title: Crib of Contempt
prose:
# Chapter 01: Crib of Contempt

Darkness first. Not the comfortable, velvety darkness of the Abyssal Halls, scented with brimstone and regret, but a thick, pressurized blackness. A suffocating, liquid dark that tasted of copper and ancient fear. I was… compressed. Every thought, every eon of accumulated fury and tactical brilliance, forced through a channel no wider than a pinhole. My consciousness, a raging inferno of will, was trapped in a container shaped like a whimpering thought.

Then, the pressure vanished, replaced by a sensory avalanche.

Light—blinding, agonizing—stabbed at retinas that were new and pathetically photosensitive. Sound—a cacophony of booming voices, tinkling laughter, and a rushing roar like the ocean in a seashell—assaulted eardrums tuned for the whispers of subjugated demons. Smells assaulted me: floral perfumes cloying and thick, sweat, something metallic and clean, and beneath it all, the warm, milk-and-musk scent of my own new body. This body. This *prison*.

I tried to clench a fist, to channel the faintest whisper of mana into a scrying mote, to *do* anything at all. The neural pathways I commanded responded with the sluggish reluctance of a glacial moraine. A tremor ran through a limb I couldn't properly locate. A gurgle, wet and furious, escaped my lips. The effort, this microscopic demand on a system not yet wired for complex thought, sent a jolt of something hot and wet spreading through the fabric enveloping my lower half.

*By the weeping void,* I thought, the internal scream silent but deafening. *I have soiled myself. I, Maledictus, Arch-Tyrant of the Obsidian Plains, have soiled myself.*

A deep, booming laugh vibrated through the very air, shaking the fragile structure of my new skull. "Ha! A fighter! Look at that kick, Seraphina! He’s got the lungs of a conqueror!"

A shadow blotted out the terrible light. A face swam into view, large and ruddy, beaming with a kind of manic, heroic pride I recognized with a hatred that transcended lifetimes. The jaw was stronger, the lines around the eyes deeper, threaded with laugh-lines instead of spell-scars, but the underlying structure was unmistakable. Alistair. The Hero of Dawn. The fool with the shining sword who had, with the help of six other equally meddling do-gooders, reduced my citadel to rubble and my essence to a screaming wisp.

He was holding me. Hoisting me aloft like a trophy fish, his hands large enough to wrap twice around my torso. The world tilted and spun. His blue eyes, bright with an emotion I refused to name, stared into mine.

*Unhand me, you sanctimonious lout!* I poured every ounce of my ancient will into the thought, trying to imbue it with the psychic weight that once made lesser demons weep. *I am Maledictus! Your reign is but a fleeting dream before the eternal night of my—*

"Aaaaargh!" The sound that tore from my throat was a thin, reedy wail, indignant but utterly pathetic. My lungs burned. My vocal cords were toys.

Alistair’s grin widened. "Hear that? A battle cry! That’s my boy! My heir!" He bounced me gently, and my world became a nauseating blur of gold-trimmed tapestries and smiling faces. Faces. Courtiers. Men and women in fine velvets and silks, their expressions a gallery of coos and congratulations. Traitors. Every last one of them. I would remember their perfumes, their ridiculous hats, the smug satisfaction in their eyes. They would be first against the wall when I reclaimed my power.

He passed me to another pair of hands. Smaller, cooler. The air shifted, the cloying floral scents giving way to something cleaner, like ozone after a lightning strike. The world steadied slightly. A face leaned close, framed by waves of dark hair threaded with silver. The eyes were a sharp, evaluating violet, missing nothing. Seraphina. The Saint of Mercy. The woman whose holy magic, channeled through that gleaming, insufferable sword, had struck the final, soul-shattering blow.

Her fingers, long and precise, brushed my forehead. The touch was light, clinical, but it carried a trace of something that made every fiber of my being recoil. Holy magic. The very energy that had unmade me, purified and sanctified and utterly loathsome. It was like having ice water laced with lemon juice dripped directly onto my soul.

A shudder wracked my tiny frame, a full-body flinch of revulsion. I tried to roll away, to sever the contact, but my muscles simply spasmed in response.

"Oh," she breathed, her voice a low, measured melody that scraped against my nerves. "He is very still, Alistair. Almost… contemplative." Her thumb stroked my cheek, another wave of that clean, awful power seeping into my skin. "He feels my presence. A good sign."

*Feels your presence?* I raged internally, trapped in the twitching meat of this infant form. *I feel the taint of the power that erased my kingdom! I feel the cosmic injustice of being cradled by my murderer! Remove your hands before I—*

I let out another gurgle, this one more of a choking cough. My body, in its infinite, humiliating weakness, decided the appropriate response to this holy contamination was to squirm and make a sound like a rusty gate hinge.

"He’s sensitive," Alistair boomed from nearby, his pride swelling audibly. "Picking up on your healing aura, Sera. A natural affinity!"

Seraphina’s lips curved in a small, private smile that did not reach her watchful eyes. "Perhaps. Or perhaps he simply dislikes being passed around like a parcel. A sensible instinct."

The indignity of it all was a physical pain, sharper than the nosebleed I was sure to develop from sheer stress. I was being analyzed like a specimen. Judged. Found… adorable. My hatred, a inferno that had burned for millennia, was being interpreted as a baby’s temperament.

My captor—my *father*, my mind supplied with a fresh surge of nausea—took me back. His hold was surprisingly secure, his large hand cradling the back of my head with a gentleness that felt like a deliberate mockery of every brutal blow we had exchanged. His booming voice resonated through my ribs, each word a tiny earthquake in my fragile skeleton.

"Look at his eyes! So focused! He’s studying me!" Alistair brought his face closer, his breath warm and smelling faintly of honeyed ale. He tapped a finger against his own jaw, right along a faded, silvery scar. "That's where the Dark Lord's shadow-claw grazed me, son! A souvenir! Right here!"

The *Grasp of Final Shadows*. A maneuver of exquisite elegance, designed not for mere physical damage but to unravel the target’s mana threads, leaving them weak and disoriented. I remembered casting it. I remembered the feeling of his holy blade deflecting my hand at the last second, the sparks of abjuration magic stinging my fingers, the scar searing itself into his flesh as he laughed, that insufferable, heroic laugh. And now it was a *souvenir*. A bedtime story anecdote. The sheer, unmitigated *audacity*.

I tried to glower. I summoned every scrap of menace I possessed, focused it on the muscles around my eyes, and *pushed*. The result was a weak scrunching of my brow, a furrowing that must have looked less like concentrated malice and more like infantile gas.

"Oh! Look!" a high, feminine voice squealed from the assembled court. "He’s frowning! So deep in thought! The prince is pondering his father’s tale!"

*Pondering?* I seethed. *I am calculating the precise angle needed to remove that scarred jaw with a dull butter knife!*

Desperation, cold and sharp, began to prick at the edges of my rage. This was untenable. This gilded prison of coos and lullabies. This body, this meat-puppet with its limited motor control and its deplorable lack of mana capacity. I had to do *something*. Something to assert my will, to leave a mark, to begin the long, arduous process of reclaiming my dominion from this humble, humiliating starting point.

A minor spell. A triviality, once. A chilling breeze, a subtle drop in temperature around my person. The *Frost of the Forsaken Whisper*. It required but a mote of mana, a whispered syllable in the mind, a conceptual nudge toward the entropy of absolute zero. I had used it to chill wine at feasts, to accentuate dramatic monologues. A party trick.

I gathered my focus. The mana pool within this body was laughably shallow, a teacup compared to the ocean I once commanded, but for this simple spell, it should suffice. I formed the incantation in my thoughts, the complex, beautiful geometry of the formula unfurling in my mind’s eye. I pushed. The pathways lit up, sluggish and narrow, but they lit.

For a glorious, terrifying second, I felt it. A connection. A thread of my will extending out into the fabric of reality, ready to weave the pattern. The air around my swaddled form began to shimmer with a faint, pearlescent frost—

And then the thread snapped.

The backlash was instantaneous and violent. Not a dull ache, but a white-hot spike of agony directly behind my eyes. It felt as if every delicate mana channel in this tiny body had been set alight with liquid fire. A coppery flood surged up my throat, and before I could even register the sensation, a hot, wet stream erupted from my left nostril.

It was not a trickle. It was a torrent. A gush of vivid, arterial red that painted the pristine white lace of my christening gown a shocking crimson. It soaked into the fabric, spreading in a grotesque, blooming flower of my own failure. The world swam. The voices around me rose in a discordant shriek of alarm.

Alistair’s smile faltered. For a fraction of a second, a flicker of something sharp and calculating crossed his features, a ghost of the warrior who had faced me in battle. It was gone in an instant, swallowed by a booming, hearty laugh that sounded just slightly too loud.

"Ha! Look at that vigor! A little warrior's nosebleed from sheer spirit!" He held me away from his body, examining the bloody mess with theatrical delight. "The lad has passion! He hears of my battle with the Dark Lord and is so overcome with righteous fervor he can barely contain himself!"

A woman in a starched apron, the nurse I assumed, bustled forward, clucking her tongue. "Such a delicate constitution, Your Majesty. His Royal Highness is very excitable today. All this stimulation is too much for a newborn."

*Delicate?* The word was a physical insult. I, who had withstood the combined assault of the Seven Heroes, the piercing of my heart by a sanctified blade, and the agonizing dissolution of my physical form, was being called *delicate*.

The nurse took me from Alistair, her hands efficient and impersonal. She produced a soft cloth, dabbed at my face and the ruined gown with practiced movements, all the while murmuring soothing nonsense. "There, there, little prince. All that fire and fight. You just rest now."

My head throbbed. The mana channels felt scorched, bruised. The humiliation was a leaden weight in my gut. I had tried to project an aura of frost and had instead produced a spectacle of blood. And they were *praising* it. Of course they were. The world had gone mad, or perhaps I had, and this was my personal, bespoke purgatory.

I was placed down. The sensation of softness beneath me, the rustle of fine sheets. A canopy overhead, embroidered with golden thread in patterns that might, to an untrained eye, look like climbing roses. To my gaze, still swimming from the magical backlash, the thorny vines formed a faint, but unmistakable, runic lattice. A ward of protection. Woven with holy magic, of course. Because why wouldn’t my crib be a gilded, sanctified cage?

The voices of my parents murmured nearby, a duet of pride and concern that grated on my frayed nerves.

"He’s perfect," Alistair said, his voice softer now, stripped of its public boom. It was intimate. Genuine. It made my skin crawl. "Just a little delicate. We’ll need to take care with him."

"We will protect him," Seraphina replied. Her tone was calm, as always, but I caught the undercurrent. A sliver of steel beneath the silk. The same tone she had used, I imagined, when discussing battle strategies in the war room, or when choosing the precise incantation to unmake an arch-demon. "From everything. Always."

*Protect me?* The thought was a razor blade in my mind. *I will dismantle your kingdom brick by brick. I will turn your beloved people against you. I will take everything you love and grind it into the dust from which it came, and then I will salt the earth so nothing ever grows there again. And I will do it while smiling.*

The nurse began to hum. A simple, tuneless melody, the kind of drowsy, nonsensical song they all seemed to favor. My fists clenched in the blankets. The tune was a violation, a sonic assault on my refined sensibilities. It was… it was…

Wait.

The melody was strangely structured. The intervals, while simple, followed a pattern. A descending minor scale, repeated, with a subtle rhythmic variation on the third iteration. It was not music. It was a mnemonic. A lullaby, yes, but one that encoded the basic steps of a minor warding charm. The kind of thing a nervous nurse might hum to a royal infant, a subconscious prayer for protection woven into song.

I hated it. I hated the simplicity, the sweetness, the utter lack of complexity. I hated that it was, objectively, not unpleasant to my new ears. I hated the way it made the throbbing in my skull recede slightly, the way the rigid muscles of my borrowed body began to relax against my will.

I focused on the tune, burning every note, every interval, into my immortal memory. Not because I liked it. But because one day, when my power was restored and my vengeance complete, I would find the composer of this ditty. I would drag them from their home. And I would have them executed by a thousand off-key lute players, playing nothing but this wretched, soothing melody, over and over, until their sanity shattered.

It was a small, petty goal. A start. In the grand, dark tapestry of my plans for this world, it was a single, insignificant black thread. But it was *mine*.

The nurse finished her song, patted my blanket-covered form, and drew the curtains of the canopy slightly, casting the crib into a gentle, golden twilight. Footsteps retreated. The heavy oak door clicked shut, muffling the distant sounds of the celebrating court.

I was alone. Trapped in the soft, warm darkness of my prison, listening to the distant echo of a lullaby I had already condemned to destruction. My body was weak. My magic was a joke. My enemies were adoring me as their long-lost son.

But I was Maledictus. And I remembered everything.

I flexed my tiny, useless fingers against the silk, feeling the ghost of power that once answered my call. The nurse’s melody lingered in the air, a soft, persistent hum.

*First,* I thought, my inner voice cold and clear amidst the ruin of my pride. *I will learn every song in this castle. And then I will burn the sheet music.*

The path forward was long. But it began here, in this swaddling, surrounded by fools.

And I was, as they so kindly noted, a fighter.

title: Can I Cast This Without Exploding?
prose:
# Chapter 02: Can I Cast This Without Exploding?

The nursery was too quiet.

I lay in my bed, the silk sheets pooling around me like liquid shadow, and stared at the canopy above. The embroidered stars—gold thread on midnight blue—were meant to be comforting. A child’s fantasy of the night sky. To me, they were a mockery. A reminder of the vast, indifferent cosmos I could no longer touch.

I flexed my fingers against the sheets, feeling the ghost of power that once answered my call. The memory of it was a physical ache, like a phantom limb. I could *see* the spell in my mind, perfect and elegant. *Watcher’s Eye*. A cantrip, nothing more. A faint, invisible sensor, no larger than a firefly, that would drift through the castle and report back to me. A tool for reconnaissance. A first step in mapping my prison.

And yet, even this—this *trivial* thing—was beyond me now.

I sat up slowly, my small body protesting the movement. The court physicians had been clear: I was delicate. Prone to fevers. Easily fatigued. A fragile little dove, they called me. *Their* little dove.

I bared my teeth at the thought.

The nursery door was closed, the heavy oak a barrier between me and the rest of the castle. Beyond it, the halls were silent, the court long since retired. The perfect time for a test.

I swung my legs over the side of the bed, my bare feet touching the cold stone floor. The chill was a shock, but I welcomed it. It grounded me, reminded me that I was still *here*, still *alive*, still *planning*.

The spell formula unspooled in my mind, a ribbon of silver and shadow. *Watcher’s Eye*. Three syllables, a flick of the wrist, a trickle of mana. I had done it a hundred times before, in a hundred different bodies. Now, I would do it in this one.

I took a deep breath, centering myself. My mana core—what little of it there was—hummed weakly in my chest, a dying ember compared to the inferno I once commanded. Fifteen units. That was my limit. Fifteen units to work with, to stretch, to *force* into compliance.

I could do this.

I whispered the incantation, my voice a lisping murmur in the dark. The words felt clumsy in my mouth, like trying to speak with a tongue too large for my skull. The syllables of the old tongue were not meant for a child’s voice, but I forced them out, each one a deliberate, precise note.

Mana trickled from my core, a thin, reluctant stream. I gritted my teeth and *pushed*, demanding more. The spell required five units. I would give it seven.

The sensor flickered into existence, a tiny, shimmering mote of light. It hovered before me, obedient, waiting for instruction.

*Go,* I thought, and it obeyed.

It drifted toward the door, slipping beneath the crack like smoke. I watched it go, my breath held, my heart pounding. The nursery walls seemed to press in around me, the weight of the castle above a physical force. But the sensor was free. It was *doing* something.

It reached the study door.

For a single, glorious instant, I *saw*. The oak desk, the holy sword mounted above it—*his* sword, the one that had pierced my chest and sent me spiraling into this wretched rebirth. The maps of my former empire, now labeled with their new, *insulting* names. *Kingdom Taxonomy*. As if they had *conquered* anything. As if they had *earned* the right to rename what was already mine.

And then—

The conduit *snapped*.

It was like a physical blow, a white-hot needle driven straight into my skull. I gasped, my hands flying to my face, my vision swimming. The backlash was immediate, brutal. My mana core, already strained, recoiled violently. Blood gushed from my nose, hot and thick, soaking into my nightgown. My stomach lurched, the room tilting around me.

I tried to cry out, but my voice was a weak, furious whimper. I clutched at the sheets, my fingers digging into the silk, my body trembling with the effort of staying upright. The pain was a living thing, a creature of fire and needles, crawling through my veins.

I had pushed too hard.

I knew it even as the thought formed. Fifteen units. That was my limit. I had taken seven for the spell, and the backlash had taken the rest. I was empty. Hollow.

And then the door burst open.

Light spilled into the nursery, harsh and golden, and Seraphina was there. My mother. The Saint of Mercy. The woman who had struck the killing blow.

Her aura flared around her, a soft, diagnostic glow. Holy magic, probing, invasive. I felt the tendrils of it brush against my scorched mana pathways, and I *hated* it. Hated the way it *saw* me, even if it didn’t *understand*.

“Lily!” Her voice was sharp with concern, but her hands were gentle as they cupped my face. “What happened?”

I didn’t answer. Couldn’t answer. My breath came in short, ragged gasps, my vision swimming with tears of pain. I focused on projecting sickness, weakness. The perfect, pitiful invalid.

Seraphina’s expression softened. “Mana depletion,” she murmured, more to herself than to me. “And a fever from the strain.” She brushed a strand of hair from my forehead, her fingers cool against my burning skin. “You overexerted yourself, my little dove.”

I wanted to scream. *I am not your dove. I am the storm that will break your wings.*

But I didn’t. I let my head loll against her hand, my body going limp with exhaustion. I was good at this. Good at playing the part they expected.

“She’s burning up,” Seraphina said, her voice tight. “Alistair!”

Footsteps thundered down the hall, and then *he* was there. King Alistair. The Hero of Dawn. My father. The man who had stood at the forefront of my destruction.

He filled the doorway, his sword drawn, his expression fierce. “Intruders?”

When he saw me, the sword clattered to the floor. His face crumpled, guilt and fear warring in his eyes. “Lily,” he breathed, sheathing the weapon with a shaking hand. “My brave girl, battling such vivid terrors!”

He crossed the room in two strides and scooped me into his arms. The hug was crushing, his armor digging into my ribs, but I didn’t protest. I let myself be held, let my head rest against his shoulder. He smelled of leather and sword oil, of sweat and something warm and *alive*. It made my skin crawl.

But I didn’t pull away.

“My poor little warrior,” he murmured, his voice thick. “You fought so hard, didn’t you?”

I didn’t answer. I didn’t have to. He wasn’t really talking to me. He was talking to the *idea* of me. The fragile, brave child he had created in his mind.

Seraphina’s hand rested on my back, her touch light. “She needs rest,” she said. “And fluids. No more late-night adventures for you, little one.”

I wanted to laugh. *Adventures.* As if I had been playing at being a hero, rather than testing the limits of my prison.

Alistair carried me back to bed, tucking me in with exaggerated care. The sheets were cool against my skin, a small relief. He sat on the edge of the bed, his hand resting on my forehead. “You’ll be alright, spark plug,” he said, his voice gruff with emotion. “Just a little fever. We’ll have you back to your mischief in no time.”

I closed my eyes, letting my breathing slow. Letting them think I was drifting off.

But my mind was a cold, calculating thing. A furnace of analysis.

I had learned something tonight. Something *useful*.

Fifteen units. That was my limit. And even then, pushing beyond five had consequences. Systemic failure. Nosebleeds. Fever. Exhaustion.

I would have to be *careful*.

But I would also have to be *smart*.

Alistair’s hand lingered on my forehead, his thumb brushing my temple. “We’ll double the guard,” he said, his voice firm. “No one gets near our little dove without my say-so.”

Seraphina made a soft, disapproving sound. “She’s not a prisoner, Alistair.”

“Of course not,” he said quickly. “But the world is a dangerous place, Sera. And our Lily is… delicate.”

I felt Seraphina’s gaze on me, sharp and assessing. “She’s stronger than she looks,” she said quietly.

I kept my eyes closed, my breathing even. But inside, I was smiling.

*Delicate.*

The word was a gift.

A shield.

A weapon.

Alistair leaned down, pressing a kiss to my forehead. “Sleep well, my brave girl,” he murmured. “The boogeyman won’t get you on my watch.”

I wanted to laugh. *You are the boogeyman,* I thought. *And you have just handed me the perfect shield.*

Seraphina’s hand squeezed my shoulder, her touch warm. “We’ll let you rest,” she said. “But first, a story. To help you sleep.”

I almost groaned. I *hated* their stories. The tales of heroes and light, of battles won and evils vanquished. They were lies. Pretty, polished lies.

But I didn’t protest. I let them think I was too weak to argue.

Alistair cleared his throat, his voice taking on the cadence of a practiced storyteller. “Once, in the darkest heart of the Obsidian Plains, there lived a terrible beast…”

I tuned him out, my mind drifting back to the study. To the maps. To the sword.

To the *possibilities*.

Fifteen units. A prison, yes. But also a *challenge*.

And I had never met a challenge I couldn’t break.

---

The story ended. Alistair’s voice trailed off, his hand patting my shoulder. “And that’s how the Hero of Dawn saved the kingdom,” he said, his voice proud.

I didn’t open my eyes. I let them think I was asleep.

Seraphina’s fingers brushed my cheek. “She’s out,” she murmured.

Alistair sighed, the bed shifting as he stood. “Poor little thing,” he said. “She’s been through so much.”

*You have no idea,* I thought.

Their footsteps retreated, the door clicking shut behind them. The nursery was dark again, the only light the faint glow of Seraphina’s diagnostic magic, lingering like a ghost.

I waited.

Counted to one hundred.

Then I opened my eyes.

The room was still. The castle beyond, silent.

I sat up slowly, my body protesting the movement. My head throbbed, my nose still tender from the earlier bleed. But I ignored the pain. It was a small price to pay.

I swung my legs over the side of the bed, my bare feet touching the cold stone. The spell formula unspooled in my mind again, but I pushed it aside. Not tonight. Tonight, I had other work to do.

I padded across the room, my nightgown whispering against the floor. The hidden drawer in my desk was where I kept my *tools*. The things I had collected. The things I had *stolen*.

I pulled it open, the wood groaning softly. Inside, a small collection of trinkets. A shard of obsidian, sharp and black. A vial of powdered silver. A lock of hair, bound with red thread.

And the crayon.

I picked it up, turning it over in my fingers. It was a deep, blood-red, the wax smooth and cool. I had taken it from the nursery art supplies, the day the court had praised my “artistic talent.”

I knelt on the floor, pulling a sheet of parchment from beneath the desk. It was one of the castle’s official documents, a tax decree I had “borrowed” from Alistair’s study. The back was blank. Perfect.

I pressed the crayon to the paper, my hand steady despite the lingering ache in my skull. The line was thick, uneven. A child’s hand. A child’s drawing.

But the *design* was mine.

A circle. Five points. A sigil at the center, simple but precise. A summoning circle. Not for a demon. Not yet. For something smaller. Something *useful*.

A familiar.

I had tried this before, of course. The first time, I had used ink. The court had found it, framed it, and hung it in the gallery as a “family portrait.” Seraphina had called it “heartwarming.” Alistair had wept.

I had wanted to scream.

This time, I was being *careful*. Crayon was less suspicious than ink. And if they found it, well. I would play dumb. *I was just doodling, Mother. I didn’t know it was bad.*

I finished the circle, my hand cramping from the effort. The crayon snapped in my fingers, the wax breaking with a soft *crack*. I stared at the drawing, my breath held.

It was *wrong*. The lines were uneven, the angles imprecise. A child’s attempt at something far beyond her skill.

But it was *mine*.

I sat back on my heels, my eyes burning with frustration. I could *see* the spell in my mind, perfect and elegant. The formula, the gestures, the precise intonation. But my body—this *wretched*, weak body—could not execute it.

I crumpled the parchment in my fist, my nails digging into my palm. The pain was sharp, grounding. A reminder of what I was. Of what I had become.

A child.

A *joke*.

I took a deep breath, forcing my fingers to relax. The parchment unfurled, the creases marring the sigil. I smoothed it out, my jaw clenched.

It would have to do.

I tucked it into the hidden drawer, beneath the other trinkets. Tomorrow, I would try again. Tomorrow, I would *succeed*.

And then—

Then, I would have my first *ally*.

A familiar. A spy. A *weapon*.

I stood, my legs unsteady. The nursery spun around me, the lingering effects of the mana backlash making my vision swim. I gripped the edge of the desk, my knuckles white.

Fifteen units.

That was my limit.

But limits were meant to be *broken*.

I crawled back into bed, pulling the sheets up to my chin. The silk was cool against my skin, a small comfort. I closed my eyes, my mind already racing ahead.

Tomorrow, I would try again.

Tomorrow, I would *push*.

And one day—

One day, I would break free.

---

The morning came too soon.

Sunlight streamed through the nursery windows, golden and bright. I blinked against it, my head throbbing. The remnants of the mana backlash lingered, a dull ache behind my eyes.

The door creaked open, and the nurse bustled in, her arms laden with a tray. “Good morning, Your Highness,” she chirped. “Time for breakfast!”

I sat up slowly, my body protesting the movement. The nurse set the tray on my lap, the scent of warm bread and honey filling the air. My stomach growled, but I ignored it. I wasn’t hungry. Not for *this*.

“Her Majesty requests your presence in the garden after breakfast,” the nurse said, straightening the blankets. “She has a surprise for you.”

I perked up at that. A *surprise*. Seraphina’s surprises were never good. Not for me.

“What kind of surprise?” I asked, my voice carefully neutral.

The nurse smiled. “Oh, I couldn’t say, Your Highness. But I’m sure you’ll love it.”

I doubted that. But I nodded, picking at the bread. The nurse bustled about the room, humming under her breath. The same tuneless melody from before. The lullaby. The *mnemonic*.

I focused on it, burning the notes into my memory. Not because I liked it. Because one day, I would find the composer. And I would make them *pay*.

The nurse finished her tasks and left, the door clicking shut behind her. I pushed the tray aside, my appetite gone. The bread was dry, the honey too sweet. Everything in this place was *wrong*.

I swung my legs over the side of the bed, my bare feet touching the cold stone. The hidden drawer called to me, but I resisted. Not now. Not yet.

I dressed quickly, my fingers fumbling with the buttons. The gown was pink, frilly. A child’s dress. I hated it.

But I wore it.

Because that was what they expected.

The garden was bright, the air warm with the scent of roses. Seraphina was waiting for me, her hands folded neatly in front of her. She smiled when she saw me, her eyes crinkling at the corners.

“Good morning, Lily,” she said. “Did you sleep well?”

I nodded, my expression carefully blank. “Yes, Mother.”

She studied me for a moment, her gaze sharp. I met it, unflinching. I was getting better at this. Better at *lying*.

“Come,” she said, holding out her hand. “I have something to show you.”

I took her hand, my fingers curling around hers. Her skin was warm, her grip gentle. I let her lead me through the garden, my eyes scanning the paths. The roses were in full bloom, their petals soft and fragrant. The gardener had done his work well.

We stopped in front of a small, circular plot of earth. The soil was dark, freshly turned. And in the center—

A crystal.

Not just any crystal. A *mana crystal*. A shard of raw, concentrated magic, pulsing faintly with inner light.

I stared at it, my breath catching. It was *beautiful*. And *useful*. And *mine*.

“Do you like it?” Seraphina asked, her voice soft.

I nodded, my throat tight. “It’s… pretty.”

She smiled. “I thought you might like it. The gardener found it in the mountains. A rare treasure.”

I reached out, my fingers brushing the crystal’s surface. It was cool, smooth. The mana within it hummed, a faint, electric vibration. I could *feel* it. Could *taste* it.

Power.

Real power.

I wanted to *scream*.

“You can plant it,” Seraphina said. “Make it part of your garden.”

I looked at her, my expression carefully blank. “My garden?”

She nodded. “Your crystal garden. The one you’ve been working on.”

I almost laughed. My *crystal garden*. The one I had *intended* to be a mana battery. A way to siphon power from the ley lines beneath the castle. A way to *break* my prison.

And now—

Now it was a *child’s plaything*.

A *pretty rock garden*.

I swallowed the bitter laugh, my fingers curling into fists. “Thank you, Mother,” I said, my voice steady. “I’ll take good care of it.”

Seraphina’s smile widened. “I know you will, my little dove.”

I knelt in the dirt, my hands brushing the soil. The crystal gleamed up at me, a beacon of what I could no longer have.

But I would have it.

One day, I would have it all.

I pressed the crystal into the earth, my fingers sinking into the cool soil. The gardener had already prepared the plot, the earth soft and yielding. I patted it down, my movements careful, precise.

“There,” I said, sitting back on my heels. “It’s perfect.”

Seraphina’s hand rested on my shoulder, her touch warm. “It is,” she agreed. “Just like you.”

I wanted to scream.

Instead, I smiled.

---

The garden became my sanctuary. A place to *think*. To *plan*.

I spent hours there, kneeling in the dirt, my hands busy with the crystals. The court praised my “artistic talent.” Alistair boasted about my “green thumb.” Seraphina watched me with quiet pride.

And I—

I *plotted*.

Each crystal was a piece of the puzzle. A node in the array I was building. A way to *harness* the power beneath the castle. A way to *break* free.

But I had to be *careful*. Had to *hide* my true purpose. Had to make them see what they *expected* to see.

A child. A *dove*.

Not the storm.

Not yet.

I pressed another crystal into the earth, my fingers trembling with the effort of restraint. The mana within it hummed, a faint, electric song. I could *feel* it, could *taste* it. Power. Real power.

And it was *mine*.

For now.

I sat back, my hands brushing the dirt from my gown. The garden was beautiful. A masterpiece of light and shadow, of color and form.

And a *prison*.

A gilded cage.

But cages had locks.

And I was *learning* how to pick them.

I stood, my legs unsteady. The garden spun around me, the lingering effects of the mana backlash making my vision swim. I gripped the edge of the bench, my knuckles white.

Fifteen units.

That was my limit.

But limits were meant to be *broken*.

And I—

I was *Maledictus*.

I would break them all.

title: With Crayons and Dark Intentions
prose:
# Chapter 03: With Crayons and Dark Intentions

The library’s children’s alcove was a cruel joke, a gilded cage within a gilded cage. It smelled of lemon oil and old paper, with a rug so plush it swallowed sound. Sunlight, filtered through stained glass depicting some forgotten hero’s triumph, painted the floor in lurid patches of red and blue. A low table, scuffed from generations of royal toddlers, held a pristine stack of parchment and a ceramic pot brimming with crayons—the blunt, waxy kind that left greasy trails. My tools. My instruments of unspeakable, preliminary investigation.

I sat cross-legged on the rug, the picture of diligent concentration. My tongue, a disobedient pink worm, poked from the corner of my mouth. My shoulders were hunched, my eyes narrowed in fierce focus.  What I was *actually* absorbed in was the precise, mathematical recreation of a Grade-Three Summoning Matrix on a sheet of cream-colored parchment.

 The Black Tome of Maledictus had etched the syntax of lesser bindings onto my soul as neatly as a scribe copies scripture.   The chalk lines of the original matrix, which should have been a foot-wide circle of power etched into stone or consecrated soil, became a wobbly, thumb-thick ring on paper. 

My first pass was rough, a sketch. I needed to ensure the anchoring glyphs were proportionally correct relative to the inner binding circle, a critical detail most apprentice sorcerers fumbled.  I went over the ring again, pressing harder, the wax building up in a satisfying, gritty ridge. My inner eye saw not a crayon drawing but the shimmering, lethal geometry of a perfect trap. *This will do for reconnaissance,* I thought, the thought sharp and cold and purely Maledictus. *A demonic gnat, a* Muscus audientis. *A low-mana servitor, easily bound, utterly invisible to lesser senses. It can flit through the halls, whisper secrets to the air, and return with the shape of my prison mapped in its tiny, buzzing mind.* The irony was a sour taste in my mouth. 

The final flourish required a key. A drop of blood, freely given, to attune the matrix to my specific mana signature. I pulled the sleeve of my cream-colored gown back, exposing the soft, unblemished skin of my wrist.  From my other sleeve, I produced the needle.  I pressed it to the pad of my finger, took a breath that was not at all shaky, and pushed. A bright, perfect bead of crimson welled up.  

I touched the drop of blood to the center of the parchment, right over the glyph of command. The parchment drank it greedily, the wax and the blood mingling in a faint, dark stain.  I could feel it, a tiny, hungry echo in the aether. It was working. The syntax was correct, even if the medium was laughable. A few more moments to let the initial resonance settle, and I could begin the actual chant. My mouth opened, the first syllable of the *Canticle of Unseen Servitude*—an Infernal lullaby, really, quite soothing—on my lips.

"Lily? What are you drawing, my love?"

The voice came from directly behind me. It was clear, warm, and as soft as the velvet curtains on the windows. It was also the single most terrifying sound in the known universe. Queen Seraphina’s voice.

Panic, cold and sharp, pierced through my concentration like a shard of ice.   In one motion, faster than I thought this clumsy, puppet limbs could manage, my hand shot out and grabbed a yellow crayon from the pot.  I uncapped it with my teeth, the plastic popping, and leaned back over my work.

My mind, that vast and ancient library, was a hurricane of aborted calculations. *Abort the ritual. Conceal the syntax. Provide an alternative, plausible explanation immediately. She is the Saint of Mercy. Her perception is a scalpel. She will see the glyphs. She will feel the resonance. She will know.*

The yellow crayon became a weapon. I jabbed it onto the parchment, in the upper quadrant of the circle. I drew a circle—a lopsided, cheerful thing—and then added stick-figure rays emanating from it. A sun. A childish, stupid sun. My hand moved faster, scribbling now, obscuring the delicate anchoring glyphs with broad, waxy strokes. I drew a tall stick figure with a straight line for a sword, a jagged triangle for a crown. I drew a slightly shorter figure with flowing lines for hair and a triangular shape that might be a dress. And between them, a much smaller figure, with two dots for eyes and a simple curved line for a smile. I linked their hands with clumsy lines.

My heart was a frantic drum against my ribs. This was madness. I had just vandalized a Grade-Three matrix with a family portrait.   The woman who was now leaning closer, her shadow falling over my work.

"It’s us, Mother," I whispered, my voice a perfect, trembling mimicry of shy pride. I tucked a stray strand of blonde hair behind my ear, the picture of a child hoping for approval.

I felt her kneel beside me on the thick rug. The scent of lavender and old paper, of clean linen and something ineffably *kind*, enveloped me. Her hand, cool and slender, came to rest on my shoulder. I fought every instinct not to flinch from the touch of my greatest enemy. She leaned in, her gaze tracing the circle, the now-obscured glyphs, the jagged, sun-shaped blotch, and the three stick figures within.

"Oh, Lily," she breathed, and her voice was thick with an emotion so potent it was almost a physical force. It was love. Awe-struck, overwhelming, *maternal* love. "It’s… it’s wonderful."

I said nothing. I kept my eyes fixed on the drawing, my expression carefully blank, my internal monologue a silent scream of pure, unadulterated humiliation. I, Maledictus, Lord of the Abyssal Halls, architect of the Obsidian Plains, author of a thousand binding pacts that had enslaved nations, had just been praised for a crayon drawing that looked like it had been produced by a particularly uncoordinated goat.

Her finger, delicate and strong, hovered over the parchment, not quite touching the wax. "Your father with his sword," she said, tracing the line of the tall stick figure’s "blade." Her finger moved to the other figure. "And me… holding your hand." A soft, choked sound escaped her throat. I dared a glance at her face. Her eyes, the color of a winter sky, were shimmering with unshed tears. Her smile was tremulous and radiant.

My mouth opened, closed. What could I say? *Actually, Mother, that jagged line is the primary vector for a demonic binding sigil, and the smaller figure represents the caster, not a loving daughter?* The words formed, acid on my tongue, and dissolved into the appropriate, childish response.

"Do you like it, Mother?" I asked, my voice a tiny, hopeful thing.

"Like it?" She let out a wet laugh, pulling me gently sideways into a hug. I went rigid, my arms pinned to my sides. "It is the most thoughtful gift I have ever received. You see us. You truly see our family." She pulled back, her hands cupping my face, her thumbs wiping at tears I hadn’t realized were leaking from my own eyes—a physiological response to stress, I told myself, nothing more. "This," she declared, her voice gaining the quiet, unshakable authority that had toppled kingdoms, "is to be framed. The finest silver frame we have. It will hang in my private study, where I can see it every day."

The humiliation was absolute. It was a physical weight, pressing down on my shoulders, making the air in my lungs feel thick and useless.  The sheer, cosmic *audacity* of it was staggering. I was a prisoner being handed the key to my cell and told it was a lovely necklace. I wanted to laugh until I choked. I wanted to scream until the glass shattered. I wanted to open my mouth and whisper the Word of Unmaking and reduce this gilded, sentimental, *insufferable* reality to a fine, grey ash.

Instead, I leaned my cheek against her shoulder, inhaling the lavender scent, and mumbled into the fabric of her gown, "I’m glad you like it, Mother."

I stood a few minutes later, a statue of internal screaming wrapped in a cream-colored gown. I watched, paralyzed, as Seraphina called for a servant with a crisp, clear snap of her fingers. A stern-faced woman in a grey dress appeared, bowing her head. My mother held the parchment out to her with the reverence one might show a holy relic.

"This is to be framed," the Queen repeated. "The finest silver frame. It hangs in my private study. See to it personally."

The servant took the drawing, her eyes flicking over it once. I saw the briefest tightening around her mouth—the trained suppression of any emotion—and then a polite, professional smile. "At once, Your Majesty."

She left. The drawing left. My abortive ritual, my reconnaissance plan, my first tentative reach for the power that was rightfully mine, was carried away to be mounted in silver and gazed upon fondly. The silence in the alcove was deafening. The sunbeam from the stained glass had moved, now illuminating the empty space on the table where my work had been.

 The court’s aesthetic and emotional judgment had not merely overridden my magical function; it had gobbled it up, digested it, and was now wearing its skin as a lovely frock. I had been outmaneuvered by sentiment. Defeated by a hug. Neutralized by a picture frame.

"Come, little dove," Seraphina said, her hand finding mine. Her palm was warm and dry, her grip gentle but firm. "Let us find some tea. You’ve been working so hard."

I let her lead me away.  The plan was ash. The circle was a portrait. And I, the Demon Lord, was being taken for tea because I’d drawn a nice picture of my family.

Later, much later, after the tea and the scones (which I ate mechanically, tasting nothing) and a tedious hour spent listening to my father regale a visiting baron with the story of how he’d once wrestled a river troll into a submission hold using only a length of rope and a well-placed knee (the troll had been trying to steal his boot, apparently), I found myself back in the library. The alcove was empty, the sunbeam gone. I stood in the center of the room, surrounded by the silent, towering shelves of books, the real grimoires, the books that held knowledge worth having.

The humiliation had cooled into something harder, more durable. A bitter, ironic resignation.  

I walked to the table where the crayons were still scattered. My fingers, moving with a slow, deliberate precision, sorted through them. Past the red, the blue, the cheerful yellow. They settled on the black crayon. It was slightly worn, the paper sheath peeling at the corners. I sat down, pulled a fresh sheet of parchment toward me, and uncapped the crayon. The smell was sharp, waxy.

My hand moved. Not with the wobbly uncertainty of a child, but with the cold, fluid certainty of a master calligrapher.  Each line was a testament to a syntax I knew better than my own name. It was a work of absolute, flawless occult precision, rendered in a child’s medium. It was beautiful in its own way, a dark and intricate flower.

When it was done, I picked up a blue crayon. Beneath the perfect black pentagram, in careful, looping, childish letters that required me to consciously slow my hand to a crawl, I wrote two words.

*My Flower.*

I left the drawing on the table, the black lines stark against the white paper, the title a joke so private and so cruel it was almost a spell in itself. I walked out of the alcove, leaving the door slightly ajar. Let them find it. Let them praise my progress in "abstract art." Let them frame this one, too, and hang it next to the family portrait.

  I was their daughter. Their delicate, artistic, brilliant daughter. And I would use that, every last, saccharine drop of it.

title: Jam, Tears, and Tactical Eating
prose:
# Chapter 04: Jam, Tears, and Tactical Eating

The nursery smelled of beeswax and stale biscuits. I sat at the low wooden table, my fingers tracing the edge of the porcelain plate where three sad little biscuits lay in a neat row. They were the kind that tasted like regret and sawdust, the kind that crumbled at the slightest pressure. The kind that made me want to summon a plague of locusts just to watch the kitchen staff panic.

But I couldn't. Not yet.

Nurse Branna was dozing in her chair by the window, her head lolling forward, her breath coming in soft, uneven snores. The afternoon light painted her face in gold, highlighting the deep lines around her eyes, the way her hands trembled slightly even in sleep.   She hummed as she worked, some tuneless little ditty that made my teeth ache. But she was thorough. I'd watched her for weeks now, noted the way she fluffed the pillows just so, the way she always made sure the sugar bowl was full before she left the room.

And the sugar bowl was full. I could see it from where I sat, its silver lid gleaming, promising sweetness and energy and the kind of quick, efficient fuel that my pathetic little body so desperately needed. But the jam pot beside it was nearly empty. A smear of red clung to the inside, the last dregs of the strawberry jam that had been served at breakfast. The good jam. The jam that made the sawdust biscuits almost tolerable.

I wanted it.

 I wanted it the way a general wants supplies. The way a siege engine wants ammunition. The way a starving man wants bread.

I watched Elara as she stacked the cups, her fingers deft, her movements practiced. She was new. New enough that she still jumped when I spoke to her, still blushed when I complimented her work. New enough that she hadn't yet learned the unspoken rules of the nursery, the delicate balance of care and deference that governed every interaction.

Branna knew those rules. Branna had been with the royal family for decades, had raised my father when he was a boy, had been there when my mother first held me as an infant. She knew when to push and when to coddle, when to scold and when to soothe. She knew that the King's pride was a lever that could move mountains, and she knew how to pull it without ever seeming to try.

But Elara? Elara was still learning. And that made her vulnerable.

I let my lower lip tremble. Just a little. Just enough to feel the first hot prick of tears behind my eyes. It was a trick I'd practiced in the mirror, a way to summon moisture on command, to make my face flush and my voice wobble. 

The lullaby composer's final, choking gasp. The way the court physicians had clucked their tongues and declared me "delicate" when I'd tried to cast my first spell. The framed portrait of my "family" that now hung in my mother's study, a testament to my artistic "talent" that was really just a summoning circle drawn in crayon.

The tears came easier now. A single, perfect drop welled up and spilled over, tracing a slow path down my cheek. I didn't wipe it away. I let it hang there, a glistening accusation, a silent testament to my suffering.

Elara turned at the sound of my sniffle. Her eyes widened when she saw the tear, her hands flying to her mouth in horror. "Oh, Your Highness! Are you alright?"

I didn't answer right away. I let the silence stretch, let her imagination fill in the gaps.  Then, when the moment was ripe, I whispered, "Elara."

My voice was small. Broken. The voice of a child who had been asked to be brave one too many times. It was a voice that made Elara's shoulders hunch, that made her take a half-step forward as if pulled by an invisible string.

"Yes, Princess?"

I looked up at her, my eyes wide and wet, my expression carefully crafted to convey a mix of vulnerability and quiet strength. "Father says I'm his brave little soldier."

"But... soldiers get rations, don't they?"

The confusion on Elara's face was almost comical. Her brow furrowed, her lips parted, her head tilted to the side like a puppy trying to understand human speech. "Rations, Your Highness?"

I nodded, my chin trembling just a little. "Rations. Extra food. For when they've been brave." I gestured to the plate of biscuits, my hand shaking slightly. "These are... they're very nice. But they're not very filling. And I've been so brave today. Haven't I?"

 Instead, 

Elara's face cycled through a series of emotions, each one more amusing than the last. Confusion gave way to dawning understanding, which in turn gave way to horrified sympathy. Her hands fluttered at her sides, her fingers twisting in the fabric of her apron.

"Oh, Your Highness," she breathed. "Of course. Of course you deserve extra rations. You're the bravest little soldier in the kingdom."

She didn't wait for permission. She didn't even glance at Branna, still dozing in her chair. She simply turned on her heel and hurried from the room, her skirts swishing against the floor, her humming replaced by the quick, determined tap of her shoes against the stone.

I watched her go, a small smile playing at the corners of my mouth. It wasn't a kind smile. It wasn't a child's smile. It was the smile of a general who had just outmaneuvered an opponent without firing a single shot.

Branna stirred in her chair, her snores cutting off with a soft snort. She blinked at me, her eyes bleary with sleep, her expression soft and indulgent. "What's all this, then? Where's Elara off to in such a hurry?"

I turned my smile on her, let it widen just a fraction, let it take on the warm, innocent glow of a child who had just been promised a treat. "She's getting me some jam, Nurse Branna. For my bravery."

Branna chuckled, the sound warm and rich and utterly devoid of suspicion. "Is she now? Well, that's very kind of her. But you know the rules, Lily. No extra sweets before dinner."

I let my smile falter, let my lower lip tremble just a little. "But Father says I'm his brave little soldier. And soldiers get rations, don't they?"

Branna's expression softened. She pushed herself up from her chair with a soft groan, her bones creaking like an old ship. "Oh, my dear. Of course they do. But you're not just any soldier. You're the King's daughter. And the King's daughter gets whatever she wants."

She crossed the room to the table, her steps slow and measured. She picked up one of the sawdust biscuits, examined it with a critical eye, then set it back down with a sigh. "Though I do wish they'd send up something with a bit more substance. These biscuits are fit for birds, not princesses."

I said nothing. I simply watched as she moved to the sideboard, watched as she opened a small wooden box and pulled out a single, perfect biscuit. It was larger than the others, golden-brown and studded with chunks of dried fruit. The kind of biscuit that was usually reserved for the King's tea, the kind that made my mouth water with anticipation.

Branna brought it back to the table and set it on my plate with a flourish. "There. That's for your bravery. But don't tell Cook I gave it to you. She'll have my head."

I nodded, my eyes wide and solemn. "I won't tell. I promise."

Branna patted my head, her fingers gentle against my hair. "Good girl. Now eat up before Elara gets back. We wouldn't want her to think I'm spoiling you."

I picked up the biscuit, my fingers closing around its warmth. It was still fresh, still soft, the scent of cinnamon and nutmeg rising from it like an offering. I took a bite, let the flavors explode across my tongue, let the sugar and spice and everything nice fuel the cold, calculating part of my mind that was already planning my next move.

Because this was only the beginning.

Elara returned a few minutes later, her cheeks flushed, her breath coming in quick little gasps. She held a small ceramic pot in her hands, its lid sealed with a strip of wax. The strawberry jam. The good jam. The jam that would give me the energy I needed to keep playing this game.

She set it down on the table with a soft thud, her eyes shining with triumph. "I found it, Your Highness. The last of the strawberry jam. Cook says it's the best batch they've made all year."

I looked up at her, my expression one of pure, childlike delight. "Oh, Elara! Thank you! You're the best!"

Elara beamed, her cheeks flushing a deeper shade of pink. "It was nothing, Your Highness. Just doing my duty."

Branna chuckled, the sound warm and indulgent. "And a fine job you're doing, too. Now, why don't you pour the Princess some milk to go with that jam? And then you can run along. I'll finish up here."

Elara nodded, her movements quick and efficient as she fetched a glass and poured the milk. She set it down beside my plate, her fingers brushing against the rim of the glass. "There you are, Your Highness. Enjoy your rations."

I smiled up at her, my eyes wide and innocent. "Thank you, Elara. You're very kind."

She curtsied, her skirts swishing against the floor. "It's my pleasure, Your Highness."

And then she was gone, her footsteps fading down the corridor, her humming once again filling the air. Branna watched her go, her expression fond, her eyes soft with affection. "That girl's got a good heart. A bit too eager, perhaps, but a good heart."

I said nothing. I simply watched as Branna turned back to the table, watched as she picked up the jam pot and broke the wax seal with a practiced flick of her fingers. She scooped out a generous dollop of jam and spread it across the fruit-studded biscuit with the precision of a woman who had been doing this for decades.

"There you are, my dear. A proper soldier's ration."

I took the biscuit from her, my fingers closing around its warmth. It was perfect. Golden and fragrant and dripping with jam, the scent of strawberries rising from it like a promise.

I took a bite, let the flavors explode across my tongue. The jam was sweet, almost cloyingly so, the strawberries bursting with juice, the sugar clinging to my teeth like a lover's embrace. It was delicious. It was perfect.

It was mine.

I ate slowly, savoring each bite, letting the sugar fuel the cold, calculating part of my mind. 

The court saw me as delicate. As sensitive. As a child who needed to be coddled and protected. And perhaps I was those things. But I was also something else. Something darker. Something stronger.

I was a soldier. And soldiers needed rations.

I finished the biscuit, licked the jam from my fingers, and sat back in my chair with a contented sigh. Branna smiled at me, her expression soft and indulgent. "There now. That's better, isn't it?"

I nodded, my eyes wide and innocent. "Much better, Nurse Branna. Thank you."

She patted my head, her fingers gentle against my hair. "You're welcome, my dear. Now, why don't you go play for a bit? I'll clean up here."

I slid down from my chair, my feet touching the floor with a soft thud. I crossed the room to the toy chest, my movements slow and deliberate. I opened the lid, peered inside at the assortment of dolls and blocks and wooden animals that lay within.

And then I closed it again.

Because I wasn't here to play. I was here to plan.

I crossed the room to the window, my steps silent against the thick rug. I peered out at the courtyard below, at the guards marching in formation, at the servants hurrying about their duties, at the world that was mine for the taking.

If only I could find a way to take it.

A sound from the corridor made me turn. Footsteps. Heavy, booted footsteps. The kind that made the floorboards creak and the walls tremble. The kind that belonged to a man who had once wrestled a river troll into submission and lived to tell the tale.

My father.

I turned just as the door swung open, just as King Alistair, Hero of Dawn, Conqueror of the Obsidian Plains, and my unwitting progenitor, strode into the room. 

"Lily!" he boomed, his voice filling the room, his arms spreading wide in welcome. "There's my brave little soldier!"

I didn't flinch. I didn't wince. I didn't let the smile slip from my face. Instead, I turned to him, my expression one of pure, childlike delight. "Father!"

He crossed the room in three long strides, his boots thudding against the floor. He scooped me up in his arms, his grip strong and sure, his laughter warm and rich. "There's my girl! I hear you've been asking for rations!"

I nodded, my chin resting against his shoulder, my arms wrapped around his neck. "Yes, Father. Nurse Branna said soldiers get rations when they've been brave."

Alistair chuckled, the sound vibrating through his chest. "That she did, my dear. That she did." He set me down, his hands gentle as he smoothed my hair, his eyes shining with pride. "And you have been brave, haven't you? My brave little soldier."

I nodded again, my expression solemn. "Yes, Father. I've been very brave."

Alistair's smile widened, his eyes crinkling at the corners. "That's my girl. And brave soldiers deserve brave rations. So I've ordered a feast for the entire nursery! Double portions for everyone! A proper soldier's banquet!"

I let my eyes widen, let my mouth form a perfect little "O" of surprise. "Really, Father?"

Alistair nodded, his expression one of pure, paternal pride. "Really, my dear. Anything for my brave little soldier."

I threw my arms around his waist, my face pressed against his doublet. "Thank you, Father! You're the best!"

Alistair patted my back, his laughter warm and rich. "Anything for you, my dear. Anything at all."

I stepped back, my expression one of pure, childlike delight. "Can I go tell Nurse Branna? Can I go tell everyone?"

Alistair chuckled, his eyes crinkling at the corners. "Of course, my dear. Of course you can."

I turned and hurried across the room, my skirts swishing against the floor. I threw open the door, my voice ringing out into the corridor. "Nurse Branna! Father says we're having a feast! Double rations for everyone!"

I heard Branna's soft chuckle, heard the scrape of her chair as she pushed herself to her feet. "Does he now? Well, that's very kind of him."

I turned back to my father, my expression one of pure, innocent joy. "Thank you, Father. Thank you so much."

Alistair smiled at me, his eyes soft with affection. "Anything for you, my dear. Anything at all."

And then he was gone, his footsteps fading down the corridor, his laughter echoing in his wake. I stood in the doorway, my smile slowly fading, my expression turning cold and calculating.

I had asked for jam. I had gotten a banquet.

I had asked for rations. I had gotten a kingdom's worth of resources.

And all it had taken was a single tear. A single, perfect tear.

I turned back to the nursery, my eyes scanning the room, my mind already planning my next move. The jam pot still sat on the table, its lid askew, its contents nearly gone. The fruit-studded biscuit lay on my plate, its crumbs scattered across the porcelain like the remnants of a battle.

I crossed the room to the table, my steps slow and deliberate. I picked up the jam pot, my fingers closing around its warmth. I scooped out the last of the jam, my tongue darting out to lick the spoon clean.

The sweetness was cloying now, the sugar coating my tongue, my teeth, my throat. It was too much. Too sweet. Too rich.

It tasted like victory.

And it tasted like ash.

Because this wasn't what I wanted. Not really.

I wanted power. Real power. The kind that came from spells and incantations and the dark, thrumming energy of the Abyss. The kind that could level cities and raise armies and reduce my enemies to nothing more than smoldering piles of ash.

But I was a child. A delicate, fragile child with a body that could barely hold fifteen units of mana, a mind that was a library with no librarian, a soul that was a supercomputer with a dial-up connection.

I set the jam pot down, my fingers lingering against the ceramic. I could feel the cold, calculating part of my mind stirring, could feel the old, familiar hunger rising within me.

Because this was only the beginning.

I had secured a resource. A trivial one, perhaps, but a resource nonetheless.

And resources were meant to be used.

I turned to the window, my eyes scanning the courtyard below. The guards were still marching, the servants still hurrying, the world still turning.

And I was still here. Still trapped. Still playing this game.

But I was learning. Oh, how I was learning.

I turned back to the nursery, my eyes scanning the room, my mind already planning my next move. The toy chest. The dolls. The blocks.

The tools of my trade.

I crossed the room to the toy chest, my steps slow and deliberate. I opened the lid, peered inside at the assortment of dolls and blocks and wooden animals that lay within.

And then I smiled.

Because this was only the beginning.

And I was just getting started.

title: Tutoring the Terror
prose:
# Chapter 05: Tutoring the Terror

The morning light slanted through the arched windows of the royal library, painting golden stripes across the polished oak table where Master Theron had arranged his teaching materials. I sat primly in my chair, hands folded in my lap, the very picture of a dutiful princess awaiting her lesson. The itch between my shoulder blades had nothing to do with the stiff brocade of my dress and everything to do with the chalk diagram slowly taking shape on the blackboard.

Theron was explaining the Law of Conservation of Mana with the enthusiasm of a man reciting a grocery list. "Now, Princess Lily, as we discussed last week, mana cannot be created or destroyed—only transformed. This is why your healing spells require such precise measurements. Too little, and the wound remains. Too much, and..." He trailed off, glancing at me with the cautious expression of someone who'd seen me faint after attempting to light a candle.

I nodded solemnly, my fingers twitching against the fabric of my skirt. The actual Law of Conservation was far more elegant than this watered-down version being taught to children. Mana wasn't just conserved—it flowed through systems like blood through veins, with pressure gradients and viscosity factors that most scholars hadn't even begun to understand. The Demon Lord's personal grimoires contained entire chapters on mana dynamics that would make Theron's head explode.

"Let us practice with a simple heating charm," Theron said, turning to the blackboard. He began drawing a spiral pattern, his chalk making that irritating squeaking sound that set my teeth on edge. "The standard Archimedean spiral creates a vortex that—"

"Actually," I interrupted, my voice sweet as poisoned honey, "the Archimedean spiral creates unnecessary turbulence at the center point. The optimal pattern for heat distribution is a logarithmic spiral with a secondary counter-spiral at the core to prevent energy loss through vortex collapse."

Theron's hand froze mid-draw. The chalk hovered above the blackboard like a question mark. "I... beg your pardon, Princess?"

I rose from my chair with the slow grace of a predator who knows her prey is already caught. The court physicians had warned me against sudden movements, so I took my time crossing the room, my slippers whispering against the marble floor. When I reached the blackboard, I took the chalk from Theron's unresisting fingers.

"May I demonstrate?" I asked, my voice dripping with false modesty.

Theron nodded mutely, stepping back as if I'd suddenly grown fangs.

I began drawing. The first spiral was perfect—a logarithmic curve that widened at precisely the right rate. Then, at the center, I added the secondary glyph, a counter-spiral that mirrored the first but rotated in the opposite direction. The design was beautiful in its efficiency, a masterpiece of magical engineering that would make any true scholar weep with admiration.

"There," I said, stepping back to admire my work. "The counter-spiral stabilizes the mana flow, reducing energy loss by approximately thirty percent. It's a refinement I developed during my studies of the Obsidian Plains' thermal matrices."

Theron stared at the diagram. His face had gone through several interesting color changes—pink, then red, then an alarming shade of purple that made me wonder if he might faint before I could. "That's... that's not in the standard curriculum," he managed finally.

"Of course not," I said, returning to my seat with the same careful slowness. "The standard curriculum is based on the simplified models developed after the Demon Lord's defeat. They're adequate for basic spellcasting but lack the precision of the original research."

Theron's eyes narrowed. "And where, exactly, did you learn about the... Obsidian Plains' thermal matrices?"

I blinked at him, all wide-eyed innocence. "Why, from the royal library, of course. Father says knowledge should be available to everyone."

This was technically true. The royal library did contain several texts on the Obsidian Plains, though none that mentioned thermal matrices in any meaningful detail. The actual knowledge had come from my own memories—from standing in the heart of the Demon Lord's fortress, watching the mana flows pulse like living things through the obsidian walls.

Theron's jaw worked silently for several moments. I could practically see the thoughts churning behind his eyes—how to reconcile this child's impossible knowledge with the delicate princess persona I'd so carefully cultivated. "Princess Lily," he said at last, "your understanding of magical theory is... advanced. Perhaps we should focus on practical applications today."

"Of course, Master Theron," I said, folding my hands in my lap again. "I'm eager to learn."

The lie tasted like ash in my mouth. I wasn't eager to learn—I already knew everything worth knowing about magic. What I needed was practice, and that was the one thing my frail body wouldn't allow.

Theron turned back to the blackboard, erasing my perfect diagram with quick, angry strokes. "Let's begin with something simpler. A basic light spell, perhaps. The standard incantation is—"

"Lux perpetua, lumen clarum," I recited automatically. "But the optimal incantation for sustained light would be lux stabilis, lumen aeternum, which reduces mana consumption by—"

"Princess!" Theron's voice cracked like a whip. He turned to face me, his face now a concerning shade of crimson. "That is quite enough. I am your tutor, not the other way around."

I tilted my head, affecting confusion. "But Master Theron, I only meant to help. Isn't that what tutors are for? To share knowledge?"

Theron's hands clenched at his sides. "To share knowledge, yes. Not to... to condescend to your elders with theories you couldn't possibly understand."

I widened my eyes, letting a single tear well up at the corner. "I'm sorry, Master Theron. I didn't mean to upset you. I just... I just want to learn."

The tear did its work. Theron's expression softened, though the purple hadn't entirely faded from his cheeks. "Of course you do, Princess. Your enthusiasm is commendable. But you must understand that magic is a complex discipline. There are reasons certain theories are taught at specific levels."

I nodded solemnly, the tear tracking down my cheek. "I understand. I'll try to be more... patient."

Theron exhaled sharply, some of the tension leaving his shoulders. "Good. Now, let's return to the basic light spell. The hand gestures are crucial—"

"Actually," I said, my voice small and hesitant, "the hand gestures for the standard light spell create unnecessary strain on the wrist. The optimal gesture would be a simple extension of the index finger, like this." I demonstrated, my finger pointing straight out with perfect precision.

Theron's face went slack. Then, without another word, he turned on his heel and strode toward the door.

"Master Theron?" I called after him, my voice trembling with false concern. "Where are you going?"

He didn't answer. The door slammed behind him with enough force to rattle the windows.

I sat perfectly still for several moments, listening to the echo of his footsteps fade down the corridor. Then, slowly, I allowed myself a small smile. It wasn't a particularly nice smile—more the kind a cat might give after swallowing a particularly plump canary.

The door to the library opened again, and Head Steward Maribel hurried in, her skirts rustling with urgency. "Princess Lily! I heard a commotion—" She stopped short when she saw me sitting alone at the table, my face carefully arranged into an expression of distress. "Where is Master Theron?"

I looked up at her, my lower lip trembling. "I... I don't know. He just... left. He was teaching me about light spells, and then he got angry, and then he just... stormed out."

Maribel's eyes widened. She crossed the room in quick strides, kneeling beside my chair. "Oh, my dear! Did he say anything? Did he... hurt you?"

I shook my head, another tear slipping free. "No. He just... he didn't like it when I corrected his diagram. I didn't mean to upset him. I just wanted to help."

Maribel gathered me into her arms, patting my back with the practiced ease of someone who'd comforted many royal tantrums. "There, there, my dear. I'm sure it wasn't your fault. Master Theron can be... temperamental at times."

I buried my face in her shoulder, letting my tears soak into the fabric of her dress. Inside, I was laughing. The old fool had walked right into my trap. Correction was the most effective form of humiliation for a scholar, and I'd delivered mine with surgical precision.

By dinner, the entire court would know about my "extraordinary grasp of magical theory." By tomorrow, I'd be the prodigy princess, the child genius who'd humiliated the royal tutor with her advanced understanding. And best of all, no one would suspect the truth—that my knowledge wasn't advanced at all. It was ancient. It was perfect. It was the knowledge of a being who'd spent centuries mastering the dark arts before being reborn in this fragile, frustrating body.

Maribel helped me to my feet, her arm around my shoulders. "Come, Princess. Let's get you to your rooms. I'll have some warm milk sent up. And perhaps... perhaps we should find you a new tutor."

I nodded, sniffling dramatically. "I'd like that. Someone who... who doesn't mind when I ask questions."

Maribel smiled down at me, her eyes warm with affection. "Of course, my dear. We'll find you the perfect tutor. Someone who appreciates your... unique mind."

As we left the library, I glanced back at the blackboard. My diagram had been erased, but the ghost of it remained—a perfect spiral with its counterpoint at the center, a symbol of efficiency and power. A symbol of what I could do, if only my body would cooperate.

The walk to my rooms was a blur of sympathetic murmurs and concerned glances from passing servants. I kept my head down, my expression appropriately solemn, but inside, I was already planning my next move. The prodigy persona was a useful one. It would give me access to resources, to knowledge, to opportunities I couldn't get as the delicate princess.

And if anyone got too close to the truth? Well. Prodigies were allowed to be eccentric, weren't they?

When we reached my rooms, Maribel settled me onto the window seat with a soft blanket and a promise of warm milk. I watched her leave, then turned to look out the window at the royal gardens below. The crystal garden was coming along nicely. The court thought it was just pretty rocks, but I knew better. Those crystals were siphoning mana from the ley lines beneath the palace, storing it drop by precious drop.

It would take time, but eventually, I'd have enough power to cast something real. Something that would make the court sit up and take notice. Something that would prove, once and for all, that the delicate princess was more than she seemed.

I smiled to myself, tracing idle patterns on the glass. The sun was setting, painting the sky in shades of gold and pink. It was beautiful, in its way. Almost as beautiful as the look on Master Theron's face when I'd corrected his precious diagram.

Almost.

---

Dinner that evening was a quiet affair. Father was in one of his storytelling moods, regaling the court with tales of his heroic exploits. Mother watched him with that fond, slightly exasperated expression she reserved for his more outrageous claims. And me? I sat at the high table, sipping my soup and listening to the whispers that followed me like shadows.

"...extraordinary grasp of magical theory..."

"...humiliated Master Theron..."

"...a prodigy, truly..."

I kept my face carefully neutral, my spoon moving from bowl to mouth with mechanical precision. Inside, I was cataloging each whisper, each glance, each murmur of admiration. The court was eating out of my hand, and they didn't even realize it.

Father finished his story with a dramatic flourish, his sword clanging against his chair as he gestured expansively. "And that, my friends, is how I single-handedly defeated the entire orc horde at Blackridge Pass!"

The court applauded politely. Mother sighed, shaking her head. "Alistair, must you always bring your sword to dinner?"

Father grinned, unrepentant. "A hero is never unarmed, my love. Besides, Lily likes the stories, don't you, my dear?"

I looked up from my soup, blinking as if surfacing from deep thought. "Hmm? Oh, yes. The stories are... very exciting."

Father beamed at me, his pride practically radiating from his pores. "There you have it! The princess herself approves!"

Mother's eyes narrowed slightly as she studied me. I kept my expression open, innocent, the very picture of a child lost in thought. After a moment, she turned back to Father with a small smile. "Indeed. Though I suspect Lily's thoughts are more on her studies than your heroic exploits these days."

Father's eyebrows shot up. "Oh? And what has our little scholar been studying?"

I set down my spoon, folding my hands in my lap. "Magic, mostly. Master Theron was teaching me about mana conservation today."

Mother's smile deepened, though her eyes remained sharp. "Was he now? And how did that go?"

I hesitated, biting my lip. "It... didn't. Master Theron left before we could finish the lesson."

Father's expression darkened. "Left? What do you mean, left?"

I looked down at my plate, my voice small. "He got upset when I... when I corrected his diagram. I didn't mean to. I just wanted to help."

Father's chair scraped back as he stood abruptly. "He what? He dared to upset my daughter? My little prodigy?"

Mother placed a calming hand on his arm. "Alistair, perhaps we should hear the whole story before you challenge anyone to a duel."

Father subsided slightly, though his grip on his sword hilt remained white-knuckled. "Very well. Lily, tell us everything."

I took a deep breath, as if gathering my courage. Then, in halting words, I told them about the lesson—the spiral diagram, my correction, Theron's anger. I made sure to emphasize how upset I'd been, how I'd only wanted to learn, how confused I was by Theron's reaction.

When I finished, Father was vibrating with indignation. "The man is a fool! A blind, stubborn fool! To walk out on my daughter, my brilliant, beautiful daughter—"

Mother's hand tightened on his arm. "Alistair. Perhaps we should speak to Master Theron before making any judgments."

Father waved a dismissive hand. "There's nothing to judge. The man is clearly incompetent. Lily needs a tutor who can keep up with her, not some doddering old scholar who can't handle a little correction."

Mother's eyes met mine across the table. There was something in her gaze—something knowing, something calculating. "And what would you like, Lily? A new tutor?"

I nodded, my expression earnest. "If it's not too much trouble. I just... I want to learn. I want to understand magic better."

Mother studied me for a long moment. Then, slowly, she smiled. "Of course, my dear. We'll find you the perfect tutor. Someone who appreciates your... unique mind."

Father clapped his hands together. "Excellent! I'll have the royal scholars assemble first thing in the morning. We'll find someone worthy of our little prodigy!"

I ducked my head, hiding my smile behind my napkin. The pieces were falling into place perfectly. The prodigy persona would give me access to resources, to knowledge, to opportunities I couldn't get as the delicate princess. And if anyone got too close to the truth?

Well. Prodigies were allowed to be eccentric, weren't they?

Mother's voice cut through my thoughts. "Lily, dear, you haven't touched your dessert."

I looked up to find a slice of chocolate cake sitting in front of me, untouched. "Oh. I... I'm not very hungry."

Mother's eyebrows rose. "Not hungry? That's unlike you."

I forced a smile, picking up my fork. "I suppose I'm still upset about Master Theron. I'll try to eat something."

Father reached over to ruffle my hair. "That's my brave girl. Don't let that old fool ruin your appetite. You're going to be the greatest mage this kingdom has ever seen!"

I took a small bite of cake, the sweetness cloying on my tongue. The greatest mage the kingdom had ever seen. If only they knew what I really was—the greatest mage the world had ever known, trapped in a body that couldn't contain me.

Mother watched me eat, her expression thoughtful. "Lily, dear, have you given any thought to what you'd like to study next? With your... advanced understanding, you could explore almost any area of magic."

I swallowed my bite of cake, considering. This was dangerous territory. I needed to appear knowledgeable but not suspiciously so. "I've been thinking about enchantments," I said at last. "The way mana can be stored in objects. It's... fascinating."

Mother's eyes gleamed. "Enchantments, hmm? That is an advanced topic. But I suppose if anyone could master it, it would be you."

Father nodded enthusiastically. "Enchantments! Like my sword! It glows when orcs are near!"
