I managed not to roll my eyes. Father's sword was enchanted, yes, but with a simple detection spell that any first-year apprentice could cast. The real enchantments—the ones that could change the world—were far beyond his understanding.

Mother's voice was gentle but firm. "Alistair, perhaps we should let Lily choose her own path. She's clearly got a mind for this."

Father opened his mouth to protest, but Mother silenced him with a look. "Lily, if you're interested in enchantments, we'll make sure your new tutor is well-versed in that area. Perhaps even someone from the Spire."

I felt a spark of interest. The Spire was the center of magical learning in the kingdom, home to the greatest scholars and mages. If I could get a tutor from there... "That would be wonderful, Mother. Thank you."

Mother smiled, reaching over to pat my hand. "Of course, my dear. We want to nurture your talents, not stifle them."

Father grinned, raising his goblet. "To our little prodigy! May her studies bring glory to Lumengarde!"

The court echoed his toast, their voices ringing through the hall. I raised my own goblet, taking a small sip of watered wine. The liquid tasted like victory.

As the dinner drew to a close, I found myself the center of attention. Nobles and scholars alike approached to congratulate me on my "remarkable insight," to ask about my studies, to praise my "natural talent." I accepted their compliments with gracious humility, my inner monologue a litany of sarcastic remarks and dark amusement.

The old man with the monocle wanted to know if I'd considered a career in theoretical magic. I told him I was still exploring my options, all while thinking about how satisfying it would be to turn his monocle into a portal to the Abyss.

The young woman with the elaborate hairdo asked if I'd like to join her study group. I told her I'd think about it, while imagining how her perfect curls would look on fire.

And through it all, Mother watched. She watched, and she listened, and she said very little. But her eyes missed nothing.

When the last of the well-wishers had drifted away, Father turned to me with a proud smile. "Well, my dear? How does it feel to be the talk of the court?"

I looked up at him, my expression carefully arranged into one of shy pride. "It feels... nice. But I just want to learn, Father. That's all."

Father's smile softened. He reached over to ruffle my hair again. "And learn you shall, my little prodigy. We'll find you the best tutor in the kingdom. Someone who can keep up with that brilliant mind of yours."

I ducked my head, hiding my smile. Oh, Father. If only you knew what that brilliant mind was really capable of.

Mother's voice cut through the moment. "Lily, dear, it's getting late. You should get some rest. Tomorrow will be a busy day."

I nodded, sliding down from my chair. "Yes, Mother. Goodnight, Father."

Father pulled me into a quick hug. "Goodnight, my brilliant girl. Sleep well."

I returned his hug, breathing in the scent of leather and steel that always clung to him. For a moment, I let myself relax into his embrace, let myself pretend that I was just a little girl, just his daughter, with no dark thoughts, no ancient knowledge, no plans for revenge.

Then I pulled away, my smile sweet and innocent. "Goodnight, Father."

As I left the dining hall, I could feel Mother's eyes on my back. She knew. Or at least, she suspected. But she would never say anything, never do anything to jeopardize the peace of her family. That was her weakness, and I would exploit it.

The walk back to my rooms was quiet. The corridors were empty at this hour, the servants having retired for the night. I moved slowly, savoring the silence, the solitude. It was the only time I could truly be myself, when no one was watching, no one was judging.

When I reached my rooms, I dismissed my maid with a wave of my hand. "I can manage on my own tonight, thank you."

The maid curtsied and left, closing the door behind her. I waited until her footsteps had faded down the corridor before I let out a long breath.

Alone at last.

I crossed to my desk, running my fingers over the smooth wood. The crystal garden was progressing nicely. The ley lines beneath the palace were strong, and the crystals were siphoning mana at a steady rate. It would take time, but eventually, I'd have enough power to cast something real. Something that would make the court sit up and take notice.

I opened the hidden drawer in my desk, pulling out the obsidian shard I'd been using to focus the mana. It was warm to the touch, pulsing faintly with stored energy. I held it up to the light, watching the way it caught and refracted the candle flames.

Soon. Soon I'd have enough power to do more than just correct diagrams and humiliate tutors. Soon I'd be able to cast real spells, to show the court what I was truly capable of.

But for now, I had a new persona to cultivate. The prodigy princess. The child genius. The delicate flower with the brilliant mind.

I smiled to myself, setting the obsidian shard back in its drawer. It was a good cover. A useful one. And if it meant I had to endure Father's puns and Mother's knowing looks a little longer?

Well. It was a small price to pay for the chance to rebuild my power.

I changed into my nightgown, blowing out the candles one by one. The room plunged into darkness, the only light coming from the moon outside my window.

As I climbed into bed, I let my mind wander back to the lesson with Master Theron. The look on his face when I'd corrected his diagram had been priceless. The way his cheeks had flushed, the way his hands had clenched at his sides—it had been almost as satisfying as casting a real spell.

Almost.

I closed my eyes, letting the darkness wrap around me. Tomorrow would bring new challenges, new opportunities. Tomorrow, I would begin the next phase of my plan.

But for now, I would sleep. And dream of spirals and counter-spirals, of mana flows and power gradients, of a world that would one day know my true name again.

Maledictus.

The Demon Lord.

Their princess.

I smiled into the darkness, letting sleep claim me. Tomorrow, the game would continue. And I intended to win.

title: Crystals, Gnomes, and Daddy's Love
prose:
# Chapter 06: Crystals, Gnomes, and Daddy's Love

The moon was wrong tonight. Too bright, too round, hanging over the palace gardens like a spotlight operated by some cosmic stage manager who wanted everyone to see exactly what I was doing. I lay in bed and stared at the ceiling and counted the hours until the household slept, which was a game I played often and always lost.

Midnight came the way it always did: slowly, then all at once, like a knife drawn across skin. The corridor outside my chambers was empty when I slipped out, bare feet silent on the cold marble. 

The garden gate was unlocked. I had unlocked it myself three nights prior, using a hairpin and a cursory knowledge of mechanical locks that predated this kingdom by several centuries. The hinges still made a noise when I pushed through, a low groan like something wounded, and I froze for a full three seconds, listening for footsteps. Nothing. The night was mine.

 Rose arbors lined every walkway, their blooms cultivated in hues ranging from cream to crimson. Fountains burbled at regular intervals, their waters lit from below by pale enchantments that made them glow like liquid moonlight. 

 I could feel them through the soles of my feet: a low hum, a pulse, the heartbeat of the world itself. They flowed beneath the palace like underground rivers, converging at points of natural power that the original builders had simply paved over and planted petunias on top of.

Amateurs.

I made my way to the southeastern corner of the garden, past the hedge maze that Father called "a delightful labyrinth of horticultural ingenuity" and that I called "a hedge maze."  The mana was sweet here, almost honeyed, with an undertone of something older and less pleasant that reminded me of the Abyssal Halls on a bad day.

My collection bag sat where I had hidden it three nights ago, tucked inside a hollowed decorative urn that the gardeners never bothered to check because it had a fake duck sitting on top of it. The duck was an abomination. I removed it with the careful disdain it deserved and retrieved the bag.

Inside, arranged in individual cloth wrappings to prevent premature resonance, were the crystals. Mana-quartz, every one of them, harvested over the course of six secret midnight excursions to the caves beneath the palace's western wing.  

  

I knelt in the dirt and began to dig.

The child's trowel I used was a gift from Father, given to me last month when I had expressed "an interest in gardening" that had made his eyes water with paternal pride. It was pink. It had a picture of a cartoon rabbit on the handle. 

But it worked. The soil was loose and dark, and within minutes I had dug the first hole: a precise cylinder, four inches deep and two inches in diameter, angled at exactly seventeen degrees from vertical to align with the ley line's flow vector. I unwrapped the first crystal—a clear one, fist-sized, with internal fractures that caught the moonlight and scattered it into prismatic shards—and pressed it into the hole.

The moment crystal touched ley line, I felt it. A whisper. A murmur. The faintest breath of mana flowing up through the soil, through the crystal's base, and into its crystalline matrix. The crystal hummed, so quietly that only someone who had once commanded armies of bound demons could have detected it. To anyone else, it would have sounded like nothing at all.

I allowed myself a small smile. Then I moved to the second position.

The work took hours. Each crystal had to be placed at a precise angle and depth, oriented so that its internal fracture planes aligned with the ley line's flow. 

So I was careful. I measured each hole with my fingers—three inches between crystals, adjusted for the natural curvature of the ley line—and I checked each crystal's orientation twice before setting it in place. The moon moved across the sky. The gardens were silent except for the fountains and the occasional rustle of something nocturnal in the hedges. By the time I had placed the eleventh crystal, my back ached and my knees were raw from kneeling on the damp earth, and I had dirt under every fingernail and something that might have been a worm in my left sleeve.

The twelfth crystal went into the ground with the same precision as the first. The thirteenth I saved.

The thirteenth crystal was special. It was the smallest of the set, barely larger than a marble, and it was not clear quartz but a deep, smoky black—the color of storm clouds and old grudges. This was the keystone, the final piece that would complete the circuit and activate the lattice. Without it, the other twelve crystals were just twelve pretty rocks sitting in holes. With it, they would become a mana battery, drawing and storing ambient energy from the ley lines in a slow, steady trickle that would accumulate over weeks and months into something useful.

I held the keystone up to the moonlight and studied it. The internal fractures caught the light and refracted it into patterns that, to anyone who knew what they were looking at, formed a perfect mathematical lattice—a map of the energy flows that would soon course through the completed array. To anyone who did not know what they were looking at, it was a dark, shiny pebble.

Like me, in a way. A small, unassuming exterior concealing something ancient and powerful and deeply, deeply unpleasant.

I knelt at the center of the lattice—the point where the twelve crystals formed a ring around an empty space—and dug the final hole. The keystone fit perfectly. I pressed it down, felt the soil close around it, and—

The lattice woke.

It was subtle. It was like feeling a single raindrop land on your skin in the middle of a storm, except the storm was mana and the raindrop was the sudden, sweet awareness of power flowing through a circuit I had built with my own hands. The crystals hummed in harmony, a chord of twelve notes that blended into a single, resonant tone just below the threshold of hearing. I could feel the ley line's energy being drawn up through the crystals, filtered and refined by their internal matrices, and channeled into the keystone, where it would pool and wait for me.

It was working.

I closed my eyes and let the sensation wash over me. The mana was thin—so thin compared to what I had once commanded that it was almost insulting—but it was there. A trickle. A breath. A single drop in an ocean I had once owned. But drops accumulate. Breaths become gales. And oceans, given time, can be drained.

"Now," I whispered to the lattice, "hide."

I stood up and brushed the dirt from my nightgown—a task that was more aspirational than practical, given the state of it—and took a step back to admire my work. The lattice was invisible. The mana flow was invisible. The keystone sat in its center like a punctuation mark, absorbing energy with the quiet efficiency of a well-designed engine. To anyone passing through the garden in daylight, they would see nothing but a circle of small stones in the dirt. A child's game. A harmless decoration.

Perfect.

I picked up the fake duck, tucked it back into the urn, and made my way back to my chambers. 

"Sleeping so soundly," she murmured, and closed the door.

I opened one eye. In the darkness, I allowed myself a smile that would have made a demon blush.

---

For three weeks, the lattice worked perfectly.

I visited it every other night, checking the keystone's energy level by touch—pressing my fingertip against its smooth surface and feeling the mana pulse beneath. It grew steadily, accumulating power the way a miser accumulates coins: slowly, carefully, one unit at a time. 

"Playing with rocks, are we, Your Highness?" she had asked, with the patient amusement of someone who had seen every form of royal eccentricity and was no longer capable of surprise.

"They're pretty," I said, which was the kind of thing a ten-year-old girl would say and was therefore exactly what I said.

Bruna had smiled and moved on. The stones remained.

On the morning of the twenty-second day, I woke to find the palace in an unusual state of organized chaos. Servants hurried through the corridors carrying trays of wine and plates of pastries. The royal banners had been freshly laundered and hung from every window. Father's voice boomed from somewhere deep in the castle, accompanied by the distinctive clanking of his ceremonial armor, which he insisted on wearing for all diplomatic occasions despite the fact that it was twenty years out of fashion and made him sound like a walking cutlery drawer.

"Visitors?" I asked my maid, who was brushing my hair with the kind of aggressive tenderness that suggested she was working through some personal grievance.

"The Beastfolk delegation, Your Highness. Prince Leo and his father's ambassadors. They arrived at dawn." She paused, brush hovering. "The King is very excited."

Of course he was. Father treated diplomatic visits the way most people treated holidays: as an opportunity to eat too much, tell stories nobody wanted to hear, and demonstrate his superiority through feats of physical strength that were impressive when he was twenty-five and merely concerning now.

I dressed in the outfit that had been laid out for me—a pale blue dress with silver embroidery that made me look like a particularly expensive piece of porcelain—and made my way to the gardens, where I assumed the official greeting would take place. I was right. The southeastern corner, where my lattice hummed silently beneath its disguise of river stones, had been chosen as the site of the reception.

My blood went cold.

Not metaphorically. I felt it actually cool in my veins, a physiological response to sudden, absolute terror that I had not experienced since the last time Seraphina had given me "the look" across the dinner table. The reception was being held in *my* garden. The diplomats would be standing *on* my ley line convergence point. 

I needed to intervene. I needed to create a distraction, redirect the reception, do *something* before—

"There she is! My little landscape artist!"

Father's voice hit me like a physical force. He was already in the garden, already striding toward me with that particular gait that managed to be both heroic and completely lacking in self-awareness, and behind him, lumbering through the garden gate like a small army of muscle and fur, came the Beastfolk delegation.

I had time for one clear thought: **I am going to dismantle this man's entire bloodline.**

Then he swept me up into a hug that lifted my feet off the ground and spun me in a circle, and all I could do was cling to his shoulders and smile.

"Father," I said, my voice muffled against his breastplate. "You're crushing my ribs."

"Ah! Sorry, sorry." He set me down and beamed at me with the radiant, uncomplicated joy of a man who had never once in his life suspected that his daughter contained the soul of a genocidal dark lord. "Lily, I want you to meet our honored guests from the Beastfolk Plains!"

 The Beastfolk delegation filled the garden path, a mass of fur and leather and poorly concealed amusement. At their head walked a man so large that he made Father look positively compact—King Ragnar of the Beastfolk Plains, whose arms were thicker than my entire body and whose beard contained, unless I was mistaken, a small bird's nest.

Beside him, slightly shorter but no less terrifying, was Prince Leo.

Leo was, by any objective standard, handsome, in the way that a hurricane is impressive. 

His eyes found mine across the garden, and he grinned. It was the grin of a predator who has spotted prey and decided, for reasons known only to his species, that the appropriate response to finding something you want to kill is to flirt with it.

"Princess Lily," he said, and his voice was a warm rumble that made the nearest rose bush tremble. "Your glow is bright today. Like a dawn-fire."

"Thank you," I said, because the correct response to a Beastfolk compliment was to accept it graciously, and because the correct response to Prince Leo specifically was to keep the interaction as brief as possible before he decided to give me another "gift" in the form of a dead rabbit. "You're very kind."

"I am not kind. I am honest. There is a difference." He took a step closer, and I took a step back, which he apparently interpreted as part of some elaborate dance. "You are avoiding me."

"I am standing still."

"A masterful strategy."

Father clapped Leo on the shoulder hard enough to stagger him, which was the kind of greeting that only made sense in the context of Hero culture, where affection was measured in bruise depth. "She's shy, lad! Give her time. She'll warm up to you once she sees what a fine specimen you are!"

"I am standing right here," I said.

Nobody heard me.

The diplomatic reception began in earnest, which meant Father started telling war stories, Ragnar started laughing at them, and the two of them began arguing about who had killed more demons during the Battle of the Obsidian Plains with the kind of cheerful one-upmanship that suggested the demons in question had been deeply annoying rather than genuinely threatening.

I stood to the side and tried to project calm while my soul screamed internally. The reception was being held directly on top of my ley line convergence point. The Beastfolk shaman—a thin, ancient creature with gray fur and eyes like chips of obsidian—was standing six feet from my keystone crystal and appeared to be *sniffing the air*.

He could sense it. I was sure of it. The mana flow from the lattice was subtle but not invisible, and to someone trained in nature-magic, it would register the way a discordant note registers to a musician. A wrongness. A pattern that didn't belong. A circle of river stones that was drawing power from the earth beneath them with the quiet, persistent hunger of something alive.

The shaman turned his head. His ancient eyes swept the garden, lingering on the flower beds, the fountains, the hedge maze. Then they settled on the circle of stones.

On my circle of stones.

I felt my heart rate spike. Fourteen years of memories and lifetimes of magical knowledge, and my body's response to mortal peril was to beat faster, like a frightened rabbit. The shaman took a step toward the stones. Then another. His nostrils flared.

**He knows. He knows, and when he tells Ragnar, and when Ragnar tells Father, and when Father asks me why I have been building magical infrastructure in the royal garden at midnight, I will—**

"There she is!" Father's voice boomed again, cutting through my spiral of panic like a sword through a particularly flimsy social fabric. He had appeared at my elbow, his hand on my shoulder, his face split by a grin so wide it threatened to bisect his head. "Lily, come here. I want to show our guests your handiwork."

"My—what?"

"Your rock garden! Bruna told me all about it. You've been working on it for weeks, haven't you? Collecting stones, arranging them just so. I told Ragnar about it, and he was very impressed. Weren't you, Ragnar?"

The Beastfolk King looked at me with the expression of a man who was being asked to be impressed by a child's hobby and had decided to commit fully. "Very impressed," he confirmed, in a voice like gravel in a tumble dryer. "Young princess has the eye. My Leo used to collect rocks too. He ate most of them, but the impulse was there."

"I have evolved beyond rock-eating," Leo said, with the dignity of a prince who had spent considerable time denying a childhood habit that was, according to the diplomatic notes, entirely accurate. "I now appreciate rocks from a purely aesthetic perspective."

Father guided me toward the circle of stones with the proprietary pride of a man showing off a new acquisition. The Beastfolk delegation followed, a murmuring mass of fur and curiosity. The shaman's eyes were on me now, sharp and bright, and I could feel his magical senses probing the air around us the way a doctor probes a wound.

I had perhaps ten seconds before he localized the mana drain.

"Look at this," Father said, kneeling beside the circle and gesturing with the expansive enthusiasm of a tour guide at a particularly boring museum. "Every stone placed just so. The way they're arranged—it's like a painting, isn't it? Bruna says she thinks it's a circle, but I told her it's more than that. It's *art*."

"It's a circle," I said.

"A circle is art, Lily! Geometry is art! Your mother always says I don't appreciate the arts, but look at this! I'm standing in front of art and I'm appreciating it!"

"The flow is…" the shaman said slowly, and every muscle in my body tensed.

Father straightened up and clapped the shaman on the back with enough force to send him lurching forward. "Unconventional, isn't it? That's Lily for you! Always thinking outside the box. I asked her why the stones were in a circle, and you know what she said? She said, 'Because circles are pretty.' Can you believe that? My daughter, the philosopher!"

The shaman blinked. He looked at Father. He looked at me. He looked at the stones again, and I could see him reaching for the mana signature, probing it, testing it—and finding nothing.

Nothing but pretty rocks.

 Father's booming voice, his radiant confidence, his absolute, unshakeable conviction that his daughter was a talented artist and not a magical engineering project had created a kind of psychic interference that had overwhelmed the shaman's ability to detect what was really happening.

"I see," the shaman said, with the careful neutrality of someone who was no longer sure what they had sensed and had decided to pretend they had sensed nothing. "Interesting shapes. Unconventional placement. The child has… an instinct."

"That's my girl!" Father said, and picked me up again, and spun me around, and the Beastfolk delegation applauded politely, and Prince Leo shouted something about how my stone-arranging skills proved I was "a woman of fierce aesthetic conviction" and that he would collect rocks in my honor, and through all of it I maintained my smile—the smile of a princess, the smile of a daughter, the smile of a girl who was watching her carefully constructed magical infrastructure get reclassified as a craft project by a man who could not stop being proud of me.

---

I returned to the garden that evening, after the diplomatic reception had devolved into an arm-wrestling tournament that Father had won by a margin that was either impressive or deeply suspicious, depending on whether you believed his claim that he had "let Ragnar have the first round."

The garden was quiet. The fountains murmured. The moon, the same moon that had watched me build the lattice, peered down through the branches of the ornamental cherry trees with what I chose to interpret as pity.

My lattice was still there. The stones sat in their circle, undisturbed, looking exactly as unremarkable as they had for the past three weeks. But something was wrong. I could feel it the moment I knelt beside the keystone—a hollow absence where the mana pulse had been, like putting your ear to a door and finding the room behind it empty.

I pressed my fingertip against the keystone's surface.

Nothing.

No hum. No pulse. No slow, sweet trickle of accumulated power. The crystal was smooth and cool and as dead as the ancient grudges I carried. I picked it up and turned it over in my hands, searching for the telltale shimmer of a charged crystal, and found nothing. It was just a rock. A dark, pretty, utterly ordinary rock.

One by one, I checked the other twelve. The same. Dead. Every crystal in the lattice had been drained of its stored mana, emptied of the weeks of accumulated energy that I had so carefully siphoned and stored and guarded. Twelve weeks of work. Gone. Not stolen—the mana was still there, dispersed back into the ambient flow, wasted, scattered like seeds on concrete.

And then I saw it.

A brass plaque, freshly installed at the edge of the garden bed, gleaming in the moonlight. I crept closer and read the inscription, which had been engraved in elegant calligraphy that I recognized as the work of the palace stonemason, the same man who carved Father's trophies and Mother's prayer stones.

*LILY'S PRETTY ROCK GARDEN*
*Arranged with love by Princess Liliana Celestia Lumengarde*
*A gift to the court and all who visit*

Beneath the plaque, written in Father's unmistakable scrawl on a piece of parchment pinned to the garden bed with a decorative silver stake, was a note:

*My dearest Lily,*

*The stonemason and I have decided that your rock garden deserves to be preserved for posterity! I've had him create a permanent installation, and several of the noble families have asked if they can commission their own "Pretty Rock Gardens" for their estates. The Duchess of Thornfield has already ordered one for her daughter's birthday!*

*Isn't it wonderful, Lily? You've started a trend!*

*Love always,*
*Father*

*P.S. The Beastfolk delegation was so impressed that King Ragnar has requested a set of "Lily Stones" for the Beastfolk embassy. I told him you'd be happy to help. Isn't that exciting?*

*P.P.S. The shaman says your rocks have "good energy." I told him that's because they're arranged with love. He seemed confused by this but appreciative.*

I set the parchment down carefully. My hands were not shaking—they were perfectly steady, because I was Maledictus, the Demon Lord, and I did not shake. My hands were simply experiencing a vibration that was entirely involuntary and had nothing to do with emotion.

The array was dead. Not damaged. Not drained by an enemy. Dead because it had been *appreciated*. Father, in his boundless, catastrophic pride, had installed a plaque that had disrupted the geometric precision of the lattice. The plaque's metal content—a cheap brass alloy with trace iron—had interfered with the crystal alignment, creating a resonance disruption that had scattered the accumulated mana like a stone thrown into a still pond. And the "permanent installation" had moved several of the crystals by fractions of inches, just enough to break the circuit and render the entire array useless.

The Demon Lord had built a magical battery, and the Hero King had unplugged it to use as a flower pot.

And I laughed.

It was a soundless laugh—the kind that comes from so deep inside you that it doesn't bother to make it all the way to your mouth, the kind that lives in the space between your ribs and your spine and feeds on the absolute, exquisite absurdity of your situation. 

Because here was the thing, the thing that made the whole nightmarish comedy of my existence so perfectly, horribly funny: Father's love was the most effective weapon I had ever encountered. More effective than any blade, any spell, any army of bound demons. It was a shield that I could not penetrate because it was not aimed at me—it was aimed at the world, and I was simply caught in its radiance. Father did not love me because I was good. Father loved me because I was *his*, and because he had decided, from the moment I was born, that everything I did was brilliant and beautiful and worthy of a brass plaque and a commission from the Duchess of Thornfield.

I picked up the dead keystone and turned it over in my hands. Smooth. Cool. Empty.

I set it back in its place among the others, where it sat among its siblings like a punctuation mark at the end of a sentence that said nothing at all. The plaque caught the moonlight and gleamed. Somewhere inside the palace, Father was probably still talking about my "artistic vision." The Duchess of Thornfield was probably already choosing stones for her daughter's birthday gift. And somewhere in the Beastfolk embassy, a set of "Lily Stones" was being arranged on a shelf by a prince who would interpret their decorative function as a profound statement about my feelings toward him.

I straightened up, brushed the dirt from my nightgown, and walked back to the palace. The guards were on their third patrol. The maid was waiting by my door with a warm cup of milk and a concerned expression. I took the milk, I smiled my princess smile, and I went to bed.

In the darkness, I held the dead keystone to my chest and felt nothing but its cold, smooth weight. 

Because that was the game. That was always the game. Not Demon Lord against Hero King, not darkness against light, not ancient evil against modern peace. It was daughter against father, and the terrible truth was that the daughter had never stood a chance.

I closed my eyes and let sleep take me, and if I dreamed, I dreamed of stones that stayed exactly where you put them, and moonlight that minded its own business, and a world where a man's love for his child did not constitute the most devastating form of magical interference known to any realm, mortal or infernal.

title: Arm-Wrestling with Destiny
prose:
# Chapter 07: Arm-Wrestling with Destiny

The block tower had taken me forty-seven minutes to construct.  I had built it as a meditation exercise, a way to center myself after the fiasco of the crystal garden, which Father had apparently discussed at length with the Beastfolk delegation during their morning audience. The blocks were a gift from the Duchess of Thornfield—hand-carved oak, sanded to a satin smoothness, each one stamped with the royal crest on its underside. 

  His grin was enormous and unapologetic, displaying a full set of very sharp teeth that he had not yet learned to moderate around small children.

"Lily!" he bellowed, spotting me by the window. "I have been looking everywhere for you! Father said you were resting, but resting is for old wolves and sick cubs, and you are neither!"

  The tower was at waist height, which for a human child was eye level, but for Leo, who insisted on walking with his chest puffed out and his chin raised like a conquering general, it was apparently below the threshold of perception.

His hip clipped the second tier.

 

"Oh!" Leo said, stopping mid-stride. He looked down at the wreckage, then up at me, and his expression shifted from surprise to something that I could only describe as delighted recognition. "You were building something! A tower! It fell!"

"Yes," I said. My voice was very even. "It did."

"Do not worry!" He crouched and began gathering blocks with the enthusiasm of a puppy collecting sticks. "I will help you rebuild! We can make it bigger! Taller! A tower that reaches the ceiling!"

I watched him pile blocks together in a chaotic heap that bore no resemblance to my original design. He was not building. He was performing the concept of building, approximating the activity with the same unselfconscious confidence he brought to everything else. Peasant children in the outer provinces stacked their firewood with more architectural integrity.

"Leo," I said, and the word came out through teeth that were, I noticed distantly, clenched hard enough to ache.

"Yes?" He looked up at me, his amber eyes bright with anticipation. His tail was wagging. The tail was always wagging. I had never met a creature so perpetually, aggressively happy, and I had spent my formative years surrounded by demons who fed on despair.

I made a decision.   I would do something far more effective. I would demonstrate, with surgical precision, the consequences of crossing a Demon Lord.

I would cast the Whisper of Dread.

The spell was a classic of the intimidation repertoire.  

It was, in short, a spell that commanded respect.

I gathered my mana. The sensation was familiar and uncomfortable, like trying to draw water from a well that had been filled with sand. My body was a vessel with a capacity of fifteen units, and the Whisper of Dread required six. Six was more than I had ever successfully channeled in this form. Six was, according to every physician and tutor who had examined me, dangerously close to the threshold at which my nose would begin bleeding and my vision would blur and I would be forced to smile weakly and claim that I had "overexerted myself."

But I was past caring about nosebleeds. I was past caring about fevers and fainting spells and the concerned looks of attendants who would carry me to bed and tuck me in and tell me what a brave little soldier I was.

I was going to make this wolf-boy understand that he was not dealing with a delicate princess. He was dealing with something far older, far darker, far more patient than anything he had ever encountered.

The spell coalesced in my chest. I shaped it with my breath, with the subtle tension of my fingers, with the focused intention of my will. It was a beautiful thing, a coil of shadow-wrought terror, and I released it toward Leo with the satisfaction of an archer loosing a perfectly aimed arrow.

It hit him.

And nothing happened.

 His fur ruffled slightly. His ears twitched. He blinked once, twice, and then his eyes widened with an expression that I had not anticipated and could not immediately categorize.

"Lily!" he gasped, dropping the armful of blocks he had been collecting. They clattered to the floor around his feet. "Did you feel that?"

I stared at him. "Feel what?"

"That!" He gestured vaguely at the air around us, his voice rising with excitement. "A prickle! A challenge! Like the moment before a storm breaks, or the instant a rival wolf steps into your territory!"

I opened my mouth. Closed it. Opened it again.

"I felt it," Leo continued, apparently not requiring my confirmation. He thumped his chest with both fists—a gesture I had seen his father make during diplomatic negotiations, always at moments of high tension. "Your spirit is fierce! I knew it! I told Father, I said, 'The little princess has a warrior's heart, I can smell it on her,' and he laughed, but I was right!"

His tail was wagging so hard now that it was creating a visible breeze. His grin had widened to the point where I could count every one of his teeth, which was an experience I would have preferred to avoid.

"A challenge," he repeated, savoring the word. "You are challenging me! Testing my mettle! This is excellent! This is wonderful! No one has challenged me since I arrived, and I was beginning to think the humans of Lumengarde had forgotten how to play!"

I had not been challenging him. I had been attempting to inflict psychic damage. The distinction seemed to be lost on him entirely.

"We must test our strength properly!" Leo declared, and before I could formulate a response, he had grabbed my wrist and was pulling me toward the heavy oak table that dominated the center of the nursery. "Arm wrestling! Yes! The classic contest of power! The true measure of a warrior!"

"Leo," I said, and my voice came out slightly higher than I would have liked. "I do not think—"

"Do not think!" he said cheerfully. "Thinking is for strategists and old men! A warrior acts! A warrior feels! A warrior grips his opponent's hand and pushes with everything he has!"

He released my wrist and vaulted onto one of the chairs, landing in a crouch on the seat. He planted his elbow on the table with a thud that made the wood shudder. His other hand beckoned to me with an enthusiasm that bordered on the deranged.

"Come! Sit! Prepare yourself for glorious combat!"

 His fingers were tipped with short, blunt claws that he had not thought to retract. His forearm, visible through the rolled-up sleeve of his tunic, was dense with the kind of muscle that came from a childhood spent climbing trees and chasing deer.

I looked at my own hand. It was pale, slender, and about as intimidating as a sparrow's wing.

The attendants had gathered at the edges of the room. I had not noticed them earlier, but now I was acutely aware of their presence—six women in identical gray dresses, their expressions ranging from amused to concerned to openly delighted. One of them, the youngest, was already pressing her hands to her cheeks in anticipation.

"Oh, Your Highness," she breathed. "You're going to arm-wrestle the Beast Prince?"

"I am not—" I began.

"She is!" Leo confirmed. "She has challenged me! It is a matter of honor now! I cannot refuse, and neither can she!"

I considered my options. I could refuse, which would be interpreted as cowardice and would likely result in Leo doubling his efforts to "build my confidence." I could attempt to win, which was laughably impossible. Or I could do what any intelligent strategist would do when faced with an unwinnable confrontation.

I could lose. Deliberately. Spectacularly.

It was not a satisfying plan. It was, in fact, a deeply humiliating plan. But it was a plan, and plans were better than chaos, and I had learned, through ten years of this absurd existence, that sometimes the best way to maintain a cover was to lean into it.

I climbed onto the chair across from Leo. The seat was too tall for me, and my feet dangled above the floor. I planted my elbow on the table, which brought my forearm to roughly the same height as his, though the comparison was not favorable. His arm was thicker than my wrist. His grip, when he took my hand, was warm and firm and entirely too strong.

"Ready?" he asked, his eyes sparkling with anticipation.

"Leo," I said, trying one last time. "I am not a warrior. I am a princess. I read books. I arrange flowers. I do not—"

"Your spirit says otherwise!" He squeezed my hand, and I felt my bones shift slightly in a manner I did not appreciate. "I can see it in your eyes! The fire! The determination! You are a fierce little soldier, and I am honored to test my strength against yours!"

I stopped trying to argue. There was no point. This creature had constructed an entire narrative about me in his head, and no amount of evidence was going to dismantle it.

"On the count of three," he announced. "One. Two. Three!"

He pushed.

I did not resist. I let my arm collapse immediately, folding beneath his pressure with a theatricality that I hoped would read as pathetic rather than deliberate. My body lurched sideways, following the trajectory of my arm, and I allowed myself to topple off the chair entirely, landing on the floor with a soft thump and a carefully manufactured gasp.

"Ow," I said, for the benefit of the attendants.

The room went silent.

Then Leo's laughter boomed out, filling the nursery with its warmth and volume. He vaulted off his chair and landed beside me, offering me his hand with the enthusiasm of someone who had just won a great victory.

"Magnificent!" he declared. "A swift and decisive defeat! You did not even try to resist! You recognized my superior strength immediately and yielded with grace!"

I took his hand. He pulled me to my feet with no visible effort, which was both humiliating and informative.

"Of course," I said, brushing dust from my dress. "You are very strong, Prince Leo."

"I am!" He puffed out his chest. "I am the strongest cub in my pack! Father says I will be a great warrior one day, perhaps even greater than him, though he says that with the kind of laugh that makes me think he does not believe it."

I had achieved the strategic defeat. I had reinforced my "delicate" cover. I had, by all reasonable metrics, succeeded.

And yet, as I looked at Leo's beaming face, I felt a new emotion stirring in my chest. It was not hatred, though hatred was familiar and comfortable. It was not frustration, though frustration was certainly present. It was something closer to bafflement—a profound, disorienting sense that I had misjudged the nature of this particular opponent.

He was not a problem to be hexed. He was not an obstacle to be removed. He was a variable, a complex and infuriating variable, one that did not respond to the tools I had spent a lifetime perfecting.

He was, in short, a challenge.

"Your Highness!" One of the attendants rushed forward, wringing her hands. "Are you all right? Should I fetch the physician?"

"I am fine," I said, managing a delicate smile. "Prince Leo was very gentle."

This was not true. Prince Leo had been about as gentle as a collapsing mountain. But the attendant beamed at my words, and Leo preened, and I realized that I had, through a combination of accident and strategy, managed to make everyone in the room happy.

It was infuriating.

"Tomorrow," Leo announced, planting his fists on his hips. "We will have a rematch! You will have time to train, to build your strength, and I will be ready to face you at full power!"

"Training," I repeated. "I do not—"

"Do not worry!" He clapped me on the shoulder, and I stumbled forward a step. "I will teach you! A great warrior teaches his rivals everything he knows, so that their victory will be meaningful when it comes!"

I stared at him. "You would teach me to beat you?"

"Of course!" He seemed genuinely surprised that I had to ask. "What is the point of victory if it is not earned? What is the point of strength if it is not tested? I want you to grow strong, Lily! I want you to be a worthy opponent! That is the way of my people!"

The attendants were cooing. The youngest one had actually clasped her hands together and was gazing at Leo with an expression of romantic fervor that I found deeply concerning.

"Prince Leo," she said, "you are so noble!"

"Noble?" He puffed out his chest further, which I had not thought possible. "I am simply a warrior who respects his rivals! It is the way of the Beastfolk Plains!"

I wanted to scream. I wanted to explain, in precise and careful terms, that I was not his rival, that I was not his friend, that I was not interested in his training or his teachings or his absurd, relentless optimism. I wanted to tell him that I was the Demon Lord Maledictus, that I had conquered nations and bound demons and reduced armies to ash, and that he, a furry eight-year-old with a tail that would not stop wagging, was not a worthy opponent but an annoyance to be endured.

But I could not say any of that. I could only smile my princess smile and nod my princess nod and accept his offer of training with the same grace I had accepted a hundred other absurd gestures of friendship.

"I would be honored," I said, and the words tasted like copper in my mouth.

Leo roared with laughter. "Excellent! Tomorrow at dawn, then! I will meet you in the training grounds, and we will begin your education in the ways of the warrior!"

The training grounds. Dawn. With a beastfolk prince who would, presumably, attempt to teach me to wrestle or throw spears or do any number of physically demanding activities that my fragile body was entirely unsuited for.

This was going to be a disaster.

I returned to my chambers with the attendants trailing behind me, their whispers a constant murmur of "how sweet" and "what a charming friendship" and "she's so brave, attempting to match the Beast Prince's strength." I closed the door to my bedroom and stood in the silence, breathing slowly, allowing the mask of the delicate princess to fall away.

The Whisper of Dread had failed. That was the first problem. My offensive magic was functionally useless against this particular target, and I needed to accept that and plan accordingly.

The second problem was that Leo had interpreted my failed spell as a challenge, and my strategic defeat as a noble concession. He was building a narrative in his head, one in which I was a fierce warrior princess who needed only training and encouragement to reach my full potential.

The third problem, and the one that troubled me most, was that I had not entirely hated the experience.

It was a troubling realization. I had spent ten years cultivating a careful distance from the inhabitants of this world, treating them as obstacles and tools rather than people. I had watched them with the detached interest of a scholar studying specimens. I had felt nothing when they praised me, nothing when they coddled me, nothing when they misinterpreted my every action as adorable or brilliant or precocious.

But Leo had looked at me—truly looked at me, with his bright amber eyes and his enormous grin—and seen something he called a fierce little soldier. He had seen strength where there was only frustration. He had seen courage where there was only calculation. He had seen a rival worth training, a warrior worth respecting, a creature worth knowing.

And some part of me, some ancient and exhausted part that had spent twenty years as a Demon Lord and ten years as a child, had felt something dangerously close to warmth.

I sat down on my bed and stared at the wall.

"Absolutely not," I said aloud.

The wall did not respond.

I was not going to develop feelings for this creature. I was not going to let his enthusiasm and his friendship and his ridiculous, wagging tail erode the careful walls I had built around myself. He was an obstacle, a variable, a problem to be solved. I would outthink him. I would outmaneuver him. I would find some way to turn his presence in the palace to my advantage, or failing that, to ensure that he left as quickly as possible.

But even as I made these resolutions, I knew, with the cold certainty of a strategist who has seen too many battles to lie to herself, that Prince Leo was not going to be easy to remove.

He was not an enemy to be defeated. He was not a threat to be neutralized.

He was a rival, and he had decided, with the unshakeable confidence of a creature who had never once doubted himself, that I was worth fighting for.

I did not know which was worse.

title: Falling for the Rival
prose:
# Chapter 08: Falling for the Rival

The training grounds smelled of sweat, leather, and the faint metallic tang of old blood.  But here, in this sunlit yard of sand and straw, it was diluted, almost pleasant, like the memory of a battle long past. I sat on a bench beneath a parasol, my skirts arranged just so, my hands folded in my lap. The attendants fluttered around me, offering sweetened tea and fanning me with ostrich feathers. I ignored them. My attention was fixed on the spectacle before me.

Prince Leo was a whirlwind of muscle and fur, his amber eyes bright with the thrill of the fight. He moved with the effortless grace of his kind, his claws digging into the packed earth as he lunged at a straw-stuffed dummy. The other beastfolk warriors—massive, shaggy figures with bared teeth and roaring laughter—cheered him on. They were a blur of motion, their bodies built for strength and speed, their voices rough with the joy of physical exertion. I watched, my expression carefully neutral, my fingers twitching against the fabric of my dress.

 And yet, as I watched Leo spin and strike, his tail wagging like a pup’s, I felt something unfamiliar stir within me. Not admiration—never that. But a flicker of something else, something dangerously close to understanding. He was alive in a way I had not been for centuries. Even now, trapped in this fragile, childish body, I could not deny the raw vitality of it.

“Lily!” Leo’s voice cut through my thoughts, loud and cheerful. He had abandoned his dummy and was striding toward me, his sword discarded in the dirt. “Watch this!”

I did not move. I did not smile. I simply tilted my head, my gaze cool and assessing. “I am watching,” I said, my voice soft but clear. “Though I fail to see the purpose of your exertions. The dummy is already dead.”

Leo laughed, a booming sound that echoed across the yard. “Not the dummy, little soldier! This!” He turned, his eyes scanning the training grounds. Then, with a grin that showed too many teeth, he pointed at me. “You!”

Before I could react, he was moving. His body blurred, his muscles coiling and releasing in a single, fluid motion. He crossed the distance between us in three strides, his arms outstretched. I had time to register the intent in his eyes—time to calculate the trajectory of his charge, the angle of his approach, the force of his momentum. I had time to plan a dozen different responses: a spell, a feint, a well-placed tripwire of shadow. But I did none of them.

Instead, I sat very still, my hands clutching the edge of the bench, my breath shallow. I was a princess. I was delicate. I was *not* a warrior.

Leo’s arms closed around me in a bear hug, lifting me effortlessly from the bench. I let out a small, undignified squeak as my feet left the ground, my skirts tangling around my legs. The court gasped—soft, delighted sounds from the ladies-in-waiting, a low chuckle from the beastfolk warriors. Queen Seraphina, standing at the edge of the yard with her arms crossed, raised an eyebrow but said nothing.

“Fear not, little soldier!” Leo declared, his voice muffled against my hair. “I shall vanquish the shadow-beast!” He spun me in a circle, his grip tight and unyielding. I clung to him, my fingers digging into his arms, my mind racing. *This is undignified. This is humiliating. This is—*

The world tilted. My stomach lurched. Leo’s foot caught on a loose stone, and suddenly we were falling. I had a brief, disorienting glimpse of the sky, then the ground rushing up to meet us. There was no time to cast a spell, no time to brace myself. There was only the impact, the jarring collision of my body with something soft and yielding.

Hay.

We landed in a heap, a tangle of limbs and straw and laughter. Leo was beneath me, his chest rising and falling with his breath, his arms still wrapped around me. His face was inches from mine, his eyes bright with amusement, his cheeks flushed from exertion. His breath was warm against my skin, smelling of mint and something wild, like the wind over open plains.

For a moment, I could not move. I could not think. I could only stare at him, my mind blank with shock. Then, slowly, the reality of the situation settled over me. I was sprawled across a beastfolk prince, my dress askew, hay tangled in my hair, my cheeks burning with something that was not anger.

*No,* I thought, my mind scrambling to regain control. *No, no, no. This is not happening. This is not—*

Leo grinned up at me, his teeth white against his sun-bronzed skin. “See?” he said, his voice rough with laughter. “We are well-matched!”

I reacted on instinct. My hand shot out, shoving at his chest. “You are a barbarian,” I hissed, my voice trembling with rage. Or at least, it *should* have been rage. Instead, it came out as a childish squeak, high and breathless. The court tittered. The beastfolk roared with laughter. Even Queen Seraphina’s lips twitched, though she quickly schooled her expression into something more regal.

I scrambled to my feet, my skirts tangling around my legs, my face burning. I could feel the heat in my cheeks, the prickling sensation spreading down my neck. My heart was pounding, my breath coming in short, sharp gasps. It was not fear. It was not anger. It was something worse—something I did not understand, something I could not control.

 I wanted to scream. I wanted to cast a spell—any spell—that would wipe that grin from his face. But I could not. Not here. Not now.

Leo rolled to his feet, his movements fluid and effortless. He brushed the hay from his tunic, his tail wagging behind him. “You are angry,” he observed, his voice cheerful. “Good! Anger is the fire that forges a warrior. You will learn to channel it.”

I glared at him, my hands clenched into fists at my sides. “I am not angry,” I said, my voice tight. “I am *disgusted*.”

Leo laughed again, the sound rich and warm. “Disgust is just anger with better manners,” he said. “Come! We will try again. This time, I will show you how to fall properly.”

I opened my mouth to refuse, but the words died in my throat. The court was watching. The Queen was watching. And I was a princess. I was delicate. I was *not* a warrior.

“Very well,” I said, my voice sweet and poisonous. “But if you drop me again, I shall ensure that your next meal is seasoned with hemlock.”

Leo’s grin widened. “A challenge! I accept!”

I turned away from him, my skirts swirling around my ankles, my face still burning. The attendants fluttered around me, brushing the hay from my dress, adjusting my sleeves, murmuring apologies. I ignored them. My mind was a storm of frustration and something else—something I refused to name.

As I walked back toward the palace, my steps measured and precise, I could feel Leo’s eyes on me. I could hear the court’s whispers, the soft coos of admiration, the laughter of the beastfolk warriors. They thought this was a game. They thought this was *fun*.

They had no idea what I was capable of.

---

The training grounds faded behind me, the sounds of clashing steel and raucous laughter growing distant. The attendants trailed after me, their voices a soft murmur of concern and admiration. “Oh, Your Highness, you were so brave!” “What a charming display of spirit!” “The Beast Prince is quite taken with you, isn’t he?”

I did not respond. My mind was elsewhere, replaying the moment over and over—the feel of Leo’s arms around me, the warmth of his breath, the heat in my cheeks. It was infuriating. It was humiliating. It was *unacceptable*.

I reached my chambers and dismissed the attendants with a wave of my hand. The moment the door closed behind them, I let out a slow, controlled breath, allowing the mask of the delicate princess to slip away. My shoulders slumped, my fingers unclenching from the fabric of my dress. The Whisper of Dread had failed. Again. Not that I had expected it to work on Leo—his beastfolk nature made him resistant to subtle magics—but the fact that he had not even *noticed* the spell grated on me. He had been too busy charging at me like an overgrown pup to sense the creeping dread I had tried to weave around him.

*This is the problem,* I thought, my mind cold and analytical. *This is the fundamental flaw in my plan.*  They saw me as a child. A prodigy, perhaps, but still a child. A creature to be coddled, to be protected, to be *laughed with*.

I paced the length of my room, my skirts whispering against the floor. The walls were adorned with tapestries, with portraits of my parents, with the framed “family portrait” I had drawn in crayon—the one that was, in truth, a summoning circle. The court thought it was adorable. The Queen thought it was a sign of my genius. I thought it was a reminder of how far I had fallen.

*I need a new strategy,* I decided. *I need to adapt.* Leo was not going to be cowed by spells or threats. He was not going to be intimidated by glares or sharp words. He was a creature of instinct, of action, of *physicality*. And if I was going to outmaneuver him, I would have to meet him on his own terms.

I stopped in front of my vanity, my reflection staring back at me. My cheeks were still flushed, my hair slightly disheveled from the fall. I looked like a child who had been playing too hard. I looked *harmless*.

I reached into the hidden drawer beneath the vanity, my fingers brushing against the obsidian shard, the powdered silver, the lock of hair. My tools. My weapons. I had spent years collecting them, planning, scheming. And yet, none of them had prepared me for this—for the way my body had betrayed me in the training grounds, for the way my heart had pounded, for the way my cheeks had burned.

 I had spent centuries in control of my body, of my emotions, of my very soul. And now, in this fragile, childish form, I was at the mercy of involuntary responses—blushing, quickened heartbeats, trembling hands. It was maddening.

I turned toward the door, my steps purposeful. The training grounds would be empty now, the court dispersed, the sun beginning its slow descent toward the horizon. It was the perfect time to begin.

---

The training grounds were quiet, the sand still warm from the day’s sun. The straw dummies stood like silent sentinels, their painted faces worn and faded. I approached one, my skirts hitched up in my hands, my bare feet silent against the packed earth. I had changed into a simpler dress, one that allowed for more movement, and my hair was tied back in a loose braid. I looked like a child preparing for a game. I looked *innocent*.

I stopped in front of the dummy, my eyes narrowing. It was a crude thing, stuffed with straw and burlap, its painted face a caricature of a monster. It was nothing like the enemies I had faced in my past life—nothing like the generals who had knelt before me, nothing like the heroes who had fallen to my spells. But it would have to do.

I reached into the pocket of my dress, my fingers closing around the small, smooth stone I had taken from the garden. It was a simple thing, unremarkable, but it would serve my purpose.  It was a minor enchantment, one that would not tax my meager mana reserves. A spell of balance, of precision. A spell to ensure that when I struck, I would not miss.

I took a deep breath, my fingers tracing the sigil in the air. The words of the incantation were soft, almost inaudible, but they carried the weight of centuries of practice. The stone in my hand grew warm, then hot, and I could feel the magic taking hold—the faintest whisper of power, like a breeze against my skin.

I stepped back, my arm drawing back, my eyes locked on the dummy’s painted face. Then, with a sharp exhale, I threw the stone.

It struck the dummy square in the chest, the impact sending a shower of straw into the air. The dummy rocked back, then forward, then back again, its movements jerky and unnatural. I watched, my expression unreadable, as it settled back into stillness.

*Not bad,* I thought, a flicker of satisfaction warming my chest. *Not perfect, but not bad.*

“What are you doing?”

I whirled around, my heart leaping into my throat. Leo stood at the edge of the training grounds, his arms crossed over his chest, his tail wagging lazily behind him. His eyes were bright with curiosity, his grin wide and unguarded.

I schooled my expression into something neutral, my fingers twitching at my sides. “Practicing,” I said, my voice cool.

Leo’s grin widened. “Practicing what? Throwing rocks?”

I did not answer. Instead, I turned back to the dummy, my mind racing. I had not heard him approach. I had not sensed his presence. He had caught me off guard, and that was a mistake I could not afford to repeat.

Leo stepped forward, his boots kicking up small clouds of dust. “You are full of surprises, little soldier,” he said, his voice warm with amusement. “I did not think you would return so soon.”

I ignored him, my eyes scanning the training grounds. There were other dummies, other targets. I could try again. I could improve.

Leo followed my gaze, his expression turning thoughtful. “You are angry about earlier,” he said, his voice softer now. “About the fall.”

I turned to face him, my expression carefully blank. “I am not angry,” I said. “I am *disappointed*.”

Leo laughed, the sound rich and warm. “Disappointed in what? In me? Or in yourself?”

I did not answer. I did not need to. Leo was already moving, his steps light and quick. He stopped in front of me, his eyes locking onto mine. “You are disappointed because you did not fight back,” he said, his voice low and serious. “Because you let me lift you. Because you let me drop you.”

I felt a flicker of something dangerous stir within me—something hot and sharp and *alive*. “I did not *let* you do anything,” I said, my voice tight. “You took me by surprise.”

Leo grinned, his teeth white against his sun-bronzed skin. “And that is the first lesson of the warrior,” he said. “Never be surprised.”

I glared at him, my hands clenching into fists at my sides. “I am not a warrior,” I said. “I am a princess.”

Leo’s grin did not waver. “And I am a prince,” he said. “But that does not mean I cannot be both.”

I opened my mouth to argue, but the words died in my throat. Leo was right, in a way. I *was* both. I was a princess, a delicate flower, a prodigy. And I was Maledictus, the Demon Lord, a creature of shadow and power and *purpose*. I could not be one without the other. Not anymore.

Leo reached out, his hand brushing against my arm. His touch was warm, his fingers calloused. “Come,” he said, his voice gentle. “Let me show you.”

I hesitated, my mind racing. I could refuse. I could walk away. I could return to my chambers and plot my next move, my next scheme. But something in his eyes—something in the way he looked at me, as if I were a puzzle he was determined to solve—made me pause.

“Very well,” I said, my voice soft but firm. “But if you drop me again, I *will* season your dinner with hemlock.”

Leo laughed, the sound echoing across the empty training grounds. “I would expect nothing less,” he said.

And so, I let him lead me back into the fray.

---

The sun dipped below the horizon, painting the sky in hues of gold and crimson. The training grounds were bathed in the soft, fading light, the shadows stretching long and lazy across the sand. Leo stood before me, his arms outstretched, his eyes bright with anticipation.

“Again,” he said, his voice rough with exertion. “This time, I will not catch you off guard.”

I did not answer. I simply stepped back, my skirts swirling around my ankles, my eyes locked onto his. I had spent the last hour learning to fall—learning to roll, to brace, to land without injury. It was humiliating. It was *undignified*. And yet, as I crouched low, my muscles coiled and ready, I could not deny the thrill of it—the rush of adrenaline, the sharp focus, the sense of *control*.

Leo lunged.

I moved.

My body reacted on instinct, my muscles remembering the lessons of the past hour. I sidestepped his charge, my hand shooting out to grasp his arm. I used his momentum against him, twisting my body and pulling him off balance. He stumbled, his eyes widening in surprise, and then he was falling—falling toward the sand, his arms windmilling as he tried to catch himself.

I did not let him.

I stepped forward, my foot hooking behind his ankle, and pushed. Leo landed with a thud, the breath rushing out of him in a startled grunt. He lay there for a moment, his chest rising and falling, his eyes wide with shock. Then, slowly, he began to laugh.

“Well done,” he said, his voice warm with amusement. “That was a proper throw.”

I stood over him, my hands on my hips, my breath coming in short, sharp gasps. My cheeks were flushed, my hair loose from its braid, but I did not care. For the first time in hours, I felt something other than frustration, other than humiliation. I felt *triumph*.

Leo rolled onto his side, propping himself up on one elbow. His eyes were bright, his grin wide and unguarded. “You learn quickly, little soldier,” he said. “I am impressed.”

I did not smile. I did not gloat. I simply nodded, my expression cool and composed. “I am a quick study,” I said. “But I am not your soldier.”

Leo’s grin did not waver. “Not yet,” he said. “But you will be.”

I turned away from him, my skirts whispering against the sand. The court would be gathering for dinner soon, and I needed to change, to compose myself, to don the mask of the delicate princess once more. But as I walked toward the palace, my steps light and quick, I could not shake the feeling of satisfaction that warmed my chest.

Leo was wrong. I would never be his soldier. But I would learn his weaknesses. I would learn his strengths. And when the time came, I would use them against him.

I paused at the edge of the training grounds, my eyes scanning the horizon. The sun had set, the sky darkening to a deep, velvety blue. Somewhere beyond the palace walls, beyond the city, beyond the kingdom, the world waited. And I would be ready for it.

But first, I had a prince to outmaneuver.

I turned back toward the palace, my steps measured and precise. The attendants would be waiting. The court would be watching. And I would be *perfect*.

As I reached the doors, I allowed myself a small, satisfied smile. Leo thought he had won today. He thought he had taught me a lesson.

He had no idea what was coming.

title: The Student Becomes the Master
prose:
# Chapter 09: The Student Becomes the Master

The morning light in the west solar was a gentle, honeyed thing, filtering through the leaded glass to illuminate motes of dust dancing in the warm air.  It was the light of appeasement, the illumination of a cage. I sat on a velvet cushion, my spine rigid, my hands folded in my lap in a pose of immaculate composure.  A mind like mine does not rest. It disassembles.

The door opened with a whisper of polished hinges. My mother, Queen Seraphina, entered first, a vision in silk the color of a summer storm. Behind her, trailing in her shadow like a nervous minnow, came the girl.

My initial assessment was swift, thorough, and utterly dismissive.   There was a faint tremor in her left wrist. Nervousness. Or perhaps, the first sign of mana fatigue from overwork. 

“Your Highness,” Seraphina said, her voice the auditory equivalent of that gentle morning light. “This is Eris of the Spire, junior magus under Archmage Mira’s direct tutelage. She has been sent to assess your aptitude and, should it prove sufficient, to begin your formal education in the arcane arts.” She placed a gentle hand on the girl’s shoulder. Eris flinched as if touched by a branding iron, then attempted to straighten into a posture of military readiness. It made her look like a startled heron.

I tilted my head, allowing a small, shy smile to curve my lips.  “It is a pleasure to meet you, Mistress Eris.”

The words came out soft, a little breathy. Perfect.

Eris’s mouth opened. A small, dry sound emerged, like a rusted hinge. She swallowed hard, her throat working. “Your Highness.” Her voice was a stammer, a fragile, cracking thing. She curtsied, a jerky, unpracticed motion. “I am to… to assess your aptitude.” She straightened, her eyes fixed on a point somewhere over my left shoulder, as if looking directly at me required more courage than she possessed. “Archmage Mira was most… insistent. She said… she said the reports from your previous tutor, Master Theron, were… unprecedented.”

My inner monologue, a steady stream of vitriol and calculus, did not pause. *Unprecedented, yes. The unprecedented discovery that a mind as profound as mine was housed in a vessel as frustratingly flimsy as this. Theron, the old fool, likely saw my correction of his pathetic Tier-Four warding circle as a miracle. He probably wept into his tea for a week after fleeing the palace. Good. Let his successor inherit his terror.*

Outwardly, I nodded, my expression one of earnest, childlike attentiveness. “Master Theron was very kind. He said I had a good ear for harmonic resonance.”

Seraphina smiled, a genuine, warm curve of her lips. “She does. She once corrected a lullaby composer on the precise interval for a soothing C-sharp minor. It was darling.” She squeezed Eris’s shoulder again. This time, the girl managed not to flinch, though a muscle in her jaw jumped. “I will leave you two to begin. Mistress Eris, tea and refreshments will be sent in. Please, make yourself comfortable. Lily is a wonderful host.” With one last, lingering look at me—a look that held its usual blend of pride and a deeper, quieter watchfulness—my mother departed.

The silence that followed her exit was thick enough to carve. I could hear the frantic ticking of the clock on the mantel, the distant cry of a servant in the gardens, the shallow, rapid rhythm of Eris’s breathing. She stood there, ramrod straight, her hands clasped behind her back, a posture of rigid discipline that was clearly costing her immense effort. 

“Would you like some tea, Mistress Eris?” I asked, my voice still a delicate, lilting thing. I gestured to the low, child-sized table between us, where a porcelain set adorned with unicorns and rainbows was laid out. My mother’s idea of appropriate tea service.

Eris’s eyes finally met mine, wide with a sort of horrified fascination. “I… I could not impose, Your Highness.”

“It is no imposition,” I said, picking up the teapot with both hands.  “Please. Sit.”

She sat, perching on the edge of the cushion opposite me as if it were a bed of nails. I poured the tea, my movements slow and deliberate, a slight, careful spill of amber liquid landing on the porcelain tray. A classic, childish mistake. I bit my lip, as if chastising myself. Eris’s rigid posture softened by a fraction. 

We sipped. The tea was chamomile, bland and soothing, designed for delicate princesses and not for fueling the machinations of a reborn demon lord. I longed for a strong, black bitter leaf, something to shock my system into alertness.

“I have prepared a standard diagnostic problem set,” Eris began, her voice gaining a sliver of confidence now that she was on the familiar ground of academic procedure. She reached into the satchel at her feet and pulled out a thin slate of polished wood, covered in faintly glowing runes. “A simple test of theoretical comprehension. Archmage Mira felt it was the best place to start.”

I nodded, my eyes wide with apparent interest. “I am ready.”

Eris placed the slate between us. The runes glowed with a soft, blue light, forming a complex equation at its center.  The kind of first-year exercise for students at the Spire who were just learning to feel the flow of mana through theoretical constructs. The runes described a simple ward, designed to deflect minor kinetic impacts. The equation balanced, but clumsily, with redundancies and wasted potential.

I looked at it. My mind, that vast and terrible library, immediately began to disassemble it. The core glyph was sound, a derivative of the Aegis Minor. The secondary runes for mana channeling were inefficient, creating a feedback loop that would waste at least thirty percent of the input energy. The tertiary glyphs, meant to dissipate excess heat, were unnecessary if the channeling was corrected. It was a textbook problem, and like all textbook problems, it was sanitized, neutered, made safe and boring.

I picked up the stylus lying next to the slate. My hand trembled as I held it, a perfect mimicry of a child’s lack of fine motor control. I made a small, thoughtful sound, a little hum in the back of my throat. Then, I began to write.

 I simplified the tertiary runes, merging three into one elegant symbol that handled both heat dissipation and ambient mana stabilization. 

I pushed the slate back toward Eris, my hand still trembling. “The charm’s core glyph is flawed,” I said, my voice quiet, hesitant, as if I were afraid of being wrong. “The channeling is wasteful, and the heat dissipation is redundant if you adjust the flow here.” I tapped the new symbol I had drawn. “It makes the ward self-sustaining against minor impacts. And it is stronger.”

I looked up at Eris, my expression one of innocent inquiry. “Is… is that better?”

The silence that followed was different. It was not the thick, nervous silence of a moment before. This was a vacuum, a sudden and absolute cessation of all sound, including, I suspected, Eris’s own breathing.

She was staring at the slate. Her face, which had been a pale, nervous canvas, had gone completely white, the blood drained from it as if by a sudden, violent spell. Her lips were parted, her eyes wide, tracing and retracing the elegant, forbidden lines I had drawn. Her slate-grey irises seemed to flicker with a light of their own, a frantic, internal computation. I watched her throat work again, a convulsive swallow. A faint, choked sound escaped her lips, something between a gasp and a sob.

Then, the color returned to her face in a sudden, violent rush, flooding her cheeks and forehead with a deep, mottled crimson. A single tear, then another, traced clean paths through the faint powder on her cheeks. She looked up at me, and the raw, unfiltered awe in her eyes was almost blinding. 

“You…” Her voice was a wreck, a ruin. “You just solved the Resonance Paradox.”

I blinked, feigning confusion. “The… the what?”

“The Resonance Paradox!” The words burst out of her, loud and fervent. She was on her feet now, the slate clutched in her hands as if it were a holy relic. “The paradox of self-sustaining kinetic wards! It has been a theoretical dead-end for two centuries! Magus Valerius proposed the base framework in the Fourth Age, but he could never reconcile the energy feedback with stable output without a third-party mana source! It is… it is considered an unsolvable problem in modern thaumaturgy! Archmage Mira herself has a paper dedicated to proving its impossibility!” She was breathing heavily, her chest rising and falling. “You solved it… like basic arithmetic!”

She took a staggering step closer, then, remembering herself, dropped into a deep, trembling curtsy. Her forehead nearly touched the floor. “You are not a prodigy,” she whispered, her voice thick with emotion. She raised her head, her tear-streaked face alight with a fervor that bordered on madness. “You are a… a living grimoire!”

I kept my own expression carefully, deliberately puzzled. Inside, however, the gears of my mind were turning with exquisite, delightful precision. *Hook set. Line tight. Now, to reel her in.*

I looked down at my hands, folded demurely in my lap. I let out a small sigh, a sound carefully crafted to convey not triumph, but a deep and weary burden. “I do not understand,” I whispered. “I just… see how it should be. It is so clear in my head. The shapes, the patterns. But when I try to explain it, or when I try to… to make it work…” I glanced at my palms, then made a tiny, helpless gesture. “My body will not listen. I am… fragile.”

A flicker of something sharp and protective crossed Eris’s face. It was exactly the reaction I had calculated.  

“It is… common for… for minds of such magnitude to be housed in vessels not yet prepared to channel their full potential,” Eris said, her voice steadier now, adopting the formal, comforting language of her academy. She straightened, wiping her eyes with the back of her hand. The scholar was reasserting control over the awe-struck girl. “Your Highness, your gift is… unprecedented. It must be nurtured. Guided.”

*Yes. Guided. Towards my goals.*

I looked up at her, allowing a single, perfect tear to well in my own eye. It was a difficult skill, but not impossible. Think of the humiliation of being swaddled. The tear spilled over, tracing a path down my cheek. “It is lonely,” I said, my voice dropping to a near-inaudible whisper. “Knowing so much, but having no one to… to understand. No one who can help me find the materials to… to explore these patterns further.”

I watched her face, saw the shift from awe to fierce, devoted protectiveness. 

I reached over, as if impulsively, and touched the sleeve of her fraying robe. “I have heard of… of certain texts,” I continued, my tone hesitant, as if confessing a terrible secret. “Old texts. From the time of my… my birthfather’s studies.” I paused, letting the implication hang in the air, heavy and fragrant. “There is a book. My mother calls it the Black Tome of Maledictus. She keeps it in the deep archives. She says it is too dangerous, too complex.” I looked at Eris, my eyes wide with manufactured longing. “I only wish I could see it. Just once. To know if… if it holds the answers I see in my head.”

The fire in Eris’s eyes changed. It was no longer the fire of awe, but of purpose. The fire of a crusade.

She drew herself up to her full, modest height. “Your Highness,” she said, her voice ringing with a newfound conviction that smoothed out her stammer entirely. “For you? For the chance to study alongside a living repository of arcane truth? I would walk through the Seven Hells themselves! I shall procure it.”

*And there it is.*

I gave her a small, watery smile, the kind of smile that breaks hearts. “You are very kind, Mistress Eris.”

She shook her head, her braid swinging. “Not kind. Duty. It is my duty to ensure such a brilliant mind is not… stunted.” She clutched the slate to her chest. “I will begin my research immediately. There are protocols, restrictions… but they can be navigated. For this.”

We sat in the gentle, honeyed light for a few moments longer, sipping our lukewarm tea. Eris began to talk, haltingly at first, then with growing enthusiasm, about the theoretical underpinnings of the Resonance Paradox, asking questions, confirming her understanding. I answered them with simple, devastating clarity, doling out breadcrumbs of my knowledge, each one a hook she would not be able to resist.

When she finally departed, her posture was transformed. She walked tall, her shoulders back, the nervous heron replaced by a woman on a mission. Her eyes shone. She did not look back.

I remained on my cushion, the tea cold in my cup. I listened to the sound of her confident footsteps receding down the marble corridor. 

The fangirl was cultivated. The scholar corrupted. The first piece of the puzzle was not merely secured; it had come to me eagerly, gratefully, promising to fetch the very key to its own undoing.

I rose, smoothing the front of my dress. My body was still frail, my mana still a pathetic trickle. But my library now had a librarian, and she was eager to fetch me the most dangerous books on the shelf. The game had advanced. And I was, for the first time since my rebirth, genuinely pleased with how it was being played.

title: Breadcrumbs and Bluff
prose:
# Chapter 10: Breadcrumbs and Bluff

The nursery floor had become a battlefield.

I knelt among scattered porcelain dolls, wooden soldiers, and stuffed creatures that had seen better centuries, each one positioned with the precision of a general reviewing her troops. The dolls in frilly gowns formed the left flank, their painted smiles turned toward the enemy. Chipped wooden soldiers held the center.
