A battalion of tin cavalry waited in reserve behind the overturned tea table that served as my command post.

 The pincer movement I was mapping would have encircled the enemy's supply lines within three days, cutting off reinforcements before the main assault even began. I had used a similar formation at the Battle of the Crimson Ford, my final campaign, the one that ended with a hero's sword through my chest and a forbidden ritual that had hurled my soul into this pink, helpless body.

A floorboard creaked.

I did not look up. I recognized the particular weight of a footstep trying not to be heard. Not a servant's shuffle, not a guard's steady rhythm. This was careful, deliberate, the step of someone who did not want to be noticed but could not help being curious.

Someone was watching me.

I kept my face angled toward the dolls, one hand adjusting a porcelain general's position. My fingers trembled, a deliberate affectation I had perfected over years: the delicate shake of a child concentrating hard. The court found it endearing. The physicians cited it as proof of my "delicate constitution." The spies found it suspicious.

Let them watch. I had everything to hide, which meant I had to be very careful about what I showed.

"Now, General," I murmured to the porcelain doll, her painted eyes staring past me with the blank vacancy of the dead. "If we advance the left flank here, we draw their forces into the valley. Terrain favors infantry on the high ground while reserves circle behind."

I moved a wooden soldier forward, then a tin cavalryman. The pattern was elegant, mathematically precise. I had once commanded armies of demons that could level cities. Now I commanded dolls that smelled faintly of lavender and old lace.

The creaking footsteps retreated.

Good. They had seen what I intended: a child playing at war, her imagination running wild with toy soldiers. They would report that the princess was "playing at generalship," a harmless game for a girl with too much time and too few playmates.

The prickle between my shoulder blades lingered. My father's court was full of eyes and ears, each reporting to some master. The merchant guilds had spies in the kitchens. Neighboring kingdoms kept agents among the visiting dignitaries. And somewhere in the shadows, moving with the silent grace that had earned him his title, was Zephyr, the Shadow Blade: the realm's master spymaster, a man who had built his reputation on unraveling conspiracies in the dark.

Zephyr saw something else. I had caught his gaze across the throne room more than once, pale eyes sharp with suspicion that never quite faded. 

He would not wait forever. Eventually he would investigate properly, and then I would have real problems.

So I needed to give him something to investigate first. Something loud, absurd, and completely wrong.

The idea took root as I adjusted the general's tiny sword. Zephyr hunted grand conspiracies, dark plots threatening the kingdom. He would never suspect that the greatest obstacle to his investigation was a ten-year-old girl and her love of baked goods. Simplicity was the most effective weapon, and I would give him so many false trails he would choke on cookie crumbs.

---

The royal gardens spread before me in carefully tended color, the manicured hedges and flowerbeds designed to impress visiting dignitaries. I crouched beside a fountain, skirts pooled in pale pink silk, scattering breadcrumbs across the flagstones. Sparrows clustered at my feet, pecking with the frantic urgency of creatures who believed the supply would vanish.

"Eat up, little friends," I said, pitching my voice to carry just far enough. "There's plenty. The bakers made extra today."

I had been aware of the two footmen since entering the garden. They stood near the eastern entrance, ostensibly tending hedges. Their boots were too clean for gardeners. Their posture too rigid for servants. Zephyr's people.

I had been conducting counter-espionage operations since before their grandparents were born.

"Here, little bird," I cooed, reaching into my waist pouch. "Something special."

 Beneath it, in careful childish letters: "THE CRUMBLE CONSPIRACY IS COMING."

I held it up for the sparrows. "See? The cookie is falling. That means the conspiracy is working. Soon there won't be any cakes left, and everyone will have to eat—" I dropped my voice to a whisper. "—plain bread."

The sparrows chirped, unimpressed.

I let my shoulders slump with the exaggerated weariness of a child carrying dark knowledge alone. "You wouldn't understand."

Behind me, one of the footmen stepped closer, his pruning shears dangling forgotten.

"Oops." The drawing slipped from my fingers and fluttered to the ground. I scrambled to pick it up, but my small, clumsy hands fumbled the task. The paper danced away from me on a gust of wind, skittering across the flagstones until it came to rest at the footman's boots.

"Oh, no," I said, voice trembling. "Please, sir, could you give that back? It's my very important drawing."

The footman bent, his movements stiff. He picked up the paper, eyes scanning it with the focused intensity of a man trained to read between lines that were not there.

"The Crumble Conspiracy," he read aloud, flat.

I snatched it from his hand. "It's nothing! Just a silly drawing. Please don't tell anyone." My chin lifted with the particular terror of a child caught where she should not be, my lower lip pushed out, my eyes brimming.

I could see the calculation behind his gaze. Weighing the drawing against his orders. Deciding whether this merited reporting.

"Of course, Your Highness," he said. "Your secret is safe with me."

I beamed, the smile of a child who trusted completely. "Thank you, sir! You're very kind."

I turned and ran, skirts flapping around my ankles, heart singing. 

Zephyr would hear within the hour.

---

My chambers were as I had left them, dolls in formation, tea table overturned. But something sat on my pillow.

A silver spoon. The handle engraved with interlocking circles and sharp lines, polished to mirror brightness. The style belonged to the Shadow Realm, Zephyr's territory: a domain of twilight palaces and cultivated silence where the Spymaster kept his secrets under lock and shadow.

"Mistress!"

I spun, spoon in hand. Baphomutt perched on the windowsill, barely larger than a cat, with leathery wings and skin the color of dried blood. His luminous eyes gleamed with adoration that was equal parts touching and terrifying.

"For Mistress!" he chirped, bouncing on clawed feet. "Baphomutt bring gift! Shiny thing!"

"You stole this from the Shadow embassy," I said flatly.

"Mistress need shiny things! Baphomutt provide!"

I closed my eyes. 

But the spoon in my hand told me something useful. It had been in Zephyr's territory until Baphomutt took it, which meant the embassy's security had gaps a well-meaning idiot could slip through. And if there were valuable objects worth guarding in a shiny room full of shadows, there might be more inside: records, documents, intelligence worth acquiring.

"Where did you find this?"

"Shiny room! Many shiny things! Dark room, many shadows! Baphomutt sneak, Baphomutt steal, Baphomutt bring to Mistress!"

A vault in the embassy. Guarded. Full of objects valuable enough to protect. And Baphomutt had moved through it without triggering a single alarm.

I filed the information away. "Thank you, Baphomutt. This is a good gift."

The imp's eyes blazed. "Baphomutt bring more—"

"No." The word was sharp enough to freeze him mid-bounce. "No more gifts without asking me first."

His wings drooped. "But Mistress—"

"Ask first. If you bring me another gift without permission, I will be very unhappy."

He nodded frantically. "Baphomutt understand! Baphomutt be good imp!"

"Good. Now go."

He vanished in a puff of sulfurous smoke, leaving behind the faint smell of brimstone and a lingering echo of chittering. I slipped the spoon into my hidden drawer alongside my other treasures and returned to the nursery floor. The porcelain general still waited, tiny sword raised. I adjusted its arm, angling the blade a fraction higher.

---

The royal kitchens roared with heat and noise the next morning. Baking bread, clattering pots, the head cook bellowing measurements over the din. Marta, broad and flour-dusted, had served the palace for thirty years. She looked up from her dough with a crinkle-eyed smile.

"Princess Lily! You should be in the nursery, not getting underfoot in my kitchen!"

I held up a basket wrapped in linen. "I came to thank you. For the crumbles."

Marta's hands stilled on the dough. "Crumbles, Your Highness?"

"The ones that keep disappearing," I said, my voice innocent and hushed. I leaned closer, glancing at the kitchen door. "I heard there's been a—" I whispered the word as if it were dangerous. "—conspiracy."

The room went quiet. A ladle paused mid-stir. Two scullery maids exchanged wide-eyed looks. The under-baker, a boy of fifteen with flour in his eyebrows, edged closer to hear.

I set the basket on the counter, pushing it toward Marta. "This is for you and the staff. For all your hard work. I wanted someone to know that I appreciate the crumbles."

I turned and left before anyone could speak. Inside the basket, tucked beneath a cloth napkin, was a note in my careful childish hand: "Thank you for the delicious crumbles! Keep up the good work!"

A simple thank-you. But Zephyr's people had torn this kitchen apart three days ago: rifled the flour sacks, interrogated the bakers, reduced the pastry chef to tears over missing sugar cookies. And now the princess had arrived with a gift basket and a whispered word about conspiracies.

 By evening, every servant in the palace would know that Princess Lily had thanked the bakers for the very crumbles Zephyr's agents had been frantically investigating. The story would swell with each retelling, gaining teeth and shadowy figures seen lurking near the pantry at midnight, until it bore almost no resemblance to the harmless seed I had planted.

None of it was true. All of it would be believed. And the one person whose job it was to separate truth from rumor would find himself drowning in so many contradictory accounts that he wouldn't know which thread to pull.

I paused on the garden path. The air smelled of crushed rosemary and warm stone. My ribs ached from holding myself taut through the kitchen performance, and I let the tension seep out through my shoulders. A sparrow landed on the fountain's rim, cocking its head as if asking whether I had more crumbs.

I had planted a seed in fertile ground and watered it with the court's own gossip. The Crumble Conspiracy would spread through the palace like a fever, growing wilder and more elaborate with each retelling, and Zephyr would chase it deeper and deeper into the dark.

All I had to do now was wait for him to trip over his own investigation.

I smoothed the front of my dress and walked back toward the nursery. The porcelain general and I had more battles to plan.

title: Zephyr's Public Meltdown
prose:
# Chapter 11: Zephyr's Public Meltdown

The throne room was a cavern of gilded absurdity, its vaulted ceiling dripping with chandeliers that cast prismatic light onto the assembled courtiers like overzealous confetti. I sat perched on a velvet cushion beside Father’s throne, my slippered feet dangling several inches above the floor. The cushion was embroidered with golden lions—his sigil, not mine. Never mine. My fingers traced the armrest’s carved edges, the wood smooth beneath my touch, worn by generations of rulers who had never once considered that the true heir to their legacy might be a ten-year-old girl with a nosebleed problem and a grudge older than the kingdom itself.

Zephyr stood before the dais, his posture rigid as a pike, a stack of parchment clutched in his hands like a man holding the last shreds of his dignity. His voice was measured, each syllable clipped with the precision of a man who had spent his life in shadows, but the tremor in his fingers betrayed him. *Pathetic.* I watched him with the detached amusement of a cat observing a particularly slow mouse. The mouse, of course, had no idea it was being watched. Or that the cat was already bored.

“Your Majesty,” Zephyr began, his voice cutting through the low hum of courtly chatter, “the Crumble Conspiracy is a credible threat. The princess’s drawings and the missing baked goods are not coincidental.”

The court erupted into laughter before he could finish. A nobleman in the front row—Lord Pembleton, if I recalled correctly—slapped his knee so hard I heard the fabric of his breeches strain. “A conspiracy! By the gods, Zephyr, you’ve outdone yourself this time!”

Father, mid-sip of wine, choked and set his goblet down with a clatter. Wine sloshed over the rim, staining the marble like a bad omen. He wiped his mouth with the back of his hand, his laughter booming through the hall. “Zephyr, my old friend, you’ve been outfoxed by a child’s imagination! A *cookie* conspiracy! I haven’t heard something this delightful since the Great Cheese Heist of ’87!”

I tilted my head, my expression the picture of innocence. “Father, perhaps Lord Zephyr is just... very thorough?” The words tasted like honeyed venom on my tongue. The court roared, the sound bouncing off the gilded walls like a flock of startled pigeons. Zephyr’s jaw clenched, the muscle twitching beneath his skin. His eyes flicked to me, dark and sharp as a blade. I met his gaze, my smile sweet, my thoughts razor-edged. *Let him wonder. Let him doubt. Let him chase shadows while I dance in the light.*

Father waved a hand, dismissing the matter with the same ease he dismissed most things—like the concept of personal boundaries or the fact that his puns were a war crime. “Zephyr, I appreciate your vigilance, but I think we can safely rule out the royal crumbles as a national security threat. Unless...” He leaned forward, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. “Unless the crumbles are a Trojan horse. A *pastry* of doom!”

The court dissolved into laughter again. Zephyr’s fingers tightened around the parchment, the edges crumpling beneath his grip. I could see the calculation in his eyes, the way his mind raced to salvage this farce. *Good. Let him spin his wheels. Let him waste his time on a conspiracy that doesn’t exist, while I weave one that does.*

“Your Majesty,” Zephyr said, his voice strained, “if I may present the evidence?”

Father sighed, but there was a glint in his eye, the same one he got when he was about to indulge in a particularly ridiculous story. “Very well, Zephyr. Let’s see what you’ve got. But I warn you—if this is another report about the royal jam going missing, I’m revoking your spymaster privileges.”

Zephyr didn’t smile. He never did. That was part of his charm, I supposed. Or his downfall. He stepped forward and slammed the first piece of parchment onto the dais. It was one of my drawings—the one of the royal bakery, complete with stick-figure bakers and a suspiciously lopsided oven. The court leaned in, their expressions shifting from amusement to outright hilarity.

Lady Whitmore, a woman whose laugh sounded like a donkey in distress, gasped. “The princess drew a *cookie*! How sinister!”

Father squinted at the drawing, then at me. “Lily, my dear, is this your handiwork?”

I nodded, my voice soft. “Yes, Father. I was practicing my... architectural sketches.”

Father beamed. “Of course! A future architect! Or perhaps a baker! You’ve captured the essence of the royal kitchens with such... *artistic flair*.”

Zephyr’s eye twitched. He flipped to the next parchment—a list of missing ingredients, written in my careful, childish hand. “Your Majesty, note the precision. The sugar, the flour, the butter—all taken in quantities consistent with crumble production. And here—” He jabbed a finger at the bottom of the page. “A note in the princess’s handwriting: *‘More crumbles, please. For the cause.’*”

The court erupted again. A young page in the back snickered so hard he nearly toppled over. Father wiped tears from his eyes, his shoulders shaking. “Zephyr, my friend, you’ve been bested by a five-year-old’s art project. I’d say that’s a new low, but you set the bar pretty high.”

Zephyr’s face was a mask of controlled fury, but I could see the cracks. His knuckles were white around the parchment, his breath coming just a little too fast. *This is too easy.* I had spent weeks planting the seeds of this conspiracy—leaving notes in the pantry, arranging my dolls in “strategic formations,” even “accidentally” mentioning the Crumble Conspiracy in front of the kitchen staff. And now, here was Zephyr, standing before the court like a fool, his reputation crumbling faster than the pastries he was so obsessed with.

I shifted in my seat, my fingers curling around the edge of the cushion. “Father, I think Lord Zephyr is just trying to keep us safe. Maybe the crumbles *are* dangerous. What if they’re... *poisoned*?”

The court fell silent. Father’s laughter died in his throat. He looked at me, his expression softening. “Lily, my dear, that’s a very serious accusation.”

I nodded, my voice trembling just enough to sell the act. “I heard the bakers talking. They said the crumbles were... *special*. Maybe someone is trying to hurt us.”

Father’s face darkened. He turned to Zephyr, his voice dropping to a growl. “Is this true? Are the royal crumbles a threat?”

Zephyr’s jaw worked, but no words came out. I could see the gears turning in his mind, the way he weighed his options. 

He chose the latter. “Your Majesty, I may have... overstated the case. The crumbles appear to be harmless.”

Father clapped him on the shoulder, his laughter returning. “There you have it! The royal crumbles are safe. Though I suppose we should keep an eye on the bakers. You never know when a man might snap and start putting *raisins* in the scones.”

The court laughed again, the sound echoing through the hall like a chorus of braying donkeys. Zephyr’s shoulders slumped, just for a moment, before he straightened and bowed. “With your permission, Your Majesty, I’ll take my leave.”

Father waved a hand. “Of course, Zephyr. And do try the crumbles while you’re at it. They’re quite good. Though I suppose you’ve already had your fill.”

Zephyr’s eyes flicked to me one last time, dark and unreadable. I met his gaze, my smile sweet, my thoughts sharp. *Run along, little spy. The game is just beginning.*

---

The moment the throne room doors closed behind Zephyr, I slipped from my cushion and curtsied to Father. “May I be excused, Father? I’d like to visit the library.”

Father’s face lit up. “Of course, my dear! But don’t stay too long. You need your rest. A growing girl like you can’t spend all day with her nose in a book.”

I nodded, my voice meek. “Yes, Father.”

I turned and made my way through the court, my steps light, my expression serene. The courtiers parted before me, their whispers following in my wake. “Such a clever child.” “So precocious.” “A credit to the kingdom.”

I ignored them. They were nothing. Pawns in a game they didn’t even know they were playing.

My chambers were a sanctuary of gilded confinement. The walls were papered in silk, the floor covered in plush rugs that muffled my footsteps. Baphomutt was perched on my desk, his beady eyes gleaming as he gnawed on the corner of a forbidden grimoire. I sighed. “Must you eat everything?”

Baphomutt chittered, his voice a squeaky rasp. “Mistress is sneaky! Like Baphomutt!”

I rolled my eyes. “Yes, very sneaky. Now put that down before you ruin the binding.”

Baphomutt dropped the grimoire with a thud and scampered to the edge of the desk, his tail twitching. “Baphomutt helps! Finds shiny things for Mistress!”

I ignored him, turning my attention to the task at hand. I pulled a sheet of perfumed parchment from my desk drawer, the paper thick and creamy beneath my fingers. The quill was already poised, the inkwell open. I dipped the nib and began to write.

*To the Shadow Blade, whose vigilance is as sharp as his wit—*

I paused, considering my words. 

*Thank you for your dedication to our kingdom’s safety. Please accept this small token of my gratitude.*

I signed the note with a flourish, my handwriting neat and precise. Then I set the quill aside and turned to the basket on my desk. It was woven from golden reeds, lined with silk, and filled with exotic fruits—dragonfruit, lychee, a cluster of grapes so dark they looked black. At the bottom, nestled among the fruit, was a single, overripe fig. Its skin was split, the sticky juice oozing onto the parchment beneath it.

Baphomutt leaned in, his nose twitching. “Mistress is giving food to enemy?”

I smirked. “Not just any food. A *message*.”

Baphomutt tilted his head. “Message is... sticky?”

I ignored him, folding the note and tucking it into the basket. Then I rang for a servant. A young maid appeared moments later, her curtsy deep, her eyes wide with awe. “Your Highness?”

I held out the basket, my voice sweet. “Please deliver this to Lord Zephyr’s quarters. With my compliments.”

The maid took the basket, her fingers brushing against the fig’s sticky residue. She didn’t notice the way the juice smeared the ink, turning my neat handwriting into an illegible blur. She curtsied again and hurried from the room, her steps quick with the importance of her task.

Baphomutt chittered, his laughter high and squeaky. “Mistress is evil! Like Baphomutt!”

I sighed, rubbing my temples. “I’m not *evil*. I’m *strategic*.”

Baphomutt scampered to the edge of the desk, his tail flicking. “Same thing!”

I ignored him, turning my attention to the next move. 

I pulled a fresh sheet of parchment from my drawer and began to sketch. A map of the palace, the corridors marked with tiny X’s. A list of names—courtiers, servants, guards. A plan. Because this wasn’t just about humiliating Zephyr. It was about *control*. About ensuring that no one ever looked too closely at the princess with the too-sharp eyes and the too-quiet smile.

Baphomutt hopped onto my shoulder, his claws pricking through the fabric of my dress. “Mistress is plotting!”

I nodded, my voice soft. “Always.”

---

The halls of the palace were a labyrinth of marble and gold, the air thick with the scent of incense and the low hum of courtly chatter. I walked with my head held high, my steps light, my expression serene. The courtiers bowed as I passed, their whispers following in my wake.

“Did you hear? Zephyr’s been reduced to investigating *pastry*!”

“I heard he’s now convinced the princess is a master of culinary espionage!”

“Such a clever child. So *precocious*.”

I ignored them. They were nothing. Background noise in a game they didn’t understand.

I turned a corner and nearly collided with Zephyr. He stood in the center of the corridor, his arms crossed, his expression unreadable. His eyes, though—his eyes burned with quiet fury.

I curtsied, my voice saccharine. “Good morning, Lord Zephyr. I do hope you’re enjoying the fruit.”

Zephyr’s jaw tightened. He didn’t answer. He didn’t need to. The silence between us was thick with unspoken words, a battlefield of glances and half-smiles.

I held his gaze for a moment longer, then turned and walked away, my steps unhurried, my heart pounding in my chest. The victory was mine. For now.

But the game was far from over.

title: Overheard and Overwhelmed
prose:
# Chapter 12: Overheard and Overwhelmed

The Book of Royal Etiquette and Protocol for Young Ladies of Noble Bearing was, objectively speaking, one of the most tedious collections of ink-stained parchment I had encountered in either of my lives.  I held it open on my lap, the spine cradled in my small hands, the text oriented upside down from where I sat curled in the window seat of the royal library.  I wasn’t reading. I was listening.

Alistair’s voice carried the distinct, resonant timbre of a man accustomed to addressing battlefields and banquet halls alike. It boomed even in a whisper, vibrating through the floorboards. “She’s not fragile, Sera. She’s *perfect*. My little miracle.” There was a sound—cloth rustling, perhaps a hand running through hair, the universal fidget of a man whose passionate declaration has met measured silence.

Seraphina’s reply was softer, as always, but it had a particular edge today. A honed quality, like a scalpel wrapped in silk. “She’s too still, Alistair. Too *knowing*. She doesn’t play like other children. She *plans*.”

My fingers tightened on the book’s spine, the cracked leather creaking under the pressure. *She sees too much.* 

The door remained a sliver.  A study in contrasts. The Hero and the Saint. My jailers. My parents.

I turned a page in the etiquette book, the rustle loud in the quiet library. 

Alistair scoffed, the sound carrying clearly through the gap. “She’s a thinker! Like you! She’s got your mind and my courage. What’s wrong with that?” 

 “I’m not saying there’s anything wrong. But she’s *different*. She needs more than just protection. She needs *guidance*.”

My breath hitched, a tiny, traitorous catch in my chest.  Guidance was the last thing I required.   Exposure. 

I stood. The movement was slow, deliberate, my legs feeling oddly heavy, as if the air in the library had thickened to syrup. I meant to leave. To slip out, back to the safety of my chambers where Baphomutt’s idiotic ministrations were a known variable. But the argument was a storm, and I found myself rooted to the spot, a sail torn from its mast.

“You worry too much,” Alistair insisted. I could hear the smile in his voice now, the fond, fatherly indulgence that was his most effective weapon against me. It was like fighting a sunbeam. “She’s got your grace, too, you know. Remember how she held her spoon at the feast last week? Properly, with the correct finger placement! A natural diplomat.”

My spoon handling. He was latching onto my spoon handling as evidence of my sound psychological development.  The sheer, crushing banality of my existence was a torment all its own.

“She held the spoon correctly because she spent three days practicing with a weighted replica before the feast,” Seraphina said quietly. “She doesn’t do things by accident, Alistair. Every smile, every word, every seemingly spontaneous gesture is… calculated.”

*Calculated.* The word sent a cold thrill through me, a rare moment of being accurately seen. And then it was immediately smothered by a wave of panic. She was too close to a truth she couldn’t possibly understand.

A footstep in the hallway beyond the study. I recognized the soft tread and the faint jingle of a teapot—Brenda, the afternoon tea servant. I pressed myself back into the window seat alcove, the Book of Etiquette held up to shield my face, a posture of studious absorption I knew would be deemed adorable if observed. The door opened wider, and Brenda slipped inside, her curtsy deep and practiced. The voices inside paused, a held breath.

“Your Majesties, your afternoon tea,” Brenda murmured. The soft clink of porcelain on a side table. “Will there be anything else?”

“No, thank you, Brenda. That will be all,” Seraphina’s voice, smooth and undisturbed.

The door clicked shut. The silence stretched for three heartbeats, four. Then Alistair spoke again, his voice lower now, but no less fervent. It was thick with an emotion I found deeply inconvenient. “I won’t have you doubting her. Not you. She’s my daughter. My *little miracle*. After everything… after all the battles, the losses… she is the one good, true thing that came from it all.”

A pause. Then Seraphina’s reply, barely above a whisper, yet it cut through the library’s stillness with chilling precision. “I know. But miracles aren’t always what they seem.”

The words hung in the air, a perfect, terrifying crystallization of the entire unspoken war within these stone walls. My chest tightened. It wasn’t pain, not exactly. It was a pressure, an unfamiliar constriction that made the air thin and my vision blur at the edges. A primal, physiological response my immortal consciousness had no protocol for. I wanted to scream. To stride into that study, to reveal the truth in all its horrific, magnificent glory, to watch the Hero’s perfect faith shatter and the Saint’s careful doubts curdle into horror. To make them *understand*.

But the words died, unborn. They turned to ash on my tongue. Because beneath the fury, beneath the humiliation, beneath the cold, strategic calculus, there was a third thing. A tiny, persistent, highly illogical variable that refused to be quantified or dismissed. It was the memory of Alistair’s laugh, deep and booming, when he’d hoisted me onto his shoulders to point out a hawk in the sky. It was the feel of Seraphina’s fingers, gentle and cool, brushing the hair from my forehead when I feigned a fever to avoid etiquette lessons. It was the taste of the honey-cakes the royal baker made specifically for me, because I’d once made a face at a plain scone and Alistair had declared them “an insult to my daughter’s palate.”

 I was a prisoner of their love, yes. But the bars were woven from sunlight and the scent of my mother’s lavender soap. And the lock… the lock might be in my own hand.

I lowered the book.  I placed the book carefully on the window seat, spine aligned with the wood, and stepped away from the library, my footsteps unnaturally loud on the marble floor. The hallway stretched before me, a canyon of portraits and potted ferns. My room was two turns and a short flight of stairs away. A sanctuary of silk sheets and hidden drawers.

My chambers were as I’d left them, cool and quiet in the late afternoon light. The air smelled faintly of potpourri and old parchment. And something else. A faint, brimstone-adjacent tang that always preceded trouble of the small, scaly, and profoundly stupid variety.

Baphomutt was perched on the corner of my bed, his bat-like ears twitching.  “For Mistress!” he squeaked, his voice a grating mix of devotion and self-satisfaction. His grin was wide, revealing far too many teeth.

I ignored him. The sight of the stolen trinket, his latest “contribution,” should have sparked the usual cold irritation. Instead, it registered with distant annoyance, like a fly buzzing in another room. I walked past the bed and sank onto the edge of it, my legs finally giving way. I sat there, hands clenched into fists on my lap, my gaze fixed on the intricate pattern of the rug.   And now, for the first time, the thought arrived with a traitorous, nauseating flicker of doubt: *What if I’m wrong?*

Not wrong about their nature. They were still the heroes who had annihilated my kingdom, slaughtered my legions, and scattered my essence to the winds. They were still the architects of my humiliation.  The realization was terrifying. It introduced a variable of catastrophic potential into all my calculations.

“Mistress is unhappy?” Baphomutt’s voice was closer now. He’d hopped onto the bed beside me, his head cocked. His yellow eyes, slitted and glowing faintly, blinked with earnest concern. “Baphomutt will get more! Shiny things! Make Mistress happy!”

I shook my head, a sharp, jerky movement. No. This was a luxury I could not afford. Guilt was a currency for mortals, for souls burdened with empathy and the illusion of free will. I was Maledictus. The Demon Lord. These people, this castle, this life of silk and misunderstanding—they were my enemies. The love I felt was a weapon turned against me, a corruption of my purpose. It had to be excised. Cauterized. I would not be a slave to sentiment. I would not let a few kind words and honey-cakes derail an eternity of calculated vengeance.

  *Miracles aren’t always what they seem.* My mother’s voice. She was right. She just had the specifics of the miracle spectacularly, catastrophically wrong. I was not a blessing. I was a curse wearing a child’s face. A curse that was, against all reason and self-preservation, beginning to understand the appeal of the blessing.

My hand moved, almost of its own accord, to the side of the bed where Baphomutt had dropped his offering. My fingers closed around the cool metal of the locket. I brought it up, holding it so the fading daylight caught the surface. It was simple, elegant silver, worn smooth with use. There was an engraving on the front. I traced the shape with my thumb. An oval, and inside it, two words in delicate script: *Our Miracle*.

A sound escaped me, not quite a laugh, not quite a sob. It was a dry, rasping exhalation of air. The irony was so perfect, so exquisitely crafted by a cruel and indifferent universe, that for a moment I almost admired it. To think that this was what they called me. This small, treasured, impossible thing.

I did not put it back down. My fingers curled around it, the metal warming to the heat of my skin. With my other hand, I reached up and tucked the chain under my pillow, hiding the locket from view.  The war for the soul of the monster they loved. I closed my eyes, the weight in my chest not lifting, but settling, becoming a part of me. A stone I would carry into battle. And for the first time, I did not know which side would ultimately claim victory.

title: Imp-romptu Theft Spree
prose:
# Chapter 13: Imp-romptu Theft Spree

The first thing I noticed when I woke was the weight on my chest. Not the usual weight of my own limbs, still sluggish with sleep, but something cold and metallic, pressing down like an accusation.  The light filtering through the curtains was soft, golden—morning light, the kind that made everything look innocent. 

A sapphire necklace lay coiled on my nightgown, the stones catching the light like captured fragments of the sky. Beside it, a ruby ring glinted, its red depths dark and hungry. And there, half-buried in the folds of my pillow, was a diamond brooch, its facets sharp enough to draw blood if I pressed too hard. 

And then there was Baphomutt.

The imp was perched on the bedpost, his clawed feet gripping the wood like a grotesque finial. His grin was wide, his yellow eyes bright with pride, his bat-like wings fluttering slightly as if he couldn’t contain his excitement. “For Mistress!” he squeaked, his voice high and reedy. “Baphomutt found shiny things! Make Mistress happy!”

I stared at him. Then at the jewels. Then back at him.

 I could already hear the questions. *Lily, where did you get these?* *Did someone give them to you?* *Why were they in your bed?*

And worse—*Did you steal them?*

I didn’t answer Baphomutt right away. Instead, I swung my legs over the side of the bed, my bare feet touching the cold stone floor.  

“Mistress is unhappy?” Baphomutt’s grin faltered, his ears drooping. His tail, which had been wagging like a dog’s, stilled. “Baphomutt did bad?”

 “No, Baphomutt. You didn’t do bad.” I reached out and patted his head, my fingers brushing against the coarse fur between his horns. He leaned into the touch, his eyes closing briefly. “But you can’t just… take things like this. Especially not from Mother’s jewelry box.”

His eyes snapped open, wide and confused. “But Mistress likes shiny things! Baphomutt sees Mistress look at shiny things!”

  But I also liked *not being executed for theft*.

“Baphomutt,” I said, keeping my voice gentle, “I *do* like shiny things. But I like them when they’re *mine*. Not when they’re stolen.”

His confusion deepened. “Stolen?”

“Taken. Without permission.”

“But Baphomutt has permission!” He puffed out his chest, his wings flaring. “Mistress is Baphomutt’s master! Baphomutt serves Mistress!”

 “Yes, Baphomutt. You serve me. But that doesn’t mean you can take things that don’t belong to me. It’s…” I searched for a word he would understand. “It’s rude.”

“Rude?” He tilted his head, his ears twitching.

“It makes people angry. It makes them think bad things about me.”

His eyes widened, and for a moment, I thought I’d gotten through to him. Then his face split into another grin. “Baphomutt will get *better* things! More shiny things! Make people not angry!”

Before I could stop him, he vanished in a puff of sulfur-scented smoke, leaving behind only the faintest shimmer in the air, like heat rising from sunbaked stone.

I buried my face in my hands.

This was not how I had planned to start my morning.

---

The jewels were a problem. A *big* problem. If I left them here, someone would find them. If I tried to hide them, someone would *still* find them. And if I tried to return them, Baphomutt would just steal them again, and then we’d be right back where we started.

I needed a solution. A permanent one.

 The surface was cluttered with books—some mine, some borrowed from the library, some *procured* through less savory means. I moved a stack of parchment aside, revealing the hidden compartment in the desk’s side.  Inside, the space was already half-full with trinkets: a silver locket I’d taken from a maid’s apron, a handful of coins from the royal treasury (borrowed, not stolen, I told myself), a small obsidian shard that hummed faintly with residual magic.

 The sapphire necklace went in first, its cool metal a stark contrast to the warmth of the wood. Then the ruby ring, its red depths dark and secretive. Finally, the diamond brooch, its facets catching the light even in the dimness of the compartment. I closed the panel, pressing until I heard the faint click of the mechanism locking into place.

There. Hidden. For now.

Almost.

I dressed quickly, choosing a simple gown of pale blue, the fabric soft against my skin. I braided my hair, my fingers moving automatically through the familiar motions. The routine was comforting, a small island of normalcy in the sea of chaos Baphomutt had unleashed.

But as I tied the ribbon at the end of my braid, I caught sight of my reflection in the mirror. My face was calm, serene. The picture of innocence. 

And that was the problem.

---

I had just finished breakfast—porridge with honey and a slice of buttered bread—when the knock came. I knew who it was before the door even opened. The knock was too soft, too precise. Only one person in this castle knocked like that.

“Come in, Mother,” I said, setting my spoon down.

The door opened, and Queen Seraphina stepped inside. She was dressed in a gown of deep emerald, the color complementing the gold of her hair, which was pulled back in an elegant twist. 

“Good morning, Lily,” she said, her voice warm but measured. “May I come in?”

I nodded, forcing a smile. “Of course.”

She crossed the room, her skirts whispering against the floor, and sat in the chair beside my desk. Her gaze flicked to the bed, then to the desk, then back to me. I kept my face carefully neutral, my hands folded in my lap.

“Did you sleep well?” she asked.

“Yes, Mother. Very well.”

She nodded, but her eyes lingered on me for a moment too long.  Seraphina was not a woman who missed much. And that made her dangerous.

“I’m glad to hear it,” she said at last. “I wanted to ask you something, Lily. Have you seen my sapphire necklace? The one with the silver chain?”

My heart stuttered in my chest. I kept my expression calm, my voice light. “No, Mother. I haven’t seen it.”

She studied me for another long moment, her gaze steady. “It was in my jewelry box this morning. But when I went to wear it, it was gone.”

I widened my eyes, feigning surprise. “Gone? That’s strange. Maybe one of the maids took it?”

Seraphina’s lips thinned slightly. “Perhaps. But the tiara from the Beastfolk envoy is also missing. The one with the emeralds.”

I forced a smile, my mind racing. “Maybe it’s a coincidence? Maybe they were misplaced?”

Seraphina didn’t look convinced. “Perhaps. But I’ll have the staff search the castle. Just to be sure.”

I nodded, my fingers tightening in my lap. “That sounds like a good idea.”

She stood, smoothing her skirts. “I’ll let you know if we find anything.”

“Thank you, Mother.”

She turned to leave, then paused at the door. “Lily?”

“Yes?”

“If you *do* see anything… unusual… you’ll tell me, won’t you?”

I met her gaze, my heart pounding. “Of course, Mother.”

She nodded, her expression softening. “Good. I’ll see you at lunch.”

The door closed behind her, and I exhaled slowly, my shoulders sagging. That had been too close. Far too close.

And Baphomutt wasn’t done yet.

---

I found him in the garden.

The royal gardens were a sprawling expanse of green, a carefully cultivated paradise of roses and lilies and manicured hedges. The air was thick with the scent of flowers, the hum of bees, the distant sound of water trickling from a fountain. It was beautiful. Peaceful.

And Baphomutt was ruining it.

The imp was crouched near the peacock enclosure, his claws digging into the dirt as he reached for one of the bird’s tail feathers. The peacock, a magnificent creature with a fan of iridescent blue and green, squawked indignantly and sidestepped, its feathers rustling. Baphomutt lunged again, his fingers just brushing the edge of a feather.

“Baphomutt,” I hissed, striding toward him. “What are you doing?”

He turned, his grin wide and unrepentant. “Mistress! Baphomutt found shiny things!” He held up the feather, its colors shimmering in the sunlight. “Pretty!”

I groaned, pinching the bridge of my nose. “Baphomutt, you can’t just take things. Especially not from the peacocks. They’re the King’s birds.”

“But Mistress likes shiny things!” he protested, his ears drooping. “Baphomutt wants to make Mistress happy!”

“I *do* like shiny things,” I said, my voice tight. “But I like them when they’re *mine*. Not when they’re stolen from peacocks or jewelry boxes or—” I cut myself off, taking a deep breath. “Baphomutt, you have to stop. You’re going to get us both in trouble.”

His eyes widened, his ears flattening against his head. “Trouble?”

“Yes. Trouble. If Mother finds out you’ve been stealing things, she’ll be angry. And if she finds out *I* knew about it, she’ll be even angrier.”

“But Mistress didn’t tell Baphomutt to steal things!”

“I know,” I said, my voice weary. “But that doesn’t matter. She’ll still think I had something to do with it.”

Baphomutt’s tail drooped, his wings sagging. “Baphomutt is sorry,” he said, his voice small. “Baphomutt didn’t mean to make trouble.”

I sighed, crouching down so I was at eye level with him. “I know you didn’t, Baphomutt. But you have to listen to me. No more stealing. No more shiny things. Not unless I tell you it’s okay.”

He nodded, his ears perking up. “Baphomutt will listen to Mistress! Baphomutt will be good!”

I reached out and patted his head, my fingers brushing against the coarse fur between his horns. “Good. Now, go. Before someone sees you.”

He vanished in another puff of smoke, leaving behind only the faintest shimmer in the air. I stood, brushing the dirt from my skirts, and turned back toward the castle.

I didn’t have the heart to tell him that it was already too late.

---

The jewels were back on my bed when I returned to my room.

I stood in the doorway, staring at them. The sapphire necklace, the ruby ring, the diamond brooch—they were arranged neatly, almost reverently, on the coverlet. And beside them, a small scrap of parchment, the edges singed as if it had been torn from a larger sheet.

I crossed the room and picked it up. The handwriting was messy, the letters uneven, but I recognized it immediately. Baphomutt’s scrawl.

*For Mistress. Baphomutt is sorry.*

  

I picked up the tiara, turning it over in my hands. The emeralds were deep, rich, their color like the heart of a forest. It was beautiful. And it didn’t belong to me.

I crossed to my desk and opened the hidden compartment. The other jewels were still there, their cold metal a stark contrast to the warmth of the wood. I added the tiara to the collection, arranging it carefully so it wouldn’t rattle. Then I closed the panel, pressing until I heard the faint click of the mechanism locking into place.

Baphomutt was a problem. A *big* problem. But he was *my* problem.

And for now, I’d have to live with him.

---

That night, as I lay in bed, I stared up at the canopy, my thoughts racing. The jewels were hidden. Baphomutt was… well, Baphomutt. And Seraphina was suspicious, but not enough to act. Not yet.

But it was only a matter of time.

I turned onto my side, pulling the blankets up to my chin. The locket Seraphina had given me was still tucked under my pillow, its weight a constant reminder of the war being waged within these walls. The war for the soul of the monster they loved.

I closed my eyes, listening to the distant sound of the castle settling for the night. The creak of floorboards, the murmur of voices, the faint rustle of the wind through the trees.

And somewhere, in the shadows, the faintest whisper of sulfur.

Baphomutt was still out there.

And he wasn’t done yet.

title: Charity as a Cover
prose:
# Chapter 14: Charity as a Cover

The knock came at precisely the wrong moment.

I was cataloguing Baphomutt's latest acquisitions—the sapphire necklace, the ruby ring, the diamond brooch, and now the emerald tiara—when the sound of knuckles against wood sent my heart into a rhythm I hadn't experienced since the Siege of the Obsidian Plains. 

I swept the jewels into the hidden compartment with a practiced motion, pressing the panel until I heard the click. 

The door opened before I could call out.

Seraphina stood in the threshold, the morning light spilling past her shoulders like a holy aura. Her expression was unreadable, which was the most dangerous expression she possessed. I had seen her face during treaty negotiations, during the Beastfolk envoy's incident with the ceremonial goat, during the time a visiting dignitary had insulted her cooking. This was the same face she wore when delivering bad news to servants who had failed her.

"Lily," she said. "We need to talk."

My stomach dropped through the floor. Baphomutt, who had been perched on the windowsill preening his wings, made a sound like a deflating bladder and vanished under the bed. The puff of smoke he left behind smelled faintly of sulfur and burnt feathers. I prayed Seraphina's sense of smell was still occupied with the morning roses.

"Good morning, Mother," I said, keeping my voice light. "I was just—"

"Those are quite pretty," Seraphina said, cutting me off.

I followed her gaze. The sapphire necklace lay on the carpet. In my haste, I had dropped one of Baphomutt's trophies. The chain glittered against the intricate weave, accusing me of crimes I had not personally committed but had certainly inspired.

I picked up the necklace. The metal was warm in my hand, the sapphires catching the light like tiny oceans.

"I found them, Mother," I said. "For the poor."

Seraphina's eyebrows rose. It was the first crack in her armor of calm, and I clung to it like a drowning demon clinging to driftwood.

"The poor," she repeated. Not a question. An invitation to elaborate, with the quiet threat of cross-examination to follow.

I nodded, letting my voice take on the wondering tone I had perfected during my years of pretending to discover things I already knew. "I heard the servants talking about the orphanage in the city. They said the children don't have enough food, let alone pretty things. So I... collected these. To sell. For them."

 The ruby ring sat beside a half-finished drawing of a spider. The diamond brooch sparkled next to a stack of storybooks. The emerald tiara rested in the open chest where I had been sorting them by value and provenance.

"I was going to tell you," I said, "but I wanted to make sure I had enough first."

Seraphina's expression shifted. The sharp edges softened, the suspicion in her eyes dimmed, and I watched the transformation with wary attention because I knew it wasn't truly over. 

"Mother, the children are so cold at night. I just wanted to help."

Her face crumpled in the way mothers' faces do when their children exceed expectations. She crossed the room and knelt before me, taking my hands in hers. The sapphire necklace dangled between us, a glittering testament to my supposed generosity.

"Oh, Lily," she said, her voice thick. "That's very thoughtful of you."

I allowed myself a small, shy smile. Inside, I was screaming.

"Your father will want to hear about this," Seraphina said, rising to her feet. "Alistair, darling, you can come in now. I know you've been listening at the door."

The King of Lumengarde, Hero of Dawn, Slayer of the Demon Lord, and the most tactically brilliant man of his generation, shuffled into the room with the sheepish expression of a child caught raiding the pantry. His holy sword was strapped to his back as always, gleaming faintly in the morning light.

"I wasn't listening," he said. "I was... patrolling. Securing the perimeter. Standard royal security protocol."

Seraphina gave him a look that could have flayed a dragon.

"Fine," Alistair admitted. "I was listening. What's this about jewels?"

I braced myself for the inevitable misinterpretation.

"Lily has been collecting jewelry to sell for the orphanage," Seraphina said, and the way she said it—as though I had personally woven the moon from silver thread—made me want to crawl into the walls. "She heard the servants talking about the children's suffering, and she decided to help. On her own. Without telling anyone."

Alistair's eyes went wide. Then they went shiny. Then the biggest, most dangerous man in the kingdom crossed the room in three strides, swept me into his arms, and spun me around like I was a sack of grain and he was celebrating a harvest.

"That's my girl!" he bellowed, and I felt my ribs creak under the force of his embrace. "Always thinking of others! That's it, that's the Lumengarde spirit! We'll feed every orphan in the city, by my sword and my daughter's generous heart!"

"I want a festival," Alistair declared, setting me down with a gentleness that belied his bulk. "A grand festival, in honor of my charitable daughter. We'll display the jewels, auction them off, raise a fortune for the orphanage. It'll be the event of the season!"

"Alistair," Seraphina said, a note of caution in her voice. "Don't you think that's a bit much? The children were very sweet, but—"

"Sweet? Seraphina, this is the most wonderful thing I've ever seen! A child who thinks of others before herself? In this day and age? It's unprecedented! It's inspiring! It's—"

"Dad," I said, my voice small and perfect. "I don't need a festival."

"Of course you don't need one," Alistair said, beaming. "That's what makes you so wonderful. But you're getting one anyway, because that's what I need. I need everyone to know how proud I am of my daughter."

I looked at Seraphina, hoping for support. She smiled at me with a gentle warmth that made my chest ache in ways I refused to examine.

"Your father has a point," she said. "Generosity should be celebrated. And if it inspires others to give, then all the better."

The court was informed by noon.

 The jewels were displayed on a velvet cushion before the throne, glittering under the chandeliers with a splendor that made my teeth ache. Every noble in Lumengarde had crowded into the hall, their eyes fixed on the small, fragile princess who had apparently discovered the concept of charity.

"—and when I found her, she was surrounded by beautiful jewels, her little hands trembling," Seraphina was telling the court, her voice carrying to every corner of the hall. "She looked up at me and said, 'Mother, these are for the poor children.' I wept, ladies and gentlemen. I wept."

I kept my smile fixed in place, my hands clasped before me in a perfect picture of maidenly modesty. Inside, I was composing a detailed plan to have the court herald who had announced me as a "prodigy of generosity" reassigned to sewage inspection duty.

"That's the most beautiful thing I've ever heard," Lady Castellan said, pressing a handkerchief to her eyes. "Your Highness, you are an inspiration to us all."

"Indeed," said Duke Aldermont, stroking his beard. "To think, a child of such tender years, sacrificing her own treasures for the less fortunate. It warms the heart."

 But Seraphina's hand on my shoulder stopped me. Her eyes were shining with pride, and I realized with a sinking feeling that anything I said would be filtered through the lens of her interpretation.

"I'm sure Lily would be happy to accept donations from anyone who wishes to contribute," Seraphina said. "She's been so moved by the support she's received."

A murmur of approval rippled through the crowd. Lord Everhart stepped forward, producing a pouch of gold coins with a flourish. "For the orphanage," he declared. "In honor of our generous princess."

"Wonderful!" Alistair boomed, clapping his hands together. "Anyone else?"

The courtiers surged forward like a tide of silk and jewels, each one eager to be seen contributing to the cause. Gold coins, silver tureens, embroidered shawls, ornate candlesticks—the pile of donations grew until the velvet cushion could no longer hold them. I watched the proceedings with a smile that was starting to hurt, my mind a whirlwind of calculations.

I was going to be sick.

No, I was going to be worse than sick. I was going to be *famous*. 

I stopped that thought before it could fully form. The cult could wait. Right now, I needed to survive the next hour without strangling a courtier with his own cravat.

"Princess Lily," a soft voice said, and I turned to find a young woman in Archmage robes kneeling before me. She had dark hair and earnest eyes, and she was looking at me with the same fervent adoration she always did.

"Eris," I said, keeping my voice pleasant. "What a pleasant surprise."

"I heard about your charity," Eris said, her voice trembling with emotion. "It's so inspiring. I brought these—" She produced a bundle of scrolls from her satchel. "—from the Spire. They contain a method for enhancing the efficiency of large-scale healing rituals. If we can implement them at the orphanage, we could treat the children's ailments more effectively."

I stared at the scrolls. They were, based on the official Archmage seals, quite valuable. And Eris had brought them as a donation.

"That's very generous of you, Eris," I said.

"Anything for you," she breathed, and I caught Seraphina's approving nod from the corner of my eye.

The afternoon devolved into a parade of similar encounters. Courtiers who had never spoken to me before approached with simpering compliments and token donations. Diplomats from other kingdoms praised my generosity to my face while mentally calculating how to leverage the story for political gain. The Beastfolk envoy presented a ceremonial dagger with a silver handle, claiming it was a traditional gift of friendship.

Through it all, I smiled and nodded and curtsied and thanked, my cheeks aching from the effort, my mind seething with resentment. By the time the last courtier had departed, I was exhausted in ways that had nothing to do with physical exertion.

I was a prisoner of my own lie.

Or, more accurately, of Baphomutt's thefts and my desperate improvisation.

The festival was announced at dinner that evening. Alistair, riding a wave of paternal pride, had outdone himself. There would be feasting and games and music. There would be a grand auction of the "recovered" jewels, with all proceeds going to the orphanage. There would be speeches and tributes and a parade, with Princess Lily as the guest of honor.

"I want her to see how much her kindness means to everyone," Alistair declared, raising his goblet to the assembled family. "I want her to know that her generosity has inspired the entire kingdom."

Seraphina smiled and nodded. Leo, who had somehow been invited to dinner, grinned at me with that infuriating mix of admiration and amusement.

"The little princess is going to be the star of the show!" he said, slapping the table hard enough to rattle the dishes. "Leo will be there! Leo will cheer the loudest!"

I returned my attention to my soup, which was excellent, and tried not to think about the fact that the only person who knew the truth about the jewels was currently hiding in my sock drawer, waiting for me to return.

I finally escaped to my room an hour later. The moment the door shut behind me, I let out a breath I hadn't realized I'd been holding. My legs gave out, and I slid down the doorframe until I was sitting on the carpet, staring at the ceiling.

"I am a prisoner of my own deception," I said aloud. The words hung in the air, heavy with irony.

Baphomutt's head emerged from under my bed, his bat-like ears twitching. "Mistress is clever!" he chirped. "Mistress tricked the evil Queen and the stupid King! They think Mistress is good!"

"Baphomutt," I said, my voice flat, "they think I'm a philanthropist. They're throwing a festival in my honor. I'll be the guest of honor at an event celebrating a lie I told to cover up your thefts."

The imp tilted his head, confused. "But Mistress is good! Mistress said the jewels are for the poor!"

"The jewels are for *me*, Baphomutt. Or they were, until you decided to return them to my bed as a guilt offering after stealing them in the first place."

"Baphomutt wanted to help!" he said, his voice taking on a wounded edge. "Baphomutt saw Mistress looking at the shiny things, so Baphomutt got them for Mistress! And when Mistress was sad, Baphomutt brought them back! Baphomutt is a good minion!"

I closed my eyes and counted to ten. Then I opened them, looked at the imp's hopeful face, and felt the familiar exhaustion settle over me like a lead blanket.

"Yes, Baphomutt. You're a very good minion. And now you're going to make sure absolutely no one sees you during the festival. Understood? No stealing, no appearing, no making things explode."

"Baphomutt understands!" He puffed out his chest, clearly proud of himself. "Baphomutt will be invisible! Baphomutt will be silent! Baphomutt will be like a shadow, like a whisper, like—"

"Like you're not there," I interrupted. "That's all I need."

He vanished with a pop, and I was left alone in the silence of my room, staring at the ceiling and contemplating the strange, cruel comedy of my existence. I was a demon lord—the most dangerous entity in the mortal realm—stuck in the body of a ten-year-old princess, being feted for a charitable act I had never intended to perform.

The irony was almost too much to bear.

I was no longer just "delicate" or "brilliant." I was now "charitable" as well. A new layer of expectation, a new false skin I'd have to wear. The court would watch me more closely, not to catch me slipping, but to see me shine. Every donation I made would be scrutinized. Every act of kindness I performed would be celebrated. I would have to maintain the facade of a generous, selfless child while quietly plotting the world's destruction.

Unless, of course, I embraced it.

The thought came unbidden, and I examined it with the same cautious attention I gave to potentially dangerous spells. My reputation as a philanthropist could be useful. It would open doors, soften suspicions, make Zephyr's paranoia look even more absurd. The cult would hear about my charity and see it as evidence of my true, saintly nature—or, conversely, as proof that I was the Demon Lord in hiding. Either way, they would be wrong, but their wrongness could be leveraged.

And the orphanage? The children genuinely needed help. I had seen them from the palace windows, thin and ragged, their faces pressed against the wrought-iron gates. The food that came from the kitchens each morning was barely enough to keep them alive. If my lie could fill their bellies and warm their beds, perhaps it wasn't such a terrible lie after all.

I hated it.

 And I hated, most of all, the warmth that spread through my chest when I remembered the way Seraphina's eyes had shone with pride.

The festival began the next morning.

The castle had been transformed overnight. Banners fluttered from every tower, ribbons twisted around every pillar, and the courtyard had been converted into a wonderland of stalls and tents and brightly colored awnings. The smell of roasting meat and fresh bread drifted through the air, mingling with the sweet scent of festival flowers. A stage had been erected at the center of the grounds, where the auction would take place.

 The dress was beautiful—Seraphina had personally overseen its creation—but it felt like armor, heavy and restrictive, binding me to the role I had chosen.

Alistair beamed at me from his seat at the high table. Seraphina sat beside him, her expression thoughtful but warm. The courtiers, dressed in their finest, had packed the festival grounds until there was barely room to breathe. At the front of the crowd, the orphans from the city stood in their newly provided clothing, their faces scrubbed and clean, their eyes wide with wonder.

I waved. The crowd cheered. I smiled. The crowd cheered louder.

The auction began with the sapphire necklace.

"To the generous citizens of Lumengarde," the auctioneer announced, holding up the chain so it caught the sunlight, "a gift from our beloved Princess Lily, who has inspired us all with her charity. Shall we start the bidding at one hundred gold pieces?"

The bids flew fast and furious. Lady Castellan offered two hundred. Duke Aldermont countered with three. A merchant I didn't recognize raised the price to five, and the crowd gasped. By the time the gavel fell, the sapphire necklace had sold for nine hundred gold pieces, and the crowd was on its feet, applauding the generosity of bidders and princess alike.

I kept my smile fixed, my posture perfect, my eyes bright. 

The ruby ring sold next. Then the diamond brooch. Each sale drew more applause, more donations, more envious whispers about the princess's good fortune. The orphans were brought forward to thank me, their small hands clutching my gown, their voices trembling as they called me "Princess Lily" and "heralds of hope" and other titles I had never wanted.

Salvation arrived in the form of an emergency.

"Your Majesties!" a messenger cried, bursting through the crowd on a lathered horse. "The Beastfolk envoy requests immediate audience! There is a problem with the North Bridge!"

Alistair's brow furrowed. Seraphina's eyes sharpened. The crowd murmured, and the auction came to a halt as the guards cleared a path for the messenger.

"Excuse me," Alistair said, rising from his seat. "Monarch business. Seraphina, take over."

"Of course," she said, rising with him. She paused, looking at me, and for a moment her expression softened into something I had seen only rarely. "You're doing wonderfully, Lily. I'm so proud of you."

I curtsied, my face burning. "Thank you, Mother."

She left, and I was alone on the dais, surrounded by a sea of faces that expected greatness. The auctioneer cleared his throat and held up the final piece—the emerald tiara.

"And now," he announced, his voice rising dramatically, "the piece de resistance! A tiara fit for a queen, generously donated by the most charitable heart in the kingdom!"

The crowd erupted in applause. I smiled, waved, and prepared to endure another hour of false adulation. But inside, I was thinking about the Beastfolk envoy's sudden arrival, and wondering—not for the first time—what fresh chaos was heading my way.

The last jewel was sold. The crowd was ecstatic. The king was beaming. The orphans were fed. And Princess Lily, the "prodigy of generosity," curtsied to the crowd with a smile that never wavered, even as a part of me screamed in silent fury.

I had turned disaster into triumph, but the cost was a new layer of expectations I could never fully escape. I was no longer just "delicate" or "brilliant." Now, I was "charitable." And that, more than anything, was the most dangerous thing any mortal had ever attached to my name.

And there was nothing I could tell them to stop.

I reached the edge of the dais, and a small hand caught my sleeve. I looked down to find a child—a girl of perhaps six, her face still bearing the marks of hunger, her eyes enormous in her thin face.

"Thank you, Princess," she whispered. "I never had a real bed before. Now I do."

 So I did what I had been doing all day.

I smiled.

"You're welcome, little one."

The girl beamed and rejoined the orphan chorus, led by their matron crying happy tears. 

Baphomutt, of course, chose that moment to appear in the shadows of the stage, his eyes gleaming with mischief.

"Mistress is happy?" he whispered.

"Go away," I hissed.

"Baphomutt wants to help!"

"Go. Away."

He vanished before I could grab him, but I caught the glint of something metallic in his claws—a spoon, perhaps, or a candle snuffer. The festival wasn't over, and neither were its disasters.

But that was a problem for later.

Right now, I had an image to maintain, and this time, I was determined to survive it.

title: Crowns and Chaos
prose:
# Chapter 15: Crowns and Chaos

The festival had reached that particular pitch of chaos where the music grew louder than the conversation, the conversation grew louder than the music, and somewhere in the middle of it all, a small girl with a demon's soul was expected to look delighted while a thousand eyes watched her every move.

I sat at the high table, which was really just a slightly elevated platform draped in gold cloth, and pushed a piece of roasted pheasant around my plate with the tip of my fork.  Too dainty and the court whispered about my "delicate appetite." Too enthusiastic and they cooed about how "the princess enjoys her food!" There was no winning, so I settled for pushing.

 

"Mistress is happy?"

The voice came from directly beside my ear, a hot whisper that smelled faintly of sulfur and stolen honey cakes. I did not flinch. I had learned, over the course of several months, that flinching only encouraged him.

Baphomutt perched on my shoulder, his tiny clawed feet digging into the velvet of my dress with the enthusiasm of a mountain climber scaling a peak. His leathery wings were folded tight against his back, and his eyes—two gleaming orbs of yellow fire—were fixed on me with the adoration of a particularly dim-witted puppy.

"Go away," I said, without moving my lips. 

Baphomutt tilted his head. "Baphomutt wants to help! Mistress looks... constipated? Baphomutt will fix!"

"Constipated," I repeated, my voice flat. "That is not—" I stopped myself. Arguing with the imp was like arguing with a wall, except the wall had better conversational skills. "I am not constipated. I am *enduring*."

"Enduring!" Baphomutt clapped his hands together, delighted. "Baphomutt knows enduring! When the Mistress endured the Archmage's visit, Baphomutt stole her quill! When the Mistress endured the Beast Prince, Baphomutt hid his boots! Baphomutt is an expert at enduring!"

I closed my eyes. Somewhere in the distant past, before I had been reborn into this gilded nightmare, I had commanded armies of demons. Legions of horrors had bowed before me. The very name Maledictus had been enough to make kings weep into their goblets.

And now I was being "helped" by a creature who thought hiding boots was a strategic maneuver.

"Baphomutt," I said, very carefully, "I do not need your help. I need you to disappear before anyone notices you. Do you understand?"

The imp's face fell. His ears, which were comically large for his tiny body, drooped. "Baphomutt only wants to help Mistress. Baphomutt is a good familiar. Baphomutt is loyal."

"You are many things," I said. "Loyal is not the word I would choose."

"Mistress is mean."

"Mistress is *practical*. Now go."

For a moment, I thought he would argue. His eyes flickered with something that might have been hurt, or might have been gas, given his diet. But then he nodded, a jerky motion that made his wings flutter, and said, "Baphomutt will find a way to help. Baphomutt will be clever!"

And then he vanished.

My stomach dropped.

 

The King had slept for sixteen hours and the court had praised his "restorative nap."

I had not slept for three days.

"Mistress Lily?"

I looked up to find one of the courtiers— "You look so thoughtful! Are you enjoying the festival?"

"Very much," I said, with the automatic sweetness of a child who had been trained to lie since birth. "The music is lovely."

"Isn't it? The minstrels came all the way from the eastern provinces. They're said to be the finest in the realm."

I nodded, as if I cared, and returned my gaze to my plate. The pheasant had congealed into a sad lump of meat. The roasted vegetables had gone cold. The bread was probably still warm, but I had no appetite.

I was too busy trying to calculate the probability that Baphomutt would do something catastrophic in the next hour.

The odds were not in my favor.

---

The scream came at precisely the worst possible moment—which is to say, any moment that involves a scream is the worst possible moment, but this one was particularly ill-timed. I had just taken a sip of watered-down wine, the only beverage deemed appropriate for a ten-year-old princess, and I nearly choked on it as the sound tore through the festival's cheerful noise.

The scream was high-pitched, female, and coming from the direction of the King's table.

I turned, my heart already sinking into my stomach, and saw the chaos unfolding.

King Alistair was patting his head with both hands, his expression shifting from bewilderment to alarm to outright panic. His hair, which he had carefully groomed for the occasion, was a mess of golden strands, and his fingers were searching for something that was no longer there.

"It's gone!" he boomed, his voice carrying across the entire festival grounds. "The crown! It's gone!"

The crowd erupted.

Guards appeared from nowhere, their armor clanking as they rushed to secure the exits.  The minstrels stopped playing mid-note, leaving an awkward silence filled only by the sound of panicked murmuring.

Queen Seraphina's eyes found me across the chaos.

They were calm. Too calm. The kind of calm that preceded a storm or a very pointed conversation about the nature of my soul. She did not say anything, but her gaze was a question, and the question was: *What did you do?*

I had done nothing. For once, I had genuinely, absolutely, completely done nothing.

Which meant Baphomutt had done something.

The realization hit me with the force of a collapsing tower, and I began to scan the crowd for any sign of the imp. 

He wanted to be seen.

Baphomutt materialized directly in front of me, perched on the edge of the high table with the casual arrogance of a creature who had no idea that he was about to cause an international incident. In his claws, clutched with the pride of a cat presenting a dead mouse, was the royal crown.

It was a magnificent thing, all gold and jewels and the weight of centuries. It gleamed in the afternoon sunlight, and for a moment, the entire festival went silent.

"For Mistress!" Baphomutt crowed, his voice high and triumphant. He dropped the crown onto my plate, where it landed with a heavy clatter, sending the remnants of my pheasant flying.

The crowd gasped.

I stared at the crown. The crown stared back at me, its jewels winking in the light like a thousand tiny accusations.

Every eye in the festival was on me.

The silence stretched.

And then, because I had spent a decade learning to think on my feet, I laughed.

It was not a genuine laugh. It was the laugh of a child who has been caught doing something naughty and is trying to pretend it was all a joke. It was high, bright, and brittle, like glass about to shatter.

"Oh, Father!" I called out, my voice carrying across the festival with the practiced clarity of a performer. "You're playing a game!"

Alistair blinked. His hands stopped patting his head, and he stared at me with the confused expression of a man who has been told that the sky is green and is trying to decide whether to believe it.

"A game?" he repeated.

I picked up the crown, holding it aloft with both hands. It was heavy—much heavier than it looked—and I had to brace my arms to keep from dropping it. "A treasure hunt! You hid the crown, and I found it! It was a game!"

"A treasure hunt," Alistair said again, his voice slow and thoughtful.

"Of course!" I beamed at him, the smile stretching my face into a mask of pure innocence. "You wanted to see if I could find it! And I did! I found the crown, Father! I won!"

For a long moment, nothing happened.

Then Alistair's face split into a grin so wide it threatened to crack his jaw. He threw his head back and laughed, a booming sound that echoed across the festival grounds and seemed to shake the very air.

"Of course!" he roared, clapping his hands together. "My little miracle, always one step ahead! She found the crown! She found the treasure!"

The crowd, which had been frozen in shock, erupted into laughter and applause. The tension dissipated like fog in the morning sun, replaced by the cheerful chaos of a festival that had just been given a story to tell.

"She's so clever!" someone cried.

"A true strategist!" another added.

"The princess is a treasure hunter!"

I smiled and waved, holding the crown aloft like a trophy, and inside my skull, I was screaming.

---

The guard who helped me down from the dais was a large man with a kind face and hands the size of dinner plates. He set me on my feet with the gentleness of someone handling a porcelain doll, and I clutched the crown to my chest like a shield.

"Your Highness," he said, his voice low and respectful, "shall I return the crown to the King?"

"No," I said, too quickly. The guard blinked. I smiled, adjusting my grip on the crown. "I mean—it's part of the game. I need to hide it again. So Father can find it."

The guard's brow furrowed. "Hide it again?"

"It's a treasure hunt," I explained, as if speaking to a particularly slow child. "He hid it. I found it. Now I hide it, and he finds it. That's how the game works."

"Ah." The guard nodded, though his expression suggested he did not fully understand. "Of course, Your Highness. Where would you like to hide it?"

I had not thought that far ahead.

"The garden," I said. "The crystal garden."

The guard nodded again and began to escort me toward the gardens, his hand hovering near my shoulder in case I stumbled. I did not stumble. I walked with the measured grace of a child who had been trained to move like a doll, my feet finding the flagstones with practiced precision.

Behind me, I could hear the festival resuming its cheerful chaos. The minstrels had started playing again, and someone was laughing, and somewhere in the distance, Alistair was telling anyone who would listen about his brilliant daughter and her amazing treasure-hunting skills.

I wanted to die.

 My mana battery array—the carefully constructed lattice of crystals and ley lines designed to siphon power from the earth itself—had been reclassified as "art" by my father, who had installed a brass plaque reading "Lily's Pretty Rock Garden" and invited the entire court to admire it.

The crystals were still there, of course. They glittered in the afternoon light, their surfaces catching the sun and scattering it into rainbows. But the precise geometry of the array had been disrupted by the plaque, the gnomes, and the decorative gravel that someone had added without my permission.

It was useless as a power source.

It was perfect as a hiding place.

I glanced at the guard, who was standing at the garden's entrance with his hands clasped behind his back. "I need to be alone," I said, with the imperious tone of a child who knows she will not be questioned. "For the hiding."

The guard hesitated. "Your Highness, I'm not sure—"

"It's a secret," I said, widening my eyes. "If you watch, it won't be a secret anymore."

The guard looked at me for a long moment. I could see the conflict in his face—the desire to protect, the fear of disobeying, the confusion of a man who had been asked to participate in a game he did not understand.

Then he nodded. "I'll wait here, Your Highness. If you need anything, just call."

I smiled at him, the sweet smile of a grateful child, and slipped into the garden.

I found a spot near the back of the garden, beneath a bush that had been shaped into a topiary rabbit. The soil was soft and dark, and I dug with my bare hands, my fingers sinking into the earth with the desperate urgency of a creature burying a bone.

The crown was heavy. It was ornate. It was covered in jewels that could feed a kingdom for a year.

I shoved it into the hole and covered it with dirt, patting the soil down until the surface was smooth and unremarkable.

Then I stood, brushed the dirt from my hands, and took a deep breath.

"Guards!" I called, my voice high and clear. "Guards! I found it!"

---

The guards arrived with impressive speed, their armor clanking as they rushed into the garden. They found me standing beside the topiary rabbit, pointing at the freshly disturbed soil with the triumphant expression of a child who had just won a very important game.

"It's here!" I declared. "The crown! I hid it, and now you've found it!"

The lead guard—a woman with a scar across her cheek and eyes that had seen too much—looked at me, then at the ground, then back at me. "Your Highness, you said you hid it. We didn't find it. You did."

"But you're finding it now," I said, beaming. "That's how the game works. You find it, and Father is happy, and everyone claps."

The guard stared at me for a long moment. I could see her trying to make sense of the situation, trying to find a logical explanation for why the princess was standing in a garden with dirt on her hands and a smile on her face.

She gave up.

"Very well, Your Highness," she said, and knelt to dig up the crown.

The crowd had gathered at the garden's edge, drawn by my cries and the sound of running guards. They watched as the guard unearthed the crown, brushing dirt from its jewels with a reverence that bordered on absurd.

"The crown!" someone shouted. "She found it!"

"The princess found the crown!"

"Treasure hunter!"

The cheers erupted, and I let myself be swept up in them. I smiled, I waved, I curtsied to the crowd with the practiced grace of a child who had spent years learning to perform.

And then Alistair was there, sweeping me off my feet and spinning me around in a circle so wide that my skirts flew out around me like a bell.

"My little treasure hunter!" he roared, his voice thick with pride. "My brilliant, wonderful, clever little girl!"

I laughed. It was high and brittle, a sound like glass shattering, but he did not seem to notice. He spun me around again, and the crowd cheered louder, and somewhere in the distance, I heard Seraphina's voice, quiet and measured.

"Alistair, put her down. She's getting dizzy."

"Nonsense!" Alistair laughed, but he set me down anyway, his hands steadying me as I wobbled. "She's a strong one, my Lily! A true strategist! She found the crown, she hid it, she found it again—why, she could run the kingdom!"

The crowd laughed. I laughed with them, the sound hollow in my own ears.

"Thank you, Father," I said, my voice sweet and clear. "I'm glad I could help."

He beamed at me, and I felt the weight of his pride like a physical thing, pressing down on my shoulders.

I had turned disaster into triumph.

Again.

---

The festival continued long into the evening, but I did not stay to enjoy it. I slipped away during the fireworks, when everyone's eyes were turned toward the sky and no one was watching the small princess making her escape.

My legs were shaking by the time I reached my room. They had been shaking since the moment the crown had landed on my plate, and I had only managed to keep them steady through sheer force of will.
