I closed the door behind me and leaned against it, pressing my palms flat against the wood and breathing in the familiar scent of my room—incense, old paper, and the faint tang of sulfur that had become a permanent fixture of my life.

Baphomutt was curled up on my bed, snoring.

He was a small creature, no bigger than a cat, and in sleep he looked almost innocent. His wings were folded over his body like a cloak, and his claws twitched occasionally as he dreamed.

I stared at him.

And I thought about the fact that Baphomutt had done this. He had stolen the crown—the *royal crown*—because he had wanted to help me.

"Next time," I said, my voice flat and cold, "I'm feeding you to the dogs."

Baphomutt snored.

I considered, briefly, whether the threat would be more effective if I repeated it. But the imp could not hear me, and even if he could, he would probably interpret it as affection.

That was the problem with Baphomutt. He was too loyal to understand when he was being threatened.

I walked to my desk and sat down, pulling out a sheet of paper and a quill. I had work to do. The festival was over, but the consequences were just beginning. The crown's disappearance would be talked about for weeks, and I needed to make sure the story stayed in my favor.

I dipped the quill in ink and began to write.

The first line was a list of potential threats. The second was a list of potential allies. The third was a reminder to myself, in the margin, to check on the mana battery's integrity.

And the fourth, written in a hand so small it was barely legible, was a question I had been trying to ignore for months.

*Why do I keep saving them?*

I stared at the words for a long moment.

Then I crossed them out, and I wrote the only answer I was willing to accept.

*Because I need them alive to destroy them later.*

It was a lie, and I knew it.

But I wrote it anyway, because the truth was too terrifying to face.

On the bed, Baphomutt snored on, dreaming of stolen crowns and loyal service and a mistress who would never, ever appreciate him.

And somewhere in the garden, beneath the topiary rabbit, the royal crown sat buried in the earth, waiting for the next chapter of the story to begin.

title: Soul Talk Over Scones
prose:
# Chapter 16: Soul Talk Over Scones

The tea party is an exercise in exquisite torture, curated for an audience of one: me. The porcelain cup in my hand is too delicate, its rim a hair's breadth from chipping, and the rosehip infusion within tastes of wilted optimism. Around the table, the daughters of Lumengarde's noble houses are a chattering flock of pastel-colored birds, their voices a high-pitched counterpoint to the delicate clink of silver on bone china.  To my right, Eris of the Spire sits with her spine so straight it could be used as a surveyor's tool, her eyes fixed on me with an intensity that would be flattering if it weren't so profoundly unsettling. To my left is the empty chair reserved for my brother, Prince Leo, who has, to his eternal credit, found a more stimulating way to spend his afternoon than listening to Lady Genevieve recount the latest scandal involving her governess's cat.

*Fascinating,* I think, tracing the rim of my cup. *The collective intellectual output of this gathering could not power a single flickering candle. They speak of ribbons, of gossip, of which courtier's son has been seen smiling at which courtier's daughter. And they expect me to participate.* I take a sip of the tea, allowing the warmth to mask the contempt I'm sure is flickering in my eyes. My body, that treacherous vessel, performs its part perfectly: a slight, thoughtful tilt of the head, a softening of the lips into what is probably interpreted as a gentle, receptive smile. 

"Isn't it just *divine* weather we're having?" chirps Lady Genevieve, her blonde curls bobbing. "Perfect for a garden stroll later."

"The roses in the Queen's garden are blooming spectacularly this year," adds Lady Seraphine, her voice a conspiratorial whisper. "My mother says it's the new compost they're using. From the royal stables."

*Ah, yes. The profound discourse.*  Eris, beside me, nods vigorously, as if I've just uttered a theorem of staggering complexity.  She is here because her mother, the Archmage Mira, insists she "broaden her social horizons," which is the Spire's polite way of saying "endure the company of people who think mana crystals are pretty rocks." Eris, for her part, treats every moment in my presence as a holy pilgrimage. It would be endearing if it weren't so convenient.

My gaze drifts to the window, where the late afternoon sun paints the gardens in shades of gold and amber. I can just see the corner of my "crystal garden," the spot where I once attempted to build a mana-siphoning array. It now sits beneath a gaudy brass plaque, labeled "Lily's Pretty Rock Garden: A Study in Natural Geometry." The ley lines beneath it hum with a power I can feel from here, a tantalizing whisper of what I could achieve if my body were not a leaky, mana-starved sieve. Instead, the array serves only to make the roses grow particularly red and to occasionally cause the garden gnomes to twitch. A failure. A monument to my current limitations.

"Your Highness is so thoughtful," Eris murmurs, leaning closer. Her breath smells faintly of mint and ozone, the signature scent of someone who spends too much time around active thaumaturgical arrays. "Contemplating the beauty of nature."

I offer her a small, shy smile. *I am contemplating the precise amount of arsenic required to poison the entire court's tea supply without leaving a detectable trace. But yes, the roses are lovely.* "Thank you, Eris. I was just thinking how nice it is to have friends over."

The other girls preen at this, their giggles rising like bubbles in champagne. They have no idea. The thought is a familiar, cold comfort. To them, I am a fragile, brilliant princess, a novelty act of prodigious talent and delicate health.  They see a child who colors in the lines very neatly and once corrected a tutor on the aerodynamic fallacies of a common incantation. The misunderstanding is my greatest shield, and my most persistent prison.

The hour of social obligation draws to a close. The noble daughters gather their reticules and their gossip, curtsying deeply as they take their leave.  Eris, however, lingers. She shifts in her seat, her hands clasped tightly in her lap, her eyes darting to me with a desperate, questioning hope. She wants to be asked to stay. She wants a private audience, a moment of scholarly communion with the object of her idolatry.

*Excellent.* The plan, a delicate, branching thing I've been nurturing for weeks, clicks into its next phase. I wait until the last echo of the departing girls' chatter has faded, until the only sound is the ticking of the grand orrery clock in the corner and the distant clang of the training grounds. The sunlight through the window has shifted, casting long, slanted bars of gold across the polished table. I set my cup down with a soft *click*, a sound that seems unnaturally loud in the sudden quiet.

"Eris," I begin, my voice dropping to a whisper, taking on a tone of grave, scholarly confidence. I lean forward slightly, a conspirator inviting another into the fold. "There is a... theoretical exercise I have been contemplating. One that requires a mind I can trust. Completely."

Eris inhales sharply, her entire body tensing like a drawn bow. "Your Highness?"

I let the silence stretch for a moment, letting her anticipation build into a thing almost painful. I trace a finger along the cool porcelain of my teacup, a slow, deliberate motion. "I have been thinking," I say, my gaze fixed on the swirling dregs at the bottom of the cup, as if the pattern there holds arcane secrets, "about the principles of soul transference."

The name of the forbidden art hangs in the air between us, a tangible, dangerous thing. Eris's face pales, then flushes a deep, vibrant crimson. Her lips part, but no sound comes out. Her hands, still clasped, are trembling. I can see the conflict warring in her eyes: the academic thrill of discussing a concept so advanced it was banned after the Fall of the Demon Lord, warring with the instinctive terror of broaching such a taboo.

"Soul... transference?" she finally manages, her voice a reedy squeak. "The forbidden art? But it's... it is the most dangerous, most unstable branch of thaumaturgy ever documented! The Spire's archives say it was the tool of the Dark Lord himself, used to possess the body of the Hero during the final siege!"

*Possess? Such a crude term.* I keep my expression one of intense, academic curiosity, masking the flicker of irritation. *It was a synaptic overlay, a forced mapping of one consciousness onto the neural architecture of another. A brilliant, if ethically questionable, application of resonance theory.* But I cannot say that. Instead, I nod, my face a mask of grave consideration. "It is. That is precisely why it is so fascinating. The theory behind it... the way a soul, a consciousness, could be... unraveled and rewoven into a new vessel. The implications for the understanding of the self, of identity, are profound."

I lift my gaze to meet hers, letting her see the depth of my "scholarly passion." "Imagine, Eris. To study it. Not to *use* it, of course. Never that. But to understand it. To map the theoretical framework. To know, in the abstract, how such a thing could even be possible." I let a breath out, a soft, wistful sigh. "It would be the discovery of a lifetime. It would change the way we understand magic itself."

Eris is leaning forward now, her earlier fear subsumed by a burgeoning, fervent excitement. The scholar in her is waking up, drawn by the siren call of forbidden knowledge. "The grimoires are locked away," she whispers, but the protest is half-hearted, already crumbling. "The only complete texts are in the Deep Archives of the Spire, sealed by Archmage Mira's own hand. And the Black Tome... the Black Tome of Maledictus is said to contain his own notes on the subject, but it is... volatile."

A faint, secretive smile touches my lips. "I have access to some materials," I say, keeping my tone light, as if discussing a borrowed book of fairy tales. "Fragments. Notes. But the theory is... complex. It requires a second mind to help structure the arguments, to catch the errors in my own reasoning. Someone with a rigorous academic background. Someone I could trust not to misinterpret the... theoretical nature of the exercise."

I turn the full force of my attention on her. It is not an easy thing, to channel a Demon Lord's focus through a child's eyes. It is like aiming a siege weapon through a keyhole. But I have had practice. "I need help, Eris. And you are the only one I can ask."

The effect is instantaneous and gratifying. Eris's spine straightens further, if such a thing were possible. Her blush deepens, but this time it is with pride, with a swelling sense of purpose. Her eyes, bright with unshed tears of devotion, lock onto mine. "You... you would trust me? With this?" she breathes. "With such knowledge?"

"Who else could I?" I ask, letting a note of weary loneliness seep into my voice. "The tutors are bound by their oaths to the Spire. My father... he would worry. My mother would ask questions I am not ready to answer. But you, Eris... you understand. You understand what it means to seek knowledge, even when others fear it."

It is a masterstroke of manipulation, and I feel a cold, familiar thrill of satisfaction as it lands. I have played to her deepest insecurity: the fear that she is not special enough, that her hard work in the Spire's shadow is meaningless. I have made her feel chosen. I have made her feel like an equal.

"I would do anything for you, Your Highness," she declares, her voice ringing with a fervor that borders on the religious. "For this... for the chance to learn with you... I would face any danger. I would brave the Seven Hells themselves."

*The Seven Hells are merely a colloquialism for the Abyssal Halls of the lower planes, and you would last approximately three minutes there before being devoured by a particularly bored minor imp,* I think, but I smile at her, a soft, grateful expression. "I know," I say. "That is why I am asking you."

 Instead, I offer her fragments, carefully selected pieces of the puzzle, framed as my own speculative musings.

"Consider the theoretical model of the soul as a resonant frequency," I say, my voice low and intense, leaning over the table as if sharing a secret. "And the body as an instrument. To transference, one would not need to *destroy* the instrument, but to *retune* it, using a sympathetic vibration to coax the soul's frequency into a new harmonic alignment with a different body's structure."

Eris's quill scratches furiously across a sheet of parchment she has produced from somewhere. Her eyes are wide, glazed with a mix of terror and ecstasy. "A sympathetic resonance cascade..." she murmurs, more to herself than to me. "The mana requirements would be astronomical. And the stability equations... they would have to account for the soul's inherent resistance to displacement..."

"Precisely," I say, nodding. "Which is why the Demon Lord's original work focused not on brute force, but on creating a state of *quantum entanglement* between the source and target souls before the transfer. To make them resonate together, briefly, as one."

I offer another piece: the concept of a "soul anchor," a fixed point of identity that could be used to pull the consciousness back to its original vessel if the transfer failed. I watch as Eris connects it to her own limited knowledge of binding spells, her mind working furiously to integrate the new, terrifyingly advanced concepts.

"This is... this is revolutionary," she whispers, her hands shaking so badly the quill rattles against the table. Her notes are a frantic scrawl, filled with half-formed equations and diagrams that are both brilliantly insightful and spectacularly wrong. "If we could prove even a fraction of this, the Spire would have to revise centuries of doctrine! They would have to recognize you—*us*—as masters!"

I sip my tea, which has gone cold. My expression is serene, unreadable. "It is just theory, Eris. Nothing more. A game of 'What If' between two friends." I let the word 'friends' hang in the air, another carefully placed hook.

*The cult of fools who worship my former self will eventually hear of this, I calculate. They will not understand the theory, but they will grasp the shape of it. They will see it as a sign, a holy blueprint for my 'rebirth.' They will begin to experiment, clumsily, fatally. Their failures will be a useful distraction. Their successes, if any, will be a resource to be harvested.* The thought sends a chill of dark amusement through me. Eris is not just my researcher; she is the first domino in a chain reaction I intend to set off across the entire kingdom. A reaction centered on the very concept of soul transference, the forbidden art that is, in fact, the secret of my own existence.

As the afternoon light begins to fade, turning from gold to a soft, bruised purple, I finally declare the session at an end. Eris looks drained, exhilarated, and utterly, hopelessly devoted. She gathers her notes, tucking them carefully into her satchel with the reverence of a priest handling holy relics.

"I will begin my research immediately," she vows, standing and giving me a deep, formal bow that is entirely too solemn for a tea party. "I will search the Spire's catalogues for every reference to sympathetic resonance, to quantum entanglement, to any theoretical model that might support your... our hypothesis."

"Be careful, Eris," I say, my voice soft with feigned concern. "Some knowledge is dangerous. Not because it is evil, but because it is powerful, and power in the wrong hands... or the wrong mind... can be catastrophic." The warning is genuine, layered beneath the performance. *Do not, for example, attempt to actually cast any of these theories with your meager mana reserves. The backlash will turn your brain to soup.*

Eris's expression is one of rapturous determination. "For you, Your Highness," she says, her voice thick with emotion, "I would face any danger. I would walk into fire."

I watch her go, her steps light, almost skipping, as she disappears down the corridor. The door clicks shut behind her. The room is silent, save for the ticking clock and the faint, distant sound of the training grounds, where Leo is probably still grunting and hitting things.

A cold, clean satisfaction settles in my chest, sharp and pure as a shard of ice. The tool has been sharpened. The seed has been planted. Eris will dig, and she will find what I have pointed her toward. She will bring it back to me, wrapped in the guise of scholarly devotion. She will become my eyes and hands in the forbidden archives of the Spire. And when the Cult of the Eternal Flame hears whispers of the princess and her "theoretical game" with soul transference, they will see not a manipulative child and her pawn, but a sign from their dark god. They will see a path to his resurrection. They will be so busy trying to build a ritual to bring him back that they will never realize he is already here, sipping cold tea in a sunlit room.

I stand, smoothing the front of my dress. My reflection catches in the windowpane, a pale, small figure against the darkening garden. For a moment, I see not Princess Lily, but a shadow of the Demon Lord Maledictus, ancient and calculating. The reflection flickers, and it is just a child again. A child who has just manipulated a loyal friend into becoming an unwitting agent of a long-forgotten darkness.

*Excellent work,* I tell myself. *Now, to review Eris's mental notes and predict the three most likely lines of inquiry she will pursue. And then, to determine how best to steer her research toward the grimoires I actually need.*

I turn from the window, my mind already racing, plotting the next phase. The tea party is over. The real work is just beginning. And somewhere, in the stables, I can hear my brother's booming laugh, a sound that promises further irritation in the very near future. I have a feeling our next encounter will require more direct, less subtle forms of manipulation.

title: Saddles, Swords, and Strategic Defeat
prose:
# Chapter 17: Saddles, Swords, and Strategic Defeat

The stables of Lumengarde were a symphony of chaos, and I was the only one who appreciated its dissonance.

Hay dust hung in golden motes, catching the late-morning light that slanted through the rafters. Grooms dashed between stalls, their arms laden with tack and buckets of feed. A stableboy with straw in his hair was trying to coax a stubborn gelding into its halter while a farrier hammered at a shoe in the corner, the rhythmic clang of iron on iron punctuating the general cacophony.

I stood at the entrance, surveying the scene with the same grim resignation I might have once reserved for a battlefield. The stables were a necessary evil—a place where beasts were housed and fed and prepared for the various indignities of royal life. In my previous existence, I had commanded legions of nightmare mounts bred in the Abyssal Halls, creatures with eyes like burning coals and hooves that left scorch marks on the obsidian plains of their homeland. They had been magnificent. Terrifying. Utterly loyal.

The pony before me now was none of those things.

His name was Buttercup, and he was the color of a particularly uninspired sunset. His mane was a shade of cream that suggested he had never once contemplated the taste of mortal fear. He was currently attempting to eat the hem of my riding dress, his large brown eyes blinking with the serene stupidity of a creature that had never once contemplated anything at all.

"You're mocking me," I said quietly, pushing his muzzle away from the fabric. "You're a horse. You shouldn't be capable of mockery. And yet."

Buttercup snorted, which I chose to interpret as an admission of guilt.

"Your Highness!"

I turned to find the Stablemaster approaching, a barrel-chested man named Harold whose face was a permanent shade of weather-beaten red. He bowed with the particular awkwardness of someone who spent more time with animals than people, his movements stiff and overly formal.

"We didn't expect you this morning, Your Highness. The Beastfolk Prince said something about a demonstration, but—"

"He did, did he?"

Harold nodded, mopping his brow with a handkerchief that had seen better days. "Yes, Your Highness. Prince Leo arrived about an hour ago with his warhorse. Said something about teaching you 'the fine art of mounted combat.'"

The fine art of mounted combat. I could already hear Leo's voice booming across the training grounds, full of that infuriating enthusiasm that seemed to be his only emotional setting. The Beastfolk prince had been a thorn in my side since his arrival, misinterpreting every assassination attempt, every subtle sabotage, every carefully crafted scheme as evidence of some imagined romantic rivalry between us.

Today, I intended to put an end to that misinterpretation once and for all.

"Where is Prince Leo now?" I asked, keeping my voice light and curious.

Harold gestured toward the far end of the stables, where a massive black stallion was being saddled by a team of grooms. The horse was a monster of sinew and muscle, its coat gleaming like polished obsidian. It stamped its hooves with a restless energy that spoke of barely contained violence, and its eyes rolled white with suspicion.

And there, standing beside it, was Leo.

He was dressed in riding leathers that did nothing to diminish his imposing frame, his golden fur catching the light in a way that made him look almost regal. His mane—the beastfolk inheritance from his father's line—was braided back from his face, and his grin was wide enough to show teeth.

"Lily!" he called, his voice carrying across the stable yard with the force of a war horn. "There you are! I was beginning to think you'd lost your nerve."

I schooled my features into a mask of polite interest and walked toward him, careful to maintain the measured, unhurried pace expected of a delicate princess. The dress I wore was a practical riding habit in deep burgundy, chosen specifically because its long skirt would make mounting a horse look appropriately challenging for someone of my "fragile constitution."

"I don't lose nerve," I said, stopping a few feet away and looking up at him. The height difference was galling. "I simply choose my battles carefully."

Leo laughed, a sound like rocks tumbling down a mountainside. "That's what I love about you, Lily. Always so serious. Always so—" He paused, searching for the word. "—intense."

I did not love anything about Leo. I was fairly certain I was incapable of loving anything about anyone, least of all a Beastfolk prince who seemed determined to interpret every interaction between us as a step in some elaborate courtship dance.

But I smiled anyway, because that was what Princess Lily did.

"Shall we begin?" I asked, gesturing toward the horses.

Leo's grin widened. "You ride, Lily? Or do you prefer to watch from the sidelines?"

The condescension was so casual, so reflexive, that it almost felt like a physical blow. I had commanded armies that had made the Seven Heroes tremble. I had brought kingdoms to their knees with a whispered word and a gesture. And this—this furred, overgrown puppy of a prince was asking me if I knew how to ride.

"I ride," I said flatly.

Leo glanced at Buttercup, who was now attempting to eat a strand of hay that had become attached to his own forelock. The pony's expression was one of profound confusion, as if the universe had presented him with a puzzle he was not equipped to solve.

"That's not a horse," Leo said, his voice thick with barely suppressed laughter. "That's a snack."

My fingers twitched.

The urge to reach for a spell—any spell—was overwhelming. A simple hex would do. Something to make his saddle grow warm, perhaps, or to turn his stirrups briefly into snakes. The formulae were already forming in my mind, elegant and precise, waiting for the mana that would bring them to life.

But my mana reserves were a pittance, and my body was a prison. Even the simplest spell risked backlash that would leave me incapacitated for hours. And Leo, with his beastfolk constitution and his infuriating immunity to my magic, would barely notice.

No. Magic was not the answer.

But sabotage?

Sabotage required no mana at all.

"I've grown rather fond of Buttercup," I said, patting the pony's neck. He responded by trying to bite my sleeve, which I deflected with practiced ease. "He may not be imposing, but he has a certain... charm."

Leo snorted. "If you say so. But a warhorse like Stormbreaker here—" He gestured to the black stallion, who bared his teeth in what I assumed was a display of aggression. "—that's a real mount. Something that'll carry you through battle and not flinch at the sight of blood."

"Stormbreaker?" I repeated, letting a note of amusement creep into my voice. "You named your horse Stormbreaker?"

"I did. It's a good name. Strong. Fierce."

"It sounds like a children's toy."

Leo's eyes narrowed, but there was a spark of delight there too. "Is that a challenge, Princess? Are you trying to goad me into proving my horse's worth?"

"Of course not," I said, widening my eyes in what I hoped read as innocent confusion. "I would never dream of such a thing."

The lie was delivered with perfect sincerity, and Leo bought it completely. He always did. That was the problem with Leo—he was so eager to see the best in everyone, so determined to interpret every interaction as a positive sign, that he was utterly blind to the machinations unfolding beneath the surface.

It was a weakness I intended to exploit thoroughly.

"I've arranged a demonstration course," Leo said, gesturing toward the training grounds visible beyond the stable yard. "Nothing too complex—a few jumps, some weaving poles, a straight stretch for speed. I thought we could make a race of it."

"A race?"

"Unless you're afraid of a little competition."

The taunt was delivered with such obvious good humor that I couldn't take offense, which was itself offensive. I was the Demon Lord Maledictus, reborn into a child's body, and I was being goaded by a young man who thought of me as a particularly challenging puzzle.

I smiled, letting my teeth show just a little. "I'm not afraid of anything, Prince Leo."

"Then let's see what you've got."

He turned to mount Stormbreaker, and I watched him go with a calculating eye. The saddle he'd brought was an elaborate affair—tooled leather, silver buckles, all the trappings of beastfolk craftsmanship. The girth strap ran beneath the stallion's belly, securing the saddle in place.

If I were to loosen that strap, just enough that it would slip mid-race...

The plan formed in my mind with the satisfying click of a well-oiled mechanism. It was simple. Elegant. The kind of sabotage that would unseat him at the most dramatic possible moment, leaving him sprawled in the dirt while I trotted past on Buttercup.

It wouldn't hurt him—I had no desire to actually injure the idiot prince. But the humiliation would be exquisite.

"Excuse me," I said, turning to Harold. "I need to visit the tack room before we begin. I should check Buttercup's saddle."

Harold nodded, gesturing toward a small door at the far end of the stable block. "Of course, Your Highness. I'll have one of the grooms bring your pony's tack to you."

"That won't be necessary," I said, already moving toward the door. "I'm quite capable of fetching it myself."

I slipped into the tack room, letting the door close behind me. The space was cramped and dim, filled with the smell of leather and saddle soap. Saddles hung from wooden racks along the walls, their stirrups gleaming in the thin light that filtered through a small window. Bridles and halters were coiled on shelves, and a barrel of oats sat in the corner, half-covered by a burlap sack.

Leo's saddle was easy to identify—it was the largest one in the room, its stitching slightly rougher than the fine Lumengarde workmanship, its buckles worn from use. I ran my fingers along the girth strap, testing the leather.

It was sturdy. Well-made. The kind of craftsmanship that would last for decades if properly maintained.

I would need to be careful.

The buckle was simple enough—a standard cinch that secured the saddle beneath the horse's belly. I loosened it slightly, just enough that a sharp turn or sudden movement would cause it to slip. Not enough to be obvious to a casual observer, but enough to be catastrophic at the wrong moment.

*There,* I thought, surveying my handiwork with satisfaction. *Let's see how well you ride when your saddle decides to betray you.*

I returned to the stable yard to find Leo already mounted on Stormbreaker, the stallion dancing beneath him with barely contained energy. The Beastfolk prince looked utterly at ease, his muscles rippling as he adjusted his grip on the reins.

"Ready?" he called, his voice bright with anticipation.

I nodded, allowing Harold to help me onto Buttercup's back. The pony was placid and unresponsive, requiring minimal guidance to follow where I directed him. He was, in short, the perfect mount for someone who wanted to appear helpless while actually being in complete control.

"Then let's begin!"

The course was laid out across the training grounds: a series of jumps formed from wooden rails, a weaving section marked by poles, and a long straight stretch that would give the horses room to run. Courtiers had gathered at the edges, drawn by the promise of entertainment. I spotted several familiar faces among the crowd—Lady Margrave with her ever-present fan, Sir Aldric the tournament champion, a cluster of young noblewomen who were already whispering behind their hands.

They were expecting a spectacle.

I intended to give them one.

We took our positions at the starting line, Leo's stallion straining against its bit while Buttercup stood placidly, occasionally attempting to eat the grass beneath his feet.

"On my signal," Leo said, raising his hand. "Three... two... one—"

He was off before the word "go" had fully left his lips, Stormbreaker surging forward with a powerful gallop that sent clods of dirt flying. I urged Buttercup forward at a more sedate pace, letting Leo take the lead.

Let him have his moment of glory. It would make the fall that much sweeter.

The first jump came quickly—a low rail set at the edge of the course. Stormbreaker cleared it with room to spare, his stride never breaking. Buttercup approached at a more cautious pace, and I had to give him a gentle nudge with my heels to encourage him over.

The weaving poles came next, and Leo navigated them with practiced ease, his body moving in perfect harmony with his mount. I followed more slowly, letting the distance between us grow.

This was all part of the plan. Let him think he was winning. Let him grow confident. When the saddle slipped, the impact would be all the more dramatic.

We rounded the final turn onto the straight stretch, and Leo urged Stormbreaker into a full gallop. The stallion's hooves thundered against the packed earth, his mane streaming in the wind. Leo was laughing, his head thrown back, glorying in the speed.

I watched the saddle.

It slipped.

The movement was subtle at first—a slight shift to one side, a wobble that Leo might have dismissed as a normal adjustment. But then the girth strap gave way entirely, and the saddle tilted at an alarming angle.

Leo's laughter cut off abruptly. He grabbed for the pommel, but it was already out of reach, sliding away from him as the saddle continued its inexorable descent. For a moment, he hung suspended, his body contorted in a position that would have been comical if it hadn't been so dangerous.

Then he fell.

The impact was soft—he landed in a patch of grass at the edge of the course, rolling with the momentum of his fall and coming up in a crouch. Dirt flecked his golden fur, and his expression was one of utter bewilderment.

"What—" he started, looking from the fallen saddle to me. "How did you—"

I trotted past him on Buttercup, maintaining a serene expression that I hoped conveyed the appropriate level of concern. "Oh dear," I said, pitching my voice to carry to the watching courtiers. "Are you all right, Prince Leo? That looked like quite a fall."

Leo blinked at me. Then, slowly, a grin spread across his face.

"Nice try, Lily!" he called, scrambling to his feet. "But I'm not that easy to unseat!"

The court erupted into cheers.

I felt my eye twitch.

He was supposed to be humiliated. He was supposed to be lying in the dirt, embarrassed and defeated, while I sailed past to victory. Instead, he was laughing, dusting himself off, looking at me with an expression of delighted approval that made my stomach churn.

"Unseated!" he declared, striding toward me. "You sabotaged my saddle! That's brilliant!"

"I have no idea what you're talking about," I said, keeping my voice flat. "Your saddle appears to have been improperly secured. Perhaps your grooms were negligent."

Leo laughed, a full-throated sound that drew more attention from the crowd. "You're a fierce rival, Lily! I knew you had it in you!"

The words hit me like a physical blow. *Fierce rival.* He had turned my sabotage into a compliment, my scheming into a game. Nothing I did seemed to penetrate the armor of his good nature; every attack was deflected and returned as affection.

I wanted to scream.

Instead, I smiled, letting my teeth show just a little. "Perhaps we should call it a draw, given the... circumstances."

"A draw?" Leo's grin widened. "Never! I was winning, and we both know it. But I'll give you credit for creativity." He stepped closer, close enough that I could smell the leather of his riding clothes and the faint, musky scent of his fur. "Next time, I'll let you win. As a favor."

The offer was so insulting, so condescending, that I nearly lost my composure entirely.

"There won't be a next time," I said, each word clipped and precise.

Leo's grin didn't waver. "Of course there will. You love the challenge." He leaned in, his voice dropping to a low murmur that was somehow intimate and infuriating in equal measure. "And so do I."

I felt my cheeks flush.

It was a physiological response, nothing more—the involuntary reaction of a body that refused to obey my will. But the courtiers saw it, and their interpretation was immediate.

"Oh, the young love!" a noblewoman sighed, pressing a hand to her heart.

I wanted to scream.

*They think I'm blushing because I'm smitten,* I realized, the horror of the situation crashing over me like a wave. *They think I'm embarrassed because I've been caught in a moment of romantic tension. They think—*

"Your Highness?" Harold's voice broke through my spiraling thoughts. "Shall I have the grooms prepare fresh mounts for a second race?"

"No," I said, the word emerging more sharply than I'd intended. "I believe we're done here."

Leo bowed, a theatrical gesture that somehow managed to be both mocking and sincere. "Until next time, Princess."

"Don't hold your breath."

"I never do."

I turned and walked away, leaving Buttercup in the care of a startled groom. The crowd parted around me, their whispers trailing in my wake like the hiss of a serpent.

*This is not over,* I told myself. *I will find a way to defeat him. I will—*

But even as I thought it, I knew it wasn't true. Leo was immune to my schemes, resistant to my magic, and utterly convinced that our interactions were part of some grand romantic courtship. No matter what I did, he would interpret it as affection.

It was a problem I could not solve with sabotage.

A problem I could not solve with magic.

A problem I could not solve at all.

---

I slammed the door to my chambers so hard that the paintings on the walls rattled.

The room was silent, save for the ticking of the clock on the mantelpiece and the soft rustle of curtains in the breeze from the open window. I crossed to my bed and flopped onto it, staring up at the canopy with a sense of defeat that was entirely foreign to me.

I was Maledictus, the Demon Lord, the scourge of the Seven Kingdoms, the architect of a thousand dark schemes. I had faced the Seven Heroes in battle. I had commanded legions of demons. I had bent the very fabric of reality to my will.

And I had been defeated by a furry prince with a winning smile and an unshakeable belief in my inherent goodness.

"It's not fair," I muttered, the words emerging unbidden from my lips.

*Fair.* What a foolish concept. The universe had never been fair, and I had never expected it to be. I had clawed my way to power through intellect and ruthlessness, through a willingness to do what others would not. I had earned my position through blood and sacrifice and an unyielding determination to succeed.

And now, I was a ten-year-old princess, trapped in a body that could barely channel enough mana to light a candle, surrounded by people who saw only what they wanted to see.

A rustling sound came from beneath my bed.

I sat up, my hand instinctively reaching for the concealed dagger I kept in my sleeve. But the sound was followed by a familiar chittering, and a moment later, Baphomutt emerged from the shadows, his leathery wings folded against his back and a riding crop clutched in his claws.

"For Mistress!" he chirped, holding the crop aloft like a trophy.

I stared at him.

"Baphomutt," I said slowly, "where did you get that?"

The imp blinked, tilting his head in confusion. "Stable. Man with red face was using it. Baphomutt thought Mistress might need it."

"Harold's riding crop?"

"Baphomutt does not know names. Baphomutt sees Mistress looking at horses. Baphomutt brings Mistress gift."

I closed my eyes, counting to ten in my head. The imp's loyalty was absolute, but his intelligence left much to be desired. He had stolen a riding crop from the Stablemaster—a man who would certainly notice its absence and report the theft to the guards.

"Not now, Baphomutt," I said, waving a hand dismissively. "I'm not in the mood for your... contributions."

The imp's wings drooped. "Mistress is sad?"

"I'm not sad. I'm—" I paused, searching for the right word. "—frustrated."

"Baphomutt can help! Baphomutt can—"

"Baphomutt can go find somewhere else to be," I interrupted, my voice flat. "I need to think."

The imp's expression was one of profound hurt, but he nodded, tucking the riding crop under his arm and scurrying toward the window. He paused at the sill, looking back at me with eyes that were far too expressive for a creature of his nature.

"Mistress is smart," he said, his voice uncharacteristically soft. "Mistress will find way. Baphomutt believes in Mistress."

And then he was gone, a dark shape against the afternoon sky, disappearing into the shadows of the castle grounds.

I lay back on the bed, staring at the ceiling.

*Mistress is smart. Mistress will find way.*

The imp's faith was touching, in its way. But faith alone would not solve my problems. I needed a new strategy, a new approach that would break through Leo's infuriating optimism and force him to see me as the threat I truly was.

What did he value? What would shake his confidence, challenge his assumptions, make him question his interpretation of our interactions?

I thought about the way he had looked at me after the race—not with suspicion, but with admiration. He had seen my sabotage as evidence of my spirit, my determination, my worthiness as a rival. He had seen my schemes as proof of my affection.

There was no way to win against someone who refused to acknowledge the game.

Unless...

I sat up, a new thought taking shape in my mind.

*What if I stopped trying to defeat him?*

The idea was anathema to everything I was, everything I had ever been. I did not yield. I did not retreat. I did not accept defeat.

But perhaps there was another way. Perhaps, instead of fighting Leo's interpretation of our relationship, I could use it. Let him think I was warming to him. Let him believe his courtship was working. And then, when he was at his most vulnerable, his most trusting...

I smiled, a cold expression that had nothing to do with warmth.

*Yes,* I thought. *That could work.*

It would require patience. It would require pretending to be something I was not. But I had spent ten years perfecting the art of deception, and I was very, very good at it.

I rose from the bed, smoothing the wrinkles from my dress. The clock on the mantelpiece ticked steadily, marking the passage of time. Outside, the afternoon light was beginning to fade, casting long shadows across the room.

*Leo thinks he's winning,* I mused. *Let him. I'll let him believe he's making progress, that his charm is wearing me down. And when he least expects it, when he's convinced he's won my heart entirely—*

The thought was interrupted by a knock at the door.

"Your Highness?" It was one of the maids, her voice soft and deferential. "The Queen requests your presence in the solar for tea."

I took a deep breath, composing my features into an expression of innocent compliance.

"Of course," I said, my voice light and sweet. "Tell Mother I'll be there shortly."

The maid's footsteps retreated down the corridor. I stood for a moment, surveying the room, my eyes lingering on the window where Baphomutt had disappeared.

*Patience,* I reminded myself. *Strategy. Long-term thinking.*

I was not defeated. I was merely... regrouping.

But as I made my way toward the solar, a small part of me wondered if I was fooling myself. Leo had a way of deflecting every attack, of turning every scheme into evidence of my affection. What if I couldn't outmaneuver him? What if his optimism was a fortress I could never breach?

I pushed the thought aside. I was Maledictus, the Demon Lord. I had conquered nations, destroyed armies, bent the world to my will.

I would not be defeated by a furry prince with a winning smile.

No matter how infuriatingly charming he might be.

title: The Demon Lord’s Guide to Sugar, Spite, and Sippy Cups
prose:
# Chapter 18: The Demon Lord’s Guide to Sugar, Spite, and Sippy Cups

The solar was warm, the kind of warmth that seeped into bones and made eyelids heavy. I sat curled in a high-backed chair, a book of children’s tales spread open on my lap, my fingers tracing the illustrations of knights and dragons. The fire crackled in the hearth, casting long shadows across the polished wooden floor, and the scent of cinnamon and cloves drifted from the teapot on the low table beside me. Mother had insisted I take a break from my studies—her words, not mine—and so here I was, pretending to be a normal, book-loving child while my mind churned with far less wholesome thoughts.

 I had heard it at least three times before, but I pasted on a polite smile and nodded along, my eyes flicking occasionally to the door. Zephyr had not been seen since the morning, and that was never a good sign.

“And then, my sweet, the troll roared—*ROOOOAR*—and I said, ‘My good fellow, if you insist on charging a toll, at least have the decency to accept coin!’” Father slapped his knee, his laughter shaking the teacups. “He didn’t, of course. Trolls never do. But I taught him a lesson he wouldn’t soon forget!”

“How brave, Father,” I murmured, my voice sweet and soft. Inside, I was calculating the structural integrity of the ceiling above his head and whether a well-placed *Minor Collapse* spell could be disguised as an accident. The mana cost would be brutal, but the satisfaction might be worth the nosebleed.

Mother sat beside me, her needlework forgotten in her lap as she watched Father with an expression that was equal parts fondness and exasperation. “Alistair, dear, perhaps Lily would like to hear a different story. One that doesn’t involve trolls or bridges.”

Father blinked, as if the idea had never occurred to him. “A different story? But this one’s her favorite!”

I opened my mouth to protest—it most certainly was not my favorite—but before I could speak, a soft knock echoed at the door. A maid peeked in, her eyes darting nervously between Father and Mother. “Your Majesties, Lord Zephyr requests an audience with Princess Liliana.”

Father’s expression brightened. “Ah! The Shadow Blade returns! Send him in, send him in!”

The maid curtsied and disappeared, and a moment later, Zephyr stepped into the room. His dark cloak was damp from the rain outside, and his sharp features were drawn into their usual frown. He bowed deeply to Father and Mother before turning his gaze to me. His eyes lingered for a fraction too long, and I felt a prickle of unease run down my spine.

“Your Majesties,” Zephyr said, his voice smooth and measured. “Princess Liliana. I apologize for the interruption, but I bring news that cannot wait.”

Mother set aside her needlework, her fingers stilling. “News, Lord Zephyr? Is something amiss?”

Zephyr hesitated, his jaw tightening. “I’m afraid so. I have received intelligence that suggests…” He trailed off, his eyes flicking to me again. “That is to say, I have reason to believe there may be a threat to the princess’s safety.”

 “A threat? To Lily? Explain yourself, Zephyr.”

Zephyr reached into his cloak and withdrew a sealed envelope. The wax seal was unmarked, smooth and unbroken. He held it out to Father, his fingers tightening around the edges. “This was left at the gate this morning. No sender. No explanation. Only this.”

Father took the envelope, his brow furrowing as he turned it over in his hands. He broke the seal and unfolded the note, his eyes scanning the contents. His expression shifted from confusion to something darker, his lips pressing into a thin line.

Mother rose from her chair, her skirts whispering against the floor as she moved to stand beside Father. “What is it, Alistair?”

Father didn’t answer. Instead, he held the note out to her, his hand trembling slightly. Mother took it, her eyes widening as she read. Then, without a word, she passed it to me.

I took the note, my fingers brushing against the rough parchment. It was a crayon drawing—crude, childish, the kind of thing a five-year-old might produce. A horse, its eyes glowing red, its mane a tangle of flames. At the bottom, scrawled in uneven letters, were the words: *For the Shadow Blade.*

I stared at the drawing, my mind racing—not with fear, but with calculation. This was no child’s prank. The symbolism was too precise, too deliberate. A demonic horse. A message meant for Zephyr. And the timing was too perfect.

I looked up, my expression carefully neutral. “How… strange.”

Father’s face was pale, his earlier joviality gone. “Strange? Lily, this is a threat. A warning.”

Mother’s hand rested on my shoulder, her fingers warm through the fabric of my dress. “Alistair, perhaps it’s nothing more than a child’s drawing. Someone playing a prank.”

“A prank?” Zephyr’s voice was sharp. “Your Majesty, this is no prank. The symbolism is clear. The demonic horse is an ancient sigil, one associated with—” He cut himself off, his eyes darting to me again. “With forces best left unmentioned in polite company.”

I tilted my head, my voice soft and curious. “Forces, Lord Zephyr? What kind of forces?”

Zephyr’s jaw clenched. “Nothing that concerns you, Princess. Suffice to say, this is a matter for the Shadow Realm to investigate.”

Father’s hand came down on Zephyr’s shoulder, his grip firm. “And investigate you will. But Lily is not to be left alone. Not until we know more.”

But I kept my expression sweet, my voice gentle. “Father, I’m sure it’s nothing. Perhaps it’s just a misunderstanding. Someone saw me drawing and thought to leave me a gift.”

Father’s expression softened, and I knew I had him. “A gift? Lily, my sweet, this is no gift. This is a warning.”

I sighed, my shoulders slumping slightly. “I suppose you’re right. But it’s still very strange. Who would leave something like this?”

Zephyr’s eyes narrowed. “That is what I intend to find out.”

Mother’s fingers tightened on my shoulder. “Lily, perhaps you should return to your rooms. I’ll have the guards double their patrols.”

I nodded, my expression one of innocent compliance. “Of course, Mother. If you think it’s best.”

Father kissed the top of my head, his beard tickling my forehead. “It’s for the best, my sweet. We’ll keep you safe.”

And that was dangerous.

---

I made my way back to my rooms, my slippers whispering against the polished stone floors. The corridors were quiet, the usual bustle of servants and courtiers muted by the late afternoon light. I kept my pace slow, my expression serene, but my mind was anything but calm.

Who had sent the note? The cult? They were the most likely culprits, but their methods were usually more… direct. A crayon drawing didn’t strike me as their style. Then again, perhaps they were growing desperate. Or perhaps this was a feint, a distraction meant to draw attention away from something else.

I turned a corner, my fingers brushing against the wall as I steadied myself. The note had been left at the gate, which meant the sender had been outside the castle walls. That narrowed the possibilities, but not by much. The cult had sympathizers everywhere, and the city was full of those who still whispered the Demon Lord’s name in the dark.

I reached my rooms and pushed open the door, stepping inside. The familiar scent of lavender and beeswax greeted me, the fire in the hearth casting a warm glow over the plush rugs and heavy drapes. I closed the door behind me, my fingers lingering on the latch for a moment before I turned the key in the lock.

I was not afraid. Fear was a luxury I could not afford. But caution? Caution was a necessity.

I moved to my desk, my fingers brushing against the smooth wood. The drawer slid open with a soft click, and I reached inside, my hand closing around the small, leather-bound ledger I kept hidden there. The ledger was a record of my observations, a catalog of the court’s weaknesses and the kingdom’s vulnerabilities. I flipped it open, my eyes scanning the pages until I found the entry I was looking for.

*Zephyr, Lord of the Shadow Realm. Suspicious. Obsessive. Prone to overreaction. Current fixation: the Crumble Conspiracy. Likely to interpret any anomaly as evidence of a larger plot. Useful as a distraction.*

I tapped my finger against the page, my mind working. The note was a problem, but it was also an opportunity. If Zephyr was focused on the cult, he would be less likely to notice other… irregularities. And if I could feed him the right information, I could steer his investigation in whatever direction I chose.

I closed the ledger and slid it back into the drawer, my fingers lingering for a moment on the small obsidian shard I kept beside it. The shard was a remnant of my past life, a fragment of the obsidian citadel that had been my home. I had carried it with me since the day I was born, a silent reminder of who I was and what I had lost.

I picked it up, turning it over in my fingers. The surface was smooth, cool to the touch, the edges sharp enough to draw blood. I pressed the pad of my thumb against one of the edges, feeling the faintest prick of pain. A single drop of blood welled up, dark and glistening in the firelight.

I watched it for a moment, my mind drifting. The blood was a reminder, a promise. I was still here. Still alive. Still Maledictus.

And I would not be defeated by a crayon drawing.

---

The knock at my door came just as the sun began to set, the golden light spilling through the windows and painting the walls in warm hues. I set aside the book I had been pretending to read and rose from my chair, smoothing my skirts as I moved to the door.

“Who is it?” I called, my voice light and sweet.

“It’s Eris, Your Highness,” came the reply, muffled through the wood. “I… I have something for you.”

I unlocked the door and pulled it open, revealing Eris standing in the hallway. Her cheeks were flushed, her eyes bright with excitement, and in her hands she held a thick, leather-bound tome. The cover was embossed with silver runes, the pages edged in gold.

My breath caught. The Black Tome of Maledictus.

I kept my expression carefully neutral, my voice soft. “Eris. What a pleasant surprise.”

Eris bobbed a quick curtsy, her fingers tightening around the tome. “Your Highness, I… I found this in the archives. It’s a grimoire, one of the oldest in the Spire. I thought… I thought you might like to see it.”

I reached out, my fingers brushing against the cover. The tome hummed with power, the runes pulsing faintly beneath my touch. It recognized me. Knew me.

I took it from Eris, my fingers curling around the spine. “Thank you, Eris. This is… quite the gift.”

Eris’s face lit up, her smile wide and genuine. “I thought it might help with your studies. There are spells in there that even the Archmage hasn’t seen. Spells of…” She hesitated, her eyes darting to the door. “Of great power.”

I opened the tome, my eyes scanning the pages. The ink was fresh, the words shifting and rearranging themselves as I watched. The tome was alive, its knowledge adapting to my presence. And it was showing me things I had not seen in a century.

I closed the book, my fingers lingering on the cover. “This is… remarkable, Eris. I don’t know how to thank you.”

Eris shook her head, her cheeks flushing. “No thanks necessary, Your Highness. It’s an honor to be of service. If there’s anything else you need, anything at all, you have only to ask.”

I smiled, my expression warm and genuine. “You’re too kind, Eris. But for now, this is more than enough.”

Eris curtsied again, her eyes shining. “I’ll leave you to your studies, then. Goodnight, Your Highness.”

“Goodnight, Eris.”

I closed the door behind her, my fingers tightening around the tome. The Black Tome of Maledictus. A grimoire of forbidden knowledge, a library of spells that had been lost to the world. And now it was mine.

I carried it to my desk, setting it down gently. The fire crackled in the hearth, the flames casting long shadows across the pages as I opened the tome once more. The words shifted, rearranging themselves into a spell I had not seen in a lifetime.

*The Word of Unmaking.*

I traced the letters with my finger, my breath catching. 

I had used it once before, in the final moments of my reign. A single syllable, spoken in desperation, and an army had been reduced to dust. But the cost had been high. I had aged decades in an instant, my body withering, my power fading.

I closed the tome, my fingers lingering on the cover. The Word was a weapon, a last resort. And I had no intention of using it. Not yet.

But it was good to know it was there.

---

The night was quiet, the castle settling into its usual rhythms. I sat at my desk, the Black Tome open before me, my fingers tracing the pages as I read. The words were familiar, the spells a language I had once known as well as my own name. But the knowledge was bittersweet, a reminder of what I had been and what I had become.

A soft scratching at the window drew my attention. I looked up, my eyes narrowing as a dark shape flitted across the glass. A moment later, the window swung open, and Baphomutt tumbled inside, his wings flapping wildly as he landed on the desk with a thud.

“Mistress!” he hissed, his voice a squeaky whisper. “Baphomutt has news!”

I sighed, my fingers stilling on the page. “Baphomutt. I thought I told you not to come in through the window.”

Baphomutt ignored me, his beady eyes gleaming in the firelight. “Mistress, the Shadow Blade is asking questions. Lots of questions. About Mistress. About the note. About the cult.”

I leaned back in my chair, my expression thoughtful. “Is he now?”

Baphomutt nodded eagerly, his wings fluttering. “He’s talking to the guards. The cooks. The stable hands. He’s even talking to the garden gnomes!”

I raised an eyebrow. “The garden gnomes?”

Baphomutt nodded again, his expression serious. “They know things, Mistress. Important things. Like where the carrots are buried.”

I pinched the bridge of my nose, my patience wearing thin. “Baphomutt, the garden gnomes are not a reliable source of intelligence.”

Baphomutt’s wings drooped, his expression crestfallen. “But Mistress, they’re very wise. And they have excellent taste in vegetables.”

I sighed, my fingers tapping against the desk. “Very well. Keep an eye on Zephyr. But do not interfere. I want to know what he’s doing, but I don’t want him to know we’re watching him.”

Baphomutt grinned, his sharp teeth glinting. “Baphomutt is the best at watching! No one ever notices Baphomutt!”

I reached into the drawer of my desk, my fingers closing around a small, wrapped parcel. I tossed it to Baphomutt, who caught it with a squeak. “Here. A reward for your… diligence.”

Baphomutt tore open the parcel, his eyes widening as he revealed the contents—a small, sugar-dusted pastry. “Ooooh! Baphomutt loves pastries!”

I watched as he devoured the treat, his wings fluttering with delight. “Just remember, Baphomutt. No more stealing. No more chaos. And no more coming in through the window.”

Baphomutt nodded, his mouth full. “No stealing. No chaos. No windows. Baphomutt promises!”

I sighed, my fingers returning to the Black Tome. “Somehow, I doubt that.”

Baphomutt finished the pastry, licking his fingers clean. “Mistress is the best! Baphomutt will go watch the Shadow Blade now!”

He flapped his wings, launching himself toward the window. I called after him, my voice sharp. “Baphomutt, the door!”

But he was already gone, a dark shape disappearing into the night.

I shook my head, my fingers tracing the pages of the tome once more. The Word of Unmaking glowed faintly in the firelight, the letters shifting and rearranging themselves as I watched. A reminder. A promise.

I closed the tome, my fingers lingering on the cover. The night was quiet, the castle asleep. But I was awake. And I was watching.

And I was waiting.

---

The knock at my door came just as the first light of dawn began to creep through the windows. I set aside the Black Tome, my fingers brushing against the cover one last time before I rose from my chair. I moved to the door, my steps silent, my expression serene.

“Who is it?” I called, my voice soft.

“It’s me, Your Highness,” came the reply, muffled through the wood. “Zephyr.”

I hesitated for a moment, my fingers lingering on the latch. Then I unlocked the door and pulled it open, revealing Zephyr standing in the hallway. His expression was grim, his dark eyes shadowed with exhaustion.

“Lord Zephyr,” I said, my voice sweet and innocent. “What brings you to my rooms so early?”

Zephyr’s jaw tightened, his fingers curling into fists at his sides. “Princess Liliana. I… I need to speak with you.”

I stepped aside, my expression curious. “Of course. Please, come in.”

Zephyr stepped into the room, his eyes scanning the space. They lingered on the Black Tome, still open on my desk, and I felt a flicker of unease. But his expression remained carefully neutral as he turned to face me.

“Princess,” he began, his voice measured. “I have been investigating the note left at the gate. The one with the demonic horse.”

I nodded, my expression solemn. “Yes. Father mentioned it. He’s quite concerned.”

Zephyr’s eyes narrowed. “As am I. The symbolism is… troubling. And the timing is too perfect.”

I tilted my head, my voice soft. “What do you mean?”

Zephyr hesitated, his fingers flexing at his sides. “The cult of the Eternal Flame has been growing bolder. They’ve been seen in the city, leaving offerings at the old shrines. And now this note, left at the gate. It’s… too coincidental.”

I felt a prickle of irritation. The cult was a nuisance, a distraction. But if Zephyr was focused on them, he would be less likely to notice other… irregularities.

I sighed, my shoulders slumping slightly. “I see. And you think the cult is behind the note?”

Zephyr’s expression darkened. “I do. And I think they may be planning something. Something that involves you.”

I wrapped my arms around myself, my expression one of innocent fear. “Me? But why would they want to involve me?”

Zephyr’s jaw clenched, his eyes flicking to the Black Tome once more. “That is what I intend to find out.”

I nodded, my expression solemn. “I see. Well, I… I trust you to keep me safe, Lord Zephyr.”

Zephyr’s expression softened, just slightly. “I will, Princess. You have my word.”

I smiled, my expression warm and genuine. “Thank you, Lord Zephyr. I… I appreciate your concern.”

Zephyr bowed, his eyes lingering on me for a moment before he turned and left the room. I closed the door behind him, my fingers lingering on the latch as I listened to his footsteps fade down the hallway.

I turned back to my desk, my eyes scanning the pages of the Black Tome. The Word of Unmaking glowed faintly in the dawn light, the letters shifting and rearranging themselves as I watched.

A reminder. A promise.

I closed the tome, my fingers lingering on the cover. The game was changing. The cult was growing bolder. Zephyr was growing suspicious.

And I was running out of time.

But I was not afraid.

I was Maledictus, the Demon Lord. And I had a plan.

title: Eyebrows on Fire, Patience on Ice
prose:
# Chapter 19: Eyebrows on Fire, Patience on Ice

The grimoire lay open on my desk, its pages catching the candlelight in a way that made the ink seem to breathe. I had been staring at the same passage for the better part of an hour, my eyes tracing the elegant curves of the Aevum Script, and I was no closer to solving the problem than when I had started.

 

 The shadows it cast were long and unhelpful, swallowing the smaller annotations in the margins of the Black Tome. I had tried angling the page toward the fire, but the letters remained stubbornly obscure, their fine strokes dissolving into the gloom like whispers into silence.

The thought sat in my chest like a stone.   I had unmade armies with a single syllable. I had rewritten the laws of thaumaturgy in my own image.

And I could not light a candle.

Well. That was not entirely accurate.  The mortifying spectacle of the court physician clucking over my "delicate constitution" while I lay there, seething with impotent rage.

In practice, my body was a sieve. The energy would leak, scatter, and twist on its way through my flawed mortal channels. The spell would either fizzle into nothing or surge out of control.

  Eris had procured it for me under dangerously thin pretenses, and if anyone else saw it, the consequences would be unpleasant.

 But the spell I was examining was complex, its structure more intricate than it first appeared. I needed to see the annotations, the small corrections in the margins that I had noticed but not yet deciphered.

I could use a lesser flame. A spark, a flicker, something small.

No. That was how disasters happened.

I looked at the candle. The candle looked back at me, its flame dancing mockingly.

A simple illumination spell. A cantrip. Something a child could manage.

I was, technically, a child. I had the body for it.

The candle flickered, and the flame died.

Darkness swallowed the room.

 The shadows pressed in around me, thick and suffocating, and I felt a familiar prickle of annoyance.

 I would not be defeated by a darkened room.

I would cast the spell.

 

I whispered the words.

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then the light began to grow.

It started as a faint glow at my fingertips, barely visible in the oppressive darkness. I felt a surge of triumph—I had done it, I had actually managed to cast a spell without—

The glow flickered.

It surged.

A blinding burst of white light exploded from my hands, filling the room with a brilliance that seared my eyes and sent pain lancing through my skull. I gasped, the sound lost in the roar of energy that rushed past my ears. Heat washed over my face, sharp and sudden, and I smelled—

Burning.

I clapped my hands to my face, my palms pressing against my eyes as tears streamed down my cheeks.  The scent of singed hair hung in the air, acrid and unmistakable.

I lowered my hands, blinking through the tears. My vision was blurred, but I could see well enough to know that my eyebrows were gone. Or rather, they were singed—reduced to a few pathetic, blackened stubs that crumbled at the slightest touch.

I stared at my reflection in the darkened window, my face a mask of horror.

This was not how the evening was supposed to go.

---

The door burst open.

I spun around, my heart hammering in my chest, as Queen Seraphina swept into the room. She was wearing her nightgown, a simple white garment that made her look almost mortal, and her dark hair was loose around her shoulders. Her eyes were wide, her expression alarmed.

"Lily! What happened?"

I forced my expression into something resembling innocent confusion. "I was... practicing a light spell. It got away from me."

"A light spell," she repeated, her voice flat.

"Yes. *Lumen Minoris*. I thought it would be simple enough." I gestured at my face, wincing as my fingers brushed against the singed remnants of my eyebrows. "I was wrong."

Seraphina crossed the room in three quick strides, her hands reaching for my face. I flinched instinctively, but she was gentle, her fingers feather-light as she tilted my chin upward and examined the damage.

"Your eyebrows," she said, her voice tight.

"Yes. I noticed."

"Your eyelashes, too."

I blinked, and a few more lashes drifted down my cheeks. I could feel the heat still radiating from my skin, the tender soreness of a burn.

Seraphina's jaw tightened. She released my chin and stepped back, her arms crossing over her chest. "You're pushing yourself too hard."

"I wasn't pushing myself. It was a cantrip. A child's spell."

"And yet you singed your eyebrows off."

Seraphina sighed, the sound heavy with exasperation. "You need rest. No more magic for a week."

"A week—"

"A week, Lily." Her voice was firm, brooking no argument. "Your constitution is delicate. You know this. The physicians have told you. I have told you. And yet you persist in attempting spells that your body cannot handle."

"I'm sorry, Mother," I said, my voice small and contrite. "I just... I wanted to read. The candle was too dim, and I thought..."

Seraphina's expression softened, just slightly. She reached out and brushed a strand of hair from my face, her touch gentle. "I understand, sweetheart. You want to learn. You want to grow. But you must be patient with yourself. Your body is still developing, and magic requires strength."

I nodded, my eyes filling with tears. 

"I'll be more careful," I said.

Seraphina studied me for a long moment, her eyes searching mine. Then she nodded, her expression easing into something almost warm. "See that you are. Now, let's get you cleaned up. I'll send for Nurse Branna."

---

Nurse Branna arrived within the quarter hour, a stout woman with gray-streaked hair and hands that moved with the practiced efficiency of someone who had spent decades tending to the royal family's various ailments. She took one look at my face and clucked her tongue.

"Oh, Your Highness! What were you thinking?"

"I was trying to light a candle," I said, my voice flat.

"A candle." Branna shook her head, her expression a mixture of exasperation and concern. "You could have asked for a lantern. Or a new candle. Or any number of things that don't involve channeling arcane energy through your delicate constitution."

"I didn't think it would be a problem."

"Clearly." She opened a small jar of pale green salve and dipped her fingers into it, the ointment releasing a faint herbal scent. "This will sting, Your Highness. Please try to hold still."

I held still as she applied the salve to my eyebrows, the cool ointment soothing the tender skin. The sting was sharp but brief, fading into a pleasant numbness that spread across my forehead.

"There," Branna said, setting the jar aside. "That should help with the burn. The salve will also encourage the hair to regrow, though it may take a few weeks."

"A few weeks."

"Perhaps a month. It depends on your body's natural healing rate." She smiled, the expression softened by genuine sympathy. "You must be more careful, Your Highness. Your constitution is delicate, and magic is a strain on even the strongest of bodies. You must not push yourself beyond your limits."

I nodded, my expression contrite. "I understand, Nurse Branna. Thank you."

Branna patted my shoulder, her touch warm and maternal. "There's a good girl. Now, I'll prepare some warm milk to help you sleep. And no more magic for the rest of the week, understand?"

"Yes, Nurse Branna."

She bustled out of the room, leaving me alone with my mother and the lingering scent of burnt hair. Seraphina was watching me, her expression unreadable.

"You should get some rest," she said.

"Yes, Mother."

She hesitated, as if she wanted to say something more. Then she shook her head and turned toward the door. "I'll check on you in the morning. If your eyebrows look worse, we'll call the physician."

"They'll be fine, Mother."

"See that they are." She paused at the door, her hand resting on the frame. "Lily. I know you want to be strong. I know you want to prove yourself. But strength is not about pushing through pain. It's about knowing your limits and working within them."

I smiled, a small, genuine thing that surprised me. "I know, Mother. I'll try."

Seraphina nodded, and then she was gone, the door closing softly behind her.

I looked ridiculous.

I set the mirror aside, my jaw tightening. 

And the grimoire was still on my desk.

I rose from the bed and crossed the room, my fingers brushing against the Black Tome's cover. The leather was warm, almost alive, and I felt a familiar pull of fascination as I opened it to the passage I had been studying.

The letters were still there, still waiting. The candle was still dark.

But I had other sources of light.

I pulled back the curtains, letting the moonlight spill into the room. It was not as bright as candlelight, but it was enough—just barely—to illuminate the page.

I sat down at my desk and began to read.

The margins of the page held a series of annotations, written in my own hand from a lifetime ago. They were corrections, refinements, observations about the spell's structure that I had never fully implemented. As I read them, a pattern began to emerge.

The spell could be simplified. The incantation could be shortened, the focus narrowed, the mana cost reduced by nearly half. It would be a pale shadow of the original, but it might be enough.

I could cast it.

 If I could adapt it to my limitations, I might be able to—

The door creaked.

"Mistress!" he squeaked, his eyes gleaming in the moonlight. "Baphomutt has brought a gift!"

"Baphomutt," I hissed, "what are you doing here?"

He scuttled into the room, his tiny claws clicking against the floorboards. In his hands, he clutched a silver candlestick—one of the pair that had been sitting on the hallway table, I realized.

"Baphomutt saw mistress was in the dark!" he announced proudly, setting the candlestick on the desk. "Baphomutt thought mistress might need light!"

I stared at him. Then at the candlestick. Then back at him.

"You stole a candlestick."

"Borrowed!" Baphomutt's expression was wounded. "Baphomutt is loyal servant. Baphomutt only wants to help!"

"You want to help by stealing the royal silver?"

"Mistress likes pretty things! Baphomutt brings pretty things!"

I pinched the bridge of my nose, feeling a headache forming behind my eyes. "Baphomutt. If you are caught, we are both in trouble. Do you understand that?"

Baphomutt tilted his head, his expression blank. "But mistress is clever. Mistress will think of something."

"Baphomutt—"

"Baphomutt believes in mistress!" He puffed out his tiny chest, his eyes shining with devotion. "Mistress will be Demon Lord again! Baphomutt will help!"

I opened my mouth to argue, then closed it. There was no point. Baphomutt's loyalty was absolute, his idiocy unbounded, and his ability to comprehend consequences nonexistent.

"Fine," I said, my voice flat. "Leave the candlestick. And go. Before someone finds you here."

Baphomutt's face split into a wide, toothy grin. "Baphomutt obeys!" He scurried toward the door, then paused, looking back over his shoulder. "Mistress's eyebrows look funny."

"Get out."

"Baphomutt is going!" He vanished through the door, his squeaky laughter echoing in his wake.

I stared at the closed door for a long moment, my hands clenching at my sides. Then I turned back to the grimoire, the moonlight spilling across its pages.

The candlestick sat on my desk, a silent reminder of Baphomutt's "help."

I set it aside and returned to my reading.

The door creaked again.

I spun around, ready to berate Baphomutt for his return, but the figure in the doorway was not the imp.

"Mother?"

Seraphina was standing in the hall, her hand resting on the doorframe. She was holding a cup of warm milk, the steam curling upward in the moonlight.

"I thought you might need this," she said, her voice soft.

I blinked, my anger fading into confusion. "You... you brought me milk?"

"You didn't drink the one Nurse Branna left."

I looked at the nightstand. The cup was still there, untouched. I had been too focused on the grimoire to notice.

"Oh. Thank you, Mother."

Seraphina crossed the room and set the fresh cup beside the old one. She glanced at the grimoire on my desk, her expression unreadable.

"You should sleep, Lily. It's late."

"I know. I just... I wanted to finish reading."

Seraphina's eyes lingered on the book. "What are you reading?"

I hesitated. The truth was dangerous, but a lie was riskier. Seraphina had a way of seeing through deception, of finding the cracks in even the most carefully constructed facade.

"It's a history," I said, my voice soft. "A chronicle of the old wars. I found it in the library."

Seraphina nodded slowly. "The old wars. The ones my husband and I fought in."

"Yes, Mother."

She was quiet for a moment, her gaze distant. Then she reached out and brushed a strand of hair from my face, her touch gentle.

"You have your father's curiosity," she said. "And my stubbornness. It's a dangerous combination."

I smiled, the expression feeling almost natural. "I'll try to use it wisely."

Seraphina's lips curved into a faint smile. "See that you do." She paused, her eyes searching mine. "Lily. If you ever need to talk—about anything—I want you to know that I'm here. No matter what."

The words settled in my chest, warm and uncomfortable. I did not know how to respond. I had spent eleven years building walls, crafting personas, hiding my true nature behind a mask of innocence. And yet, somehow, this woman kept finding ways to slip through.

"Thank you, Mother," I said, my voice barely above a whisper.

Seraphina nodded, and then she was gone, the door closing softly behind her.

I sat on the bed, staring at the cup of warm milk. The grimoire was still open on my desk, the moonlight still spilling across its pages. But the words seemed less important now, the spell less urgent.

I picked up the cup and took a sip. The milk was warm and sweet, flavored with honey and a hint of cinnamon.

I did not know what to make of this. I did not know what to make of any of it.

I would find a way. I would not be deterred.

But tonight, I would sleep. I would let my body heal. I would let my eyebrows grow back.

And tomorrow, I would begin again.

I closed the grimoire and set it aside, then blew out the candle that Baphomutt had brought. The room was dark, but the moonlight was enough to guide me to the bed.

I lay down, staring at the ceiling. The singed skin on my forehead throbbed, a dull ache that reminded me of my failure.

But it was a temporary setback. A minor inconvenience.

I would not be stopped by something as trivial as singed eyebrows.

I closed my eyes, letting the darkness swallow me.

And I slept.

title: Kidnapped by Incompetents
prose:
# Chapter 20: Kidnapped by Incompetents

The garden was too quiet today, the kind of quiet that settled in my ribs like wet wool. I sat on the stone bench beneath the rose trellis, my sketchbook balanced on my knees, the charcoal stick moving with deliberate precision across the page. The air smelled of damp earth and blooming roses, cloying and thick. It was the scent of a place that had never known fire, never known the clean bite of ozone after a spell gone right.

Around me, the garden stretched in manicured perfection—hedges trimmed into geometric shapes, flowerbeds arranged in symmetrical patterns, a fountain burbling in the center like a contented infant. It was all so carefully contained, so utterly lacking in anything that might hold my interest. 

The first shadow fell across my page before I noticed the shift in the light. A flicker of movement, too fast for the garden’s usual stillness. My fingers tightened around the charcoal, but I didn’t look up. Not yet. I finished the final curve of the binding glyph, my lips moving silently as I traced the incantation’s phonetic structure in my mind. The third syllable needed to be aspirated, not guttural. A common mistake, and a fatal one if you were trying to summon something you couldn’t control.

The second shadow joined the first.

I exhaled through my nose, slow and controlled, and finally lifted my gaze. Two figures stood at the edge of the rose trellis, their robes dark and unadorned, their faces obscured by deep hoods. They weren’t gardeners. They weren’t courtiers. They weren’t even the usual palace guards, who at least had the decency to announce themselves before interrupting what they assumed was a princess’s idle doodling.

I tilted my head, just slightly, and let my voice carry the faintest edge of irritation. “Can I help you?”

The taller of the two figures took a step forward. His voice was a rasp, like dry leaves scraping stone. “The vessel has been chosen. The time is now.”

I blinked. Then I blinked again, slower this time, letting my confusion show. “I’m sorry, what?”

The second figure moved faster than I expected. A sack descended over my head before I could react, the rough fabric scratching against my cheeks, the scent of stale incense and something metallic—blood, perhaps—filling my nose. Strong arms lifted me off the bench, and for a single, disorienting moment, I was weightless. Then my back hit something hard, and the world tilted.

I didn’t scream.

I took inventory.

The sack was thick, but not thick enough to block out all light. I could see the faint outline of my captors’ legs as they moved, their steps quick and silent. Professionals, then. Not Zephyr’s people—they would have sent someone with less subtlety, someone who would have enjoyed the drama of it. And not Leo’s either. The Beastfolk didn’t bother with sacks. They just threw you over their shoulders and growled.

No, these were cultists. The kind who thought they were being clever.

I let my body go limp, feigning fear. It wasn’t difficult. My heart was pounding, not from terror, but from the sheer inconvenience of this. I had a grimoire to finish adapting, eyebrows to regrow, and a very important lesson to teach Prince Leo about the consequences of calling me “sweet cheeks” in public. Being kidnapped was not on the agenda.

The journey was short. A few turns, a staircase descending, the cool kiss of underground air against my skin. Then the sack was yanked off, and I was set down on my feet.
