The chamber was dim, lit only by flickering candles set into iron sconces along the walls. The air smelled of damp stone and old blood, the kind of scent that clung to the back of your throat.

I took it all in with a single sweep of my gaze—the circular chamber, the robed figures arranged in a loose semicircle, the crude sigils painted on the floor in what looked like rust. The leader stood at the center, his hood pushed back to reveal a face that was all sharp angles and fanatical eyes. His lips curled into something that might have been a smile.

“The vessel has arrived,” he said, his voice echoing off the stone. “The time of resurrection is at hand.”

I rubbed at my wrists where the ropes had chafed, then looked up at him. “I’m sorry, but I think there’s been a mistake.”

The cultists exchanged glances. The leader’s smile faltered. “Mistake?”

I nodded, my expression carefully neutral. “Yes. You see, I’m not a vessel. I’m a princess.”

A murmur rippled through the group. The leader’s eyes narrowed. “You lie. The signs were clear. The bloodline, the power—”

“Ah,” I said, holding up a finger. “There’s your first error. Bloodline has nothing to do with it. The ritual you’re attempting requires a willing participant, not just a convenient one. And as for power—” I gestured vaguely at myself. “Do I look powerful to you?”

The leader’s jaw tightened. “You are the daughter of the Hero and the Saint. The blood of the conquerors runs in your veins. That is power enough.”

I sighed. “You’re confusing lineage with aptitude. Just because my father can swing a sword doesn’t mean I can. And just because my mother can heal a wound doesn’t mean I can’t cause one.” I paused, letting the words hang in the air. “But that’s not the real problem, is it?”

The leader’s hands clenched at his sides. “And what is the real problem?”

I stepped forward, my slippers whispering against the stone. The cultists flinched, but I ignored them, crouching down to examine the sigils on the floor. My fingers hovered just above the painted lines, tracing the shapes without touching them. “The third syllable of the incantation is aspirated, not guttural. You’re pronouncing it wrong. And this binding glyph—” I tapped the air above a particularly sloppy curve. “It’s upside down. If you complete the ritual like this, you won’t summon anything. You’ll just make a very loud noise and possibly collapse the ceiling.”

The cultists froze.

The leader’s breath hitched. He dropped to his knees in front of me, his hands trembling as he reached out. “Then... then you are the vessel. You must be. How else would you know these things?”

I let my lips curl into a faint smile. “I read a lot.”

The cultists didn’t laugh. They didn’t even breathe. The leader’s eyes burned with something like hope, like desperation. “Guide us, vessel. Show us the true path. We have waited so long for this moment.”

I looked around the chamber, at the eager faces, the trembling hands, the candles flickering like dying stars. They were so certain. And they were so wrong.

But they were also useful.

I stood, brushing imaginary dust from my skirts. “Very well. But we’ll need to start from the beginning. The ritual is delicate. One misstep, and—” I mimed an explosion with my hands. “Well. Let’s just say you won’t like the results.”

The leader scrambled to his feet, his face alight with devotion. “Yes, vessel. Anything you say.”

I nodded, already turning toward the sigils. “First, we’ll need to correct the glyphs. The alignment is off by three degrees. And the candles—” I pointed to the sconces. “They’re in the wrong positions. The light needs to intersect at the exact center of the circle. Otherwise, the resonance will be unstable.”

The cultists moved as one, their robes whispering against the stone as they adjusted the candles, repainted the glyphs, murmured corrections under their breath. The leader hovered at my elbow, his voice a constant stream of questions. “Like this, vessel? Is this correct?”

I corrected him. Again. And again.

The ritual dagger was brought forward on a velvet cushion, its blade gleaming in the candlelight. The metal was dark, almost black, the edge serrated like a row of teeth. The leader held it out to me, his hands steady now, his voice reverent. “The final step, vessel. The blood offering.”

I extended my hand, palm up. The dagger was cold against my skin, the metal biting just enough to draw a thin line of blood. I didn’t flinch. “Of course.”

The leader’s voice rose in a chant, the words clumsy, the syntax all wrong. The cultists joined in, their voices a discordant hum. The dagger flared with a sickly yellow-green light, the same color as a bruise. The light crawled up my arm, tracing the veins beneath my skin, and I felt the first tug of the siphon.

It wasn’t pain. It was the sensation of something being slowly, inexorably drained from me—like water trickling from a cracked cup. My fingers went numb. My vision blurred at the edges.

The cultists gasped, their eyes wide with awe. “The power flows!” the leader cried. “The Lord stirs within you!”

I gritted my teeth. Fools.

The siphon was a crude spell, designed to feed energy from a “willing” vessel to an empty rune matrix. But the matrix wasn’t empty. It was keyed to a resonance frequency that didn’t match the intended entity. They were trying to pour my life force into a circle meant to summon me.

The irony was almost too much.

I locked eyes with the leader, my expression shifting from passive vessel to something older, colder. “You are doing it backwards.”

The cultists froze.

The leader’s mouth opened and closed. “Vessel?”

I pulled my hand back, ignoring the searing cold that now blanketed my arm up to the elbow. “The flow is wrong. You are feeding the circle, not the god. The siphon is drawing from the vessel’s core, but the matrix is keyed to a resonance frequency that doesn’t match the intended entity. This will create a void, not a presence. You will collapse the ritual and take half this cave with it.”

The leader’s face went pale. “But... but the texts said—”

“The texts were wrong,” I said flatly. “Or perhaps you misread them. Either way, if you complete the ritual as it stands, you will die. All of you.”

A ripple of fear passed through the group. The leader’s hands trembled. “Then... then what do we do?”

I looked down at the dagger, still clutched in his grip. The yellow-green light flickered, dimming as the siphon’s hold weakened. “You let me correct it. And you pray to whatever gods you worship that I don’t decide to let you fail.”

The leader dropped to his knees, his voice a whisper. “We are yours to command, vessel.”

I smiled. It was a small, private thing, sharp at the edges. “Good. Now, let’s begin again.”

---

The ritual took hours.

I corrected the glyphs, adjusted the candle positions, realigned the sigils. The cultists watched in rapt silence, their eyes wide, their breath shallow. Every so often, one of them would whisper a prayer, their voice trembling with devotion. It was pathetic. And yet, there was a part of me—a small, traitorous part—that understood their desperation. They wanted to believe. They needed to believe.

I let them.

When the final glyph was complete, I stepped back, my arms crossed over my chest. The chamber was silent, the air thick with anticipation. The leader looked at me, his eyes burning with hope. “Is it... is it ready?”

I nodded. “It is.”

He exhaled, his shoulders sagging with relief. “Then we may begin.”

I held up a hand. “Not yet.”

The leader froze. “Vessel?”

I gestured to the dagger, still resting on its cushion. “The blood offering is the final step. But it must be done correctly. The blade must be heated to precisely thirty-seven degrees Celsius. Any hotter, and the blood will coagulate too quickly. Any colder, and the resonance will be unstable.”

The leader’s eyes widened. “We... we did not know this.”

“Of course you didn’t,” I said, my voice dry. “You’ve been working from a children’s version of the ritual.”

The cultists exchanged glances. One of them, a woman with a scar running down her cheek, stepped forward. “We will heat the blade, vessel. As you command.”

I watched as they prepared the dagger, heating it over a small brazier, testing the temperature with careful fingers. The leader hovered at my side, his voice a constant murmur. “You are truly the vessel, aren’t you? The Dark Lord’s chosen.”

I didn’t answer. I didn’t need to.

When the dagger was ready, the leader held it out to me, his hands steady. “The final step, vessel.”

I took the dagger, my fingers curling around the hilt. The metal was warm now, almost alive. I pressed the flat of the blade against my palm, feeling the heat seep into my skin. The cultists began to chant, their voices rising in a crescendo, the words clumsy, the syntax still slightly off.

I closed my eyes.

And then I spoke.

Not the incantation. Not yet. Instead, I spoke the Word of Unmaking.

It was a single syllable, a breath of sound, a whisper that carried the weight of the universe. The dagger flared white-hot in my grip, the light searing my eyes even through my closed lids. The cultists screamed, their voices raw with terror. The chamber trembled, the stone groaning as the ritual circle dissolved into nothingness.

And then, silence.

I opened my eyes.

The cultists were on their knees, their faces pale, their eyes wide with shock. The leader stared at me, his mouth open, his voice a whisper. “What... what have you done?”

I looked down at the dagger. The blade was gone, reduced to a smear of ash on my palm. I brushed it away, my voice calm. “I saved your lives.”

The leader’s breath hitched. “But... the ritual...”

“Was flawed,” I said. “Beyond repair. If I had let you complete it, you would have died. All of you.”

The cultists exchanged glances. The woman with the scar stepped forward, her voice trembling. “Then... then you are not the vessel?”

I smiled. It was a slow, dangerous thing. “Oh, I am. Just not the one you were expecting.”

The leader’s eyes widened. “You... you are the Dark Lord.”

I didn’t answer. The silence was answer enough.

The cultists dropped to their knees, their voices a chorus of awe. “Forgive us, Dark Lord. We did not know. We did not understand.”

I looked around the chamber, at the trembling figures, the flickering candles, the remnants of the failed ritual. They were so small, so fragile. 

I could have killed them. I could have let the ritual collapse, let the cave bury them beneath tons of stone. It would have been easy. It would have been just.

But I didn’t.

Instead, I stepped forward, my voice soft. “Rise.”

The cultists obeyed, their eyes still wide, their breath still shallow. The leader looked at me, his voice a whisper. “What do we do now, Dark Lord?”

I looked down at my hands, at the faint scars where the dagger had cut, at the ash still clinging to my skin. “Now,” I said, “you listen.”

And they did.

---

The journey back to the palace was uneventful.

The cultists escorted me to the garden, their heads bowed, their voices hushed. They left me at the edge of the rose trellis, their eyes burning with devotion, their hands trembling with awe. The leader pressed a small, black stone into my palm, his voice a whisper. “A token of our loyalty, Dark Lord.”

I closed my fingers around the stone, feeling the faint pulse of magic within it. “Go,” I said. “And do not return until I call for you.”

They left without another word.

I stood in the garden, the stone heavy in my hand, the scent of roses thick in the air. The sun was setting, the sky painted in shades of gold and pink. It was beautiful. It was boring.

I sighed, tucking the stone into the pocket of my dress. Then I turned and walked back toward the palace, my steps quick, my mind already racing with the problem of how to explain this to my parents.

---

The throne room was empty when I arrived, the golden filigree dull in the fading light. I hesitated at the door, my fingers curling around the black stone in my pocket. 

I took a deep breath.

And then I stepped inside.

My father was the first to notice me. He turned, his face lighting up with a smile so bright it made my chest ache. “Lily! There you are, my little spark! We were beginning to worry.”

I forced a smile, my cheeks aching with the effort. “I’m sorry, Father. I was... sketching in the garden.”

My mother stepped forward, her eyes sharp, her voice soft. “You’ve been gone for hours, Lily. We sent the guards to look for you.”

I nodded, my fingers tightening around the stone. “I lost track of time.”

My father chuckled, ruffling my hair. “Ah, the curse of the artist! I remember when I used to get lost in my training. Hours would pass, and I wouldn’t even notice.” He paused, his expression turning serious. “But you must be more careful, Lily. The world isn’t as safe as it once was.”

I looked up at him, my voice small. “I know, Father.”

My mother’s gaze lingered on me, her eyes searching. “Lily,” she said, her voice careful. “Is everything all right?”

I hesitated. Then I nodded, my voice barely above a whisper. “Yes, Mother. Everything’s fine.”

She didn’t believe me. I could see it in her eyes. But she didn’t press. Instead, she reached out, brushing a strand of hair from my face. “You’re trembling,” she said. “Come. Let’s get you some warm milk.”

I let her lead me from the throne room, my father’s laughter following us like a shadow. The stone in my pocket felt heavier with every step.

I had spent eleven years planning for this moment. Eleven years preparing for the day when I would reclaim what was rightfully mine.

And now, I wasn’t sure I wanted it anymore.

---

The milk was warm and sweet, the honey and cinnamon coating my tongue like a lie. I sat at the small table in my room, the grimoire open in front of me, the candle flickering in the draft. Baphomutt was curled up in the corner, his tiny form twitching in his sleep, his snores a soft, rhythmic hum.

I took another sip of milk, my fingers tracing the edges of the page. The spell was still there, waiting. The adaptation was still possible.

But my mind wasn’t on the grimoire. It was on the stone in my pocket, on the cultists’ faces, on the way my father’s smile made my chest ache.

I set the cup aside and picked up the stone, turning it over in my fingers. It was smooth, cool to the touch, the magic within it a faint, pulsing warmth. A token of loyalty. A reminder of what I was.

What I could be.

I closed my eyes, the stone heavy in my palm. The Word of Unmaking still echoed in my mind, the memory of the dagger’s light searing my vision. I could have killed them. I could have let the cave collapse. I could have ended them.

But I didn’t.

I opened my eyes, my gaze falling on the grimoire. The spell was still there, waiting. The adaptation was still possible.

I would find a way.

But not tonight.

Tonight, I would sleep.

And in the morning, I would face the problem of how to explain to my parents that their daughter had just saved a cult of fanatics from themselves. Again.

title: Amateurs at the Altar
prose:
# Chapter 21: Amateurs at the Altar

 No, this was a different cold. A deliberate cold. A cold with intent.

The cult leader's hand was steady as he pressed the flat of the dagger against my palm, and the metal drank warmth from my flesh the way a sponge drinks water.   The binding was wrapped in strips of leather that had been treated with something that smelled like burnt herbs and desperation. And the runes etched along the blade's spine were so poorly executed that I had to squint to recognize them at all.

I was strapped to an altar carved from a single block of black stone, my wrists bound with ropes that had been woven with protective charms—protective charms that were, I noted with mounting irritation, tied incorrectly. The knot pattern was wrong. The charms were facing the wrong direction. The rope itself was the wrong grade for ritual binding, too stiff and too thick, the kind a farmer might use to secure a load of firewood.

The chant began.

I recognized the third stanza of the Binding of the Vessel before the second line, and the recognition was so insulting that I almost laughed out loud. The Binding of the Vessel.  

These fools were performing it with a kitchen knife and a prayer.

The third stanza, mangled beyond recognition, came out as a series of garbled syllables that bore only a passing resemblance to the original Infernal.  And whoever had transcribed the ritual had clearly been working from a copy of a copy of a copy, each generation adding its own layer of errors like sediment accumulating on a riverbed.

The blade flared with a sickly, yellow-green light.

And I felt the tug.

It wasn't pain, exactly. It was an emptying. A horrible pulling sensation from the center of my being, as if something vital was being siphoned through a straw too small for the task. Like trying to drain an ocean through a drinking straw, the flow was slow and agonizing, and the thing being drained was me. I felt my essence—my mana, my life force, the very substance of my soul—being pulled from the core of my being and channeled into the dagger, then directed outward into the rune circle that had been painted on the cave floor in what I sincerely hoped was red ochre and not something worse.

I recognized the spell's signature instantly. A crude, parasitic siphon, designed to feed energy from a willing vessel to an empty rune matrix. It was the magical equivalent of a child trying to light a candle with a bonfire. Technically possible, but catastrophically mismatched.

The fools.

They were trying to pour my life force into a circle meant to summon me.

The metaphorical slap in the face was worse than the physical drain. Here I was, Maledictus, Lord of the Abyssal Halls, conqueror of the Obsidian Plains, the terror that had made the Seven Heroes sweat through their armor—and I was being mugged by my own would-be priests. Drained by a ritual so incompetent that my past self would have wept with secondhand embarrassment. If my former generals could see me now, they would have died of laughter before I could punish them for it.

The cult leader's voice rose in fervor, the corrupted words of the chant pouring from his lips with the confidence of a man who had no idea he was reciting gibberish.  The dagger remained pressed against my palm, its cold seeping deeper into my bones with every passing second.

I catalogued the spell's flaws as it worked. The siphon was drawing from my core, yes, but the containment matrix was misaligned—the rune for "contain" had been written as the rune for "release," which meant the energy was bleeding out into the cave instead of being stored.  And the directional flow was reversed, pulling energy from the vessel into the circle instead of using the circle to anchor the vessel's power for the summoning.

If this ritual had been performed by anyone with even a fraction of my knowledge, it would have worked. But these people had the intellectual rigor of a cabbage patch and the magical aptitude of a brick.

 I watched the light creep past my wrist, past my elbow, and I felt my fingers go numb, the world tilting slightly at the edges. The sensation was deeply unpleasant—not painful, exactly, but wrong. A violation of the natural order, as if my body was being turned inside out and examined by creatures that had no business looking.

The cultists gasped and murmured. I could hear the excitement in their voices, the barely contained glee of people who thought their desperate gamble was paying off. They pressed closer, their robed forms crowding around the altar, their faces illuminated by the sickly glow of the dagger's light.

"The awakening!" one of them hissed, a woman with a scar across her cheek and a voice like a rusty hinge. "The vessel stirs!"

"She glows," another breathed, a young man with wide, terrified eyes and a beard that looked like it had been chewed off by a nervous animal. "The Lord's light fills her!"

 "Feel the power flow, vessel! The Lord stirs within you!"

I felt something stir, all right.  I ran through the entire catalog of my former vocabulary—Infernal, Abyssal, and the Old Tongue that predated both—and I still felt understated. There was a specific word in the Old Tongue, a compound of several concepts, that meant "the act of being so monumentally stupid that the universe itself pauses to reconsider your existence." I used it three times in a row.

*You absolute imbeciles*, I thought, as the siphon continued its agonizing work. *You have the Demon Lord himself in your grasp, and you're trying to drain him like a tapped keg. You could have asked. You could have made a deal. You could have done literally anything other than this monumentally stupid ritual.*

But they hadn't asked. They hadn't dealt. They had kidnapped me, strapped me to an altar, and begun chanting the magical equivalent of a child's nursery rhyme at me. And now they were stealing my life force, drop by agonizing drop, and they didn't even know what they were consuming.

 The cultists were feeding on my essence, and they didn't even know what they were eating. It would be like a starving man discovering a feast and taking one bite before setting the rest on fire.

 

I studied the siphon's matrix as it worked.  One good push in the right place, and the whole thing would collapse like a house of cards in a hurricane.

One push. That was all I needed. But the drain was making it hard to focus. The light had reached my shoulder now, and my vision was starting to blur at the edges. I needed to act before the siphon took too much of me.

I locked eyes with the leader.

My expression shifted. I couldn't see it, but I felt it—a hardening of the jaw, a coldness in the gaze, the subtle rearrangement of features that transformed me from a passive, frightened vessel into something ancient and furious. 

"You are doing it backwards," I said.

My voice cut through the drone of voices like a blade through silk. The cultists froze. The leader's mouth opened and closed, opened and closed, a fish gasping for air it couldn't find. The chanting stopped entirely, replaced by a ringing silence that echoed off the cave walls.

"Vessel?" he managed. The word came out as a squeak, stripped of all the dramatic weight he had been trying to invest in it.

I pulled my hand back, ignoring the searing cold that now blanketed my arm up to the elbow. The dagger came with me, still pressed against my palm, its sickly light flickering as the contact was broken. The siphon sputtered, trying to maintain the connection, but I had already severed the flow.

"The flow is wrong," I said, my voice flat and clinical. "You are feeding the circle, not the god. The siphon is drawing from the vessel's core, but the matrix is keyed to a resonance frequency that doesn't match the intended entity."

I paused, watching the confusion spread across their faces like ink on wet paper. The leader's brow furrowed. The scarred woman's mouth twisted. The young man with the chewed beard looked like he was about to be sick.

"This will create a void, not a presence," I continued, each word landing like a hammer blow. "You will collapse the ritual and take half this cave with it."

My correction was not helpful. It was an indictment. A declaration of incompetence delivered in the tone of a tutor grading a failed examination. 

A gasp rippled through the cult.

"She speaks," someone whispered, their voice trembling. "The vessel speaks with the Lord's voice."

"Her words are sacred," another added, more loudly, a note of desperate hope creeping into their voice. "She corrects our errors. She guides our hands."

The leader stared at me, his face a mask of conflicting emotions. Fear. Awe. Confusion. A desperate hope that I was wrong, that his ritual wasn't the disaster I was describing. His hands were shaking around the dagger's hilt, and I could see the sweat glistening on his forehead in the torchlight.

  My vision blurred at the edges, the cultists' faces dissolving into smears of torchlight and shadow.

I dropped to the ground, catching myself on one hand, the stone floor cold against my palm.  

I looked at the rune circle on the floor. Its glyphs were glowing erratically, some already cracking from the strain. Hairline fractures spiderwebbed across the stone, and I could see the containment matrix beginning to fail—not all at once, but in fits and starts, like a dam springing leaks. One glyph in particular, the one that governed the flow of power from circle to summoning point, was glowing a furious, unstable red.

The cultists were panicking now. Their chanting had devolved into a cacophony of desperate prayers and confused shouts. The scarred woman was backing away from the altar, her hands raised as if to ward off a blow. The young man with the chewed beard had collapsed to his knees, his face buried in his hands. The leader was still holding the dagger, his knuckles white, his face a rictus of terror.

But I wasn't looking at them anymore. I was looking at the flaw.

There it was. The single syllable in their corrupted chant that, if inverted, would destabilize the entire matrix. It was buried in the fourth stanza, a word that had been mistranscribed so badly that it had become a different word entirely—one that, when spoken with the correct inflection, would trigger a sympathetic resonance. The word was supposed to be *vethra*, meaning "to bind," but the transcription had turned it into *vethraen*, meaning "to release." If I spoke it with the proper inflection, it would unravel the binding matrix from within.

 But it would use the dagger's own stolen energy against it, turning the siphon into a feedback loop that would shatter the ritual construct.

The question was whether I could survive the backlash.

I took a breath.  

It was not a word of any mortal tongue. It was a key—a sound that didn't belong in their litany, a dissonant note in their symphony of ignorance. It scraped the air, vibrating at a frequency that made the torch flames gutter and the stones hum. It hung in the air for a moment, dark and final, a sound that had no business existing in this cave, in this world, in this reality.

 The yellow-green light shattered, fracturing into a thousand shards of dissipating energy that scattered like startled fireflies. The shards arced through the air, some of them winking out of existence, others embedding themselves in the cave walls with a sizzling sound.

 The glyphs that had been glowing moments before were now blackened, ruined, their meanings erased beyond recognition. The entire circle was a ruin, a scarred testament to the cult's incompetence.

  My chest felt hollow, scraped out, as if something vital had been removed and not replaced.

The cultists were frozen. Their faces were masks of terror and awe, their mouths hanging open, their eyes wide and unblinking.  The metal was crumbling, rusting, decaying before our eyes—the artifact's power consumed by the feedback loop I had triggered.

The cave was silent save for the sound of my ragged breathing and the crackle of the dying torches.

The leader's voice, when it finally came, was barely a whisper. "What... what did you do?"

I looked up at him. My vision was still blurry at the edges, but I could see the terror in his face, the desperate need to understand what had just happened. He was on his knees now, the dagger forgotten on the floor beside him, his hands trembling.

I smiled. It was not a kind smile. It was the smile of someone who had just demonstrated, in front of an audience of fanatics, that their entire belief system was built on a foundation of sand.

"I fixed your mistake," I said.

And then the darkness took me.

title: A Word That Breaks Worlds
prose:
# Chapter 22: A Word That Breaks Worlds

The first thing I noticed was the smell: ozone, scorched stone, and the sharp, coppery tang of fear-sweat. It clung to the back of my throat like wet wool, and I knew, with the deep bone-memory of a thing long familiar, exactly where I was.

The second thing was the silence. 

I was on the floor. Cold stone pressed against my cheek. Grit stuck to my skin.  Blood. Of course. My body's preferred method of announcing that I had used too much magic, which was to say: any magic at all.

I opened my eyes. The torchlight was a smear of orange and gold, blurring at the edges of my vision. For a long moment I was content to lie there, counting the beats of my own heart, feeling the way my body pressed into the stone as if it wanted to become part of it. Every joint ached. Every breath came shallow, scraped through a throat that felt raw and distant, like it belonged to someone else.

The cult leader was on his knees. I could see him through the curtain of my hair, a large man in dark robes, his face the color of wax that had been left too close to a flame. His hands hovered in front of him, open and trembling, as if he were trying to catch the pieces of something that no longer existed. The dagger was gone. What remained of it lay scattered around his knees—shards of rust-colored metal flaking into dust, the artifact's power consumed by the feedback loop I had triggered.

"What... what did you do?" he whispered. He wasn't asking me. He was asking the air, the cave, the empty space where his life's work had been. "What did you do?"

I pushed myself up.

The movement unleashed a cascade of small agonies—my shoulder, my ribs, the deep throbbing at the base of my skull. My vision swam, tilted, and stabilized. I swayed on my knees, one hand pressed flat against the stone floor to hold myself upright. The cultists watched me. All of them. Their faces were masks of terror and awe, their mouths slack, their eyes glistening in the torchlight like those of frightened cattle.

I let the silence stretch. Let them look at the child they had drugged, bound, and dragged to their altar. Still alive. Still breathing. Still absolutely furious.

The fury was a strange thing. It had been waiting beneath the exhaustion, patient as a buried root. They had taken me from my bed in the middle of the night. They had wrapped me in cloth soaked with some soporific that left my limbs heavy and my thoughts wrapped in cotton wool. They had dragged me through a tunnel system that smelled of damp earth and old blood, and they had laid me on a stone altar beneath a ceiling painted with crude, anatomically enthusiastic renderings of my former self. Then they had produced a dagger, said a great many flowery things about vessels and resurrections, and begun to drain me like a cup of well water.

The arrogance of it. The sheer, staggering presumption.

I understood, distantly, where their logic had failed. They had found fragments of the old texts, the ones that spoke of the Demon Lord's return in blood and sacrifice. They had built a ritual around those fragments with the care of a child assembling a siege engine from pictures of a kite. And they had concluded, in their infinite foolishness, that the vessel for Maledictus's return needed to be destroyed in order for Maledictus to return. They had never stopped to consider that perhaps the vessel was already occupied.

The leader's mouth opened and closed. He made a sound that might have been a word, but it came out as nothing more than a dry click. The other cultists pressed themselves against the cave walls, robes rustling as they tried to become part of the rock. The smoldering remains of their precious circle lay between us—cracked, blackened, ruined, its meanings erased beyond recognition.

I looked at those ruins, and something cold and familiar settled into my chest. Not the exhaustion. Not the pain. Something older. Something that had been waiting, patient as a buried root of its own.

 I was drained. Hollowed out. My mana reserves were a puddle evaporated by noon sun. My body felt like a wineskin that had been emptied and then stomped on by a celebratory crowd. But my mind was not the mind of the exhausted child who had been carried from her bed. That child was gone, pushed aside by the thing that lived beneath her ribs, the thing that had spent twenty years pretending to be a princess and was now, finally, allowed to breathe.

I was Maledictus. And these ants had tried to sacrifice me to me.

I let myself feel that for a moment. Let it wash through me like a tide of black water, cold and clarifying. Then I pushed myself to my feet.

The movement made the leader flinch. He scrambled backward on his knees, his robes catching under his legs, his hands splayed in front of him as if to ward off a blow. The cultists in the back of the cave made small animal sounds—whimpers muted by the hands they had clamped over their mouths.

I did not spare them the dignity of a glance. My attention was on the circle. On the ruined glyphs and the cracked stone where their binding had failed. They had tried to trap a principle in a bottle. They had built a ritual to contain a soul they did not understand, to drain a power they could not measure, to channel a force that had, in my previous incarnation, dissolved three armies at the Battle of the Hollow Chasm in the time it took to clear one's throat.

And they had done it with a dagger that was a failed prototype of an immortality project I had abandoned centuries ago.

The insult was almost poetic.

I took a breath. The air tasted of copper and ash, and the cold in my chest had spread, numbing my ribs, making it hard to draw a full breath. My hands were trembling. 

I ignored it.

The leader found his voice again. "Please," he said, and the word came out cracked, desperate, stripped of all the grandeur he had been posturing with only minutes ago. "Please, the ritual was pure. We followed the texts—the true texts, the ones that your... that the Dark Lord's apostle preserved—"

"Your texts were wrong," I said. My voice came out small and hoarse, which was fitting for a ten-year-old with a throat full of dust. I made sure it carried anyway. "You built the binding from a third-generation copy of a translation of a fragment. The original instructions specified a hand that had never spilled blood, a heart that had never known malice, and a soul that had never touched the void. The binding was meant to hold a manifestation of pure, indifferent truth. You used a knife that steals life and a circle drawn by murderers."

The leader stared at me. His lips moved. No sound came out.

"You couldn't have bound me," I said, "even if you had done it correctly."

I felt it then—the cold thing stirring behind my eyes. Not a spell. Not a trick. Just the awareness of what I was, finally surfacing after years of pretending to be something small and sweet.

The torchlight guttered. The temperature in the cave dropped, not by degrees but by a sudden, shocking margin, as if someone had opened a door to a winter that didn't exist in this season. The leader's breath fogged in front of his face, and he made a sound like a wounded dog. The cultists nearest the walls gasped, their breath clouding too, their eyes going wide and white.

I did not need the full incantation. The old words, the ones that had unmade armies and leveled citadels, were overkill for a circle of this size. I needed only the concept. The principle. The true name of the thing they had so grossly misapplied.

They had tried to bind a soul. I would show them what a soul could do.

I look—no. I looked at the leader, and I let him see what was behind my eyes. Not the void. Just the edge of it. The dark that had lived in the Abyssal Halls, when they were mine, when the obsidian columns echoed with the screams of heroes who had been arrogant enough to challenge me. The dark that had survived death, reincarnation, diapers, and lullabies.

The air grew heavy. The weight of the cave seemed to settle onto the cultists' shoulders, and somewhere near the altar a torch began to gutter, as if the flame itself was trying to escape.

The leader's breath came in short, sharp gasps. The fog from his lips didn't dissipate—it hung in the air, frozen, suspended, like a ghost waiting for permission to leave.

He knew. In that moment, he knew something was deeply, terribly wrong. His mouth was opening, closing, forming questions he didn't dare speak aloud.

I opened my mouth.

The syllable that fell from my lips was not a word of any human language. It was not a word of elvish or dwarven or the old tongue or the beastfolk's throat-sounds or the Spire's precise, mathematical cant. It was a sound that existed before language, before meaning, before the world itself had decided what it wanted to be.

It scraped the air.

I felt it leave me as a vibration, a frequency that pulled the heat from the stones, that made the torch flames bend away from me as if they were bowing, that resonated in the bones of every creature in the chamber—the cultists, the rats in the walls, the distant bats in the upper chambers—with the same deep hum of a bell that has given up trying to be silent.

The syllable hung in the air. Dark. Final. A single note of negation.

And I felt the cost.

It was not pain. Pain I knew how to endure; pain was a language I had spoken fluently across two lifetimes. This was something else. A cold spot bloomed in my chest, a patch of absence where I could feel... less. Like a page being torn from a book, but slowly, methodically, leaving behind only the thin white scar of the binding. I felt a few pages of my future collapse into nothing—days, weeks, perhaps a season, excised from the calendar of my life with the clean precision of a surgeon's blade.

The sensation was not painful. It was deeply, unnervingly wrong. A reminder that this power was not free, and never had been. The Word of Unmaking did not ask for mana. It asked for time. For the raw currency of existence, drawn directly from the ledger of one's life.

I felt years drain from my bones. Not in a dramatic way—no sudden aging, no cracking voice or graying hair. Just a subtle, profound shift, as if the floor of my future had shifted a few steps closer to the edge of a cliff I hadn't yet seen.

The syllable touched the cracked rune circle.

There was no explosion. No grand spectacle. No flash of light or roar of thunder, no screaming fissure tearing through the earth. The world's ending, I had learned long ago, rarely arrives with acclamation. It slips in quietly, wearing the face of a normal day, and it changes everything with a single, unremarkable gesture.

The runes un-happened.

 Gray. Then white. Then nothing. The carved channels smoothed over, the stone filling itself in like water closing over a thrown stone, until the floor was as pristine as the day it had been cut from the mountain.

The circle dissolved. Not broke, not shattered, not crumbled. Dissolved. Inert. Perfect. A smooth stretch of stone that might have been mistaken for the cave's natural floor, and indeed, after a moment, I could not have pointed to the spot where the glyphs had been. The stone did not remember it had ever been touched by chisel or magic.

The dagger in the leader's hand crumbled.

I watched it happen. The ruined metal, already flaking and corroding, turned to fine gray dust that spilled through his fingers like sand. He tried to clutch at it, to hold on to the last relic of his faith, but the dust poured through his grip and scattered across the floor where it blended with the ash from the failed ritual. 

The silence that followed was absolute.

The cultists stared at the blank floor. Their eyes moved across the empty stone, searching for the lines that had been there moments before, finding nothing. The leader—his fingers still spread, still sifting through the dust of his broken world—made a sound like a man who had forgotten how air worked. He dropped to all fours. His body convulsed, racked by dry heaves that produced nothing but spittle and strangled gasps.

Then the screaming began.

Not screams of pain. These were screams of existential terror, the kind that came from a soul that had just watched its entire cosmology collapse into a puddle of un-matter. They came from the back of the cave, from the cultists who had huddled there, from the ones who had been closest to the walls when the temperature dropped and the dark thing in the child's eyes had opened its own eyes.

"The Dark Lord's voice!" one of them shrieked, his voice climbing past reason into a register I hadn't known adult men could reach. "He has rejected us! The sacrifice was an insult—a mockery—He is not returning!"

"He is here!" another screamed. "He is here, He is here, He is HERE—"

The word caught. Spread. They scrambled over each other to flee, robes tangling, elbows finding faces, boots sliding on the smooth stone where their sacred circle had been. Masks dropped. Ceremonial daggers clattered to the floor, forgotten. One cultist tripped over a fallen torch and went down in a heap, only to be trampled by the ones behind him who had stopped trying to maintain any semblance of dignity or order.

They were not fleeing a child. They were fleeing the thing they had seen in my eyes—the dark that had looked back at them from the heart of the abyss. And in their terror, they had found a story that made sense to them. The Dark Lord was not returning. He was already here. He had been here all along. And they had tried to feed him to himself.

The absurdity of it was almost enough to make me laugh.

I watched them go. My expression was empty. My body was still trembling from the strain, my vision swimming at the edges, the cold spot in my chest pulsing with a dull, wrongness that I suspected would take a very long time to heal—if it healed at all. I had spent a sliver of my life to erase their ritual. I had traded a few pages of my future for the privilege of watching them flee.

It had been worth it. I was surprised to find I meant that.

The tunnel mouth emptied. The sounds of panicked screaming faded into echoes, then into nothing. The cave was silent again, save for the crackle of dying torches and my own ragged breathing.

I leaned against the cold cave wall. My legs had stopped wanting to hold me, and I let the stone take my weight, feeling the chill seep through my torn dress and into my bruised shoulders. The leader was still on the floor, his retching having subsided into low, wet sobs. He did not look up as the last of his followers abandoned him.

I let a bitter smile touch my lips.

"Idiots," I whispered to the empty chamber. "You were trying to sacrifice me to me."

The leader let out a sound that might have been a laugh, if laughter could be made of despair. He pressed his forehead to the smooth stone where his circle had been, his hands spread flat on the floor as if begging the rock to take him too.

The torches guttered. One by one, they died, leaving only the faint gray light of distant dawn creeping through a crack in the cave ceiling. The cold spot in my chest pulsed again, and I pressed a hand to it, feeling the absence beneath my ribs like a hole where a tooth used to be.

I had won. I had survived. And I had just spent a sliver of my life to do it.

In the new darkness, I heard it—the distant thunder of boots, echoing through the tunnels. Many boots. Armored boots, moving fast, moving with purpose.

And above them, barely audible but unmistakable, a voice. A bellow, raw with fury and fear, echoing off stone walls.

"LILY!"

I closed my eyes. 

Father was coming.

title: Saint or Devil? Both?
prose:
# Chapter 23: Saint or Devil? Both?

The boots were not merely thunder. They were a landslide, a battering ram of armored feet pounding through the tunnels with a rhythm that shook loose dust from the cave ceiling and sent small stones skittering across the smooth stone floor where the cult's circle had been. The torches had mostly died, leaving only the thin gray light of early dawn filtering through the crack overhead, and in that half-darkness the sound of approaching men was enormous. I let my head fall back against the cold wall. My limbs had turned to something heavier than lead — something molten and slow, as if my bones had been replaced with cooling ore. The cold spot in my chest pulsed with each heartbeat, a dull and persistent wrongness that I did not have the energy to examine.

The cult leader had stopped sobbing. He lay crumpled on the floor, his hands still spread flat against the stone where his sacred circle had been, his forehead pressed to the rock as if he were listening for something buried beneath it. When the boots grew loud enough to shake the dust from his hood, he did not move. He had given up. I almost felt a flicker of respect for him — at least he had the decency to accept his failure without more screaming.

"LILY!"

The roar came down the tunnel like a physical force, bouncing off the walls and multiplying until it seemed to come from everywhere at once. My father's voice, raw with terror and fury, the voice of a man who had once bellowed challenges at the gates of my obsidian citadel and had somehow never lost that particular edge of desperation. I closed my eyes. There was no point in pretending to be strong. I was not strong. I was a ten-year-old girl who had just spent a sliver of her lifespan erasing a ritual circle with the Word of Unmaking, and I felt every single one of those stolen pages pressing against the inside of my ribs.

The boots arrived. A flood of them — royal guards in full plate, their swords drawn, their faces masks of urgency and fear. They filled the cave mouth and then parted, and through the gap strode King Alistair of Lumengarde, the Hero of Dawn, my father, his holy sword blazing with white-gold light that made me squint. His eyes found me immediately. He had been scanning the room for threats, his jaw set, his free hand already reaching for a spell — and then his gaze landed on me, small and pale against the cave wall, my torn dress stained with dust and what might have been a trace of blood from my nose, and his face broke open like a child's.

The sword went back into its sheath with a click I heard clearly across the cavern. He crossed the space in three strides that ate the distance like a predator's, and then he was on his knees before me, his armored gauntlets reaching for me and then stopping, hovering, as if he was afraid I would shatter if he touched me wrong. His hands were shaking. I had never seen my father's hands shake. They had held a sword against the Demon Lord's legions without trembling; they trembled now at the sight of his daughter with dirt on her face.

"My little miracle," he breathed, and the words came out cracked and uneven. "My Lily. Are you hurt? Did they harm you? Did any of them touch you, I swear by the dawn itself I'll —" His voice broke on the last word, and he stopped talking.

He scooped me up. It was not the careful, ceremonial lift of a king carrying his daughter through a formal occasion. It was the desperate clutch of a man who had just found something precious that he had been certain was lost forever. His arms banded around me, plate armor cold against my back, leather padding rough against my cheek, and the scent of him — steel oil and old sweat and the faint trace of the pine soap he used — filled my nose. I let my head fall against his shoulder. I did not have the strength to hold it up, and I was not going to waste energy pretending otherwise.

"They were bad men," I said into his shoulder. My voice came out small and reedy, which was not entirely an act. "They drew a circle and said mean things. They tried to take something from me."

A shiver ran through me — and I was surprised to find that it was genuine. The memory of the ritual, the dagger pressing against my palm, the chanting rising like a tide of filth, the moment when I had reached into the depths of my own soul and spent a piece of my future to make them stop — all of it pressed against me at once, and my body responded before my mind could stop it. My father's arms tightened around me. A growl rumbled up from his chest, a sound I had heard only in war stories, the noise a man makes when he wants to kill something.

"The Eternal Flame," he said, and his voice had gone flat and cold. "I know their kind. Filth who dress up cowardice as faith. They'll be dragged before the courts, every last one of them, and I'll personally —"

"Alistair." Queen Seraphina's voice cut through the cave like a blade through silk. She had entered behind him, silent as a shadow, and I had not heard her at all — which was deeply unsettling, because I had spent centuries learning to track the movements of everyone in a room. She walked past the guards, past her husband, past the sobbing cult leader on the floor, and stopped in the center of the cavern where the circle had been. She stood there for a long moment, her hands clasped before her, her eyes closed. Then she extended her right hand, palm down, and let it hover over the spot where the cult's ritual had drawn its lines.

She did not chant. She did not gesture. She simply stood there, eyes closed, her fingers spread, and I felt the weight of her attention like a physical thing pressing down on the air. The cold spot in my chest pulsed again, and I pressed my face harder into my father's shoulder to hide the expression that wanted to cross my face.

When Seraphina opened her eyes, her brow was furrowed. I had never seen her brow furrowed. The Saint of Mercy was a woman of serene certainty, of unshakeable calm, of the quiet confidence that comes from having personally delivered the killing blow to the most powerful dark being in the world. She did not frown. She did not look confused.

She looked confused now.

"The energy signature is gone," she said, and her voice was soft, almost wondering. "Completely. Not dispersed — there's no trace of it bleeding into the stone, no residue in the air, no echo in the ley lines beneath us. It's as if the ritual never happened at all." She paused, and her eyes found me over my father's shoulder. There was something in them that I could not name. "Erased."

The word hung in the air. I could feel my father's chest rise and fall beneath me, could feel the tension in his arms as he registered his wife's tone. He did not understand what she was saying, not really. He was a warrior, not a mage; for him, magic was a tool, a weapon, something to be used and then put away. He had never had to think about what it meant for a ritual's energy to be erased rather than dispersed.

But I knew. And Seraphina knew. And the question she asked next, soft and weighted with implications I could not afford to address, fell into the silence like a stone into deep water.

"Lily. What happened here?"

I buried my face deeper into Alistair's shoulder. The wool of his surcoat was scratchy against my cheek, and I focused on that sensation — the itch, the texture, the mundane physicality of it — to keep my voice steady. "They drew a circle," I said, muffled. "And they said mean things. And then the circle went away." I let my voice wobble. "The nice man who was talking — he said the circle was wrong. He said the Lord was angry. And then they all started screaming and running."

It was a masterpiece of selective truth. Every word was technically accurate. The cult leader had said the circle was wrong, had said the Lord was angry, had screamed and run — well, had tried to run, before his followers trampled him. The circle had gone away because I had spent a page of my future to erase it with the Word of Unmaking, but that was not a detail I needed to share.

My father's arms tightened around me. "The Lord," he repeated, and the growl was back in his voice. "They dared to invoke their filth in my kingdom, near my daughter — I'll have their tongues for it."

"Alistair." Seraphina's voice was gentle but firm. She had crossed the cavern and now knelt before us, her skirts pooling on the dusty stone, her hands reaching out to frame my face. Her fingers were cool against my cheeks. She turned my head gently, examining me with the clinical precision of a healer — my eyes, my nose, my cheeks, the faint shadow of a bruise where the cult leader had grabbed me. Her thumb brushed over the corner of my mouth, where a trace of dried blood from my nosebleed still lingered. She studied it for a moment, then let her hand fall.

Her fingers found my wrist. She pressed two fingers to my pulse point, her eyes drifting closed again, and I felt the faint push of her magic — a gentle, probing warmth, like sunlight filtered through silk, searching for wounds, searching for curses, searching for anything that should not be there. I held my breath. The warmth flowed over my skin, through my veins, around the cold spot in my chest.

It paused there. I felt it — a hesitation, a ripple in the flow of her magic as it encountered something it could not read. The void where my stolen lifespan had been. The hole in my future.

Then the warmth withdrew, and Seraphina opened her eyes.

Her expression had settled into serene certainty — the mask she wore when she had decided on a truth and would not be moved from it. "She is unharmed," she said. "The circle was unstable and collapsed. The cultists fled." She looked past me, at the guards who had secured the whimpering cult leader and were dragging him to his feet. His hood had fallen back, revealing a gaunt face streaked with tears and snot, his eyes wide and staring at me with an expression I could not quite parse — fear, yes, but something else beneath it. Something like reverence.

Seraphina did not look at him. She kept her eyes on me. "This is not a dark ritual," she said, and her voice carried through the cavern with the weight of scripture. "It is a blasphemous one. They used corrupted rites and were punished for their presumption. The circle rejected them because it was never holy to begin with — merely a mockery of true power. Lily is untouched."

She placed her hand on my head. Her palm was warm, her fingers gentle, and the gesture was a benediction — a mother's blessing, a saint's protection. The words she spoke next were meant to comfort.

"She is protected."

I felt them like a brand. A hot iron pressed against the soft tissue of my soul. Protected. Yes. Protected by the fact that I was the very creature they had been trying to summon, protected by my own stolen knowledge, protected by the pages of my own future that I had burned to make their circle vanish. I was protected in the same way a spider is protected by its web — I had built the trap myself, and now I was stuck in the center of it, waiting to see what flew in.

"Take them," my father said to the guards, jerking his chin toward the cultists. "All of them. I want every name, every face, every rat-hole they crawled out of. And I want them tried for treason against the crown and the kingdom." His voice had gone hard again, the voice of a king rather than a father. "No one threatens my daughter and walks away with their tongue."

The guards saluted and hauled the cult leader away. He did not resist. He did not even look at me. But as they dragged him toward the tunnel mouth, he began to laugh — a low, wet, broken sound that echoed off the walls and raised the hairs on my arms.

"The Lord's judgment," he said, and his voice was cracked and strange, the voice of a man who had seen something that had broken something important inside him. "The Lord's judgment has come. She is the vessel. She is the vessel and the contents, the cup and the wine, the mouth and the word —" The guards cuffed him, and the laughter cut off.

My father's arms tightened around me. "Ignore him," he said. "He's mad. They're all mad."

I did not say anything. I was not sure he was wrong.

---

The journey back through the tunnels was a blur of torchlight and echoing footsteps. My father carried me the whole way, his arms steady, his stride unhurried despite the guards flanking us. The cold spot in my chest pulsed with each of his steps, a dull ache that I tried to ignore. The air changed as we climbed — from the damp, mineral smell of deep stone to the cleaner scent of morning, and then to the perfumed warmth of the castle corridors.

Word had spread ahead of us. I could see it in the faces of the servants who pressed themselves against the walls as we passed — the wide eyes, the hushed whispers, the hands clasped to mouths. By the time we reached my rooms, the story had already grown to twice its size. The Princess had been kidnapped by a dark cult. The Princess had faced them alone. The Princess had been found untouched, protected, a miracle.

I heard fragments of it as Nurse Branna fussed over me, as the physician was called and then dismissed with a wave of Seraphina's hand, as the warm bath was drawn and I was lowered into water that smelled of lavender and chamomile. My father refused to leave. He sat on the stool beside the tub, his armor still on, his hands clasped in his lap, watching me as if I might disappear if he looked away.

"I should have been there," he said. His voice was rough. "I should have been faster. I should have —"

"Father." I reached out and put my damp hand on his gauntlet. The gesture was automatic, a piece of the mask I wore, but his reaction was not. His eyes went bright with moisture, and he caught my hand in both of his and pressed it to his chest.

"My little miracle," he said. "My brave, brave girl."

I let him hold my hand. I let him believe it. The water was warm, and the cold spot in my chest ached, and I did not have the strength to argue with a man who loved me so completely and understood me so little.

---

When I was finally alone, the bath long cold and the servants dismissed, I stood before the mirror in my bedchamber. The candles had burned down to stubs, casting long shadows across the walls. I wore a simple linen nightgown, my hair still damp and brushed flat against my skull, and I looked exactly like what I was supposed to look like: a small, pale, exhausted child who had been through an ordeal and come out the other side.

My eyes were clear. My face was composed. There were shadows under my eyes, but they could have been from fear or exhaustion or the natural pallor of a delicate constitution. Nothing about my reflection suggested that I had spent a sliver of my lifespan to erase a ritual circle with the Word of Unmaking. Nothing suggested that I was the Dark Lord Maledictus, reborn in the body of my enemy's daughter, wearing an innocence that was as much a prison as the gilded walls around me.

I touched my chest. The cold spot was still there, beneath my sternum, a place where the warmth of my own life did not quite reach. It ached, dully, like a bruise on a rib. I had traded pages of my future for the privilege of watching those fools flee. I had spent a piece of myself to protect a family I had once sworn to destroy.

A miracle. A protection. The irony pressed against me like a physical weight, heavy and cold, and I stood there in the candlelight with my hand over my heart and felt, for the first time since my rebirth, the full and terrible weight of being alone.

The cult thought I was a saint. The court thought I was a miracle. My father thought I was a blessing. My mother suspected something she could not name and chose not to look too closely.

No one knew the truth. No one could know the truth. I was the only being in the world who knew what I was — and I was not entirely certain anymore that I knew what I was becoming.

The candles guttered. The shadows leaned in. I stood before the mirror and watched the girl in the glass, and the girl in the glass watched me back, and neither of us had any idea what to say.

title: Daddy's Little Monster
prose:
# Chapter 24: Daddy's Little Monster

The journey was a smear of sensation and shadow. I was aware, in fragments, of being lifted, of the world tilting dizzily. My cheek rested against a surface that was hard, warm, and faintly vibrating. It smelled of worn leather and cold steel, a familiar, aggressive scent that made something old and deep in my soul want to recoil. Alistair’s armor. I was being carried against his chest. The vibration was his heartbeat, a steady, powerful thrum beneath my ear that did not match the erratic fluttering in my own ribcage.

I heard his voice, but the words were muffled, as if coming through deep water. “—move faster! The physician, now!” A command, edged with the kind of authority that bent the world to its will. Servants’ boots scuffed on stone, voices murmured urgent replies. A blanket was draped over me, the wool coarse against my cheek, scratching faintly with each of his strides. 

The cold spot in my chest, that aching void where a sliver of my life had been excised, pulsed with a dull, insistent throb. It was the price. The down payment on my survival.   And I had paid for it in years I would never live, in warmth my blood would no longer carry.

I drifted. The thrum of Alistair’s heart was a dark lullaby. The ache was a counter-rhythm. Occasionally, I would surface enough to feel a hand brush my hair back, to hear a whispered endearment that tasted like ash. Then the dark would fold me up again, soft and absolute.

 Then, the weight of a proper eiderdown coverlet, pressing me into the mattress. The air smelled of beeswax polish, dried lavender, and the lingering, faint ozone tang of my mother’s healing magic. My bedroom.

I kept my eyes closed for a long moment, cataloging. The distant, muffled sounds of the castle settling into its evening rhythms. The slight dip in the mattress to my left, indicating a weight. A scent, stronger now, of clean linen and that subtle, human musk that clung to my father even after bathing. He was here.

I opened my eyes.

The room was lit by a single candelabra on the bedside table, casting a warm, golden glow that did little to dispel the shadows clustering in the corners. And there he was, sitting in the brocaded armchair that was usually reserved for my music tutor. He had changed out of the armor, now wearing a simple tunic and trousers, the colors muted in the soft light.  He had not slept. The evidence was written in the pallor of his skin, the slight tremor in the hand that rested on the chair arm.

I made a small sound, a dry click in my throat. The effect was instantaneous. He leaned forward, his entire bearing shifting from exhaustion to a vibrant, fierce alertness.

“There she is.” His voice was a low rumble, rough with disuse and emotion. “My brave girl.”

He reached out. His hand, the hand that had wielded the Dawnbreaker to cleave my obsidian fortress in twain, that had ended the reign of Maledictus with a stroke of holy light, came to rest on my forehead.  I flinched, a tiny, involuntary jerk.

He noticed, of course. His expression flickered with concern. “Sore? The healer said there would be bruises. Those foul cultists… I should have torn them apart myself.”

“Father.” My voice emerged as a whisper, scraped raw. “You’re here.”

“As if I would be anywhere else.” He smiled, but it was a strained thing, not reaching the exhaustion in his eyes. “You gave us a fright, Lily. A terrible fright. When we found you… the circle was gone. Just bare stone. And you were lying there, so still…”

I remembered. The fading chant, the crumbling dagger, the desperate, wrong incantation I had corrected. And then the Word, a syllable of pure negation on my tongue, costing me breath and blood and time. The circle hadn’t just been broken. It had been unwritten, erased from the very fabric of the space. My mother had sensed that. I could tell by the way she had examined me earlier, her hands glowing with diagnostic light, her brow furrowed not with suspicion, but with a healer’s deep perplexity. She had found the void, the absence where the ritual’s energy should have been, and where a part of my own life force now resided as a deficit.

“You faced monsters,” Alistair continued, his voice thickening. “Alone. In the dark. And you came out… unharmed. Pure.” He swallowed hard, his Adam’s apple bobbing. He looked away for a moment, blinking rapidly, before meeting my gaze again. His eyes were shining, bright with unshed tears of pride. “You are the bravest person I have ever known. Even braver than I was in the Scorching Fields.”

The Scorching Fields. The final battlefield, the plains of ash and shattered obsidian where I had made my last stand. Where he had earned his epithet, the Hero of Dawn, by meeting my hellfire with a sun of his own making.  He was praising my bravery while extolling his greatest victory over me. The hand on my forehead was the hand of my destroyer, now stroking my hair with the gentle care of a man who has never known true loss. The irony was a blade twisting in a wound I hadn’t known I still possessed.

“I saw it,” he whispered, leaning closer. His breath was warm on my cheek. “The light around you. Your mother says the magic was all gone, that the cultists’ circle was inert. But she knows. She says you have a light that protects you.” He shook his head, a small, certain motion. “They’re wrong, of course. The light isn’t around you. It *is* you.”

He believed it. Every syllable. I could see the absolute, unshakeable faith in his eyes, the conviction of a man who had never had reason to doubt the fundamental goodness of his world, or of the daughter he thought he had made.  It was love, unconditional and profound, aimed at a version of me that did not exist, and yet felt, in this moment, like the only thing keeping me from shattering.

A hot, traitorous pressure built behind my eyes. My throat tightened. This was weakness. A system error. The Maledictus did not *feel* this sentimental, human affection. It was a liability, a vulnerability to be exploited, not internalized.  Not a creature who felt the sting of tears at the sound of his voice cracking with pride.

 I turned my head slightly, burying my cheek into the pillow, breaking the contact of his hand. My movement was sluggish, weighted with the bone-deep exhaustion that clung to me like a second skin.

“Sleep,” Alistair whispered, misunderstanding my movement as weariness. He pulled the eiderdown up more snugly around my shoulders, tucking it along my sides with a meticulous care that was almost comical in its intensity. “My little miracle. Sleep now. You’re safe. You’re home.”

He settled back in the chair, the wood creaking softly. Then, he began to hum.

It was a lullaby. An old one, a simple melody I recognized from the deepest, most tangled archives of my memory. A tune from before the war, from a time when such gentle sounds might have been part of my existence. But Alistair did not hum it with any technical skill. He was tone-deaf, a fact well-known to the court but usually masked by his booming speaking voice. Here, in the quiet intimacy of my sickroom, the flaw was laid bare. The melody wandered, the pitch wobbled, and he occasionally skipped a beat entirely, his humming trailing off before picking up again a measure later.

 

And yet.

The warmth in the room was not just from the candles. It radiated from him, a physical presence, a shield of simple, paternal devotion. His bad humming filled the spaces between the shadows, a defiant, off-key proclamation that here, in this room, nothing dark could touch me. 

I lay still, face half-buried in the pillow, feigning the drift toward sleep he expected. I listened to the tuneless lullaby. I felt the weight of the blankets, the silk against my skin, the phantom warmth of his hand still lingering on my forehead. The hero’s song was a discordant wreck. It was the auditory equivalent of a bludgeon dipped in honey. It was stupid, and sentimental, and completely, infuriatingly effective at unraveling my composure.

Exhaustion, profound and absolute, began to pull me under, a soft, dark tide. The cold spot was a stone in my chest, the warmth a stubborn ember beside it. My last coherent thought before the darkness claimed me fully was a bitter, bewildered admission that tasted like defeat.

*The Hero’s song is awful. And I… do not entirely hate it.*

The lullaby continued, wavering and true, as I fell.

***

I drifted in a state of half-awareness, a gray space between the abyss of true sleep and the sharp pain of full consciousness. Fragments of sensation intruded. The scratch of a wool blanket being adjusted. The cool touch of a damp cloth on my brow. My mother’s low, measured voice speaking to my father in the doorway, a murmur of medical terms and reassurances that I absorbed without processing. *Magical exhaustion, yes. The void she mentioned… an after-effect of the trauma. No lingering taint, her aura is bright, almost blindingly so.* The Saint, misreading the absolute void where my power had drained as a purity of light. The irony was so thick I could have choked on it.

More time passed. The candle guttered and was replaced. The castle noises faded to a deep quiet. The weight beside my bed remained constant. Alistair did not leave.

At some point, I must have truly slept, because the next thing I knew, a pale, watery light was filtering through the heavy curtains. The candles had burned to nubs. The armchair was empty. But the impression of presence lingered in the slight disarray of the cushion, the faint warmth still clinging to the fabric.

I lay still, staring at the canopy above my bed. The embroidered stars and moons, done in silver thread, seemed to mock me with their serene, celestial indifference. My body felt heavy, drained, as if all the marrow had been turned to lead. The cold spot was a persistent, dull ache, a permanent resident now. The trauma, they called it. A polite term for the self-inflicted wound of using the Word.

The door opened softly. It was Nurse Branna, her round face creased with concern. She carried a tray with a bowl of broth, steam rising in delicate curls, and a piece of toast cut into neat triangles. She moved with practiced quiet, setting the tray on the bedside table and fluffing my pillows with efficient, gentle hands.

“Your Highness is awake. Good. The king was most insistent you have sustenance the moment you stirred.” She arranged the pillows behind my back, propping me up with a care that made me feel like a fragile porcelain doll. “He’s just gone to brief the Queen on the… proceedings. The cultists are in the deepest cells. A right proper mess, that was.”

I said nothing, watching her. The simple, domestic normalcy of her actions felt alien after the night’s emotional onslaught.

“Now,” she said, her voice taking on a brisk, nurturing tone. “A few spoonfuls of broth to start. Doctor’s orders. No excitement, no strain. Just rest and building back your strength.” She lifted the bowl, a delicate porcelain thing painted with bluebells, and brought a spoonful to my lips.

The broth was rich, savory, and warm. It soothed my raw throat. I swallowed mechanically, my eyes still fixed on the space where my father had sat. Nurse Branna’s chatter filled the silence, a comforting drone about the weather, the garden, a funny thing the kitchen cat had done. It was noise designed to restore equilibrium, to paper over the cracks with the familiar.

I let it wash over me, a meaningless stream. My mind was elsewhere, caught in a loop. The feel of his hand. The sound of his broken song. The weight of the title he’d given me. *Miracle.* A word for something sacred, something inexplicable, something good. I was none of those things. I was a calculated deception, a walking lie, a vessel for a vengeful, ancient consciousness. Yet, the word clung to me, sticky and persistent.

When Branna left, promising to return in an hour to change the water in my basin, the silence of the room settled back in, heavier now. I sat with it, sipping the last of the broth. The numbness from the night before was receding, and in its place was a new, uncomfortable awareness. 

He saw a light. He saw bravery. He saw his little girl, his miracle, preserved and pure after facing darkness. He saw all of that, and he loved it with a totality that was terrifying. And I, Maledictus, the Dark Lord Reborn, the architect of a thousand schemes, felt the corrosive effect of that love doing something my own power never could. It was getting inside me. Not through force, but through a slow, steady seep, like water through stone. It was rewriting the calculations, introducing new variables I couldn't quantify. The cold spot was a void of my own making, a cost of my own power. The warmth was an invasion, unsolicited and potent.

I did not want this. This complication. This *affection*. It was a liability beyond measure. Affection could be exploited. Affection could lead to hesitation. Affection was the antithesis of the cold, clear vengeance that had sustained me for a decade in this prison of flesh.

And yet, when I closed my eyes, I could still feel the ghost of his calloused hand on my brow. I could still hear the melody, terrible and true.

 And somewhere beneath that hatred, in a place I refused to examine, the warmth spread, stubborn and unyielding.

The next time the door opened, it was my father again. He had changed into his formal tunic, the crest of Lumengarde embroidered over his heart, but his hair was still damp from washing, and he looked no more rested than he had in the night. He carried a small, covered dish.

“Thought you might want something sweet,” he said, his voice softer than usual, as if not to startle me. He set the dish on the table and uncovered it. A slice of honey cake, glistening with glaze. “From the kitchens. Your favorite.”

He looked at me, waiting. The adoration was back in his eyes, clear and bright, undimmed by time or sleep. The guilt coiled tighter in my gut. I was a poison. A corruption in his perfect, happy world. And he was offering me cake.

“Thank you, Father,” I murmured, my voice small. The mask felt like it was melting, fusing to my skin.

He smiled, and this time, it reached his eyes, crinkling the corners. “That’s my girl. We’ll have you up and about in no time. Perhaps a turn in the gardens later? The sun is good for the constitution.” He reached out, then seemed to think better of it, letting his hand fall to his side. “Just rest today, though. Doctor’s orders. And mine.”

He lingered, watching me take a tentative bite of the cake. 

When he finally left, promising to return after his council meeting, the cake was gone and the room felt emptier than before. I stared at the empty plate, at the crumbs clinging to the porcelain. The cold spot pulsed. The warmth lingered, a ghost of touch and sound and a terrible, beautiful, misplaced faith.

I was Maledictus. I did not feel this. This sentimental, human weakness. It was a bug in my code, a glitch in the resurrection matrix. And yet, as the morning light grew stronger, chasing the last shadows from the corners, I found myself not pushing the warmth away, but simply existing alongside it, the two sensations warring in the silent space behind my ribs. The hero’s daughter. The villain’s soul. A little miracle, wrapped in a lie.

title: Demanding Demonic Pets
prose:
# Chapter 25: Demanding Demonic Pets

The broth was lukewarm and too salty, but I sipped it anyway, letting the porcelain bowl hide my face while my father’s voice boomed through the room like a poorly tuned war horn. He was recounting the capture of the cultists again—how the royal guards had cornered them in a ravine, how not a single arrow had been loosed, how the cult leader had wept like a child when confronted with the might of Lumengarde. I nodded at the appropriate moments, my fingers tightening around the spoon just enough to feel the metal bite into my skin. 

*Focus,* I told myself. *This is data. The Hero of Dawn is proud, predictable, and utterly unaware that his greatest enemy is currently wearing a nightgown with embroidered bunnies.*

Alistair leaned forward, his elbows resting on his knees, the fabric of his tunic straining slightly over his shoulders. He had changed into something more formal since last night, but his hair was still damp at the temples, curling slightly where it met his skin. The scent of soap and something faintly metallic—probably the remnants of whatever oil he used to polish his armor—drifted toward me. I resisted the urge to wrinkle my nose. The man smelled like a blacksmith’s forge, and I had spent the last decade in a body that preferred the scent of old books and candle wax.

“And then,” he said, grinning like a man who had just invented storytelling, “the cult leader—what was his name, Stablemaster?”

The Stablemaster, a gaunt man with a face like a disappointed hound, cleared his throat from his post by the door. “High Priest Veldrin, Your Majesty.”

“Right, Veldrin!” Alistair clapped his hands together, making the broth in my bowl ripple. “He looks at me, and he says, ‘You don’t understand what you’ve done!’ And I say—”

“‘You’re right,’” I murmured, my voice soft. “‘I don’t.’”

Alistair blinked, then threw his head back and laughed, the sound filling the room like a physical force. “Exactly! Oh, Lily, you’ve got my sense of humor. That’s my girl.” He reached out as if to ruffle my hair, then seemed to think better of it, letting his hand drop back to his knee. “You should’ve seen his face. Like he’d swallowed a lemon whole.”

I set the bowl aside, my fingers lingering on the smooth edge of the porcelain.  I hated it. Hated the way my body betrayed me by enjoying something so mundane, so *human*. But the drain from the Word of Unmaking had left me weaker than I cared to admit, and even the simplest spells felt like trying to lift a mountain with a teaspoon.

*This is temporary,* I reminded myself. *A setback. A necessary cost.*

Alistair was still talking, his voice a steady, comforting rumble. “The physician says you’ll be up and about in a few days. Maybe a turn in the gardens? The sun’s good for the constitution.”

I let my gaze drift toward the window, where the morning light spilled across the floor in golden rectangles. The gardens. Where my mana battery had been repurposed into a decorative curiosity, where the court ladies now left offerings of polished stones at the base of the topiary rabbit like it was some kind of shrine. The thought made my teeth ache.

“Father,” I said, letting my voice take on a hesitant, dreamy quality.  “The recovery is… dull.”

He leaned in instantly, his eyes brightening. “Of course it is! You’re a miracle, Lily. You shouldn’t be cooped up in here like some invalid.” He waved a hand dismissively. “What do you need? A puppy? A kitten? A falcon? I’ll have the Stablemaster fetch you one by sundown.”

I shook my head, letting my lower lip tremble just slightly.  “I saw a picture in a book,” I said, my voice barely above a whisper. “Of a horse. But not a normal one. A special one.”

Alistair’s grin widened. “A horse! Now that’s a proper pet for a princess. We’ll get you the finest mare in the stables. White as snow, with a mane like silk—”

“No,” I said, cutting him off before he could launch into another heroic monologue about the virtues of white horses. I let my fingers twist together in my lap, a gesture I had learned made me look small and uncertain. “Not white. Black. Like… like the night sky. And with…” I hesitated, letting my voice trail off as if the next part was too silly to say aloud. “With red eyes. Like a storybook nightmare.”

The room went very still.

The Stablemaster made a sound somewhere between a cough and a squeak. Alistair’s grin faltered, his eyes flickering toward the man by the door as if seeking confirmation that he had heard me correctly. I kept my gaze fixed on my hands, my heart hammering against my ribs. *Too much. Too demonic. He’ll see through it. He’ll—*
