Then Alistair laughed.

It started as a chuckle, deep and warm, and then it grew, swelling until his shoulders shook and his eyes crinkled at the corners. He slapped his knee, his laughter filling the room like a physical force, and I felt something inside me twist. Not fear. Not relief. Something worse. Something that felt suspiciously like disappointment.

“A black pony with red eyes!” he wheezed, wiping at his eyes with the back of his hand. “Oh, Lily, that is the most wonderfully morbid thing I have ever heard! You have your mother’s taste for the dramatic and my love for the absurd!” He turned to the Stablemaster, who looked like he had just been told his favorite horse had been replaced with a demon. “You hear the lady! Find the darkest colt you can! And for the eyes… well, we’ll have the royal artificer tint its tack, eh? Or maybe a nice conjurer for a glamour? Surprise me!”

The Stablemaster bowed so deeply I thought he might tip over. “At once, Your Majesty.” He scurried from the room like a man fleeing a burning building, and I was left staring at my father, my carefully crafted request now lying between us like a live coal.

Alistair was still grinning, his earlier mirth fading into something softer, more affectionate. “You’re something else, you know that? A black pony with red eyes. I love it.” He reached out, his calloused fingers brushing against my cheek. I forced myself not to flinch. “You’ll have to name it something suitably dramatic. How about… Midnight?”

I swallowed the urge to correct him. *Midnight is pedestrian. If you’re going to indulge this fantasy, at least do it properly. Nyx. Vesper. Umbra.*

“That sounds lovely,” I said instead, my voice small.

Alistair beamed, clearly taking my lack of enthusiasm as shyness. “That’s my girl. We’ll have it brought to the courtyard tomorrow. You can meet it when you’re feeling up to it.” He pushed himself to his feet, his joints popping like kindling in a fire. “I’ve got a council meeting to attend, but I’ll check on you later. Try to rest, all right? Doctor’s orders.”

I nodded, watching as he strode toward the door, his boots thudding against the floor. He paused at the threshold, turning back to look at me. “And Lily?”

“Yes, Father?”

“No more talk of nightmares, all right? You’re safe here.” He smiled, and for a moment, I saw the man who had stood against the darkness and won. The man who had looked into the abyss and refused to blink. “You’re my miracle.”

The door clicked shut behind him, and I was left alone with the silence and the weight of my own thoughts.

*He doesn’t see it.*

The realization settled over me like a shroud. I had expected suspicion. Hesitation. At the very least, a flicker of doubt. But Alistair had seen my request for what it was—a child’s whimsy, dark and dramatic, but ultimately harmless. He had taken my carefully constructed test and turned it into a gift, wrapping it in love and indulgence like it was nothing more than a pretty bauble.

And that was the problem.

I had spent years probing the limits of his perception, testing how far I could push before the mask slipped. But the mask wasn’t slipping. It wasn’t even *bending*. It was expanding, stretching to accommodate every dark, twisted thing I threw at it, until even the most blatant displays of malice were reinterpreted as quirks of a precocious child.

*He doesn’t see the demon. He sees the daughter.*

The thought was a blade between my ribs, sharp and unexpected. I pressed a hand to my chest, my fingers brushing against the cold spot where the Word had carved away a piece of me. It pulsed in response, a steady, rhythmic ache that was becoming as familiar as my own heartbeat.

I should have been pleased. This was what I had wanted, wasn’t it? A father who loved me so completely that he would never suspect the truth. A court that saw my schemes as genius, my malice as charm. It was the perfect cover. The ultimate infiltration.

So why did it feel like a cage?

I exhaled sharply, forcing the thought away. *Emotions are a liability. Focus on the objective.*

The pony was a test. A probe. And it had yielded valuable data. Alistair’s reaction had been clear: he would indulge any request, no matter how dark, as long as it was framed as a child’s fancy. 

Forbidden grimoires. Artifacts. Access to restricted sections of the library.

Power.

The thought sent a shiver down my spine, but it wasn’t fear. It was anticipation. The cold spot in my chest throbbed in agreement, a silent reminder of what I was capable of. What I *would* be capable of, once I had the resources to match my knowledge.

I pushed myself up from the bed, my legs unsteady beneath me. The physician had left a walking stick propped against the nightstand, a gnarled thing of polished oak with a silver handle shaped like a roaring lion. I ignored it, taking a tentative step toward the window. The floor was cold beneath my bare feet, the stone leaching the warmth from my skin.

Outside, the courtyard was alive with activity. Servants scurried like ants, their arms laden with baskets and trays. A group of guards marched in formation, their armor glinting in the sunlight. And there, in the center of it all, was the Stablemaster, his face a mask of barely contained panic as he barked orders at a cluster of grooms.

I watched as one of the grooms led forward a small, sleek pony, its coat as dark as polished obsidian. It was a pretty thing, with a glossy mane and a tail that swished lazily in the breeze. The groom held it steady while another man—probably the royal artificer—knelt beside it, his hands moving in quick, precise gestures. A faint shimmer of magic rippled over the pony’s eyes, and for a moment, they glowed a deep, unnatural red before settling into a more natural, if still striking, hue.

*Not demonic,* I thought, my lips curling into a frown. *Just a glamour. A trick of the light.*

It was the illusion of darkness, wrapped in adoring indulgence. A gift from a doting father, interpreting his daughter’s request as nothing more than a child’s whimsy.

The groom led the pony toward the center of the courtyard, where a small crowd had gathered. I recognized a few of the courtiers—Lady Elara, with her perpetually pinched expression, and Lord Cedric, who was currently laughing at something the Stablemaster had said. They were all watching the pony with varying degrees of amusement, their voices carrying through the open window in a low, excited murmur.

I pressed my palm against the glass, my breath fogging the surface. The pony was not evil. It was not even particularly remarkable, beyond its coat and the glamour on its eyes. It was a well-bred animal, nothing more. And yet, as I watched it nuzzle the groom’s hand, its ears twitching with curiosity, I felt something inside me shift.

This was not the test I had expected. The pony was a prop, a distraction. The real test had been Alistair’s reaction, and he had passed with flying, misguided colors.

I turned away from the window, my fingers curling into fists at my sides. The cold spot pulsed, a steady, insistent reminder of what I had lost—and what I could still gain.

The next day, the pony would be brought to me. A gift. A symbol of my father’s love.

And I would accept it.

Because a pony with red eyes was just the beginning.

---

The morning dawned bright and clear, the kind of day that made the castle’s stone walls glow like honey in the sunlight. 

I dressed quickly, choosing a simple gown of deep blue with silver embroidery along the sleeves.  I twisted my hair into a loose braid, letting a few strands escape to frame my face. 

When I stepped into the courtyard, the pony was already there, tethered to a post near the fountain. It was smaller than I had expected, its legs slender and its head bowed slightly as it nosed at a pile of hay. The glamour on its eyes had faded overnight, leaving them a more natural brown, but the Stablemaster had clearly taken Alistair’s request to heart. A thin band of red-dyed leather circled its head, the color bright against its dark coat, and a matching ribbon had been woven into its mane.

It was ridiculous.

It was perfect.

I approached slowly, my slippers whispering against the cobblestones. The pony lifted its head as I drew near, its ears twitching forward with interest. Its eyes were wide and dark, the red leather doing little to disguise their natural color. It was, in every way, an ordinary pony.

And yet, as I reached out to touch its neck, I felt a strange, unexpected thrill run through me. Its coat was warm beneath my fingers, the muscles beneath the skin shifting as it turned to nuzzle my palm. It made a soft, contented sound, its breath hot against my skin, and I found myself smiling before I could stop myself.

*Pathetic,* I thought, even as my fingers curled into the softness of its mane. *It’s just a pony.*

But it wasn’t. Not really. It was a symbol. A promise. A reminder that my father would give me anything I asked for, no matter how dark, as long as I framed it as a child’s fancy.

The Stablemaster cleared his throat behind me, and I turned to find him standing a respectful distance away, his hands clasped behind his back. “Your Highness,” he said, bowing slightly. “His Majesty thought you might like to take him for a ride. There’s a saddle and bridle inside, if you’re feeling up to it.”

I glanced toward the stables, where a groom was leading out a small, ornate saddle. It was a pretty thing, the leather tooled with gold and silver, the stirrups sized for a child’s feet. The sight of it made something inside me twist, a strange, uncomfortable sensation that I refused to name.

“I’m not sure,” I said, my voice carefully hesitant. “I’ve never ridden before.”

The Stablemaster’s expression softened. “No need to worry, Your Highness. Midnight is as gentle as they come. He’ll take care of you.”

*Midnight.* The name grated against my nerves like sandpaper. It was too simple, too safe. But I nodded anyway, letting him lead the pony toward me. The groom brought the saddle forward, and I watched as they fitted it onto the pony’s back, the leather creaking softly as they tightened the girth.

I let them help me onto the pony’s back, my legs dangling awkwardly on either side. The saddle was higher than I had expected, the pony’s warmth seeping through the fabric of my gown. I gripped the reins tightly, my knuckles white, and the pony shifted beneath me, its muscles bunching as it adjusted to my weight.

“Easy,” the Stablemaster murmured, his hand resting on the pony’s neck. “He knows you’re new to this. Just let him guide you.”

I nodded, my throat suddenly dry. The pony took a tentative step forward, and I tightened my grip on the reins, my heart pounding in my chest. It was just a pony. Just a simple, ordinary pony.

And yet, as it carried me forward, its hooves clicking against the cobblestones, I felt something inside me uncoil. A tension I hadn’t even realized I was carrying. The cold spot in my chest pulsed, but for once, it didn’t feel like a void. It felt like a challenge.

The courtyard was alive with activity, the usual bustle of servants and guards paused as they watched me ride. I caught sight of Alistair standing near the fountain, his arms crossed over his chest, a proud smile on his face. He waved, and I lifted a hand in response, my fingers trembling slightly.

*This is power,* I thought, as the pony carried me forward. *Not the kind I was born with. Not the kind I lost. But power all the same.*

And for the first time in a long time, I let myself imagine what it might be like to wield it.

---

The ride was short, little more than a circuit of the courtyard, but by the time I dismounted, my legs were trembling and my palms were slick with sweat. The Stablemaster and groom helped me down, their hands steady beneath my elbows, and I let them guide me to a bench near the fountain.

Alistair was there in an instant, his face alight with pride. “Well? What do you think?”

I looked up at him, my breath still coming in quick, shallow gasps. The pony—Midnight—stood a few paces away, its head bowed as it nibbled at the grass near the fountain. The red leather around its eyes caught the sunlight, glinting like a warning.

“He’s… wonderful,” I said, my voice soft.

Alistair beamed, clapping his hands together. “I knew you’d love him! And just wait until you see what the artificer can do with his tack. We’ll have him looking like a proper nightmare in no time.”

I forced a smile, my fingers twisting together in my lap. The pony was nothing like what I had envisioned. It was small, gentle, utterly ordinary. And yet, as I watched it nuzzle the groom’s hand, I felt something inside me shift.

This was not the test I had expected. But it was a test all the same.

And I had passed.

The next few days passed in a blur of activity. The pony—Midnight, much to my continued annoyance—became a fixture in the courtyard, and I found myself spending more and more time with him. 

It was a weakness. A distraction.

And yet, I couldn’t bring myself to care.

Alistair, of course, was delighted. He took every opportunity to praise my “bond” with the pony, his voice booming through the courtyard as he recounted my “bravery” to anyone who would listen. The courtiers humored him, their smiles polite and their eyes carefully blank as they watched me ride. Only Seraphina seemed to notice the way my fingers trembled when I gripped the reins, the way my breath hitched when the pony took a step too quickly.

“You’re tense,” she said one afternoon, her voice quiet as she watched me dismount. “Are you sure you’re feeling well?”

I forced a smile, my fingers brushing against the pony’s neck. “Just tired. It’s been a long day.”

Seraphina’s gaze lingered on me for a moment longer, her eyes sharp and assessing. Then she nodded, her expression softening. “Perhaps a rest, then. The physician said you’re still recovering.”

I nodded, letting the groom lead the pony away. The cold spot in my chest pulsed in agreement, a steady, insistent reminder of what I had lost. But for once, the ache of it didn’t feel like a wound. It felt like a promise.

That night, I lay in bed, staring up at the canopy above me. The room was quiet, the only sound the distant murmur of the guards changing shift outside my door. I pressed a hand to my chest, my fingers brushing against the cold spot. It was still there, a void where a sliver of my lifespan had been carved away. But it no longer felt like an absence. It felt like a beginning.

I closed my eyes, letting my thoughts drift. The pony was a test. A probe. And it had yielded valuable data. Alistair’s reaction had been clear: he would indulge any request, no matter how dark, as long as it was framed as a child’s fancy.

The thought sent a shiver down my spine, but it wasn’t fear. It was anticipation. The cold spot pulsed in agreement, a silent reminder of what I was capable of. What I *would* be capable of, once I had the resources to match my knowledge.

I turned onto my side, my fingers curling into the sheets. The pony was just the beginning. A symbol. A promise.

And I would use it.

Because a pony with red eyes was nothing compared to what came next.

title: Library Espionage 101
prose:
# Chapter 26: Library Espionage 101

The physician’s verdict arrived at breakfast, delivered with the same solemnity one might reserve for announcing the birth of a new heir. “Her Highness is fit for light activity,” he declared, his voice echoing slightly in the grand dining hall. I kept my eyes on my porridge, stirring it with exaggerated care,  

Alistair clapped his hands together so hard the silverware rattled. “Excellent! What do you say, Lily? A project to celebrate your recovery? Something to keep that brilliant mind of yours occupied.” He beamed at me, his eyes alight with the kind of pride that made my teeth ache. I forced my lips into a small, shy smile, the kind that made the courtiers coo and Seraphina’s gaze sharpen just a fraction.

“I’ve always been fond of the library,” I said, my voice soft, hesitant. “Perhaps I could help organize it? Just a little. To learn.” The words tasted like ash in my mouth, but I kept the smile plastered on. The library was the heart of the castle’s knowledge, and knowledge was power. 

Alistair’s face lit up like a torch. “A scholar in the making! Just like your mother.” He turned to Seraphina, who was watching me with that quiet, assessing look of hers. “What do you think, my love? Lily, reorganizing the royal archives?”

Seraphina’s fingers stilled around her teacup. “It’s an ambitious project for a child,” she said carefully. “The library is vast. And Master Theron is… particular about his domain.”

I lowered my eyes, letting my lashes flutter against my cheeks. “I wouldn’t want to overstep. I just thought… perhaps I could learn from him. If he’d allow it.” The lie slid off my tongue with practiced ease. 

Alistair waved a hand dismissively. “Nonsense. Theron would be honored to have your assistance. Wouldn’t you, Theron?” He turned to the librarian, who had been hovering near the doorway like a nervous sparrow. Master Theron’s fingers twisted together, his knuckles white against the dark fabric of his robes.

“Of course, Your Majesty,” he said, his voice thin. “It would be an honor to guide Her Highness.” His eyes darted to me, and I could see the wariness in them. 

I inclined my head, the picture of demure gratitude. “Thank you, Master Theron. I promise I won’t be any trouble.”

Alistair laughed, the sound booming through the hall. “Trouble? Lily? Never. You’re the most diligent child I’ve ever met.” He ruffled my hair, and I resisted the urge to flinch. The cold spot in my chest pulsed, a reminder of the lifespan I had sacrificed to save myself from the cult. 

---

The library was a labyrinth of towering shelves and dust motes dancing in the sunlight that filtered through the high, arched windows. The air smelled of old parchment and candle wax, the scent thick enough to taste. 

“This is the main collection,” he said, gesturing to the rows of books that stretched into the shadows. “We have texts on history, philosophy, magic—though the latter are restricted, of course.” His eyes flicked to me, gauging my reaction.

I nodded, my expression carefully blank. “Of course. I wouldn’t dream of overstepping.” 

Theron relaxed slightly, though his fingers still twitched at his sides. “Your Highness mentioned wanting to learn. Perhaps we could start with something simple. The royal genealogies, perhaps? They’re quite fascinating.”

 “I’ve heard there are texts on magical theory. For beginners, of course. Just to understand the basics.”

Theron’s eyebrows shot up. “Magical theory? That’s rather advanced for—”

“For a child?” I finished, my voice soft. “I know. But I’ve always been curious. And Father says curiosity is the first step to wisdom.” 

Theron hesitated, then nodded. “Very well. I’ll fetch a few introductory texts. But you must promise to be careful. Magic is not a toy.”

I nodded, my eyes wide and innocent. “I promise.”

As soon as he turned his back, I let the mask slip. My fingers curled into fists, my nails biting into my palms.  

Theron returned with a stack of books, their spines creaking as he set them on the table. “These should do for a start. They’re quite basic, but they’ll give you an idea of the fundamentals.”

I reached for the top book, my fingers brushing against the leather cover. It was warm, as if it had been waiting for me. “Thank you, Master Theron. I’ll take good care of them.”

He nodded, though his eyes lingered on me for a moment longer than necessary. “I’ll leave you to it, then. If you need anything, I’ll be in my office.”

I waited until he was out of sight before I let out a slow breath. 

I stood, my chair scraping against the stone floor. The library was vast, but I had time. And patience. I would find what I was looking for.

---

The first week passed in a blur of dust and ink. I catalogued texts, created a new indexing system, and “discovered” several “lost” volumes of royal poetry. The poetry was dreadful, but it served its purpose. It distracted Theron, made him think I was nothing more than a precocious child with a love of books.

Theron, to his credit, was a fast learner. He began to relax around me, his initial wariness giving way to something akin to pride. “Her Highness has a remarkable mind,” he told a group of courtiers one afternoon, his voice warm with admiration. “She’s reorganized the entire poetry section in a week. And her notes! Impeccable.”

The courtiers cooed, their eyes soft with affection. “Such a diligent child,” one murmured. “She recovers by improving the castle.”

I ducked my head, letting my hair fall forward to hide my expression.  What I cared about were the hidden alcoves, the false shelves, the sections marked “restricted” that I now had a legitimate reason to browse.

Theron, bless his nervous heart, was my unwitting guide. He showed me the library’s true architecture, pointing out the hidden nooks and crannies with the pride of a man who had spent his life among books. “This section is for historical texts,” he said, gesturing to a shelf near the back. “And this one is for—”

“Restricted,” I finished, my eyes flicking to the small, unobtrusive sign. “What’s in there?”

Theron hesitated. “Texts that are… not suitable for general reading. Ancient magic, forbidden rituals. The kind of knowledge that’s better left buried.”

I nodded, my expression carefully neutral. “I understand. But if they’re part of the library’s collection, shouldn’t they be properly catalogued? For historical accuracy?”

Theron’s fingers twisted together. “I suppose. But they’re not for—”

“For children,” I finished again, my voice soft. “I know. But I’d like to learn, Master Theron. To understand why they’re forbidden.”

Theron sighed, but he nodded. “Very well. But you must promise not to touch anything. Just look.”

I promised, my fingers crossed behind my back. I had no intention of keeping that promise.

---

The restricted section was exactly what I had hoped for. The shelves were lined with texts on demonology, soul transference, the Word of Unmaking. My fingers itched to pull them from the shelves, to devour their contents, but I forced myself to be patient. I was a child, a prodigy, a curiosity. I had to play the part.

I spent three afternoons “examining” the texts, committing their critical passages to memory before returning them to their shelves. The accounts of the Demon Lord’s weaknesses were flawed, riddled with inaccuracies and half-truths. The Heroes had never truly understood the power they had faced. But the partial diagram of the soul-anchor ritual was promising. With the Codex Animarum to cross-reference, I could piece together the missing fragments.

Baphomutt, of course, was a constant source of chaos. The imp had taken to “helping” by stealing small trinkets and hiding them in the forbidden section. One afternoon, I found Master Theron’s favorite quill tucked behind a tome on necromancy, its feather bent and its inkwell cracked.

Theron was horrified. “That’s my best quill! How did it—”

I gasped, my hand flying to my mouth. “Oh no! It must have fallen during my purge. We must be thorough, Master Theron. We can’t have anything out of place.” I retrieved the quill, holding it out to him with a solemn expression. “Here. It’s safe now.”

Theron took the quill, his eyes filled with gratitude. “Thank you, Your Highness. You’re a lifesaver.”

I smiled, my fingers curling into my palm. The quill was returned, but now I knew exactly where the most sensitive texts were located. Baphomutt’s chaos was consistently useful, a fact I acknowledged with a grudging mental note to not feed him to the dogs. For now.

---

The month drew to a close, and I presented my new organizational chart to the King and Queen.  Demonology was filed under “Applied Geomancy,” poison lore under “Theoretical Herbalism.” The restricted section was buried beneath a labyrinth of cross-references, its true contents obscured by the sheer volume of mundane texts.

Alistair examined the chart, his eyes wide with admiration. “Lily, this is incredible! You’ve organized the entire library in a month. You’re a prodigy of administration.”

I curtsied, my cheeks flushed with false modesty. “Thank you, Father. I just wanted to help.”

Seraphina took the chart from Alistair, her eyes scanning the titles. Her fingers stilled on “Applied Geomancy,” and I held my breath. But she only smiled, her expression soft. “It is very thorough, Lily. You’ve done well.”

I curtsied again, my heart pounding. The library was mine. The game had changed.

---

That night, I lay in bed, staring up at the canopy above me. The cold spot in my chest pulsed, a steady, insistent reminder of what I had lost. But for the first time, the ache of it didn’t feel like a wound. It felt like a promise.

I had spent a lifetime wielding power like a blade, carving my name into the bones of the world. But now, I was learning the art of infiltration. The library was just the beginning. I would uncover the secrets the Heroes had buried, piece together the rituals they had feared, and reclaim the power that was rightfully mine.

And when I did, they would never see it coming.

title: Poison-Proof Prince
prose:
# Chapter 27: Poison-Proof Prince

The small drawing room on the eastern wing of the palace smelled of lavender and old varnish, a room selected specifically for its lack of strategic value.  The drawing room was my stage. The tea was my weapon. And the audience of one was already approaching, if the thunderous footsteps in the corridor were any indication.

*Thud. Thud. Thud.* Each footfall landed with the grace of a falling anvil.

 He was enormous, as always, a wall of golden fur and corded muscle poured into formal attire that the court tailors had labored over for weeks. The silver-embroidered tunic strained across his shoulders, the delicate threadwork shimmering like captured starlight against tawny fur. He looked like a war bear stuffed into a birthday cake.

"Lily!" He announced my name the way a siege engine announces a wall. "I brought you a gift!"

He thrust his arms forward, presenting his offering with the solemn gravity of a general presenting battle standards. In his massive hands, he held a stuffed bear. The bear's head was sewn on backwards, its button eyes staring at its own felt rump with an expression of permanent existential bewilderment. One of its arms was longer than the other, and the stitching along its belly was a chaotic topography of knots and tangles, as though it had been assembled during an earthquake by someone working from a verbal description of a bear they'd heard about once in a dream.

I stared at the bear.

I stared at Leo.

My mind, that vast and terrible repository of infernal knowledge, could not categorize what I was seeing.  But this creature — this misshapen, backwards-headed, lopsided monstrosity — existed beyond any classification system I had ever devised.

"To match your fighting spirit!" Leo declared, his voice filling every corner of the room like water through a cracked dam. "The court seamstress wept when I described what I wanted. She wept with joy, I think!"

*She wept, certainly. Whether from joy is a matter of considerable debate.*

I accepted the bear with both hands, my fingers curling into the cheap stuffing. Its button eyes swiveled to stare at me. One of them was loose. It felt like looking into the face of cosmic indifference. "It's... very thoughtful, Prince Leo."

"Leo!" He corrected, beaming. "We are past formalities, you and I. We have sparred! We have shared tea! I have seen you glare at me with the fury of a winter hawk! These are the bonds of true friendship."

*Bonds of true friendship.* 

I set the bear on the side table, positioning it upright against the wall so its reversed head faced the room with quiet, accusatory judgment. Leo noticed and grinned, apparently interpreting my careful placement as pride of display.

"You will treasure it always," he said, with a certainty that precluded any response.

*In my next life, if such a thing exists, I will ensure this bear is burned first.*

---

The tea service arrived carried by a junior servant whose name I had never bothered to learn — a pale, nervous creature who moved through the drawing room like a mouse through a cat's territory. She set the tray on the low table between the chaise longue and the stiff-backed chair Leo had claimed, her hands trembling just enough to make the porcelain rattle.  

 The pot was warm under my fingers as I lifted it, and I poured Leo's cup with the steady, precise movements of someone who had once administered poisons to an entire embassy of rival warlocks. My smile was serene. My eyes were calm. My left hand rested in my lap, where the small cloth packet had been transferred from my pocket, its contents — a fine, tasteless powder brewed from *Radix purgantis*, a rare root harvested from the marshlands south of the Scorching Fields — had already been dissolved into his cup during the pour.

 Within an hour of ingestion, it would initiate a thorough and deeply unpleasant cleansing of the digestive tract — not lethal, but profoundly inconvenient, guaranteed to send its victim running for the nearest privy with the urgency of a man fleeing a collapsing building. The goal was not death. Death was too quick, too clean, and far too final to serve my purposes. The goal was *humiliation*. A prince of the Beastfolk, doubled over in agony in the corridors of the Lumengarde palace, attended by every court physician and gossipping servant within earshot — the image would linger in diplomatic memory for decades. The beastfolk delegation would withdraw in shame. Leo's carefully cultivated reputation for indomitable constitution would crumble. And I, small and quiet and overlooked, would be the architect of it all, sipping my own unpoisoned tea with the satisfaction of a plan perfectly executed.

"I hope you enjoy it, Prince Leo," I said, my voice light and girlish, pitched to the exact frequency that the court had come to associate with precocious innocence. "I blended this myself. The jasmine is from the royal gardens, and the mountain herb is said to aid in recovery after vigorous exercise."

*A vigorous exercise of his colon, specifically.*

Leo accepted the cup. It looked comically small in his hands, like a thimble held by a giant. He raised it to his nose and inhaled deeply, his nostrils flaring, his eyes closing in concentration. For a moment, the drawing room was silent except for the faint crackle of the fire in the hearth and the distant, ever-present hum of the palace's ambient magical wards.

"Smells like a challenge!" Leo opened his eyes, grinning with the unshakable confidence of a man who had never met a problem he couldn't solve by being louder. "I accept!"

He drained the cup in a single, convulsive gulp. His throat bobbed. He smacked his lips appreciatively, twice, then set the cup down on the table with a decisive *clink*.

"Excellent," he pronounced. "Light. Clean. There is a strength in it that sneaks up on you, like a fox in tall grass. You have a gift, Lily."

*I have several gifts, none of which you are currently appreciating.*

---

I settled back into the chaise longue, my own cup cradled in both hands, and began to count.

Five minutes. Leo was talking about his morning training, his hands carving broad, sweeping arcs through the air as he described a grappling technique he had developed — or more accurately, *invented on the spot*, since beastfolk combat traditions favored spontaneity over formal curriculum. His voice filled the room, bouncing off the floral wallpaper and settling into the curtains like smoke. I let it wash over me, a meaningless tide of words, while my internal clock ticked with the precision of an hourglass.

Ten minutes. Leo had moved from grappling to a recounting of his most recent wrestling match with the ambassador from the Northern Marches, a barrel-chested man known for his stubbornness and his collection of ceremonial arm-rings. According to Leo, the match had lasted three hours, involved two broken chairs, and ended with the ambassador conceding after Leo sat on him. He described this sequence of events with unflagging enthusiasm, apparently unaware that sitting on one's opponent was not, in any formal combat tradition, a recognized finishing move.

Fifteen minutes. The fire in the hearth had burned lower, the embers settling into a bed of orange light that cast long, trembling shadows across the floor. Leo was still talking. I was still waiting. The *Radix purgantis* should have begun its work by now — the standard onset period was fifteen to twenty minutes, depending on the individual's weight and the state of their stomach. Leo was large, admittedly, but he had also consumed the entire dose in a single gulp, which should have accelerated the effect. I shifted my grip on my teacup, the porcelain cool against my fingers, and allowed myself a moment of mild professional concern. The root was fresh. I had verified its potency myself, crushing it with a mortar and pestle at dawn while Baphomutt watched from atop the wardrobe, offering what he considered helpful commentary in broken Common.

Twenty minutes. Nothing. Not a grimace. Not a stomach cramp. Not the faintest flicker of discomfort crossing Leo's broad, golden face. He was describing, now, how he had challenged the Northern Marches ambassador to a rematch and won by pinning him to the floor of the throne room during a diplomatic reception, an event that had apparently delighted King Alistair and horrified Queen Seraphina in equal measure.

Twenty-five minutes. I took a slow sip of my own tea, tasting nothing but jasmine and herbs, and began to reconsider my assumptions. Perhaps the root had degraded. Perhaps the storage conditions in the palace pantry had compromised its alkaloid structure. Perhaps I had miscalculated the dosage. But no — my measurements had been exact, my methodology sound. This was the same compound I had once used to incapacitate the entire court of the Shadow Throne, an operation that had earned me the epithet "the Silent Hand" among the infernal courts.

Thirty minutes. Leo smacked his lips again, the same appreciative gesture as before, and reached for the teapot.

"More tea, Lily? This is excellent. It has a..." He paused, searching for the word, his brow furrowing with uncharacteristic thought. "...a lingering kick. Like a good stew. Warming."

My hand moved of its own accord, pouring a second cup with the mechanical precision of someone whose plans were dissolving faster than sugar in hot water. *A lingering kick.* He was describing the poison as a *flavor note.* He was critiquing the *mouthfeel* of his own purgative. 

*Is his stomach made of the same stone as his skull? Is the beastfolk digestive system an iron forge, capable of transmuting any substance into base energy? Did I waste a perfectly good rare root on a man who metabolizes poison the way lesser beings metabolize breakfast?*

I watched him drink the second cup. He drank it in two gulps this time, savoring each with the deliberation of a wine connoisseur. His ears — those ridiculous, tufted appendages that swiveled independently of each other like the turrets of a small, furry fortress — flicked forward with pleasure.

"Three cups, then," Leo announced, pouring himself a third without waiting for my permission, an act that in any other context I would have catalogued as a minor diplomatic offense worthy of a strongly worded letter. "Your tea is as fierce as you are, Lily. It warms the belly and tests the constitution. A true tea for warriors."

He said this while looking directly at me, his amber eyes bright with what I initially interpreted as mockery, but slowly, reluctantly, and with the taste of ashes I was not permitted to use as a metaphor, recognized as *genuine admiration.* He was not mocking me. He was not suspicious. He was not even mildly inconvenienced. He was *delighted.* He had consumed three cups of a purgative tea — three cups that would have reduced most human adults to a state of near-death intestinal distress — and he was describing it as a *compliment.*

My plan had not merely failed. It had been *reinterpreted.* The poison had become a flavor. The humiliation had become an endorsement. The weapon had become a gift.

---

"You may court me with this tea anytime," Leo added, with a wink that involved his entire left side.

The sentence landed in my ears and detonated. *Court me.* He was using the word *court me* to describe the act of serving him poison tea. The sheer, titanic magnitude of his misunderstanding was almost impressive. I had once witnessed a demon lord's castle collapse into the Abyss after a warding matrix failed catastrophically, and that event had seemed, in retrospect, more orderly than this conversation.

I set my own cup down on the table with a soft *click.* The sound was small, almost inaudible beneath the continued enthusiasm of Leo's monologue, but it carried the weight of a declaration of surrender — not to him, specifically, but to the fundamental absurdity of my situation. 

Leo was now discussing, at length, a hunting expedition he had undertaken the previous week in the forests north of Lumengarde, during which he had allegedly wrestled a bear. Not killed. *Wrestled.* He had pinned the bear, introduced himself, and released it as a sign of respect. The bear, according to Leo, had looked at him with what he described as "profound gratitude" before lumbering away into the undergrowth.

*I have ruled kingdoms of fire and shadow. I have commanded armies that blackened the sky. I have unmade walls with a single syllable of forbidden speech. And this man — this lumbering, bear-wrestling, tea-guzzling, pun-spouting catastrophe in formal attire — has defeated me without lifting a finger.*

 The cult had failed to sacrifice me. Leo was failing to be poisoned by me. I was beginning to sense a pattern in my life that I did not appreciate.

"Leo," I said, and he stopped mid-sentence, his ears perking forward with the eager attentiveness of a dog hearing a familiar word. "Do you... feel any discomfort?"

"Discomfort?" He considered the question with the seriousness of a philosopher confronting a moral dilemma. "Only the discomfort of knowing that this tea will soon be gone and I will have to drink something lesser for the rest of the day. A tragedy."

*He is immune. Not through magical resistance, not through antidote, not through any form of supernatural protection. He is simply... built this way. The beastfolk constitution is not a metaphor. It is a geological fact.*

"You are staring at me," Leo observed, his tone suggesting this was a compliment he was generous enough to share. "Most people look away when I speak. My father says it is because my enthusiasm is 'overwhelming.' But you stare right through me, Lily. Like you are trying to solve a puzzle." He leaned forward, and the chair beneath him groaned in quiet protest. "I like this about you. You are not afraid."

*Oh, I assure you, Prince Leo. Fear is not what you are seeing. What you are observing is the precise expression of a being whose entire operational framework has just been rendered obsolete by a man who arm-wrestled a bear and called it diplomacy.*

"Very well," I said, and my voice came out softer than intended, the words carrying a weight that had nothing to do with the tea and everything to do with the realization that settling in behind it, slow and inevitable as a glacier. "Would you like a biscuit?"

I lifted the plate of shortbread from the side table — the one I had prepared alongside the tea, because even failed plans deserve a supporting cast. Leo accepted a biscuit with both hands, his claws careful not to crush the delicate pastry, and bit into it with the same enthusiastic precision he brought to everything.

"Outstanding," he said, crumbs cascading down the silver embroidery of his tunic like an edible avalanche. "Lily, you are a woman of many talents. The tea, the biscuit, the way you glare at me as though plotting my demise — it is all part of your charm."

He took a second biscuit. Then a third. I watched him eat, my hands folded in my lap, my expression fixed in the polite, attentive mask I had perfected over years of court performance. Inside, beneath the mask, something was shifting — not the cold spot, which remained its constant, humming presence, but something warmer and infinitely more troublesome. It was the same sensation I had felt when Alistair had wrapped me in his arms after the cult's kidnapping attempt, the same reluctant, unwanted warmth that I had no name for and no desire to examine.

Leo finished the plate and patted his stomach with both hands, a gesture of satisfaction so pure and uncomplicated that it bordered on aggressive. "Your hospitality is the finest I have encountered, Lily. When I return to the Plains, I will tell my father that the princess of Lumengarde serves tea that could tame a wild river and biscuits that could end a war."

"Your father will be... impressed," I managed.

"He will be *furious,*" Leo corrected, grinning. "He will demand I bring him a dozen servings on my next visit. You have created a diplomatic obligation, Lily. Congratulations."

*A diplomatic obligation. Of course. My failed assassination attempt has resulted in an international commitment to produce pastries. This is what my existence has become.*

I stood, smoothing the front of my dress, and curtsied — the practiced, graceful motion that the court had taught me, the one that made the ladies-in-waiting coo and the tutors nod approvingly. Leo stood as well, his full height nearly scraping the ceiling of the small drawing room, and I had to tilt my head back to meet his eyes.

"Thank you for the bear," I said, glancing at the backwards-headed monstrosity still perched against the wall, its button eyes staring into the middle distance with the vacant wisdom of the profoundly confused. "It is... unique."

"As are you," Leo replied, and his voice had dropped, just slightly, from its usual booming register to something almost gentle. "I mean that, Lily. Among all the people I have met in this palace — the warriors, the scholars, the politicians — you are the only one who has ever made me feel that I am not being fully understood. It is... refreshing."

I stared at him. For one disorienting moment, I could not determine whether he had just paid me an extraordinary compliment or delivered the most devastating insult I had ever received. Possibly both.

"Until next time," he said, and bowed — the beastfolk bow, a deep, sweeping gesture that was equal parts respect and theatrical flourish. He turned, ducked through the doorway, and his footsteps began their thunderous retreat down the corridor.

I stood alone in the drawing room, surrounded by the fading scent of pine and wildflowers, the empty tea service, the plate of crumbs, and the backwards-headed bear. The fire had burned to embers. The shadows had lengthened. And the room, which had felt so carefully prepared for a scene of triumphant revenge, now felt like what it truly was: a small, quiet place where a small, quiet girl had attempted to do something terrible and had produced, instead, a pleasant afternoon of tea and conversation.

I sank back into the chaise longue and pressed my fingers to my temples.

*The poison failed. The humiliation failed. The man drank three cups and asked for more. He interpreted every signal — the glare, the silence, the tea itself — as evidence of attraction. He is not my enemy. He is not my rival. *

Baphomutt materialized on the armrest of the chaise, his tiny form wreathed in the faint sulfurous haze that accompanied his appearances. He sniffed the air, spotted the backwards bear, and tilted his head at an angle that suggested either curiosity or a dislocated neck.

"Mistress's tea plan?" he squeaked.

"Failed."

"Mistress will poison him next time?"

"Probably."

"Baphomutt will steal his boots."

"No."

"Baphomutt will steal his *other* boots."

"Go away."

The imp vanished with a pop and a whiff of brimstone, leaving me alone with my thoughts, which were neither pleasant nor productive. I reached for the bear and turned it in my hands, studying its reversed head, its mismatched arms, its expression of permanent, baffled surprise. It was, in its way, a perfect representation of every relationship I had in this palace: nothing was what it appeared to be, nothing worked as intended, and the only rational response was to hold the evidence and stare at it until it made sense.

It did not make sense.

I set the bear on the mantelpiece, next to a porcelain vase of dried lavender, where it sat facing the wall like a penitent at prayer. Then I gathered the tea service, carried it to the kitchen corridor, and deposited it with the washing staff, who accepted it with the practiced blankness of servants who had learned not to ask questions about the princess's activities.

In my room, I pulled the cloth packet from my pocket — the one that had contained the *Radix purgantis* — and examined its empty interior. The powder was gone. The root was spent. My plan was a memory. And Prince Leo was probably, at this very moment, telling every person he encountered about the wonderful tea the princess had served him and how it proved, beyond all doubt, that she was interested in him romantically.

I folded the packet into a precise square, tucked it into the hidden drawer alongside the obsidian shard and the red crayon, and closed the drawer with a click that sounded, to my ears, like the final punctuation on a very long and very stupid sentence.

Tolerance. The word surfaced in my mind with the reluctant clarity of a diagnosis. Not hatred — I already hated him, and hatred was familiar, comfortable, a tool I knew how to wield. Not fear, not respect, not the cold calculus of strategic alliance. Tolerance. The grudging, exasperated acceptance that some obstacles could not be removed, only endured. Prince Leo was a permanent feature of my landscape, like the weather, or Baphomutt, or the cold spot in my chest where a piece of my lifespan had been carved away by my own hand. He could not be poisoned. He could not be intimidated. He could not be outwitted, because he did not recognize the game being played. He existed in a state of perpetual, blissful misinterpretation, and there was no force in heaven, earth, or the Abyssal Halls capable of dislodging him from it.

I sat on the edge of my bed, kicked off my shoes, and reached for the Black Tome of Maledictus from its hiding place beneath the mattress. The leather was cool and familiar under my fingers, its pages shifting and rearranging as I opened it, eager to show me something new. I ignored the tome's silent suggestions and turned instead to the section on *Radix purgantis*, searching for any detail I might have overlooked — any variable, any interaction, any reason why a dose that should have reduced a grown man to a groaning wreck had instead produced a satisfied smile and a request for more.

The text was clear. My dosage had been correct. My preparation had been flawless. The root was potent, fresh, and properly administered.

There was no explanation for Leo's immunity.

I closed the book, set it aside, and stared at the ceiling. Somewhere in the palace, Leo was probably still talking. Somewhere, Alistair was probably listening to him with the delight of a father who had found another person equally enthusiastic about loud noises and physical contact. And somewhere, the cold spot in my chest was humming its quiet, persistent note, reminding me that the most dangerous enemies were not the ones who fought you, but the ones who loved you without permission.

I pulled the covers over my head and considered, for the first time in many years, the possibility that I was simply outmatched.

title: Reading My Own Autopsy
prose:
# Chapter 28: Reading My Own Autopsy

The knock arrived at an hour I had earmarked for productive brooding, which is to say, just after breakfast, when the palace corridors were quiet and the threat of well-meaning family members had not yet materialized. I was seated at my desk with the Black Tome open to a section on metabolic resistance in beastfolk physiology, a topic I had been forced to confront with increasing urgency since Prince Leo had proven immune to the *Radix purgantis*. The living grimoire kept helpfully rearranging the text to emphasize the words "substantial constitution" and "accelerated hepatic filtration," as if the book itself were mocking me.

The knock came with a distinctive triple-tap, eager and slightly too fast, the signature of exactly one person in the entire kingdom.

I closed the Black Tome, slid it beneath a geography workbook, and arranged my features into a mask of polite welcome. "Come in."

The door swung open and Eris of the Spire entered in a state I could only describe as scholarly detonation.   She clutched something to her chest, wrapped in rough cloth, and her eyes were luminous in a way that made me brace for the worst.

"Your Highness!" She gasped the words, breathless. "I found it. I found it!"

I set down my pencil very carefully. "Found what, Eris?"

She took two unsteady steps into the room and lowered the bundle reverently onto my desk, as though it contained a blessing. Her hands were trembling. I noticed ink beneath her nails, and a small paper cut on her index finger that had bled and dried and been ignored.

"The *Codex Animarum*," she said, her voice cracking with a kind of devotional pride. "The complete treatise on theoretical soul transference."

I looked at the cloth-wrapped object on my desk. The room felt suddenly warmer, or perhaps colder, or perhaps both at once.

"I found it in the deepest archive of the Spire," Eris continued, words tumbling out in increasing haste. "The lower vaults, the ones that require three signed affidavits and a blood sample to enter. I had to promise the Archivist three moonlit sermons, which I have not yet begun to compose and which I suspect will be extremely poor because my voice goes rather shrill in large spaces, and she also required a first-edition copy of *Advanced Thermodynamics for Battle-Mages*, which I do not possess but which I believe my cousin's old mentor's former colleague-in-arms may have, assuming he has not sold it to fund his gambling habit, which is a real risk for him, and—"

"Eris."

She stopped, blinking, her mouth still open around half a syllable.

I rose from my chair, summoning the full power of my practiced persona: the curious princess, gently overwhelmed by her friend's generosity. "You found the book. You brought it here. That is what matters."

The blush that suffused her face was visible even beneath the scattered ink. "I thought of you immediately! When we spoke of it at the tea party, your insights were so brilliant. I knew you would appreciate the rigor of this text." She pressed her hands together, the gesture of a supplicant before an altar. "I have been seeking it for weeks. Since our conversation. I could not let it fall into the hands of someone who would not understand its significance."

The book sat between us, humble in its cloth wrapping, weighing perhaps three pounds. It felt heavier.

"May I?" I asked, extending my hands.

"Yes! Please! I saved the unsealing for you—I could not bear to open it without you present."

My fingers encountered cloth, then beneath it, leather.  As I drew the covering away, the title emerged in gold leaf that had faded to the color of old bronze: *Codex Animarum*.

The binding was not the work of a press but the labor of a master artisan, the spine tooled with geometric patterns that I recognized as protective sigils, subtle variations of wardings I myself had designed in a previous lifetime. The recognition arrived as a shock, a hand squeezing my chest.

I opened the first page.

The script was elegant and disciplined, each letter formed with the precise, unhurried strokes of a scholar who believed that knowledge deserved ceremony. The ink was a deep brown-faded to the color of dried blood in places, and the margins were dense with annotations in a smaller, more cramped hand, suggesting that the text had been studied and argued with and ultimately revered by generations of readers.

I turned a page at random.

The diagram occupied the upper half of the page, rendered with exacting care: a soul-anchor, its geometry perfect. Nested triangles. Intersecting circles. Heretical runic flourishes at each cardinal point. It was the same configuration I had glimpsed in the seized texts in the royal library days earlier, but this was not a partial copy or a corrupted transcription. This was the source. The true image, complete in every particular.

The same geometry I had developed, refined, and used.

*This is not theory.*

The realization arrived without preamble, brutal in its clarity. This book was a dissertation, a systematic examination of a phenomenon that real scholars had studied with real rigor. The author of this text, whoever she was, had devoted decades to understanding the mechanics of what I was. She had compiled reports from the Demon Wars, analyzed testimonies, and constructed a complete theoretical framework for the magic that had saved my existence and damned it in the same breath.

*This is my story, dissected and explained by scholars who never knew the subject was alive and reading over their shoulders.*

I forced a smile. It was a practiced smile, a product of ten years of careful construction, and today it required more effort than it had ever demanded before. "Eris, this is a wonder. You are a marvel."

She practically vibrated. "I have notes! Preliminary observations on the first three chapters, though I confess I struggled with the methodology section. The author's insistence on treating the soul as a purely energetic phenomenon rather than a spiritual one is rather—" She caught herself, her blush deepening. "I mean to say, I found it challenging. I thought perhaps, when you have had time to study it, you could explain the parts I could not understand. Your insights are always so—"

"The chapter on paradoxes," I heard myself say. "You mentioned it."

Eris nodded eagerly. "The Paradox of the Bound Vessel," she said, and the words were clinical, scholarly, entirely without malice. But they landed like a blow all the same. "I read it twice and had to set the book down, because my understanding was not equal to the author's arguments. The concept is so strange—a soul that is intact, fully coherent, but bound to a vessel some fundamental way that it does not belong in."

Her words hung in the air.

*A being whose soul is intact but bound to an incompatible vessel.*

I looked down at the chapter heading, visible through the pages I had already opened: *The Paradox of the Bound Vessel*. The script was elegant, the phrase illuminated with gold and blue. The scholar had chosen it carefully, understanding that the phenomenon deserved a name worthy of its strangeness.

She had described me without ever knowing she was doing so.

My knuckles went white against the cover.

"Your Highness?" Eris's voice, small and uncertain. "Are you well?"

I was not well. I was a demon lord trapped in the body of his enemy's daughter, reading a scholarly analysis of his own spiritual condition written by a woman who had died centuries before I was reborn. The irony was so vast it made my teeth ache.

But I had a role to play.

I lifted my eyes to Eris, and my smile was gentle, curious, the smile of a brilliant young princess delighted by the intellectual challenge before her. "I am more than well, Eris. I am moved." The lie emerged smoothly, coated in earnestness. "That you would go to such lengths for me, that you would promise moonlit sermons and sacrifice your academic standing to bring me this text—it means more than I can say."

The blush peaked.  "Your insights at the tea party changed how I think about the fundamental nature of consciousness," she said, murmuring. "I could not let such brilliance go unshared."

"Shall we discuss it?" Eris asked, pulling a battered notebook from her sleeve. It was stuffed with loose pages, marked with the careful tabbing system of a dedicated scholar. "I have prepared questions for the first three chapters. I thought we could start with the author's treatment of consciousness as a discrete entity, and then—"

"Eris." I held up one hand, the gesture gentle and apologetic. "Let me absorb it first. This is a profound gift, and I want to give it the full attention it deserves. I will study it thoroughly, and we can discuss your insights once I have graced my mind with the full scope of the author's arguments."

It was perfect. The phrasing, the cadence, the slightly formal diction that made me sound like a bookish child eager to do justice to a friend's generosity. Anyone hearing it would smile indulgently and think what a lovely young scholar Princess Lily was.

Eris nodded so vigorously her hair threatened to escape its remaining pins. "Of course! Of course. I understand completely." She tucked the notebook back into her sleeve, already planning. "I shall begin sourcing the secondary texts the author references in her bibliography. There are at least three lost works mentioned, and I have a contact in Verra who specializes in—"

"That would be wonderful."

"—and if I can locate even one of them, we will have a complete picture of her source materials, which will make our analysis so much stronger—"

"Eris," I said, gently. "Go. You have already given me a gift beyond measure. Allow me to study it."

She obeyed, flustered and delighted. At the door, she turned and performed a small, uncoordinated curtsey that nearly sent her into the doorframe. "I shall return with notes," she promised. "I shall return with so many notes."

The door shut behind her.

The room was silent.

I sat very still for a long moment, the *Codex Animarum* heavy in my lap, my hands resting on its pale leather cover. The texture was smooth against my fingers, cool in a way that had nothing to do with temperature. Somewhere in the palace, Eris was probably already plotting her next research project. Somewhere, no doubt, a student in the Spire's lower archives was wondering why the moonlit sermons required three when the Archivist had never imposed such a fine before.

None of that mattered.

I rose from my chair, crossed to the door, and turned the key in the lock.  The bolt slid home.

I returned to my desk and faced the book.

*Codex Animarum.* The most dangerous object I had ever owned. More dangerous than the Black Tome, which at least was alive with my own power and would never betray me. This was different. This was a mirror, polished by a stranger, reflecting an image I had never allowed myself to examine directly.

It was also a manual.

The scholar who had written it had proposed methods of analysis. But methods of analysis could be repurposed as methods of alteration. A soul that was understood was a soul that could be modified. The Black Tome had refused to let me copy spells because it knew I could not cast them, but it had never suggested that my condition might be changed. It had accepted the prison my body had become as a permanent reality.

This book did not accept anything. It questioned everything.

I opened it to the first chapter, the title inscribed in elegant blue ink: *On the Nature of the Soul as a Non-Corporeal, Malleable Energy Pattern.*

I read.

The author's prose was dense but not impenetrable—the language of a mind comfortable with paradox, willing to ask uncomfortable questions and follow them to their conclusions. She wrote of the soul not as an immutable essence, but as a configuration. A pattern of energy that could be observed, measured, and, in theory, adjusted. She cited sources I half-remembered, grimoires I had read in my younger centuries, treatises I had dismissed as speculation but that had apparently contained more truth than I had credited.

She cited reports from the Obsidian Plains.

I stopped breathing for a moment. The text before me described an encounter with a demonic entity whose spiritual signature had indicated a soul of unusual integrity, unusually focused, unusually *badly matched* to its physical form. The scholar had noted the discrepancy with professional curiosity.

*While alive to read the notes,* I thought. *I am studying my own autopsy, while still alive to read the notes.*

The cold spot in my chest pulsed again, steady and rhythmic, like a second heartbeat. I placed my hand over it, pressing through silk and skin, and the pulse continued beneath my palm. It was no longer merely a wound, a void, an absence. It was something more now. A marker. A reference point. A feature of the configuration the scholar was describing.

 But it was fused now with something else. Something colder. More analytic.

*She got so much wrong,* I thought. *But she built a framework. A language. A working model of what I am.*

I turned the page and found a diagram of the soul's proposed energetic anatomy: channels, nodes, anchor points. The author had labeled each with the meticulous care of a cartographer mapping uncharted territory. Some of the labels were incorrect, products of incomplete information and guesswork. But many were not.

She had drawn me a map of myself.

In the margin, a small notation caught my eye, written in a hand that was not the author's—a later reader, one of the scholars who had studied the text across the centuries. *A Rune of Command, inscribed at the primary anchor point, might theoretically regulate the channeling of foreign energy.*

I read the annotation three times.

*Rune of Command.*

I had not considered that.

The book had been a gift from Eris, who had acquired it through the sacrifice of moonlit sermons and first-edition textbooks and the goodwill of archivist who had no idea what she was releasing into the world. Eris, who believed she was helping a brilliant young princess pursue a purely theoretical interest in forbidden magic. Eris, who had placed in my hands the most complete framework for understanding my condition that I had encountered in ten years of searching.

I closed the book gently, the way one closes a text that might bite back if startled.

Then I opened it to the chapter on the Rune of Command and began to read in earnest.

The terror was still there. But curiosity was a brighter fire, and it had been so long—so very long —since I had allowed myself to feel that particular heat. I was a scholar again. A student again. A demon lord studying his own reflection, not to flinch from it, but to map its contours.

Outside, the bells chimed the hour. I did not hear them.

I turned the page.

title: Pillow Runes and Paranoia
prose:
# Chapter 29: Pillow Runes and Paranoia

I woke to the sensation of something wrong.

Not the wrongness of a nightmare—those I had grown accustomed to, the echoes of battles fought in obsidian halls, the screams of armies I once commanded. This was quieter. A presence. A weight on my chest that had not been there when I fell asleep.

My eyes snapped open.

The bedchamber was dark, the embers in the fireplace casting long, wavering shadows across the silk hangings. And there, in the exact center of my immaculate bed, lay a single sheet of thick parchment. It was the kind used for royal decrees, the kind that required a scribe’s steady hand and a king’s seal. Not the kind of thing one found on one’s pillow unless one was expecting a very formal assassination.

I sat up slowly, my fingers already reaching for the dagger I kept hidden beneath my pillow. The parchment did not move. It did not breathe. It simply lay there, a silent accusation.

No one entered my chambers without announcement. No one.

I snatched the parchment, my heart hammering against my ribs. The dagger came with it, gripped tightly in my other hand. The metal was cold, familiar. A tool. A promise.

The parchment was heavier than it looked. I held it up to the dim light, and my breath caught.

It was not a drawing this time.

It was a glyph, burned into the paper with precise, searing heat. The edges were crisp, the lines unbroken. A Rune of Command. Not the crude, jagged thing I had once sketched in crayon and been praised for as "artistic." This was a perfect, textbook rendering, complete with the subtle sigils of binding and domination that marked it as something far more dangerous than a child’s scribble.

I traced the lines with my fingertip, feeling the faint residue of heat. The rune was flawless. Not the work of a cultist, not the desperate scrawl of a fanatic. This was the work of someone who understood the architecture of the soul and will. Someone who had studied the forbidden texts of the Demon Wars. Someone who knew exactly what they were doing.

My stomach twisted.

This was impossible.

I was ten years old. Even if I had been born with the knowledge of centuries, I lacked the years of dedicated study required to produce something like this. The rune was not just a symbol—it was a key. A weapon. A statement.

And it had been left on my pillow.

I looked around the room, half-expecting to see Zephyr lurking in the shadows, or perhaps one of the cultists, their eyes alight with fanatical glee. But the chamber was empty. The door was still locked. The windows were latched.

Whoever had done this had not needed to break in. They had simply… placed it there. As if they had every right to enter my most private space.

I set the parchment down on the bedside table, my hands trembling. The dagger I kept close. The rune seemed to pulse in the dim light, a silent challenge.

I had spent years crafting my persona. The delicate princess. The precocious genius. The child who drew pentagrams in crayon and was praised for her "artistic flair." The girl who fainted after casting a simple light spell and was prescribed warm milk and extra naps.

But this—this was not a child’s game.

This was evidence.

I thought of the ledger I had seen in Zephyr’s study, the one where he meticulously recorded my "suspicious" behaviors. The dolls arranged in military formations. The "crystal garden" that was, in truth, a failed mana battery. The thank-you fruit baskets that had sent him on a wild goose chase about a "Crumble Conspiracy."

All of it seemed so trivial now.

This rune was not trivial.

I stood, wrapping my robe around me, and moved to the fireplace. The embers still glowed, casting enough light to see by. I knelt, striking a flint to coax the flames back to life. The fire caught, crackling softly.

I held the parchment over the flames, watching as the edges began to curl and blacken. The rune distorted, the lines warping in the heat. The smoke curled upward, carrying the scent of burning parchment and something else—something older, something that smelled like the Abyssal Halls.

As the last of the rune vanished into ash, I whispered the words that had become my mantra, the lie I told myself and the world.

"Just a clever little girl."

The words tasted like smoke in my mouth. They were ash. They were nothing.

I was no longer investigating a precocious child.

I was investigating a concealment.

And concealments, in my experience, only concealed one thing: a truth too dangerous to be seen.

---

The fire burned low as I sat in the chair by the hearth, staring at the pile of ash. The rune was gone, but the weight of it remained. A silent accusation. A threat.

I thought of the Black Tome of Maledictus, the grimoire Eris had procured for me at great personal cost. The tome that had contained the Word of Unmaking, the spell that had nearly cost me a sliver of my lifespan. The tome that had described my condition with eerie accuracy, that had drawn a map of my own soul.

The tome that had mentioned the Rune of Command.

A Rune of Command, inscribed at the primary anchor point, might theoretically regulate the channeling of foreign energy.

I had not considered that before. The idea had been there, in the margins, a footnote to a footnote. But now it was here, in my hands. Or rather, it had been.

I stood, pacing the length of my chamber. My bare feet made no sound on the thick rugs. The night was quiet, the palace asleep. But I was awake, and I was thinking, and I was afraid.

Not of the rune itself. I knew what it was. I knew what it could do. I knew how to counter it, how to break it, how to turn it against its caster.

What I did not know was who had sent it.

The cultists were the obvious answer. They had tried to sacrifice me once before, believing I was a vessel for the Demon Lord’s return. But this was not their style. Their magic was crude, their rituals theatrical. This rune was precise. Academic. It was the work of a scholar, not a fanatic.

Eris?

No. Eris was brilliant, but she was also young, and she lacked the depth of knowledge required to craft something like this. She worshipped me, yes, but she did not understand the full scope of what I was. She thought I was a prodigy. A genius. A child touched by greatness.

She did not know I was the greatness itself.

Zephyr?

He was the most likely candidate. The Shadow Blade. The man who had stolen my grimoires, who had sabotaged my escape routes, who had stood beside the Saint as she delivered the killing blow. He was suspicious of me, yes, but he was also methodical. He would not leave a rune on my pillow. He would present it as evidence. He would demand answers.

Unless he was testing me.

I stopped pacing, my fingers curling into fists.

That was it. It had to be.

Zephyr was testing me. Probing my reactions. Waiting to see if I would recognize the rune, if I would panic, if I would give myself away.

I exhaled slowly, forcing my hands to relax.

If that was the case, then I had already failed.

I had burned the rune. I had destroyed the evidence. I had given him exactly what he wanted—a reaction.

But what else could I have done?

I could not leave it there. I could not risk someone else finding it. The maids, the tutors, my parents. If they had seen it, they would have asked questions. Questions I could not answer.

I thought of my father, of the way his face lit up when he spoke of my "brilliance." Of my mother, of the way her eyes narrowed when she thought I wasn’t looking, when she sensed something was wrong but could not put her finger on it.

I thought of the ledger. Of Zephyr’s meticulous notes. Of the way he had looked at me during the Crumble Conspiracy, his eyes sharp with suspicion, his mouth a thin line of frustration.

He was getting closer.

I could feel it.

And now, with this rune, he had proof. Or at least, he thought he did.

I moved to the window, pulling back the heavy curtains. The night was dark, the moon a sliver in the sky. The gardens below were quiet, the paths empty. Somewhere out there, Zephyr was watching. Waiting.

I let the curtain fall back into place.

I could not go to my parents. Not with this. Not yet.

If I told them about the rune, they would demand answers. They would call for an investigation. They would turn the palace upside down, and in the process, they would uncover things I could not explain. The Black Tome. The Word of Unmaking. The cold spot in my chest, the void where a sliver of my lifespan had been excised.

No. I could not tell them.

But I could not ignore this either.

I needed answers. I needed to know who had sent the rune, and why. I needed to know what Zephyr knew, and how close he was to the truth.

And there was only one place I could get those answers.

The restricted archives of the Royal Academy.

The ones sealed after the Demon Wars.

The ones that contained the records of my defeat.

I turned away from the window, my mind made up.

I would not go to the King. I would not go to the Queen.

I would go to the archives.

And I would go alone.

---

The decision settled over me like a cloak. Heavy. Necessary.

I moved to my wardrobe, pulling out a simple dress—dark blue, unadorned. The kind of thing a princess might wear for a quiet morning in the library. Not the kind of thing one wore for breaking into a restricted archive.

I dressed quickly, my fingers fumbling with the buttons. My hands were still trembling, but I forced them to still. I could not afford mistakes. Not now.

I pulled on a pair of soft leather boots, the kind that made no sound on stone floors. I braided my hair, pinning it up in a way that would not draw attention. I looked at myself in the mirror, at the wide eyes, the pale face, the child’s body that was both my prison and my shield.

I looked like a princess.

I looked like a child.

I did not look like a demon lord.

I did not look like a threat.

I turned away from the mirror, moving to the hidden drawer in my desk. The one where I kept the things I could not explain. The obsidian shard. The powdered silver. The lock of hair from the Beastfolk shaman who had sensed something in me, something he could not name.

And the red crayon.

I took the crayon, turning it over in my fingers. It was worn down to a nub, the paper peeled back to expose more of the wax. I had used it to draw summoning circles, to sketch pentagrams, to leave messages for Baphomutt when I could not risk speaking aloud.

I set it down, my fingers brushing against the Black Tome of Maledictus. The grimoire was bound in black leather, the pages yellowed with age. It was a living thing, a text that rewrote itself based on the reader’s knowledge. It had shown me the Word of Unmaking. It had shown me the map of my own soul.

And now, it had shown me the Rune of Command.

I opened the tome to the page where the annotation had been, the one that had mentioned the rune. The page was blank. The tome had decided I no longer needed that information.

I closed it with a snap, my jaw tightening.

I would not find answers in the Black Tome. Not this time.

I moved to the fireplace, kneeling before the hearth. The ashes of the rune were still there, a dark smudge against the white stone. I reached out, brushing my fingers through them. They were cool now, inert. The magic was gone.

I stood, wiping my hands on my dress.

I would need supplies. A candle. A quill. Parchment. Something to take notes with, something to record what I found.

I moved to my desk, pulling out a fresh sheet of paper. I dipped my quill in ink, my hand steady now. I wrote quickly, my letters small and precise.

*Restricted Archives. Demon Wars. Rune of Command. Zephyr.*

I folded the paper, tucking it into my sleeve.

I would not be able to enter the archives alone. The restricted section was guarded, the texts locked away behind wards and keys. But I knew someone who could get me in.

Someone who worshipped me.

Someone who would do anything I asked.

I moved to the door, pressing my ear against the wood. The hallway was quiet. The palace was still asleep.

I turned the handle, slipping out into the darkness.

---

The corridors of the palace were empty at this hour, the torches guttering low. The stone floors were cold beneath my boots, the air still and quiet. I moved quickly, my footsteps silent, my breath steady.

I knew the way to Eris’s chambers. I had been there before, under the guise of a "study session." She had shown me her collection of grimoires, her notes on magical theory, her attempts to replicate the spells I had described to her.

She had shown me everything.

And now, I would ask her for one more thing.

I reached her door, pressing my hand against the wood. I could hear her breathing on the other side, slow and even. She was asleep.

I knocked softly, then harder when she did not answer.

A rustle of fabric. A muffled curse. The sound of feet hitting the floor.

The door creaked open, and Eris peered out, her hair tousled, her eyes bleary with sleep. She blinked at me, then gasped, dropping into a curtsey so deep she nearly toppled over.

"Your Highness! I—what—is something wrong?"

I smiled, the expression feeling brittle on my face. "Nothing is wrong, Eris. I simply… I had a thought. A question. And I knew you would be the one to answer it."

She straightened, her cheeks flushing. "Of course, Your Highness. Anything. What do you need?"

I stepped inside, closing the door behind me. Her chambers were small, cluttered with books and scrolls. The air smelled of ink and candle wax. A single candle burned on her desk, casting long shadows.

"I need to visit the restricted archives," I said, my voice low. "The ones sealed after the Demon Wars."

Eris’s eyes widened. "The restricted archives? But—those are forbidden. No one is allowed in without special permission from the Archmage."

"I know," I said. "But I believe there is something there that I need to see. Something about the Rune of Command."

Eris’s breath caught. "The Rune of Command? But—that’s forbidden magic. Dangerous. Why would you—"

"I have my reasons," I said, cutting her off. "And I trust you, Eris. I trust you to help me."

She hesitated, her fingers twisting together. "Your Highness, if we’re caught—"

"We won’t be," I said. "We’ll go now, while the palace is still asleep. We’ll be in and out before anyone knows we’re there."

Eris bit her lip, then nodded. "All right. I’ll help you. But we’ll need to be careful. The archives are warded. There are traps. Alarms."

"I know," I said again. "That’s why I came to you."

She flushed, her eyes shining. "I won’t let you down, Your Highness."

I smiled, the expression feeling more genuine this time. "I know you won’t."

---

Eris moved quickly, pulling on a dark cloak and stuffing a satchel with supplies. A lockpick. A candle. A small vial of oil to silence squeaky hinges.

I watched her, my fingers tapping against my thigh. I had chosen her for a reason. She was brilliant, yes, but she was also young, eager to please. She had spent her life in the shadow of the Archmage, desperate to prove herself. And when she had met me, she had seen something in me that she recognized. A kindred spirit. A prodigy.

She did not know that the prodigy was a lie.

She did not know that the girl she worshipped was the very thing her people had fought to destroy.

And I would not tell her.

Not yet.

Eris turned to me, her satchel slung over her shoulder. "Ready?"

I nodded.

We slipped out into the hallway, moving quickly, quietly. The palace was still asleep, the torches guttering low. We took the servants’ passages, the narrow, winding corridors that the maids and footmen used to move unseen.

Eris led the way, her steps sure, her breath steady. She knew these passages well. She had used them before, to sneak into the library, to study forbidden texts, to prove herself to the Archmage.

Now, she was using them for me.

We reached the archives, a heavy wooden door set into the stone. The air here was colder, the silence deeper. The door was warded, the wards humming faintly, a low vibration that I could feel in my teeth.

Eris knelt, pulling out her lockpick. She worked quickly, her fingers deft, her breath steady. The wards flickered, then died, the hum fading into silence.

The door creaked open.

We stepped inside.

The archives were vast, the shelves stretching into darkness. The air smelled of old parchment and dust. The candle in Eris’s hand cast a small pool of light, illuminating the titles of the books nearest to us.

*Treatise on the Binding of Elemental Spirits.*
*The Demon Wars: A Retrospective.*
*The Anatomy of the Soul: A Theoretical Framework.*
