I moved to the shelves, my fingers brushing against the spines. The books were old, the leather cracked with age. Some of them were written in languages I recognized—Infernal, the old tongue, the script of the Abyssal Halls. Others were in languages I did not know, their letters strange, their meanings lost to time.

Eris moved beside me, her candle casting long shadows. "What are we looking for, Your Highness?"

I hesitated. I could not tell her the truth. Not yet.

"A text on the Rune of Command," I said. "Something that explains its structure. Its purpose."

Eris nodded, her eyes scanning the shelves. "There’s a section on forbidden magic. Back there." She pointed to the far end of the archives, where the shelves disappeared into darkness. "But it’s heavily warded. We’ll need to be careful."

I followed her, my heart pounding. The wards here were stronger, the hum louder, a vibration that set my teeth on edge. Eris knelt again, pulling out her lockpick. She worked quickly, her fingers moving with practiced ease.

The wards flickered, then died.

The shelf creaked open.

I stepped forward, my eyes scanning the titles.

*The Runes of Power: A Comprehensive Guide.*
*The Demon Lord’s Grimoire: A Forbidden Text.*
*The Soul and the Sigil: The Theory of Command.*

I pulled the last one from the shelf, my fingers trembling. The book was heavy, the cover worn. I opened it, my eyes scanning the pages.

The Rune of Command is not merely a symbol. It is a key. A weapon. A tool of domination. It is the means by which the will of one may be bent to the will of another, by which the soul may be bound, the mind enslaved.

I turned the page, my breath catching.

The rune must be inscribed at the primary anchor point, the nexus of the soul’s energy. It must be activated with a precise incantation, a sequence of syllables that resonates with the target’s own mana signature.

I thought of the rune on my pillow. The perfect lines. The precise sigils.

Someone had known exactly what they were doing.

I turned another page, my eyes widening.

The Rune of Command was not merely a tool of domination. It was a tool of regulation. A means of controlling the flow of foreign energy, of channeling mana without backlash.

A means of bypassing the limitations of the body.

I thought of my own body, of the frail, childish form that could barely contain the knowledge of centuries. Of the mana capacity that was a teaspoon to a barrel. Of the backlash that came with every spell, the nosebleeds, the fainting, the exhaustion.

If I could inscribe the Rune of Command at my primary anchor point…

I could cast without limits.

I could be whole again.

I closed the book with a snap, my mind racing.

Eris looked at me, her eyes wide. "Your Highness? Did you find what you were looking for?"

I nodded, my fingers tightening around the book. "Yes. But I need to take this with me."

Eris hesitated. "But—it’s forbidden. If we’re caught—"

"We won’t be," I said. "Trust me, Eris."

She nodded, her eyes shining. "I do, Your Highness."

I tucked the book into my sleeve, my heart pounding. I had what I needed. Now, I needed to act.

I turned to Eris, my expression carefully neutral. "Thank you, Eris. You’ve been a great help."

She flushed, her cheeks turning pink. "Anything for you, Your Highness."

I smiled, the expression feeling brittle. "I know."

We slipped out of the archives, moving quickly, quietly. The palace was still asleep, the torches guttering low. We took the servants’ passages back to our chambers, our footsteps silent, our breath steady.

When we reached my door, Eris curtseyed deeply. "Goodnight, Your Highness."

I nodded, watching as she disappeared down the hallway.

Then I stepped inside, closing the door behind me.

I moved to my desk, pulling out the book. I opened it, my eyes scanning the pages.

The Rune of Command.

The key to my freedom.

I traced the lines of the rune with my fingertip, my mind already working.

I would need ink. Parchment. A steady hand.

And I would need to be careful.

If I was caught…

But I could not think of that now.

I had a rune to inscribe.

And a soul to reclaim.

title: Healing Spell Havoc
prose:
# Chapter 30: Healing Spell Havoc

The royal gardens in late morning are a contradiction I've come to appreciate on a purely aesthetic level: meticulously ordered chaos, every rose pruned to a specific height, every hedge coaxed into geometric submission, yet alive with the hum of insects and the lazy drift of pollen on warm air. I walked the gravel path with my hands clasped behind my back—a posture that Nurse Branna calls "regal" and that I adopted because it keeps my fingers from trembling in plain sight. The cold spot in my chest had become a familiar passenger, a coin of frost embedded between my lungs, reminding me with every shallow breath that the Word of Unmaking had taken its price and would take more if I was careless.

I was not planning to be careless today. Today, I was planning to be *methodical.*

The rose bushes along the eastern wall were in full bloom, a riot of crimson and pale pink that the head gardener maintained with near-religious devotion. I paused beside the tallest hedge, ostensibly to admire a particularly large bloom, and allowed my gaze to drift into the tangle of thorns and stems beside it.

There. Caught in the lattice of woody branches, a sparrow. Small, brown, ordinary in every conceivable way. It fluttered weakly, one wing extended at an angle that suggested the bone beneath had decided to pursue an independent career. The other wing tucked tight against its body, trembling. Its black bead-eyes caught the light as it chirped, a thin, reedy sound that barely carried past the hedge.

I studied it with the dispassion of a scholar examining a diagram.

*A practical test.* The thought surfaced like a bubble in still water, cool and clinical. *A low-stakes subject. Healing is a fundamental of channeling, a flow of restorative energy from the caster to the recipient. If I can manage this—Sanctum Minoris, the simplest mending formula—perhaps I can begin to map the boundaries of what this body will allow.*

I had memorized Sanctum Minoris roughly three hundred years ago, during what I now grimly recognized as my "optimistic phase," when I believed that comprehending every branch of magical theory would grant me immunity to its practical consequences. The spell was elementary. A child's first healing cantrip, taught in nurseries across the five kingdoms. Warm light, gentle flow, mend the break, ease the pain. The formula was so simple it was practically an insult to the discipline.

The problem had never been knowledge.

"Your Highness?"

The voice came from behind me, accompanied by the crunch of boots on gravel. I turned to find a groom—young, freckled, wearing the green-and-gold livery of the stable staff. He held a currycomb in one hand and had the earnest, slightly desperate expression of someone who had been assigned to check on me because the palace considered me a walking liability.

"Is something amiss, Your Highness? Did you need assistance?"

*Yes,* I thought. *Fetch me a functioning circulatory system and approximately four hundred units of mana. Then we can discuss assistance.*

"I am quite well, thank you," I said aloud, deploying the voice I had cultivated for these interactions: soft, measured, with just enough hesitation to suggest a shy child choosing her words carefully. "I was merely observing this sparrow. It appears to have injured itself."

The groom peered at the rose bush. "Poor thing. I can fetch it out, Your Highness, if you like. Maybe take it to the kitchen for—"

"That won't be necessary." The words came out sharper than intended, and I saw his eyebrows lift. I softened my tone, clasping my hands in front of me in what I hoped read as girlish concern rather than the reflexive response of a predator guarding its specimen. "I mean—perhaps we should let it rest? I've read that frightened animals sometimes worsen their injuries when handled by strangers. Might you check on the stables instead? I'm sure the horses need attending."

He hesitated, glancing between me and the sparrow with the conflicted expression of someone torn between duty and the desire to not argue with royalty. The desire won, as it usually does.

"Of course, Your Highness. I'll be just over there if you need anything." He gestured vaguely toward the stable block and retreated, his boots crunching a diminishing rhythm on the path.

I waited until he was well out of earshot. Then I knelt.

The gravel bit into my knees through the thin fabric of my dress, and I ignored it. I reached into the rose bush with careful hands, threading my fingers between thorns that pricked at my skin without drawing blood—another small mercy in a life defined by their absence—and cupped the sparrow in my palms.

It was lighter than I expected. Its heartbeat pulsed against my skin in rapid, panicked bursts, a flutter so fast it felt like a single continuous vibration. The broken wing hung between my fingers, the bone clearly displaced beneath a ruffle of feathers. The bird chirped once, a high, thin note that sounded, to my ears, less like pain and more like accusation.

I held it close to my chest and closed my eyes.

*Sanctum Minoris.* I called the formula to the forefront of my mind, laying it out in the luminous architecture of intention that I had once wielded with the ease of breathing. The spell was a lattice of intent: three primary channels directing restorative energy from the caster's mana reserves into the recipient's damaged tissue, each channel subdivided into secondary filaments that guided the healing along natural biological pathways. In theory, it was elegant. In practice, it was the magical equivalent of asking a creek to fill a reservoir.

I gathered what I could.

Mana, for me, was not a river or even a stream. It was a thin trickle at the bottom of a dry well, barely enough to wet the stones. I coaxed it upward through channels that resisted and sputtered, pulling the raw energy from wherever this wretched body stored its pitiful reserves—some dark, cramped cellar that I could only access by straining against the walls of my own flesh. The effort produced an immediate response: a pressure building behind my eyes, heavy and insistent, as though someone were pressing their thumbs against my temples from the inside. A high, thin ringing started in my ears, overlaying the ambient garden sounds with a metallic whine.

I ignored both. I had endured worse. I had endured the Hollow Chasm. I had endured the Saint's killing blow. I could endure a noseache and a headache.

The lattice took shape in my mind, shimmering and precise, each strand of intent aligned exactly as the formula demanded. I visualized the flow of energy, the warm golden current that would move from my hands into the bird's body, seeking the break, mending it, knitting bone to bone and feather to feather. I whispered the incantation under my breath, the syllables soft and practiced, each one a lock tumbling open.

For a single, breathless instant, I felt it. A connection. The lattice caught, the energy began to flow, and I felt the sparrow's tiny body respond—a warmth in its wing, a flicker of the break beginning to align. *It's working.*

Then the lattice shattered.

The mana did not flow where I directed it. It *recoiled*, slamming backward through my channels with a violence that stole my breath. The energy, raw and furious and utterly uncontrolled, detonated outward from my hands in a burst that I felt rather than saw—a pulse of force that ripped through the delicate lattice and scattered its components like glass thrown against a wall.

The sparrow did not heal.

It *exploded.*

Not violently, not with blood or bone fragments—the spell had been too weak for that level of destruction. Instead, there was a soft, almost gentle *poof*, and suddenly my hands were full of feathers. Downy, brown, white-tipped feathers that erupted in a cloud around me, filling the air with a drifting, silent snowfall. A faint smell of ozone hung in the wake of the burst, sharp and metallic, mixed with something warmer—something that might have been the ghost of living tissue.

I sat there, kneeling in the gravel, my hands open and empty and trembling. Feathers settled on my dress, in my hair, on the tops of my shoes. The air around me drifted with the last few stragglers, spinning lazily downward.

My ears rang. The pressure behind my eyes had intensified to a dull, throbbing ache that pulsed in time with my heartbeat. I looked down at the pile of feathers in my palms—a small, soft mound that bore no resemblance to the living creature that had been there seconds ago—and then at my own hands. They were shaking. Not subtly, not the gentle tremor I had learned to disguise with careful posture. They were shaking openly, visibly, the fingers jittering like a child who had held a sparkler too close.

*The energy dispersal matrix was unstable.* I catalogued the failure with the same clinical detachment I applied to everything, because the alternative was to feel, and feeling was a luxury I could not afford. *The reformative lattice collapsed under the strain of the rebound. The subject was too fragile to absorb the kinetic return. The mana flow was insufficient, the conversion rate catastrophic, the containment—nonexistent.*

I stared at the feathers.

*I killed it. I tried to heal it, and I killed it.*

The cold spot in my chest pulsed, a sharp little throb of agreement, as though the void where my lifespan had been excised was nodding in recognition of a kindred emptiness.

"Your Highness!"

The voice arrived before the footsteps. Nurse Branna came hurrying down the gravel path with the particular urgency of a woman who had been watching from a distance and had finally decided that whatever was happening warranted intervention. She was a stout woman, broad-shouldered, with the kind of no-nonsense practicality that made her indispensable and occasionally terrifying. Her apron was dusted with flour—she had been baking, probably scones, because the universe delighted in reminding me that my prison was padded with pastries.

She skidded to a stop beside me, her eyes widening as she took in the scene: me, kneeling, covered in feathers, hands trembling, face—what was my face doing? I didn't have the energy to check.

"Oh! Your Highness! What happened? Are you hurt?" She was already reaching for me, her hands warm and firm on my shoulders, scanning my face with the focused attention of someone looking for injuries.

I blinked. The world felt slightly tilted, as though the garden had shifted a few degrees off its axis while I wasn't looking. The ringing in my ears was fading, replaced by the distant, steady sound of the garden fountain—a trickle of water over stone that grounded me in the physical world with more effectiveness than any anchor spell.

I took a breath. Then another. The pressure behind my eyes eased to a manageable throb, and my hands, while still trembling, had slowed to something that could pass for the aftermath of excitement rather than magical catastrophe.

I looked at Nurse Branna's worried face, and I felt the mask settle back into place—the mask I had worn for ten years, the one that smiled and tilted its head and said the right things in the right tones. It was second nature now. Muscle memory. The only kind of memory this body seemed eager to retain.

"The energy dispersal matrix was unstable," I said. My voice came out flat and clinical, the tone I used when explaining to tutors why their simplified spell diagrams were fundamentally wrong. "The subject couldn't contain the reformative flow. The rebound was..." I searched for the word that would satisfy a nurse who knew nothing about magical theory. "...unexpected."

I said it the way one might discuss a failed baking experiment. As if I had attempted to make a cake and it had fallen, rather than attempting to mend a living creature and reduced it to a cloud of feathers.

Nurse Branna looked at the feathers. She looked at my hands. She looked at my face, still dusted with down, a single brown feather perched absurdly on my left ear.

I watched the calculation happen behind her eyes—the gears turning, the worry rearranging itself into something more manageable.

"Ah." Her expression softened from alarm into a kind of respectful understanding. "You were testing the containment field parameters! Very advanced, Your Highness. I've heard the scholars at the Spire debate those same limits." She nodded, as though this explained everything, and began gently brushing feathers from my hair. "The rebound effect is quite dangerous with unstable matrices. You're very brave for attempting it."

*Brave.* I almost laughed. The sound would have come out broken.

"Perhaps," she continued, her practical mind already moving to solutions, "we should start with plants next time? Wounded ferns, or a damaged vine. Much more resilient tissue. The containment matrix would have more room to operate." She said this with the confident authority of a woman who had spent decades managing the aftermath of children's enthusiasms, from scraped knees to, apparently, exploded birds.

"That's—" I paused, recalibrating. The correct response was not *That is the most condescending assessment I have heard since the Hero of Dawn tried to explain the concept of sovereignty to me using cookie shapes.* The correct response was something a ten-year-old girl would say. "That's a really good idea, Nurse Branna. Thank you."

I stood, using her offered hand for balance, and brushed the remaining feathers from my dress. They clung to the fabric with the obstinate loyalty of things that had nowhere else to go. Several more drifted down from my hair as I moved, adding to the small pile on the ground.

A few courtiers had gathered at the edge of the garden path, drawn by the commotion. I recognized them: Lady Morvaine, whose diamonds were always slightly too large for her fingers; Lord Cassander, who smelled of pipe tobacco and self-satisfaction; and young Countess Ashwell, who had the particular talent for being present wherever gossip was born. They stood in a loose cluster, watching with the avid attention of people who had nothing better to do and had found it.

"Practicing her containment fields!" Lady Morvaine whispered to Lord Cassander, though her whisper carried with the practiced volume of someone who wanted to be heard. "So diligent!"

"Wonderful technique for one so young," Lord Cassander murmured back, puffing his chest. "I've always said the princess has a gift."

*You've always said whatever requires the least amount of thought, Cassander. It's the cornerstone of your career.*

I nodded at Nurse Branna, as though accepting her advice with the gratitude appropriate to a well-bred child. "An excellent suggestion, Nurse. Fetch me a wounded fern, perhaps. Or—I should like to examine the root systems of the climbing roses. For structural analysis."

This was not entirely a lie. Root systems fascinated me for reasons that had nothing to do with gardening and everything to do with mana flow through organic networks, but the courtiers didn't need to know that. What they needed to see was a princess who had attempted something ambitious, failed spectacularly, and was calmly moving on to the next experiment with the unshakeable poise of a born scholar.

I turned and walked away from the cloud of feathers, my steps measured, my posture straight despite the ache behind my eyes and the tremor I could still feel in my fingertips. Behind me, I heard Nurse Branna bustling to collect the evidence of my failure, murmuring something about "brave attempts" and "learning opportunities" to the watching courtiers.

I did not look back.

The gravel path stretched ahead of me, bordered by roses and manicured hedges and the quiet, implacable beauty of a garden that had never tried to be anything other than what it was. I walked it with the careful, deliberate steps of someone crossing a minefield, which was not far from the truth. Every step was a calculation. Every breath was a managed resource. The cold spot in my chest hummed its low, persistent note, and I felt—in the same instant—the warmth that spread from somewhere near my heart, the contradictory signal that my body produced when I thought about the people waiting for me in the palace. Father, with his booming laugh and his terrible puns. Mother, with her quiet watchfulness and her warm hands.

I hated that warmth almost as much as I hated the cold.

The feathers were still settling behind me, a final, delicate punctuation mark on a sentence I wished I hadn't attempted to write. The sparrow was gone—not dead in any conventional sense, because there was nothing left to *be* dead. It had simply been unmade, reduced to its component parts by a channel of magic too weak to carry what I had forced through it.

*This body is a cage,* I thought, and the thought was so familiar it might have been carved into my bones. *A cage of flesh and limitation, with no exit, no lever, no key. I know the theory. I can visualize the spell. I can feel the lattice forming in my mind with the precision of a master architect drawing blueprints. And when I try to build it, the materials crumble in my hands.*

I touched the cold spot through my dress, pressing my palm flat against my chest. It did not respond to the touch. It was not, after all, a physical thing—or rather, it was the physical absence of something that had been removed. A page torn from the book of my remaining years, leaving a ragged edge that would never heal.

The Rune of Command could fix this. The book in my desk drawer said as much: a means of regulating foreign energy, of channeling mana without the limitations imposed by a body that was never designed to hold what I carried. The Rune could be inscribed at my primary anchor point, the nexus of my soul's energy, and it would act as a buffer between my knowledge and my flesh—a translation layer that would allow the torrent of my understanding to pass through the narrow channel of this child's body without destroying everything it touched.

But to inscribe the Rune, I needed steady hands. I needed mana—more than the pathetic trickle this body produced. I needed time, and privacy, and a set of materials that I was still procuring with the agonizing patience of someone building a ship in a bottle.

And I needed to not explode any more birds.

I reached the palace steps and paused, looking back over my shoulder at the garden. From this distance, the cloud of feathers had mostly settled, leaving a faint, pale dusting on the rose bushes that would probably be attributed to a recent molt from one of the garden's resident doves. Nurse Branna was gone. The courtiers had dispersed, carrying their gossip with them like seeds on the wind. By evening, the story would be that Princess Lily had conducted a sophisticated magical experiment in containment theory, and that the resulting feather explosion was a calculated demonstration of energy dispersal principles.

The myth of the prodigy grew thicker with each failure, woven from the threads of other people's willingness to believe that everything I did was intentional.

I climbed the steps, my hand on the railing, my legs unsteady in a way that I disguised as fatigue rather than the aftermath of magical backlash. The great doors of the palace opened before me—held by a footman who bowed—and I stepped into the cool, polished interior, leaving the garden and its small tragedy behind.

*Mana prison,* I thought, and the phrase carried a double meaning that only I could appreciate. The cage was not merely the limitation of my body's mana capacity. The cage was the *understanding*—the vast, precise, terrible understanding of what I could do if the prison did not exist, held in perfect clarity behind eyes that could barely stay open after the effort of mending a bird's wing.

I made it to my chambers before the nosebleed started. A thin red line dripped from my left nostril, warm against my upper lip, and I pressed a handkerchief to it with the resigned efficiency of long practice. The handkerchief came away spotted, a Rorschach pattern of failure that I folded into a square and tucked into the washbasin for the laundry staff to find.

Another entry in the log of strange stains that Princess Lily's chambers seemed to produce on a weekly basis. The palace staff had stopped asking questions. They assumed I was clumsy. They assumed I was fragile. They assumed, and their assumptions were a wall I had built brick by brick, and I would continue to build it until it reached the sky.

I sat at my desk, the stolen book still hidden in its drawer, and stared at the wall.

The feathers were gone. The bird was gone. The proof of my failure had been swept up and composted and forgotten by everyone except me.

And the cold spot in my chest pulsed on, steady as a second heartbeat, marking time in a currency I could not afford to spend.

title: Keys to Deception
prose:
# Chapter 31: Keys to Deception

The grand hall had been transformed into a temple of sound, which was ironic, because the sound about to be produced was going to be a monument to mediocrity dressed in silk and candlelight.

 Two hundred and thirty-seven nobles, give or take, arranged in concentric arcs of escalating importance. The outer rings held the minor barons and their overdressed spouses, their perfume a chemical fog that would have choked a lesser being. The inner circle contained the dukes and duchesses, the military commanders, the foreign dignitaries—each one wearing the particular expression of strained attention that accompanied mandatory cultural events.

I had been preparing for this moment for three weeks. Not the performance itself—that was trivial. The sonata was a simple piece in C major, composed by some court musician whose name I had already forgotten and whose talent I had already assessed as adequate at best. No, the preparation had been in the presentation. 

My fingers found the opening notes, and the hall fell silent.

The sonata was structured in three movements, each one a study in predictable harmonic development. The composer had followed every rule of classical form without understanding any of the reasons behind those rules. The result was technically correct and utterly soulless—a piece of music that had been assembled rather than composed, each phrase placed where convention demanded rather than where emotion required.

 My fingers moved across the keys with the fluidity of someone who had internalized the instrument's mechanics so thoroughly that conscious thought was unnecessary.

This was the danger. This was the tell I could not hide.

I had been playing the piano for exactly fourteen months. In that time, I had progressed from "charming child picks out simple melody" to "concert-level performance" with a speed that should have raised alarms in anyone with a functioning brain.

But the court saw what it wanted to see. The court saw a prodigy, a miracle, a testament to the combined genius of the Hero King and the Saint Queen. The court saw exactly what I needed them to see.

The first movement ended. I allowed myself a brief pause, letting my hands rest on the keys as I had practiced, my head tilted slightly as if I were listening to the final chord fade into silence. The gesture was calculated to suggest deep musical sensitivity, a child overwhelmed by the beauty she had just created.

 She was not applauding. She was not smiling. She was watching me the way a jeweler watches a diamond, searching for the flaw that would reveal it as a clever fake.

I continued to the second movement.

The andante section was slower, more contemplative, and I used the change in tempo to study the audience. Most of them had already stopped listening, their attention drifting to the more interesting pursuits of cataloging each other's jewelry and calculating the political implications of who was seated next to whom. The performance was merely an excuse for the gathering, a cultural obligation that had to be endured before the real business of court intrigue could begin.

 His suspicion was a constant, low-level annoyance, like a pebble in my shoe that I could not quite shake loose.

The second movement built toward its climax, a predictable crescendo that the composer had clearly intended to be the emotional heart of the piece. I played it with technical precision, my fingers dancing across the keys with a facility that I had spent years cultivating in my previous life and had carefully disguised as "natural talent" in this one.

The third movement was a rondo, lively and energetic, designed to send the audience home with a spring in their step and a tune in their heads. 

When the final chord faded into silence, the hall erupted in applause.

I rose from the bench, executed a small, perfect curtsy, and allowed a shy smile to cross my face. The courtiers murmured their appreciation. I could hear the whispers carrying through the hall—"remarkable," "extraordinary," "a true prodigy"—each word a brick in the wall of my carefully constructed persona.

The performance was over. But the real test was just beginning.

---

The aftermath of the recital was a blur of congratulatory whispers and insincere compliments, each one delivered with the particular blend of envy and admiration that characterized courtly praise. 

"And what a natural ear you have, Your Highness!" A portly courtier—Baron something-or-other, I had never bothered to learn his name—beamed down at me with the condescending warmth of an adult addressing a particularly clever pet. "Such instinctive musicality! One would think you were born with a conservatory's knowledge!"

I smiled up at him, my eyes wide and innocent. "Thank you, my lord. Though I must confess, the piece's harmonic architecture is rather conventional. The composer's use of parallel fifths in the development section was technically correct but artistically timid, and the applied diminished seventh in the recapitulation felt like a concession to tradition rather than a genuine expressive choice."

"Such... scholarly words from our little musician!" The Baron's laugh was nervous, high-pitched. "It is as if you were born with a conservatory's knowledge!"

I tilted my head, affecting a look of childish puzzlement. "Father says I read the liner notes in his old songbooks too carefully."

 The Baron patted my head with a relief that was almost palpable, and I allowed myself to be guided back toward the refreshment table, where a glass of lemonade and a plate of petit fours awaited.

I sipped the lemonade—too sweet, as always, the palace's pastry chef had a heavy hand with sugar—and surveyed the room from beneath my lashes. 

The Queen had heard my analysis. The Queen had seen the gap between the innocent child and the scholarly mind. And the Queen, I suspected, had filed that information away for later consideration.

I finished my lemonade and allowed myself to be drawn into another conversation, this time with a duchess who wanted to discuss the weather. I responded with appropriate childish enthusiasm, discussing the recent rainfall with the same manufactured wonder I might have used to discuss a particularly interesting species of beetle.

But my mind was elsewhere, turning over the implications of Seraphina's attention like a stone in my pocket, testing its weight, examining its edges.

The performance had been flawless. The cover had held. But the cracks were beginning to show.

---

The last guests departed as the sun sank below the horizon, painting the marble corridors in shades of amber and rose. I made my way toward my chambers, my legs aching from the hours of standing and curtsying and pretending to be delighted by conversations that had contained less intellectual stimulation than a conversation with a particularly dull rock.

I was halfway down the corridor when Seraphina emerged from a side passage, her steps silent on the polished floor. She moved with the fluid grace that had earned her the title of Saint, her white and gold robes catching the fading light like captured sunlight.

"Lily." Her voice was low, pitched for private conversation rather than public address. "A moment, please."

I stopped, turned, and curtsied with practiced grace. "Mother. Did you enjoy the recital?"

Seraphina's expression was unreadable. She studied me for a long moment, her gaze traveling across my face as if she were reading a text written in a language only she could understand.

"Your technical grasp is formidable, Lily," she said at last. "It is rare to see such analysis in a child, however gifted."

I shifted my posture, allowing a calculated slump of childish fatigue to enter my shoulders. "It is just patterns, Mother." I pitched my voice soft, guileless, the voice I had practiced for hours in front of my mirror. "Like the shapes in the carpet or the order of the stars. Notes are only little shapes that make feelings."

Seraphina's expression softened, the sharp edge of inquiry melting into something that might have been concern. She stepped forward and brushed a strand of hair from my forehead, her touch gentle but probing, as if she were searching for something beneath my skin.

"Patterns can be exhausting to chase," she said quietly. "You must also rest your mind, not just your fingers."

I nodded, the image of obedient compliance. "Yes, Mother. I will rest."

I watched her go, my expression carefully composed into the tired smile of a child who had been praised too much and was ready for bed. 

Seraphina's suspicion was a patient predator. It had been lurking in the shadows of her gaze for years, growing stronger with each slip, each tell, each moment of brilliance that I could not fully disguise. And tonight, I had given it fresh meat.

My cover, though intact, had grown thinner. And the cold spot in my chest pulsed on, steady as a second heartbeat, marking time in a currency I could not afford to spend.

I made my way to my chambers, my steps measured, my breathing even, my mind already working through the implications of the evening's events. The recital had been a success. The performance had been flawless. But the cost of that perfection was rising, and I could not afford to pay much more.

 And for just a moment, I allowed myself to feel the weight of what I had become.

A demon lord in a child's body, playing a role that grew more complex with each passing day, surrounded by people who loved a girl who did not exist.

I pushed away from the door and crossed to my desk, where the hidden drawer waited with its precious cargo. The Black Tome. The Rune of Command. The tools I would need to bridge the gap between my knowledge and my flesh.

 And somewhere in my chest, the cold spot pulsed on, patient and eternal, a reminder of the price I had already paid and the prices yet to come.

The cage was me. And I was the only one who could break it.

title: Crimes in the Kitchen
prose:
# Chapter 32: Crimes in the Kitchen

The afternoon light fell in slanted gold bars across the Aubusson rug of my solar, illuminating dust motes that drifted with the lazy disregard of entities unburdened by demonic intellects trapped in fragile, mana-starved vessels. I was cross-referencing the energy signatures of three lesser binding circles from memory against the diagrams I’d memorized from the Codex Animarum, trying to isolate the precise variable that made one stable enough for a weak caster to manipulate. The hollow ache behind my ribs was a dull, persistent reminder of the Word’s price. My fingers itched to sketch, to trace the theoretical adjustments, but the hidden drawer remained shut. Surveillance was heightened since Mother’s pointed comments about my “patterns.” 

Which is why the subsequent disruption was so exquisitely, predictably infuriating.

A sound like a small, furry avalanche preceded him. A thud, the chime of a knocked-over silver bell, the faint, petulant squeak of a toy soldier being stepped on, and then my solar door burst inward with enough force to rattle its hinges. Baphomutt, my long-suffering, eternally loyal, and spectacularly witless imp minion, tumbled through the opening in a flurry of stained linen and frantic energy. His bat-like ears were askew, his mismatched eyes gleaming with the manic light of a job he believed well done. In his grubby, clawed hands, he held aloft a single piece of parchment, its surface mottled with what I instantly identified as butter, cinnamon, and a faint, greasy thumbprint.

“Mistress!” he chittered, his voice a high, excited screech that set my teeth on edge. “Look! Look what Baphomutt has secured! The great secret! The Master Chef’s treasure, for you!”

He scampered forward, thrusting the parchment at me with the trembling pride of a war dog presenting a particularly mangy kill. My initial flicker of interest—perhaps a map, a coded message, something with tactical utility—died a swift and merciful death as my eyes processed the document. It was written in Chef Marcel’s precise, looping hand, the ink slightly smeared by what I deduced was a hasty removal from some flour-dusted surface.

*Royal Shortbread of Lumengarde: Yield 4 Dozen.*
*Ingredients: 2 cups sifted all-purpose flour, ¾ cup caster sugar, 1 cup cold unsalted butter (cubed), 1 tsp vanilla extract, ¼ tsp salt, zest of one lemon…*

It was the recipe. The *shortbread* recipe. Not a state secret, not an arcane formula, not even a particularly well-guarded household account. It was the recipe for the buttery, crumbly confections Chef Marcel baked for Father’s teatime, the ones he guarded with the ferocity of a dragon hoarding gold, more out of professional pride than any genuine security concern.

*Absolute, unmitigated disaster.*

“Baphomutt,” I said, my voice very quiet while the inner monologue screamed in a dialect of hellfire and fury. “What, precisely, do you believe you have accomplished?”

His chest puffed out. “Baphomutt stole the Master Chef’s most prized formula! For Mistress! Now Mistress can bake the golden treasures whenever she wishes! No more begging the fat man!” He grinned, a wide, jagged expression that showed far too many teeth. “Mistress will be happy. Mistress will have all the cookies. The fat man will cry.”

 Now I was being presented with a pilfered biscuit recipe by a creature whose primary strategic contribution was hiding jewels in my sock drawer and causing olfactory disturbances that were blamed on the kitchens.

The sheer, cosmic indignity of it threatened to crack the carefully maintained composure of my current vessel. My hands, small and childish, clenched in the silk of my dress. *Threat assessment: Chef Marcel will realize the recipe is missing within the hour. His initial reaction will be theatrical rage. His second will be a methodical search. His third, given the known ‘unusual smells’ emanating from my chambers since the bath salt incident, will be to direct suspicion here. The court, already primed by the Crumble Conspiracy, will amplify this into a narrative of culinary espionage. Zephyr will see confirmation. Seraphina will observe. Father will find it hilarious and commission an ode to my domestic enthusiasm.*

“Mistress is quiet,” Baphomutt noted, his ears drooping slightly. “Mistress is not pleased? But… the treasure…”

“The ‘treasure’,” I said, taking the parchment between two fingers as if it were contaminated, “is a recipe for shortbread. A pastry. You have stolen a pastry recipe from a man whose entire professional identity is wrapped up in that pastry. You have committed a crime of negligible material value but catastrophic symbolic weight.”

He blinked, his reptilian brain visibly churning. “The… fat man will be sad?”

“The fat man,” I clarified, “is Royal Chef Marcel, a man with the ear of the Queen and the ferocity of a cornered badger when his culinary domain is violated. He will not merely be ‘sad.’ He will be a force of nature. He will tear this palace apart, stone by stone, to find the perpetrator. And when he cannot find an intruder, he will look inward. He will look for culprits among the staff. And he will look,” I added, my voice dropping to a whisper that held more genuine menace than any shout, “at me. Because my chambers already smell faintly of sulfur and failed alchemy. Because I am known to ‘experiment.’ Because, to a man whose world revolves around butter and sugar, this will look like a prank. A prank that undermines his authority.”

Baphomutt’s lower lip trembled. “But… Baphomutt only wanted to please Mistress…”

“You have pleased me,” I said flatly, folding the parchment with precise, angry movements. “You have presented me with a logistical catastrophe wrapped in butter-stained vellum. Go. Hide. And do not ‘please’ me again today.”

He slunk away, his tail dragging on the floorboards, radiating an aura of wounded devotion that grated on my already frayed nerves. I stared at the folded recipe in my hand. The hollow space behind my ribs pulsed. This was the chaos I was chained to, the unpredictable variables that threatened to unravel plans measured in decades.

The distant, booming sound of Chef Marcel’s voice reached me even through the closed door and down the corridor. It was a sound of pure, unadulterated rage, pitched to carry.

“—sabotage! Culinary treason! Someone has laid hands to the Royal Shortbread! My life’s work! Plundered from under my very nose, while I was proofing the almond croissants! This is an affront! An insult to the Crown’s palate! I shall have the culprit’s hide, and I shall render it into lard!”

His accusations, I noted with weary precision, were casting a wide net. The courtiers would be whispering within minutes. I needed to act, and I needed to act now, not with denial, but with the only weapon this form permitted: aggressive, disarming redirection.

I folded the recipe into a smaller square and slipped it into the pocket of my dress. Then I smoothed my hair, arranged my features into an expression of mild, concerned curiosity—a look I had practiced to perfection—and stepped out into the corridor.

The chaos was just beginning to bloom. Two footmen were exchanging panicked glances. A maid scurried past, clutching a feather duster like a shield. And at the far end of the hall, a knot of courtiers had formed, their heads bent together. I ignored them, walking with the measured, slightly unsteady gait of a child who is trying very hard to appear calm. My destination was the source of the thunderous voice.

I found Chef Marcel in the main kitchens, which were in an uproar. He was standing in the center of the flagstone floor, his flour-dusted apron tied over his vast, tomato-red face, gesticulating with a rolling pin at a quartet of terrified sous-chefs. Steam seemed to rise from his bald head.

“—every surface! Check every shelf! The recipe was here, I tell you, tucked in the folio of household accounts where it has been for thirty years! Someone has taken it! And when I find them, they will be kneading dough with their teeth!”

“Chef Marcel?”

He spun, his eyes wild with fury. The sight of me, his Highness’s daughter, standing in his domain, seemed to short-circuit his rage into baffled consideration. “Princess Lily! What brings you to my kitchens? This is no place for—”

“Your distress is palpable,” I said, widening my eyes slightly, letting a tremor of concern enter my voice. “I heard the commotion from my rooms. Was something… misplaced?”

My feigned ignorance was a masterstroke. The fury drained from his face, replaced by the heavy burden of explaining a great injustice to an innocent. He drew himself up, drawing in a breath that expanded his considerable chest. “Misplaced, Your Highness? Nay, not misplaced. *Stolen*. The Royal Shortbread recipe, the very heart of this kitchen, has been filched! Plundered from the book of accounts! It is a disaster!”

I let my hand flutter to my mouth, timing the gasp perfectly. “Oh, how dreadful! That is your most famous creation! The one Father adores! But…” I paused, tilting my head, my expression shifting from shock to thoughtful concern. “But perhaps… perhaps it is not a theft for malice?”

He narrowed his eyes, suspicious. “What do you mean, child?”

“Well,” I ventured, stepping a little closer, my voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. “I have been reading. In the library, about flavor alchemy. It says that recipes are not static things, but evolving equations. Balances of taste and texture that can be… improved. Refined.” I looked up at him, my face the picture of earnest, childish deduction. “What if it wasn’t stolen *from* you, but *borrowed* by someone wishing to *improve* it? For the Crown? For your own artistry?”

The suggestion, so earnest and framed in the language of advancement, short-circuited the Chef’s rage into baffled consideration. Chef Marcel’s mouth opened, then closed. His anger, directed at a vague, malevolent thief, had no purchase on this concept. A thief was an enemy. An ambitious apprentice or a misguided scholar attempting to “improve” his masterpiece? That was a problem of a different order. It was a problem of *artistry*.

“Improve…” he murmured, the rolling pin lowering to his side. His brow furrowed. “The ratio is perfect. The vanilla must be *just* so. Who would think to improve it?”

“Someone who admires it greatly, I suppose,” I said softly. “Someone who sees the potential in a classic. It is a form of flattery, in a way. Though a very frustrating one.” I gave a small, sad smile. “If only there were a way to recreate it, to prove the original’s perfection… or perhaps even find the improvement, if it exists.”

The seed was planted. I watched it take root behind his eyes, the shift from victimized chef to challenged master. The problem was no longer finding a culprit, but proving the supremacy of his art.

“Recreate it,” he said slowly, testing the words. “From memory. Yes. The proportions are in my head, if not on parchment. A test. To see if any ‘improvement’ can be made.” He looked at me then, really looked at me, with something other than kitchen-fury or deference to my rank. It was the appraising glance of one craftsman to another. “You have an interest in the balance of flavors, Princess?”

“Only a reading interest,” I demurred, lowering my eyes. “The theory. I have no skill at the practice.”

“Nonsense,” he declared, a new energy in his voice. “Theory is the skeleton! Come. You shall assist. We shall recreate the Royal Shortbread from scratch, and you will see the care required. Perhaps your ‘flavor alchemy’ will offer a thought, even if it is only to show why the old ways endure.”

*Checkmate.*

I followed him deeper into the kitchens, my heart rate elevated not with fear, but with the cold thrill of opportunity. This was reconnaissance. This was access.

The royal kitchens were a realm unto themselves, a hot, fragrant, chaotic universe of copper and flame. I was given a stool at a large preparation table, my sleeves rolled up, my hands washed with unnecessary thoroughness. Chef Marcel, now a general marshaling his forces, began measuring with a speed and certainty that was impressive. I watched, my outer demeanor one of rapt, innocent attention.

*Inner mapping: Main preparation area. Three ovens, temperature variance noted in the brickwork. Cool store to the north, heavy door, lock appears mechanical, not magical. Spice cabinet along the east wall, rare ingredients on high shelves, likely catalogued but not physically secured. Guard rotation… two guards outside the main doors, changing shift with the dinner bell. Minimal patrols through the kitchens themselves; it’s a staff-only zone. Storage for silver and plate in an adjacent pantry, visible through that doorway. Access points from the garden via that service entrance, used for deliveries…*

I passed Chef Marcel a sifter when he gestured for it, my movements careful and helpful.

“The butter must be cold,” he instructed, demonstrating. “Not merely cool. Cold. It creates the layers. The short.”

“Because the water in the butter turns to steam during baking, creating pockets,” I said, the words slipping out before I could fully censor them. I bit my lip, looking down. “That is what the book said. About puff pastry. Is it similar?”

Chef Marcel stared at me, the sifter forgotten in his hand. I felt a spike of alarm—had I gone too far? But then he broke into a slow, wide grin. “Precisely, Your Highness! Precisely! The principle, if not the exact method. You have a head for the science of it.” He looked back at his dough, shaking his head in wonder. “A true prodigy. Even in the culinary arts.”

I bowed my head, hiding the flicker of genuine amusement. *Prodigy. Yes. That is what I am.* I proceeded to measure sugar with meticulous care, my small hands surprisingly steady as I leveled the measuring cup. I suggested, timidly, that perhaps a pinch of ground cardamom might “balance the lemon,” and he paused, considering it, before nodding thoughtfully. He didn’t use it, but he considered it. That was the victory.

As we worked, the story of the morning’s drama filtered through the kitchens. Lily, the young princess, had come to help Chef Marcel in his hour of crisis. Lily, with her knowledge of “flavor alchemy,” was collaborating on the recreation. The narrative was solidifying, smoothing over the sharp edges of suspicion and replacing them with the softer contours of my own bizarre, adorable legend.

A courtier peered in from the doorway, whispering to her companion. “Look, she’s measuring the flour herself. What dedication.”

“Such a helpful child,” another murmured. “And to think, they said the recipe was stolen. Perhaps it was just misfiled.”

The chaos was now my cover. The imp’s idiocy was being laundered through my supposed brilliance into a story of proactive, scholarly investigation. Baphomutt, I realized, was not merely a liability. He was an agent of unpredictable, yet ultimately exploitable, chaos. A force I could channel.

The recreation was completed as the afternoon light began to turn amber. The results were not identical to Chef Marcel’s version—my suggestion of slightly less vanilla had been overruled, and the baking time had been adjusted by a minute he swore by—but they were close. Very close. He held up a shortbread cookie, golden-edged, and inspected it with the critical eye of a master. Then he bit into it. A slow, deep satisfaction spread across his features.

“Acceptable,” he pronounced, which was high praise indeed. He handed me a cookie. It was warm, crumbly, and tasted of butter and victory.

“Now,” he said, clapping his floury hands together, making me jump. “You, Princess. You have a steady hand and a theoretical head. You are to have permanent access to my kitchens, for study. Not for cooking,” he added quickly, seeing my expression, “but for observation. For your ‘flavor alchemy.’ It seems the Crown’s prodigy is also a culinary savant!”

I curtsied, the movement clumsy but endearing. “Thank you, Chef Marcel. You are too kind.”

As I left the kitchens, the cookie crumbly in my hand, I caught a glimpse of a familiar, shadowy form detaching from the rafters high above the cool store. Baphomutt’s eyes glinted down at me. I gave him the barest nod, then held up the cookie, making him see it. Then I popped it into my mouth and chewed slowly, deliberately, holding his gaze. His expression shifted from hopeful to crestfallen. I let him watch me swallow. Then I gave him a single, slow blink, my eyes cooling with a message he, in his simple, demonic way, would understand: *This was the reward. For now. Be more useful next time.*

He vanished back into the shadows, chastened. I walked back to my chambers, the taste of butter on my tongue, the hollow ache a quiet presence, and a new, permanent pass to the palace kitchens secure in my pocket. 

I reached my room and closed the door, leaning against it as I finally let my face go slack. The performance had been draining. I crossed to my desk, opened the hidden drawer, and placed the folded, butter-stained recipe inside, next to the Black Tome and the Rune of Command. Another trophy from a war of attrition, fought with sugar and spite. My fingers brushed the cool, dark cover of the Tome. The real work waited. But tonight, for a moment, I would allow myself the quiet, smug satisfaction of a crisis averted and a territory claimed. The cage remained, but I was learning to decorate it with interesting new locks. And, I thought, recalling the warm, crumbly perfection of the shortbread, with interesting new flavors.

title: Necromancy and Napkins
prose:
# Chapter 33: Necromancy and Napkins

The garden was a dappled lie.

Sunlight filtered through the leaves of the ancient oak, painting shifting patterns on the stone path. The air smelled of roses and damp earth, of lemon cakes and the faint, metallic tang of old magic.  But Eris had requested a "private tutorial," and I had, with the patience of a spider weaving its web, guided the conversation toward exactly this topic.

I sipped my tea. The porcelain was delicate, the rim painted with tiny golden stars. It was the sort of cup one used for innocent things—birthday wishes, polite compliments, the occasional lie. My fingers, small and still slightly sticky from the honey cake I’d eaten earlier, curled around the warmth. The steam curled upward, carrying the scent of bergamot and something darker, something that didn’t belong in a garden tea party.

Eris leaned forward, her notebook already open, her quill poised. Her eyes were bright, eager. 

"Princess," she said, her voice hushed with reverence, "you mentioned Theoretical Manifestation yesterday. I’ve been thinking about it all night. The way you described perception as a mutable construct—it’s revolutionary."

I set my cup down with careful precision. The clink of porcelain on porcelain was the only sound in the garden besides the distant chirp of birds. "Revolutionary is a strong word," I said, my voice light, almost playful. "It’s merely an extension of existing principles. The mind is a lens, Eris. And lenses can be ground to different specifications."

Eris’s quill scratched furiously across the page. "Yes! Exactly! The *lens* of perception! But how do you stabilize the illusion without the anchor rune? The texts all say it’s impossible to cast without it—without risking caster disorientation, or worse."

 But Eris didn’t need to know that. Not yet.

"Ah," I said, tilting my head as if considering the problem for the first time. "That is the puzzle, isn’t it? Let’s treat it as a game. If you were to cast the spell without the anchor, how would you compensate for the instability?"

Eris’s brow furrowed. She was clever, I’d give her that. But cleverness was a tool, and tools could be wielded by those who knew how to guide them. "I suppose," she said slowly, "you could reinforce the energy matrix with a secondary focus. A physical object to act as a conduit, perhaps? Something to ground the spell’s resonance."

I nodded, as if this were a reasonable suggestion. "A valid approach. But what if the object itself is the problem? What if the instability isn’t in the spell’s structure, but in the way we perceive it?"

Eris’s quill stilled. She looked up at me, her eyes wide. "Perception as the variable," she murmured. "Not the spell, but the caster’s *understanding* of it."

I reached for another honey cake, my fingers brushing the crumbs on the plate. "Precisely. The spell isn’t a wave, Eris. It’s a recursive echo. A reflection of a reflection, bending back on itself until the original source is indistinguishable from the illusion."

 To her, it was simply another brilliant insight from the princess who had already rewritten half the Spire’s curriculum in her head.

Her breath hitched. The quill trembled in her hand. "A recursive echo," she repeated, her voice barely above a whisper. "That’s… that’s not in any of the texts."

"Perhaps not," I said, taking a bite of the honey cake. It was too sweet, cloying. I swallowed it anyway. "But that doesn’t mean it’s wrong."

Eris’s face went pale. Then flushed. Then pale again. Her fingers tightened around the quill until her knuckles turned white. "You’re saying the spell isn’t just about manipulating energy. It’s about *understanding* the nature of perception itself. That the caster’s mind is the true medium."

I set the honey cake down. "Yes."

She stared at me, her lips parted, her eyes shining with something dangerously close to worship. "That’s… that’s not a game. That’s an equation of beauty. And you see it whole, while I can only ever trace the edges."

The words were quiet, trembling. A single tear slid down her cheek, then another. She didn’t wipe them away. She just sat there, her notebook forgotten, her quill dripping ink onto the page like a slow, melancholy rain.

I watched her, my inner monologue a cold, satisfied hum. *Excellent. The manipulation is complete.*

 "There, now," I said, my voice soft, almost maternal. "You’re the one with the *Codex*, remember? Your mind is a finely tuned instrument. Mine is just… unusually shaped."

Eris sniffed. She clutched her notebook to her chest like a lifeline. "Unusually shaped," she repeated, her voice thick with emotion. "That’s one way to put it."

I withdrew my hand, letting it fall back into my lap. The gesture had been calculated—just enough contact to seem comforting, not enough to be intrusive. 

I picked up my teacup again, taking a slow sip. The tea was lukewarm now, but I didn’t mind. The taste was secondary to the performance. "Shall we move on to the next puzzle?" I asked, my voice bright. "I’ve been thinking about the linguistic roots of the incantation. The original phrasing is fascinating—it’s almost as if the words themselves are a kind of spell."

Eris nodded eagerly, her tears still glistening on her cheeks. "Yes. Please. I want to understand it all."

I smiled. "Of course. Let’s begin with the first syllable. It’s not just a sound, Eris. It’s a *concept*."

---

 But the air between us had shifted, thickened. Eris’s notebook was now a sacred text, her quill a wand, her every word a prayer.

I outlined the spell’s components with the dry precision of a cartographer mapping uncharted territory. The linguistic roots of the incantation, the precise geometric focus required, the volatile energy matrix that underpinned it all. I spoke of the spell as if it were a theoretical exercise, a mental puzzle to be solved over tea and honey cakes. But in my mind, it was so much more.

It was a weapon.

It was a key.

It was the first step toward reclaiming what had been taken from me.

Eris scribbled furiously, her hand moving in quick, jagged strokes. Every now and then, she would pause, her eyes distant, her lips moving silently as she worked through the implications of what I’d said. Once, she gasped aloud, her hand flying to her mouth as if she’d just realized something profound.

I didn’t ask what it was. I didn’t need to. I already knew.

"Princess," she said suddenly, her voice trembling with excitement, "what if the energy matrix isn’t linear? What if it’s *fractal*? A self-replicating pattern that grows more complex the deeper you go?"

I tilted my head, considering. "An interesting thought. But fractals require a seed, Eris. A starting point. What would the seed be in this case?"

She bit her lip, her brow furrowing. "The caster’s intent? Or perhaps the target’s perception? If the spell is recursive, then the seed could be the first layer of the illusion itself."

I nodded slowly, as if this were a revelation. "A plausible theory. But intent is a slippery thing. It’s not always reliable."

Eris’s eyes lit up. "Unless you *control* it. Unless the caster’s intent is so precise, so *focused*, that it becomes the seed itself."

I reached for another honey cake, my fingers brushing the crumbs. "And how would you measure that precision?"

She hesitated. "I… I don’t know. But you do, don’t you? You see it. You *understand* it."

I took a bite of the honey cake, chewing slowly. The sweetness was almost unbearable. "Perhaps," I said, swallowing. "But understanding is only the first step. The next is application."

Eris’s quill hovered over the page, her hand trembling. "Teach me," she whispered. "Please."

I set the honey cake down. "Very well. Let’s begin with the basics. The spell’s energy matrix is a lattice, Eris. A web of interconnected points. Each point is a node, and each node is a choice. The caster’s job is to weave those choices into a coherent whole."

Eris nodded eagerly, her eyes never leaving my face. "And the anchor rune? Where does it fit in?"

I smiled. "The anchor rune is a crutch. A way to force the lattice into a specific shape. But what if you didn’t need it? What if you could weave the lattice freehand, so to speak?"

Eris’s breath hitched. "You’re saying it’s possible to cast the spell without the anchor?"

I nodded. "Possible, yes. But not easy. It requires a level of precision that most casters can’t achieve. A level of *understanding* that most casters don’t even know exists."

Eris’s eyes widened. "But you do."

I didn’t answer. I didn’t need to. The truth was written in the way she looked at me, in the way her hands trembled around her quill, in the way her tears had dried but left their mark on her cheeks.

She worshipped me.

And worship, I had learned, was a very useful thing.

---

The tea party dragged on. The sun climbed higher in the sky, the shadows shortening, the air growing warmer. Eris’s notebook was now a mess of scribbles and diagrams, her quill running low on ink. I had lost count of how many times I’d refilled my teacup, how many honey cakes I’d eaten. The sweetness was cloying, but I forced myself to swallow each bite, to keep up the performance.

Eris, for her part, had stopped eating entirely. She was too engrossed in the spell, too enthralled by the possibilities. Every now and then, she would look up at me, her eyes shining with something like awe, and I would feel a flicker of something dark and satisfied curl in my chest.

*This is how you build an army,* I thought. *Not with swords, not with threats, but with knowledge. With devotion.*

I outlined the final component of the spell—the incantation itself. 

Eris repeated them after me, her voice hesitant at first, then growing stronger. The syllables rolled off her tongue like a prayer, like a vow. I corrected her pronunciation gently, my voice soft, my tone patient. "Not quite," I said. "The second syllable should be sharper. Like a blade cutting through silk."

She tried again, her voice trembling. This time, the syllable was perfect.

I smiled. "Better."

Eris’s face flushed with pride. "I think I understand it now. The spell isn’t just about creating an illusion. It’s about *rewriting* reality. Even if it’s just for a moment."

I nodded. "Reality is a construct, Eris. And constructs can be dismantled."

She stared at me, her eyes wide. "You make it sound so simple."

"It is simple," I said. "The hard part is believing it’s possible."

Eris’s quill stilled. She looked down at her notebook, at the pages of scribbles and diagrams, at the incantation written in her own hand. Then she looked back up at me, her expression suddenly vulnerable. "I don’t know if I can do it," she whispered. "I don’t know if I’m smart enough."

I reached across the table, my hand hovering just above hers. "You are," I said, my voice firm. "You’re the one with the *Codex*, remember? The one who solved the Resonance Paradox. You’re smarter than you think."

Eris sniffed, her eyes glistening. "But you’re… you’re *you*. You see things no one else can see. You understand things no one else can understand."

I withdrew my hand, letting it fall back into my lap. "And yet, here you are, understanding them too. That’s not nothing, Eris."

She shook her head, her tears spilling over. "It’s not the same. It’s not *yours*."

I sighed, as if this were a problem I’d encountered before. "Eris, listen to me. Knowledge isn’t a finite resource. It’s not something you take from someone else. It’s something you *build*. And you’re building it right now, with every word you write in that notebook."

Eris wiped her eyes with the back of her hand, leaving a smudge of ink on her cheek. "But what if I’m not good enough? What if I can’t do it?"

I leaned forward, my voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. "Then you’ll try again. And again. And again. Until you *are* good enough."

Eris stared at me, her breath hitching. "You really think I can do it?"

I smiled. "I know you can."

She nodded, her tears drying, her expression hardening with determination. "I won’t let you down."

I picked up my teacup, taking a slow sip. "I know you won’t."

The lie tasted like honey.

---

The garden was quiet now, the only sounds the distant chirp of birds and the scratch of Eris’s quill. She had stopped crying, but her hands still trembled as she wrote, her eyes still shone with that dangerous, worshipful light.

I watched her, my inner monologue a cold, calculating hum. *She is mine now. Not just her mind, but her heart. Her devotion. Her loyalty.*

It was a useful thing, devotion. It could be shaped, molded, turned into something sharp and deadly. Or something soft and pliable. Whatever I needed it to be.

I set my teacup down, the porcelain clinking softly against the saucer. "Eris," I said, my voice gentle, "there’s one more thing I want to show you."

She looked up, her eyes bright. "Yes?"

I reached into the pocket of my dress, my fingers brushing the cool metal of the Rune of Command. I had taken it from the restricted archives last night, slipping it into my pocket while Eris distracted the archivist with questions about soul transference. It was a small thing, no larger than a coin, its surface etched with intricate glyphs that hummed with power.

I placed it on the table between us, my fingers lingering just long enough to feel the faint pulse of energy beneath my skin.

Eris’s eyes widened. "What is that?"

I smiled. "A tool. One that might help you with the spell."

She reached for it, her fingers trembling. "May I?"

I nodded. "Go ahead."

Eris picked it up, her breath catching as she felt the energy thrumming through it. "It’s… it’s alive."

"Not alive," I said. "Just… aware. It responds to intent."

Eris’s eyes flicked up to mine. "Intent?"

I nodded. "The same intent that powers the spell. The same precision, the same focus. The rune is a conduit, Eris. A way to channel energy without the anchor."

She stared at it, her fingers tightening around the metal. "It’s forbidden."

I shrugged. "So is the spell we’ve been discussing. But that hasn’t stopped us, has it?"

Eris hesitated. Then, slowly, she nodded. "No. It hasn’t."

I leaned back in my chair, my voice light. "Then let’s not let a little thing like forbidden knowledge stand in our way."

Eris’s face flushed with excitement. "What do I do with it?"

I reached for another honey cake, my fingers brushing the crumbs. "Hold it in your hand. Focus on the spell. On the lattice, the nodes, the choices. Let the rune guide you."

Eris nodded, her eyes never leaving the rune. She closed her fingers around it, her breath steadying, her expression growing serious. I watched as her lips moved silently, as her eyes fluttered closed, as the faintest glow began to emanate from between her fingers.

I smiled.

It was working.

---

The glow faded. Eris’s eyes snapped open, her breath coming in quick, shallow gasps. "I felt it," she whispered. "I felt the energy. It was… it was like the spell was *alive*."

I nodded. "That’s the rune’s power. It amplifies intent, focuses it. But it’s not a crutch, Eris. It’s a tool. And tools can be dangerous in the wrong hands."

Eris looked down at the rune, her expression suddenly wary. "What do you mean?"

I reached across the table, my fingers brushing hers as I took the rune back. The metal was warm now, humming with residual energy. "The rune doesn’t just amplify intent. It *feeds* on it. The stronger the intent, the more power it draws. And if the intent is… unstable…"

I let the sentence hang in the air, letting Eris fill in the blanks.

She swallowed. "It could be dangerous."

I nodded. "Very."

Eris’s eyes flicked up to mine. "But you’re not afraid of it."

I smiled. "I understand it. That’s the difference."

Eris stared at me, her expression a mix of awe and fear. "You’re not just a princess, are you?"

The question was quiet, hesitant. I tilted my head, my voice light. "What do you mean?"

Eris shook her head, as if dismissing the thought. "Nothing. It’s just… you’re so much more than anyone realizes."

I laughed, the sound bright and innocent. "I’m just a girl who likes puzzles, Eris. Nothing more."

She didn’t believe me. I could see it in her eyes, in the way her fingers trembled around her quill, in the way she looked at me as if I were something holy.

But she didn’t push it. She just nodded, her voice soft. "Of course."

I slipped the rune back into my pocket, the metal cool against my skin. "Now," I said, my voice bright, "shall we return to the spell? I want to discuss the energy matrix in more detail. There’s a particular node that’s been giving me trouble."

Eris nodded eagerly, her notebook already open, her quill poised. "Yes. Please."

I smiled.

The trap was set.

---

The sun was beginning to dip below the horizon by the time the tea party ended. The garden was bathed in golden light, the shadows long and lazy. Eris’s notebook was now a mess of scribbles and diagrams, her quill running dry, her hands stained with ink.

She looked up at me, her eyes shining. "Princess," she said, her voice soft, "thank you. For today. For everything."

I smiled, my voice gentle. "You’re welcome, Eris. I’m glad you found it… enlightening."

She nodded, her expression suddenly vulnerable. "I just… I want you to know how much this means to me. How much *you* mean to me."

I reached across the table, my hand patting hers awkwardly. "I know."

Eris sniffed, her eyes glistening. "I won’t let you down. I promise."

I withdrew my hand, letting it fall back into my lap. "I know you won’t."

She stood, her chair scraping against the stone path. "I should go. I have… I have a lot to think about."

I nodded. "Of course."

Eris hesitated, her fingers tightening around her notebook. Then, suddenly, she leaned down and pressed a quick, shy kiss to my cheek. "Thank you," she whispered.

I didn’t move. I didn’t react. I just sat there, my expression carefully neutral, my inner monologue a cold, satisfied hum.

*Excellent.*

Eris straightened, her face flushed. "I’ll see you soon, Princess."

I smiled. "I look forward to it."

She turned and hurried away, her footsteps quick on the stone path. I watched her go, my fingers brushing the Rune of Command in my pocket.

 I picked up my teacup, taking a slow sip. The tea was cold, but I didn’t mind. The taste was secondary to the victory.

Eris was mine now. Body, mind, and soul.

And soon, she would be my hands. My eyes. My voice in the dark.

I set the teacup down, my fingers brushing the crumbs on the plate. The honey cakes were gone, the lemon cakes untouched. The garden was empty, the sunlight fading.

I stood, smoothing my dress, my fingers lingering on the Rune of Command. The metal was cool, humming faintly against my skin.

It was time to return to my chambers.

Time to plan the next move.

Time to weave the next illusion.

I smiled, my inner monologue a dark, satisfied whisper.

*Let the game begin.*

title: Accidental Heroics
prose:
# Chapter 34: Accidental Heroics

They had assembled to watch me make a fool of myself. The least I could do was oblige them efficiently.

The training ring was a circle of packed earth scuffed by generations of boots, hooves, and the occasional desperate scrape of a practice blade following a particularly decisive defeat. The air hung thick with the smell of sweat and leather — the perfume of athletic endeavor, or perhaps its tombstone. 

"Honored friends!" he bellowed, his voice carrying across the training yard with the kind of volume that made me think his ancestors had communicated across entire mountain ranges. "Today, the fierce rose of Lumengarde tests her thorns against the fangs of the Beastfolk! A formal spar — to first yield!"

He punctuated the declaration by raising his practice sword overhead, and the crowd responded with a smattering of applause. 

I smiled.  I tilted my head just so, letting a strand of silver hair fall across my face, and I saw several of the court ladies press their hands to their hearts.

*Adorable,* they were thinking. *So brave. So hopeless.*

Let them think it. In a few minutes, this would be over.

My practice sword felt like a lead bar in my hands. My grip was technically correct — centuries of swordsmanship in my previous life had left their mark, even if this ten-year-old body had never held a blade before Leo's "training" had begun — but my fingers lacked the strength to maintain the proper hold for more than a few moments. The hilt wobbled. The blade dipped. I adjusted my stance, and my boots slipped slightly on the loose earth.

Leo, by contrast, looked like he had been born with a sword in his hand. He stood opposite me with an easy confidence that spoke to years of training, natural athleticism, and the bone-deep certainty of someone who had never once been betrayed by their own body. He was a full head taller than me, broad-shouldered, with the golden-furred ears of a wolf pricking forward from his mane of tawny hair. His grin could have been carved from sunlight, and it was directed at me with the persistence of a lighthouse beam.

He looked like he was about to attend a birthday party.

I looked like I was about to attend my own funeral.

"Your Highness," I said, pitching my voice to carry exactly the right note of nervous deference. "Perhaps we should reconsider. I'm certain there are more qualified sparring partners available. Someone who wouldn't bore you with their incompetence."

Leo threw his head back and laughed, a booming sound that startled several birds into flight from the nearby trees. "And that is why you are so magnificent, little rose! You seek to test me even before the spar begins! "

I blinked. That hadn't been a feint. That had been a sincere request to end this farce.

"No, I just thought —"

"Your strategy is obvious to a trained eye," he continued, striking a heroic pose that made his furred ears swivel proudly. "But I am not so easily deceived! Leo reads your words as a blade reads its edge — sharp, deceptive, aimed to find the gaps in his guard!"

I stared at him. My mind, which had spent centuries plotting the downfall of kingdoms, produced absolutely nothing but static.

"Right," I said. "Shall we begin?"

He nodded, settling into a fighter's stance with an easy grace that made me want to scream. The crowd pressed closer to the wooden fence that ringed the training ground, a wall of expectant faces. I spotted my father near the back, practically vibrating with excitement beside one of his knights. His holy sword — Dawnbreaker, the blade that had ended my previous life — was slung at his hip even though this was a training exercise. That man wore his weapon to breakfast. My mother stood beside him, her serene expression belying the sharp edge in her eyes. She was always watching. Always cataloging.

And there, near the stables — a figure in dark robes who had somehow found a shadow to stand in despite the afternoon sun. Zephyr. The Shadow Blade. Watching me with the intensity of a man who suspected a teacup of being a particularly dangerous poisoner.

*Focus,* I commanded myself. *The plan is simple. Lose quickly. Lose clearly. Lose without injury.*

 A quick, clean defeat would reinforce the "delicate princess" persona I had constructed, and Leo would return to the Beastfolk Plains satisfied with his victory. The best outcomes in life were the ones that required minimal effort and generated maximal boredom in my opponents.

The only question was how to lose without making it suspicious.

I had already noticed the answer during my approach to the ring: a shallow divot in the packed earth, probably left by some previous sparring match. A natural, unremarkable imperfection. I would stumble on it during our first exchange, fall, and drop my sword. The match would end. I would be led away to drink warm milk and plot in peace.

"Begin!" Leo announced, as though the authority to begin rested with him rather than with the actual royalty present. It probably did, honestly. His father was a king. Mine was a man who challenged visiting dignitaries to arm-wrestling.

He moved fast — much faster than I remembered from our previous training sessions. His first strike was a testing blow: an overhead swing designed not to hurt, but to measure my reaction time and the strength of my guard.

I raised my sword to parry.

The impact was like being hit by a falling tree. The shock jarred my teeth, sent a tremor up my arms, and nearly wrenched the blade from my fingers. My entire body shuddered with the force of it, and I felt the vibration travel through my bones all the way down to my toes. My teeth clicked together. My vision blurred for half a heartbeat.

This was going to hurt.

But I had a plan. I let the momentum of the parry carry me backward, my feet moving in a stumbling, graceless shuffle that would have made my old weapons master weep. I twisted slightly, feeling for the divot with my heel.

There.

My foot caught on the edge of the depression. I gave a small gasp — genuinely surprised, because the catch was more abrupt than I had anticipated — and pitched backward. The fall was not entirely uncontrolled. I managed to twist so that I landed on my hip rather than my tailbone, and I let go of the sword so that it clattered across the packed earth, spinning to a stop several feet away.

I lay there for a moment, staring up at the sky. The clouds were nice. Puffy. White. Completely indifferent to my humiliation.

The crowd sighed — one collective, sympathetic exhale. I heard a few murmurs of concern, someone clucking their tongue, and my father's voice rising above the noise with something that might have been "That's my girl!" or possibly "She's practicing falling!" It was hard to tell with him.

*Good,* I thought. *It's over.*

I pushed myself up onto my elbows, prepared to accept my defeat with gracious humility. In my peripheral vision, I saw Leo approaching, his sword lowered. He extended a hand toward me.

I reached up to take it.

And then he opened his mouth.

"A feint!" he declared, his voice ringing with excitement.

I froze, my hand hovering an inch from his.

"You feigned a loss of footing to draw my focus downward!" he continued, gripping my wrist and hauling me up with far more force than necessary. I stumbled forward and nearly crashed into his chest before steadying myself. "You prepared a counter from the ground! But I read the shift in your shoulder! I recognized the trap!"

I blinked up at him.

"What?"

"That's why you dropped the sword so casually," he said, his eyes bright with the fervor of a man who had just solved a puzzle that had never existed in the first place. "A deliberate bait! You wanted me to advance, to press my advantage, so that you could catch me off balance from below!"

"No," I said slowly, clearly, with the careful enunciation one might use with a child. "I fell. I dropped my sword. The match is over."
