Leo laughed, a booming, delighted sound. "And even now, you deny your genius! The misdirection extends beyond the battlefield and into the realm of words! Magnificent! Truly magnificent!"

I felt my left eye twitch.

The crowd, which had been murmuring in sympathy moments ago, shifted to a different murmur. One of interest. One of speculation. I caught snatches of conversation from the spectators pressed against the fence.

"Did you see the way she fell? That was perfect form."

"She planned the whole thing. The princess is more than she appears."

"Look at her face — she's not even breathing hard."

That last one was because I was breathing very hard, actually, but I was doing my best to hide it, which apparently read as composure.

A cold sensation crept down my spine, settling in that spot in my chest where the Word of Unmaking had left its permanent absence. This was not going according to plan.

Leo was still holding my arm, his grip large enough to have wrapped around my wrist twice. "Your blade, little rose," he said, releasing me with a flourish. "Let us test your strategy further."

He retrieved my practice sword from the dirt and held it out to me, hilt first. His expression was one of genuine admiration, and I recognized with a sinking feeling that correcting him would be pointless. He would interpret any denial as further evidence of my cunning. To refuse to continue would confirm his suspicion that I had been playing at something. To continue would fuel his delusion further.

I took the sword. Because there was no other option.

"Fine," I said, and the word came out through gritted teeth.

We squared off again. This time, I decided, I would be more careful. No more controlled stumbles. No more theatrical gestures. I would simply be *bad* — uncoordinated, sloppy, the way a ten-year-old girl who had never held a sword in her life might fight.

I attacked first. A wild, mistimed swing designed to go wide and leave me off balance.

Leo dodged it with theatrical flair, spinning away and striking a dramatic pose. "An angular approach! You seek to confuse me with unexpected vectors!"

I blinked. "What?"

"Your commitment to unpredictability is inspiring!" He lunged, and I flinched backward, nearly tripping over my own feet. "Yes! You use chaos as a weapon! The unorthodox is your shield!"

I tried a different approach. I gave up on attacking and simply stood there, holding my sword at an awkward angle, waiting for him to strike. Surely a straightforward defense would be too boring for him to misinterpret.

Leo paused, staring at me. His ears twitched.

"Ah," he said, nodding slowly. "The stillness. The immobility. You are inviting me to commit, forcing me to reveal my technique before you counter with your own devastating strategy."

"No," I said. "I'm literally just standing here."

"A master stroke of reverse psychology!" He applauded, the pommel of his sword clinking against his palm. "You wish me to believe you are unprepared, so that I will lower my guard! But I see through it, little rose! I see through it all!"

Behind him, I saw one of the guardsmen exchange a look with another. They were starting to believe him.

I tightened my grip on the sword and swung at him — not with any real intent, just a desperate, flailing attempt to make physical contact and end this madness.

Leo sidestepped, caught my sword on his own, and used the momentum to spin me around. I stumbled, catching myself on the fence. The wooden rail groaned under my weight.

"Excellently deceptive footwork!" he announced cheerfully. "You turn your own momentum into a defensive repositioning!"

"Is there anything I do that you will not interpret as brilliance?" I demanded.

He considered this. "No," he said, as though it were a compliment.

I screamed internally. Then externally, just a little, because it was either that or commit a murder in front of a hundred witnesses. The sound came out as a small, frustrated growl, and Leo's eyes widened with what I could only describe as adoration.

"A battle cry! The fierce rose reveals her thorns at last!"

The crowd oohed. Someone clapped. My father shouted something about "Lily's fighting spirit" and "chip off the old block."

We circled each other. The sun was warm, the earth was dusty, and Leo was still talking.

"Your stance suggests the classic Lumengarde school," he observed, ducking under a clumsy swing that was literally just me trying to make him stop talking, "but the flailing quality you have added introduces a layer of organic chaos that cannot be taught! A blend of discipline and wildness! The storm in a teacup!"

"Sword fighting is not a tea ceremony," I muttered.

"Ha! Even your metaphors challenge convention! You reject the traditional imagery, just as you reject traditional combat norms!"

I had no response to that. There was no response to that.

The spar continued. I grew increasingly desperate, and my desperation translated into increasingly erratic movements. I swung too high. I swung too wide. I stumbled over my own feet. At one point, I tried to dodge a lunge and ended up executing what Leo called "an elegant pirouette" — which was actually just me trying to keep my balance after my heel caught on another divot.

"You dance around my attacks like a leaf in the wind!" he proclaimed.

"I'm trying to fall over," I said flatly.

"Of course! You wish to draw me into a false sense of security! Just as you did with your initial stumble!"

So I did the only thing I could do. I attempted a theatrical surrender.

I raised my free hand, spread my fingers, and opened my mouth to say the words that would end this nightmare: "I yield."

But my flailing sword arm — the one still holding my practice sword — chose that exact moment to lower, and the flat of my blade smacked against Leo's with a sharp, metallic *clang.*

The impact sent a vibration up my arm. I felt my grip loosen. The sword twisted in my hand, and somehow — through a sequence of physics I would later calculate with the careful detachment of a scholar studying a natural disaster — the motion caught Leo's blade at precisely the wrong angle.

His sword spun out of his grasp.

It arced through the air in a glittering spiral, carving a shimmering path against the afternoon sunlight, and embedded itself in the packed earth at the edge of the ring. It stood there, quivering, like an exclamation point at the end of a sentence no one had meant to speak.

The training ground went silent.

I stared at the sword.

Leo stared at the sword.

The crowd stared at the sword.

I felt the cold spot in my chest pulse with something that might have been either dread or laughter. The two were becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish.

Leo turned to me slowly. His face was lit with an expression I had never seen before: pure, unadulterated admiration, as if he had just watched the sun write him a love letter.

"You..." His voice was hushed, reverent. "You orchestrated the entire sequence. The feints. The misdirection. The self-deprecation. The surrender as the final trap, to draw me into complacency. And then — *the disarmament.*"

"That was an accident," I said, with the flat, desperate emphasis of a woman watching her house burn down.

He wasn't listening. He had already turned to address the crowd.

"Behold the fierce rose of Lumengarde!" he proclaimed, gesturing at me like I was a museum piece that deserved its own wing. "Not a weakling to be protected, but a cunning strategist in training! Today, she has proven herself my equal upon the field of honor!"

The crowd erupted — not in a wild roar, but in a wave of knowing nods, appreciative murmurs, and scattered applause. The guardsmen who had been exchanging dubious glances now looked at me with something approaching respect. I saw my father pumping his fist in the air, beaming with pride. Even my mother wore a faint smile that I couldn't quite parse.

"My little rose," Leo said, crossing to retrieve his sword and then presenting it to me with a formal bow, "I have been blind to your genius. No more. From this day forward, I will treat you as I would any worthy opponent — with the full measure of my respect, my attention, and my admiration."

That was worse. That was so much worse.

I took the sword he was offering, because I didn't know what else to do with it, and stood there in the center of the training ring while the crowd applauded and Leo continued to speak about my heroic potential and my "inimitable strategic mind." My fingers curled around the hilt of his practice sword. The leather grip was warm from his hand.

And then, in the middle of all that, I felt something strange.

A bubble of laughter.

It rose up from somewhere deep in my chest, from the place where the cold spot lived, and it wasn't a cold laugh. It was warm. It was absurd. It was the laugh of a woman who had spent years plotting the destruction of her enemies and had just been publicly declared the intellectual equal of a wolf-eared muscle brain because she had tripped over a hole in the ground.

*Oh no,* I thought. *I've been infected by this place.*

But the laughter kept rising, and I had to bite the inside of my cheek to keep it contained. Not because I wanted to hide it — I obviously couldn't — but because it was a genuine laugh, and the last thing I needed was for Leo to see that and interpret it as affection.

"Your smile," Leo observed, catching sight of my twitching lips. "You are pleased by my recognition! It is a worthy moment between rivals!"

"It's a muscle spasm," I said.

"Of course! A muscle spasm you will add to your arsenal of misdirection! Brilliant!"

As the crowd began to disperse and Leo continued to offer his effusive praise, I thought about my next move. I needed to redirect the narrative. I needed Zephyr to follow another false trail while I worked on the Rune of Command in peace. I needed—

*Jam,* I thought suddenly.

It was absurd. It was petty. It was exactly the kind of thing that would drive the Shadow Blade to distraction.

I smiled — a real smile this time, with edges sharp as glass. Leo saw it and preened, thinking it was for him.

It wasn't.

"Your Highness," I said sweetly, "would you excuse me? I need to draw a picture."

He blinked. "A picture? Of what?"

"A jar of jam," I said. "The conspiracy."

Leo looked at me with reverence. "Even in art, you pursue strategy. Magnificent."

I didn't correct him. I just walked away, my practice sword still clutched in my hand, my mind already turning toward crayons and a certain spymaster's desk.

title: Jam, Spies, and Sanity
prose:
# Chapter 35: Jam, Spies, and Sanity

The office was a monument to order. Every quill stood at attention in its brass holder, each one identical in height and angle. The ink bottles were arranged in a precise gradient from midnight blue to pale lavender, their caps aligned with a compass rose I had etched into the desk's surface years ago. The maps on the wall—all forty-seven of them—hung with military exactness, their corners weighted by identical obsidian paperweights.

No dust. No clutter. No chaos.

That was the point. Order was armor. Order was the difference between a master spy and a man who got lost in the noise of his own suspicions. I had built this office to be my fortress against the world's confusion, a place where every variable was accounted for and every threat could be measured against the cold mathematics of intelligence.

And there, in the center of my desk, sat a piece of chaos.

The crayon drawing was crude. That was the first insult. The artist—if one could use such a term—had clearly spent no more than ninety seconds on the entire composition. A jar, bulbous and uneven, rendered in a shade of purple that had no business existing in nature. The label was a scribble, barely legible, but I had decoded it within moments of finding the thing: *THE CONSPIRACY*.

The jar had a face. Furious, scribbled eyes. A mouth open in what might have been a scream or a threat. The entire image was framed by a border of jagged lines that could have been flames or could have been the desperate attempts of a child to contain her own rage.

I had been staring at it for the better part of an hour.

 A personal, laughing dismissal of everything I had dedicated my life to. 

I had to prove them wrong.

The problem was the word "conspiracy." It was too specific. Too pointed. The drawing did not say "jam" as a casual subject. It said "THE CONSPIRACY" in block letters, as if the jar itself was the villain of the piece. Which meant, if I was reading this correctly—and I always read things correctly—that there was a conspiracy involving jam. Or a conspiracy *about* jam. Or a conspiracy that used jam as its cover.

The royal kitchens had been searched during the Crumble Conspiracy fiasco, but my operatives had been looking for pastry-based weapons, not preserves. The distinction mattered. The crumble caper had been a deliberate misdirection, a colorful lie designed to waste my resources. But jam was different. Jam was sticky. Jam was persistent. Jam could hide things.

I stood, my chair scraping against the floor in a manner that would have shamed me under normal circumstances. My hand went to the dagger at my belt—a comfort, not a threat—and I began to pace. The drawing watched me from the desk, its scribbled eyes following my movements with the uncanny certainty of something that knew it had gotten under my skin.

"Jam," I said aloud, testing the word. "The conspiracy."

 Whoever had sent this message knew that I would be forced to investigate, knew that the investigation would make me look ridiculous, knew that I would go anyway because I could not afford to ignore a potential threat to the crown.

And they were right.

I stopped pacing and retrieved my cloak from the hook by the door. The fabric was black, darker than the space between stars, woven with a silencing enchantment that had taken me three years to perfect. I had worn it during the infiltration of the Iron Citadel. I had worn it when I extracted the traitor from the heart of the Beastfolk court. I had worn it when I discovered the truth about the Whispering Vault.

Tonight, I would wear it to break into the royal pantry and sniff jam.

The hallways of the palace were quiet at this hour. The guards knew my shadow, knew the particular stillness that preceded my passage. I moved through the corridors like a rumor, leaving no trace, my boots making no sound against the marble. The kitchens were located in the eastern wing, past the great hall and the wine cellars, down a narrow staircase that smelled of bread and smoke and something sweet that clung to the air like a memory.

The pantry door was unlocked. Of course it was. The palace staff had no reason to fear an intruder who wanted to steal preserves. I slipped inside and let the door close behind me, the darkness swallowing me whole.

For a moment, I simply stood and breathed.

The pantry was a cathedral of sustenance. Shelves rose to the ceiling, laden with jars and kegs and sacks and bundles. The air was thick with competing scents—cinnamon and cloves, honey and vinegar, the sharp tang of pickled vegetables and the warm, yeasty promise of rising dough. Somewhere in the darkness, a mouse skittered across a shelf, its tiny feet making a sound like distant applause.

I began my work.

The jam was organized by type, a fact that spoke well of the pantry staff. Strawberry occupied the eastern shelf, arranged in neat rows of identical jars. Blackcurrant sat on the western wall, slightly fewer in number, their labels bearing a more ornate script. Apricot—the variety depicted in the drawing—was on the central island, stacked in a pyramid formation that suggested pride of place.

I started with the strawberry.

The first jar was sealed, its lid smooth and unbroken. I held it up to the sliver of moonlight that crept through the high window, examining the contents for anomalies. The jam was a deep, rich red, studded with seeds, its surface glossy and still. No residue on the glass. No discoloration along the rim. No sigils or markings that I could detect with my enhanced vision.

I opened the lid and inhaled.

Jam. That was all. Just jam—sweet, fruity, utterly ordinary. The kind of jam that appeared on royal breakfast tables every morning, consumed by kings and queens and princesses who were almost certainly involved in a conspiracy that I could not yet prove.

I replaced the lid and moved to the blackcurrant.

I was a master spy reduced to sampling preserves, and the humiliation burned in my chest like a brand.

The apricot was my last hope, and I approached it with the caution of a man approaching a live bomb. The jar was larger than the others, its contents a golden amber that caught the moonlight and held it. I lifted it from the pyramid, careful not to disturb the arrangement, and turned it over in my hands.

Nothing.

I opened the lid. The scent was apricot, of course—sweet, slightly tart, with a hint of something floral that I could not identify. I dipped a finger into the substance and tasted it, my tongue cataloging the flavors with the precision of a wine merchant assessing a rare vintage.

Jam. Perfectly normal, if slightly over-sweet, jam.

My paranoia screamed that this was the deception. The normalcy was the false front. The jam was a disguise, a mask worn by something far more sinister that lurked beneath the surface. I pressed my ear to the glass, listening for the tell-tale hum of a trapped voice or the whisper of a curse. The jar was silent. It was the silence of a thing that had nothing to hide, and that silence was the most damning evidence of all.

"Clever," I murmured. "Very clever."

I was still holding the jar to my ear when the door swung open.

The girl was young—no more than fourteen, with a round face and a mop of brown hair escaping from under her cap. She carried a bundle of linens in her arms, the white fabric piled so high that she had to peer around it to see where she was going. She froze in the doorway, her eyes widening as they adjusted to the darkness and found me standing there, illuminated by a sliver of moonlight, holding a jar of apricot jam against my ear like a man listening for a heartbeat.

"Lord Zephyr?" Her voice was a squeak, barely audible over the sudden thundering of my own pulse. "Is... is there a poison in the preserves?"

The question was innocent. The question was a child's attempt to make sense of an impossible sight. But to me, it was a verdict. A judgment. A confirmation of everything I feared about how this investigation was going to be perceived.

I straightened, my dignity a tattered cloak that I wrapped around myself with as much grace as I could muster. "Routine safety audit," I said. My voice was clipped, professional, the voice of a man who conducted routine safety audits of jam at midnight on a regular basis. "The crown's stores must be verified against potential contamination."

The maid blinked. Her gaze dropped to the jar in my hand, then to the open strawberry jar on the shelf behind me, then back to my face. I could see her trying to process what she was seeing, trying to fit the legendary Shadow Blade into a category that made sense.

She failed.

"Of course, my lord," she said, and curtsied. 

I replaced the jar on the shelf, my movements slow and deliberate. The sticky residue on my gloves felt like a brand, a permanent mark of my shame. I turned to face the maid, and I could see her backing away, her foot catching on the hem of her apron, her arms tightening around the linens as if she expected me to lunge.

"Carry on," I said, and swept past her into the corridor.

I did not run. Running would have been an admission of defeat. But I walked faster than was dignified, my cloak billowing behind me, my jaw clenched so tightly that my teeth ached. The maid's voice followed me down the corridor, floating after me like a ghost.

"The Shadow Blade... sniffing jam..."

I pretended not to hear.

The walk back to my office was a blur of dark corridors and burning shame. I passed the guards without acknowledging them, their salutes falling on deaf ears. I climbed the stairs to my tower, my boots echoing against the stone, each step a drumbeat of failure.

The door to my office clicked shut behind me, and I stood in the darkness, letting the silence settle around me like a shroud.

The drawing was still there. Of course it was. The jar with its furious face, screaming at me from the center of my desk. I crossed to it, my hand reaching out, my fingers hovering over the crude crayon lines.

The jam conspiracy was a phantom. A lie. A joke crafted by someone who knew exactly how to push my buttons, who knew that I would chase any lead, no matter how absurd, because I could not afford to ignore a potential threat.

But the source of the notes was real.

The demonic horse. The rune of command. And now this—a jar of jam with a screaming face, a mocking declaration that the conspiracy was real, that it was everywhere, that I would never find it because I was too busy chasing my own tail.

I sank into my chair, the leather creaking beneath me. The drawing stared up at me, and I stared back, and for the first time in years, I felt the weight of my own inadequacy pressing down on my shoulders.

I was no longer hunting a threat. I was being hunted by a prankster, and my own methods had become the joke.

The worst part was that I was going to keep investigating anyway. Because that was what I did. That was who I was. The Shadow Blade did not give up, did not surrender, did not admit defeat in the face of a crayon drawing.

I pulled a fresh sheet of parchment from my drawer and began to write my report.

*Subject: The Jam Conspiracy*
*Status: Ongoing*
*Preliminary findings: The preserves are clean. This is itself suspicious. Recommend—*

I stopped. What did I recommend? That we confiscate all jam in the kingdom? That we interrogate the apricot growers? That I continue to break into pantries at midnight and listen to jars for signs of life?

I crumpled the parchment and threw it across the room.

The drawing continued to scream at me from the desk. In my mind, I could hear the maid's voice again, asking if there was poison in the preserves. I could see her curtsy, polite and terrified, as she backed away from the legendary Shadow Blade and his jar of jam.

I had been a master of shadows, a whisper in the dark, a blade that struck without warning. I had brought down empires and exposed conspiracies that would have shattered kingdoms. And now I was being undone by preserves.

The cold, logical part of my mind—the part that had kept me alive through decades of danger—offered a new theory. What if the jam was not the conspiracy? What if the jam was a symbol? A message meant to convey something deeper, something about the nature of the threat I was facing?

Jam was sweet. Jam was innocent. Jam was the kind of thing that a child might draw, a child who wanted to mock the adults who thought they were in control.

A child.

The thought struck me like a physical blow. I leaned forward, my eyes fixed on the drawing, my mind racing. The crayon. The crude lines. The furious face. The label that had been written with the careful, deliberate strokes of someone who was still learning to form letters.

The princess.

I had suspected her for months. The doll formations. The rune of command. The strange way she moved through the palace, always watching, always calculating, always one step ahead of everyone around her. But I had never been able to prove anything, and every time I tried, I ended up looking like a fool.

The Crumble Conspiracy. The fruit basket. The thank-you notes.

And now the jam.

I picked up the drawing, holding it carefully by the corners, and studied it with the attention I usually reserved for enemy codes. The face on the jar was not just furious. It was *determined*. It was the face of something that would not be stopped, would not be contained, would not be silenced.

It was the face of a conspiracy that was not jam at all.

I set the drawing down and reached for a fresh piece of parchment. My hand was steady now, my mind clear. I had a new theory, a new lead, a new direction.

The princess was the conspiracy. The jam was just her way of telling me that she knew I was watching.

I began to write a new report, my quill moving across the page with renewed purpose. The words came easily now, flowing from my mind to the paper in a stream of cold, precise prose. I documented everything—the demonic horse, the rune of command, the drawing of the jar. I noted the patterns, the escalation, the mocking tone that bordered on contempt.

I did not mention the maid. Some humiliations were best left unrecorded.

When the report was finished, I folded it into a tight square and tucked it into the inner pocket of my cloak. Tomorrow, I would begin a new phase of my investigation. I would watch the princess more closely. I would follow her every move, catalog her every gesture, analyze her every word.

I would find the truth.

The drawing sat on my desk, still screaming, still mocking, still watching me with its furious, scribbled eyes. I did not look at it again. I could not afford to. If I looked at it, I would see the truth—that I was being outmaneuvered by a child, that my carefully ordered world was crumbling around me, that the jam conspiracy was just the beginning.

I blew out the candle and sat in the darkness, my hands folded in front of me, my mind churning with suspicions and fears and the desperate hope that I was wrong.

I was not wrong. I was never wrong.

But for the first time in my career, I wished I was.

title: Sleepy Spells and Fatherly Wisdom
prose:
# Chapter 36: Sleepy Spells and Fatherly Wisdom

The state dinner was a gilded prison of polite suffering.

I sat beside my father, King Alistair, my fingers tracing idle patterns on the damask tablecloth while the visiting diplomats droned on about trade tariffs and territorial grazing rights. The candlelight flickered, casting long, wavering shadows that danced like restless spirits across the walls. My father, however, was in his element—booming with laughter, clapping visiting dignitaries on the back, his voice a thunderous counterpoint to the delicate clink of silverware. He leaned toward me, his breath warm with the scent of spiced wine. "These dull men will put even *you* to sleep, my little star," he whispered, his eyes crinkling with amusement.

I forced a smile, my cheeks aching with the effort. *If only he knew how right he was.* The truth was, I had spent the last hour calculating the precise mana cost of *Lassitudo Animi*, a cantrip designed to induce mild mental fatigue. It was trivial magic, requiring little more than a thread of power—something even my pathetic mana reserves could manage without immediate backlash. The sigil was simple: a spiral, tightening inward like a noose of boredom. Under the table, my fingers traced it into the fabric of my dress, the threads catching slightly beneath my nails.

The duke from the northern provinces was mid-sentence, his voice a monotonous hum as he extolled the virtues of his region’s wool. I tuned him out, focusing instead on the spell’s intent. *Boredom. Fatigue. A dimming of enthusiasm.* The words formed in my mind, sharp and precise, a counterpoint to the duke’s droning. I exhaled, releasing a whisper of mana toward my father. The spell connected—a delicate thread of energy, invisible but tangible, like the faintest tug on a fishing line.

For a moment, it worked. I felt the spell take hold, a subtle shift in the air. My father’s laughter faltered, his smile wavering as if caught in a sudden gust of wind. His fingers, which had been drumming an enthusiastic rhythm on the table, stilled. His eyes, usually so bright with mirth, grew heavy-lidded. *Yes. This was it.* The perfect, petty revenge for an evening of tedium.

Then the spell snapped.

It wasn’t a violent backlash—no explosion of energy, no searing pain. Instead, the mana surged back into me like a wave breaking against a cliff, not with force, but with a profound, leaden weariness. My eyelids fluttered, my posture slumping as if my bones had turned to lead. A yawn escaped me, wide and utterly genuine, my jaw cracking with the effort. I clapped a hand over my mouth, but it was too late. The damage was done.

My father turned, his laughter softening into concern. "Tired, my little star?" he asked, his voice warm with affection. "The dull men *are* putting you to sleep!" He didn’t question the cause, only the symptom. With effortless strength, he lifted me from my chair, cradling me against his chest like a child half my age. I was too exhausted to protest, my head lolling against his shoulder, the scent of wine and leather and something uniquely *father* filling my senses.

*This was not the plan.*

I had intended to dim his enthusiasm, to make him *less* of a presence, not *more*. And yet, here I was, enduring the exact opposite of my goal: more of him, not less. His arms were warm, his heartbeat steady beneath my ear, and the hum of his voice as he carried me through the torch-lit corridors was a lullaby I hadn’t asked for. He sang—if one could call it that—a tuneless, off-key melody that was somehow more noise than music. I should have been seething. I should have been plotting. Instead, my inner monologue, usually a torrent of sarcasm and diabolical scheming, was sluggish, as if my thoughts were wading through honey.

*This is a tactical failure of the highest order,* I thought, my mental voice slurring slightly. *I have been outmaneuvered by my own incompetence.*

The corridors passed in a blur of flickering torchlight and the distant murmur of courtiers. My father’s humming grew louder, his grip on me tightening slightly as if to ward off the very idea of sleepiness. "You’ll feel better after a nap," he declared, his voice booming in the quiet hallway. "And tomorrow, we’ll have a proper adventure! Maybe a ride through the gardens, or—"

"Or a lesson in swordplay," I mumbled, my voice muffled against his shoulder. It was a reflex, a habit born of months of enduring his well-meaning but misguided attempts to "toughen me up." The words slipped out before I could stop them, and I immediately regretted them. Swordplay was the last thing I wanted—my body was a prison of frailty, and the thought of wielding a blade with any semblance of skill was laughable. But my father, ever the optimist, took it as enthusiasm.

"Ah, so you *are* awake!" he said, his voice bright with pride. "I knew you were just resting your eyes. You’ve got the spirit of a warrior, my Lily. Just like your old dad!"

I didn’t correct him. There was no point. Instead, I let my eyes drift shut, feigning sleep while my mind raced. *This is temporary,* I told myself. *A setback. A minor humiliation.* But the warmth of his embrace, the steady rhythm of his steps, the way his voice softened when he spoke to me—it was all too much. Too *real*. Too *human*.

We reached my chambers, and he pushed the door open with his shoulder, the hinges creaking softly. The room was bathed in the soft glow of a single enchanted lantern, its light flickering like a dying star. My bed, a monstrous thing of silk and down, awaited me, and my father carried me to it with the same care he might have shown a fragile artifact. He set me down gently, his large hands clumsy as he fussed with the silk duvet, tucking it around me with the precision of a man who had never made a bed in his life.

"Better?" he asked, his voice a low rumble.

I nodded, my eyelids heavy. The exhaustion was real now, a weight pressing down on me, and I couldn’t tell if it was the backlash of the spell or the sheer emotional toll of the evening. My father smiled, his face softening in the dim light. "That’s my girl," he said, brushing a strand of hair from my forehead. His fingers were calloused, rough against my skin, but his touch was gentle. "Sleep well, my little star. Tomorrow, we’ll show those dull men how a Lumengarde shines."

He turned to leave, his boots scuffing softly against the stone floor. As he reached the door, he paused, his hand resting on the frame. "Oh, and Lily?" he said, his voice light with amusement. "Nice try with the spell, by the way. The duke *was* talking a lot."

My eyes snapped open.

*He knew.*

The realization hit me like a physical blow, and for a moment, I forgot to breathe. My father chuckled, the sound rich and warm, and then he was gone, the door clicking shut behind him. The confession of guilt lodged in my throat, a lump of words I couldn’t force out. *He knew.* And he was *amused.*

I lay there, staring at the ceiling, my mind racing even as my body begged for sleep. The spell had failed. Spectacularly. Not only had it not worked as intended, but it had backfired in the most humiliating way possible, leaving me exhausted and at the mercy of my father’s doting affection. And yet, despite everything, there was a part of me—a traitorous, insidious part—that didn’t entirely hate the outcome.

*This is unacceptable,* I thought, my mental voice growing fainter as sleep pulled at me. *I am Maledictus. I do not* like *things.*

But as the darkness closed in, I couldn’t deny the warmth in my chest, the way my father’s laughter still echoed in my ears. It was a warmth that had nothing to do with magic and everything to do with the man who had carried me to bed, who had hummed off-key and called me his little star.

And for the first time in a long time, I let myself wonder if that warmth might be worth something after all.

---

The next morning, I woke to the sound of birds chirping outside my window and the faint, familiar scent of strawberry jam. My head throbbed slightly, a remnant of the previous night’s magical backlash, but the exhaustion had faded, leaving only a dull ache behind my temples. I sat up slowly, my fingers brushing against the silk sheets, and took stock of my surroundings.

The room was as I had left it—neat, orderly, the enchanted lantern still casting its soft glow. But something was different. On my bedside table, a small silver tray held a plate of toast, a jar of jam, and a folded note. I reached for the note first, unfolding it with careful fingers.

*"My dearest Lily,"* it read, in my father’s bold, looping script. *"I hope you slept well. I’ve asked the kitchen to prepare your favorite breakfast—strawberry jam, just the way you like it. Join me in the gardens when you’re ready. We’ll have that ride I promised. Love, Father."*

I set the note down, my fingers lingering on the paper. The jam was a recurring joke between us—a symbol of my "delicate constitution" and his unwavering indulgence. But today, it felt different. Today, it felt like a peace offering.

I dressed quickly, choosing a simple gown of pale blue, the fabric soft against my skin. The mirror reflected a girl who looked far too innocent for the thoughts swirling in her head. I scowled at my reflection, but the expression only made me look younger, more vulnerable. *Useless,* I thought. *Absolutely useless.*

The gardens were alive with the sounds of morning—birds singing, bees buzzing, the distant murmur of servants going about their duties. My father was waiting for me near the stables, his back to me as he adjusted the saddle on a sleek black mare. He turned as I approached, his face breaking into a grin. "Ah, there she is! My little star, ready for an adventure!"

I forced a smile, my cheeks aching with the effort. "I’m not sure I’d call a ride an adventure," I said, my voice light. "But I suppose it’s better than another state dinner."

My father laughed, the sound booming across the courtyard. "That’s the spirit! And who knows? Maybe we’ll find a dragon to slay along the way."

I rolled my eyes, but the gesture was lost on him. He lifted me onto the mare with ease, his hands steady and sure. The horse shifted beneath me, its muscles rippling with barely contained energy. I gripped the reins tightly, my knuckles white, and tried to ignore the way my stomach twisted with nerves. I had ridden before, of course, but never with any real skill. My body was not built for such things.

My father mounted his own horse, a massive stallion that snorted and pawed at the ground. "Ready?" he asked, his eyes bright with excitement.

I nodded, though I wasn’t sure I was. The mare took off at a gentle trot, and I clung to the saddle, my body swaying with the motion. My father, ever the showman, urged his stallion into a gallop, and the mare followed suit, her hooves pounding against the earth. The wind whipped through my hair, tugging at the strands, and for a moment, I forgot to be afraid. For a moment, I forgot to be anything but a girl on a horse, riding beside her father.

We slowed as we reached the edge of the gardens, the path winding through a grove of fruit trees. My father dismounted first, then lifted me down, his hands warm on my waist. "There," he said, setting me on my feet. "Not so bad, was it?"

I shook my head, though the truth was more complicated. The ride had been exhilarating, terrifying, and utterly unlike anything I had experienced in my past life. There were no grand battles here, no armies to command, no souls to consume. Just the wind, the sun, and the steady presence of my father beside me.

We walked for a while, the path leading us deeper into the gardens. The trees were heavy with fruit, the air sweet with the scent of ripening peaches. My father plucked one from a low-hanging branch, polishing it on his sleeve before handing it to me. "For you," he said, his voice soft.

I took it, my fingers brushing against his. The peach was warm from the sun, its skin velvety beneath my touch. I bit into it, the juice running down my chin, and my father laughed, handing me a handkerchief. "You’re a mess," he said, but his eyes were warm.

I wiped my chin, my fingers lingering on the fabric. "I suppose I am," I said, my voice quiet.

My father studied me for a moment, his expression unreadable. Then, without warning, he pulled me into a hug, his arms wrapping around me with a strength that was both comforting and suffocating. "You’re my mess," he said, his voice muffled against my hair. "And I wouldn’t have it any other way."

I stiffened, my body instinctively resisting the embrace. But then, slowly, I relaxed, my arms wrapping around him in return. It was a small thing, a fleeting moment, but it was enough to send a jolt of panic through me. *This is dangerous,* I thought. *This is weakness.*

But as my father pulled away, his smile brighter than ever, I couldn’t bring myself to care.

---

The rest of the day passed in a blur of small, meaningless moments. We returned to the palace, where my father regaled me with stories of his youth—tales of battles won and enemies vanquished, all told with the same enthusiasm he might have used to describe a particularly good meal. I listened, my expression carefully neutral, my mind racing with the implications of the morning’s events.

That evening, as I sat in my chambers, a knock sounded at the door. Before I could answer, it swung open, revealing Queen Seraphina. She carried a tray laden with a steaming cup of tea and a plate of biscuits, her expression unreadable. "I thought you might like some company," she said, her voice quiet.

I nodded, my fingers tightening around the edge of my book. "Of course," I said, my voice carefully light.

Seraphina set the tray down on the table beside me, her movements graceful and precise. She poured the tea with the same care she might have used to mix a potion, the steam rising in delicate curls. "You seem different today," she said, her eyes meeting mine. "More at ease."

I took a sip of the tea, the warmth spreading through me. "Do I?" I asked, my voice carefully neutral.

Seraphina studied me for a moment, her gaze sharp and assessing. "Your father tells me you enjoyed your ride this morning," she said. "He was quite pleased."

I set the cup down, my fingers tracing the rim. "He’s easily pleased," I said, my voice dry.

Seraphina smiled, a small, private thing. "He is," she agreed. "But that doesn’t mean his happiness isn’t genuine."

I said nothing, my mind racing. Seraphina’s presence was always a reminder of the careful balance I had to maintain—the girl I pretended to be and the demon I truly was. She was observant, far more so than my father, and I could never quite shake the feeling that she saw more than she let on.

She reached out, her fingers brushing against my cheek. "You look tired," she said, her voice soft. "Perhaps you should rest."

I nodded, my throat tight. "Perhaps I should," I agreed.

Seraphina stood, her skirts whispering against the floor. She paused at the door, her hand resting on the frame. "Sleep well, Lily," she said, her voice warm. "And remember—you are loved."

The door clicked shut behind her, leaving me alone with my thoughts. I stared at the tea, the steam now curling lazily in the air, and wondered, not for the first time, what it would be like to be truly loved. Not as a vessel for a demon’s soul, not as a prodigy or a miracle, but as a girl. A daughter.

The thought was dangerous, treacherous. And yet, as I climbed into bed, the silk sheets cool against my skin, I couldn’t bring myself to push it away.

---

The next morning, I woke to the sound of Baphomutt’s chittering. The imp was perched on the foot of my bed, his beady eyes gleaming with mischief. In his paws, he clutched a small, folded parchment, the wax seal already broken. "Mistress!" he squeaked, holding it out to me. "Important letter!"

I sat up slowly, my head throbbing with the remnants of the previous day’s exhaustion. "Where did you get this?" I asked, my voice sharp.

Baphomutt’s ears drooped. "From the hallway!" he said, his voice defensive. "It was just lying there!"

I snatched the parchment from his paws, my fingers trembling slightly as I unfolded it. The script was florid, the ink dark and heavy, and the sigil at the bottom—a flame encircled by a serpent—was unmistakable. The Cult of the Eternal Flame.

*"To the Saint of the New Dawn,"* the letter began, *"we humbly beseech your blessing. The hour of our Lord’s return draws nigh, and we seek only to serve. Grant us your favor, and we shall ensure your place at His side when the old world is remade."*

I crumpled the parchment in my fist, my heart pounding. The cult. Again. They had been quiet since the failed ritual, their attempts at resurrection thwarted by my own hand. But now, they were back, and this time, they weren’t threatening me. They were *worshipping* me.

Baphomutt tilted his head, his ears perking up. "Mistress angry?" he asked, his voice small.

I glared at him, my fingers tightening around the parchment. "You could say that," I said, my voice tight.

The imp’s ears drooped further. "Baphomutt sorry," he said, his voice contrite. "Baphomutt just wanted to help."

I sighed, my anger fading as quickly as it had come. Baphomutt was an idiot, but he was *my* idiot. "You did," I said, my voice weary. "Just… next time, bring me the letter *before* you break the seal."

Baphomutt nodded eagerly, his tail wagging. "Yes, Mistress!" he said, his voice bright.

I set the crumpled parchment aside, my mind racing. The cult’s letter was a problem—a big one. But it was also an opportunity. If I played my cards right, I could use their misguided devotion to my advantage. Maybe even turn them into a tool.

But first, I had to deal with the immediate threat. The letter had been delivered to *me*, not my parents. That meant someone—Baphomutt, most likely—had intercepted it before it could reach them. But if Seraphina or Alistair found out about this, they would ask questions. Questions I couldn’t answer.

I stood, my legs unsteady, and crossed to my desk. The drawer slid open with a soft click, revealing the hidden compartment where I stashed forbidden trinkets and stolen jewels. I added the crumpled letter to the collection, my fingers lingering on the parchment for a moment before I shut the drawer.

Baphomutt watched me, his eyes wide. "Mistress okay?" he asked, his voice small.

I turned to him, my expression carefully neutral. "I’m fine," I said, my voice light. "But we have work to do."

The imp’s ears perked up. "Work?" he asked, his voice eager.

I nodded, my mind already racing with possibilities. "Yes," I said. "And this time, we’re going to do it right."

Baphomutt grinned, his sharp teeth glinting in the morning light. "Baphomutt ready!" he said, his voice bright.

I smiled, but the expression didn’t reach my eyes. The cult’s letter was a reminder—a warning. The world was still out there, waiting, watching. And I was still Maledictus, no matter how much I might wish otherwise.

But for now, I had a plan. And if there was one thing I was good at, it was turning chaos into opportunity.

Even if that opportunity came in the form of a misguided cult and an overenthusiastic imp.

title: Fan Mail from Fanatics
prose:
# Chapter 37: Fan Mail from Fanatics

The morning light crept through my curtains like an unwelcome visitor, pale and hesitant, as if it too knew something was wrong. I had barely slept. 

Baphomutt had been uncharacteristically quiet since delivering his disastrous package. He perched on my windowsill now, his leathery wings folded tight against his spine,  

"Mistress," he squeaked, his voice barely above a whisper. "Baphomutt has bad feeling."

I stared at him. "You? Have a bad feeling? You once ate a cursed amulet because you thought it was a berry."

"Was not berry," he said defensively. "Was berry-shaped. Very deceptive."

I pinched the bridge of my nose, feeling the familiar ache of an oncoming headache.  

"The letter," I said, keeping my voice low. "You found it in the hallway. Are you certain no one saw you pick it up?"

Baphomutt's ears drooped. "Baphomutt was very sneaky. Very quiet. Like shadow."

"Like a shadow that leaves a trail of stolen silverware and demonic graffiti," I muttered.

"Mistress wounding," he said, pressing a tiny claw to his chest. "Baphomutt's heart is small but feels big things."

  The Eternal Flame. The symbol of my former glory, twisted into something reverent and pathetic.

*"To the Saint of the New Dawn,"* I read again, my eyes tracing the florid script. *"We humbly beseech your blessing. The hour of our Lord's return draws nigh, and we seek only to serve. Grant us your favor, and we shall ensure your place at His side when the old world is remade."*

Who had been defeated by the Seven Heroes and reborn as a ten-year-old princess with the mana capacity of a damp sponge.

But not in the way they thought. Not even close.

"Mistress," Baphomutt said again, his voice more insistent. "Baphomutt hears footsteps."

I froze. My ears, attuned to the subtle rhythms of the palace, caught it a moment later: the soft, measured tread of someone walking with purpose. Not a servant's hurried patter or a guard's heavy boots. This was the deliberate, unhurried pace of someone who owned every corridor they walked.

Seraphina.

I shoved the letter beneath my pillow, my movements swift and practiced. The motion was barely complete when the door swung open, and my mother stepped inside, her presence filling the room like morning light through stained glass.

Queen Seraphina, the Saint of Mercy, was a study in contrasts. Her robes were the color of winter frost, pale and pristine, but her eyes held the warmth of a hearth fire. Her hair, silver-gold and impossibly smooth, was pinned in an elaborate arrangement that somehow managed to look effortless. She moved with the grace of a dancer and the precision of a surgeon, and her gaze, when it landed on me, was sharp enough to cut glass.

"Lily," she said, her voice carrying that particular blend of affection and scrutiny that only a mother could achieve. "You're awake early. And you look..." She paused, her head tilting slightly. "Troubled."

 "Just a dream, Mother. Nothing to worry about."

"A dream." She repeated the word as if tasting it, her eyes never leaving mine. "You've been having quite a few of those lately."

"Children have dreams," I said, keeping my voice light. "It's what we do."

Seraphina's lips curved into a smile that didn't quite reach her eyes. "Indeed. Though most children dream of ponies and birthday cakes, not..." She gestured vaguely. "Whatever it is that causes you to wake with that look on your face."

 

"I'm fine," I said, the words coming out more firmly than I felt. "Really. It was just a strange dream."

Seraphina studied me for a long moment, her gaze probing, searching. Then, mercifully, she let it drop. "Very well. But if you're feeling unwell, you must tell me. Your constitution is delicate, and I won't have you pushing yourself too hard."

"Yes, Mother."

She crossed to my bed, her hand reaching out to brush a strand of hair from my forehead. The gesture was tender, maternal, and it sent a spike of guilt through my chest that I ruthlessly suppressed.  He did not feel his mother's gentle touch and want to lean into it.

But I wasn't Maledictus anymore, was I? I was Lily. And Lily was a good daughter, a sweet princess, a prodigy of magic and generosity and all the things the court adored.

"Mother," I said, the word slipping out before I could stop it. "Do you ever wonder if... if the person you are is the person you were meant to be?"

Seraphina's hand stilled on my forehead. Her eyes, warm and sharp and impossibly knowing, met mine. "All the time," she said softly. "Every day. But I've learned that the person you are is shaped by the choices you make, not the ones you wish you could take back."

She said it so simply, so matter-of-factly, that I almost believed her. Almost.

"Now," she continued, her tone shifting to something lighter, "I came to tell you that your father has planned another of his 'family bonding' activities for this afternoon. Something involving a scavenger hunt and, if I know your father, far too much enthusiasm."

I felt my lips twitch despite myself. "A scavenger hunt?"

"He's already hidden the clues. I believe one of them involves the crystal garden and a very confused garden gnome."

The image was so absurd, so perfectly Alistair, that I couldn't stop the small laugh that escaped me. It was a genuine sound, unguarded and real, and it caught me off guard.

Seraphina smiled, and for a moment, the sharpness in her gaze softened. "There's my girl. I was worried I'd have to fetch the physician."

"I'm fine, Mother. Truly."

"Good." She leaned down and pressed a kiss to my forehead, her lips cool against my skin. "I'll see you at breakfast. And Lily?"

"Yes?"

"Whatever it is that's troubling you," she said, her voice dropping to a near-whisper, "you can tell me. No matter what it is. I'm your mother. I'll always listen."

The words settled over me like a blanket, warm and suffocating in equal measure. I nodded, not trusting my voice.

Seraphina swept out of the room, her robes whispering against the floor. The door closed behind her with a soft click, and I was alone again, the silence pressing in from all sides.

I pulled the letter from beneath my pillow, the parchment crumpling in my grip. The cult's words burned in my mind, their reverence a poison I couldn't purge.

*Saint of the New Dawn.*

*The hour of our Lord's return draws nigh.*

They didn't understand. They couldn't understand. They had built an entire theology around a lie, and I was the unwilling cornerstone of their delusion.

Baphomutt crept closer, his tiny claws clicking against the windowsill. "Mistress sad?"

"I'm not sad," I said, the words flat. "I'm furious."

"Furious is good," he said, nodding sagely. "Furious means Baphomutt should hide."

"Stay."

He froze mid-creep, his eyes wide. "Mistress?"

I stared at the letter, my mind churning. The cult was a threat, yes, but not the kind I was used to. They didn't want to kill me. They wanted to worship me. To define me. To shape me into their image of what their Lord's vessel should be.

And that was worse. So much worse.

If they had threatened me, I could have destroyed them. If they had tried to sacrifice me again, I could have turned their own ritual against them. But this—this gentle, reverent poison—was something I couldn't fight with fire and fury.

I needed a different approach.

"Baphomutt," I said slowly, the gears of my mind turning. "How good are you at intercepting mail?"

The imp's eyes brightened. "Very good! Baphomutt is expert at stealing letters. Once stole love letter from knight to lady. Very romantic. Very stolen."

"Good." I tucked the letter into my sleeve, my mind already forming a plan. "I need you to watch the palace entrances. If anyone delivers anything—a letter, a package, a message—I need to know about it before anyone else does."

"Baphomutt understand! Baphomutt will be like shadow. Like wind. Like—"

"Just don't get caught."

The imp's ears drooped slightly, but he nodded with the solemnity of a creature who had no idea what he was agreeing to. "Baphomutt will not fail mistress."

"You say that every time."

"And Baphomutt means it every time!"

I sighed, the sound escaping through my nose in a long, weary exhale. "Just go. And Baphomutt?"

"Yes, Mistress?"

"Be careful."

The imp's beady eyes widened, and for a moment, something that might have been confusion flickered across his face. Then he grinned, his sharp teeth glinting in the morning light. "Mistress worried about Baphomutt!"

"Don't make it weird."

"Baphomutt will be so careful! So sneaky! So—"

"Go."

He vanished through the window with a flutter of leathery wings, leaving me alone with the letter and the cold spot in my chest and the growing, gnawing certainty that the cult's misunderstanding was only going to get worse.

I stood, smoothing my dress, and slipped the letter into the hidden drawer where it had spent the night. The parchment settled among the trinkets and stolen jewels, its presence corrupting the space like a drop of ink in a glass of water.

I would have to deal with this. Soon. Before the cult's reverence spiraled into something I couldn't control.

But first, I had to survive breakfast.

---

Breakfast was, as always, a production.

The royal dining hall was a cavernous space, its ceilings vaulted with carved stone and its walls lined with tapestries depicting the glorious victories of the Seven Heroes. The long oak table gleamed with polish, set with silverware that had been polished to a mirror shine and porcelain plates painted with delicate scenes of pastoral life. The smell of fresh bread and honeyed ham wafted through the air, accompanied by the gentle murmur of servants attending to their duties.

King Alistair sat at the head of the table, his broad shoulders filling the carved oak chair like it had been made for him. Which, I supposed, it had. He was a mountain of a man, all muscle and good humor, with a jaw that could crack walnuts and a laugh that could shake the rafters. 

"Lily!" he boomed, his face splitting into a grin as I entered. "There's my little genius! Come, sit! I've saved you the good seat!"

"Good morning, Father," I said, sliding into the chair he'd indicated. "I trust you slept well."

"Like a baby!" he declared, slapping the table with enough force to make the silverware jump. "Woke up at dawn, did a hundred push-ups, then went for a run around the castle walls. Nothing like a good sweat to get the blood flowing!"

"Delightful," I said, my voice carefully neutral.

Seraphina, seated at the other end of the table, raised an eyebrow but said nothing. Her gaze flicked to me, then to the doorway, then back to her plate. She was always watching, always cataloging, always filing away details for later examination. It was exhausting.

"So," Alistair said, leaning forward with the eager expression of a man about to reveal a brilliant plan, "I've been thinking about this afternoon's scavenger hunt."

"Have you now?" Seraphina said, her tone mild.

"I have! I've hidden clues all over the palace. The first one is in the crystal garden—I've taped it to the underside of the garden gnome's hat."

"The one that twitches?" I asked, unable to help myself.

"The very same! That gnome has been acting strangely ever since you planted those crystals, Lily. I think it's possessed by the spirit of a mischievous fairy."

"I'm sure it's just a draft," I said.

"Draft, my eye! That gnome has personality!" Alistair laughed, a booming sound that made the chandeliers tremble. "Anyway, the scavenger hunt is going to be epic. I've hidden clues in the library, the training grounds, even the throne room!"

"The throne room?" Seraphina said, her eyebrow climbing higher. "You hid a clue in the throne room?"

"Behind the left armrest of the throne! Very sneaky. No one will ever look there."

"Except for the dozens of guards and courtiers who pass through the throne room every day."

Alistair waved a dismissive hand. "Details, details. The point is, we're going to have a grand adventure, just like the old days!"

"Father," I said, the word slipping out before I could stop it, "do you ever miss it? The adventure, I mean?"

Alistair's grin faltered for just a moment. "Miss it? Lily, I have everything I could ever want right here. A beautiful wife, a brilliant daughter, a kingdom that loves me. What more could I ask for?"

"The honeyed ham?" I suggested.

He laughed, the sound filling the hall. "You're a cheeky one, aren't you? Just like your mother."

"I'm nothing like my mother," I said, the words coming out sharper than I intended.

"Lily?" he said, his voice softer now. "Are you alright?"

I forced a smile, the mask sliding back into place. "I'm fine, Father. Just tired. I didn't sleep well last night."

"Ah, bad dreams?" He reached across the table and patted my hand, his grip warm and steady. "I used to have those too, back in the old days. You know what helped? A good breakfast and a hearty laugh. So eat up, and I'll tell you the story of the time I wrestled a wyvern for its treasure hoard."

"Did you really wrestle a wyvern?" I asked, despite myself.

"Of course not! I shot it with an arrow and then claimed the treasure. But the wrestling story sounds better."

Seraphina let out a soft sigh, but there was affection in it. "Alistair, you're going to give her bad habits."

"Bad habits? I'm giving her life lessons! The most important one being: if you're going to tell a story, make it a good one."

I picked up my fork and took a bite of the honeyed ham, the sweetness coating my tongue. It was good. Everything in this palace was good, polished and perfect and suffocating in its domesticity.

And somewhere out there, a cult was worshipping me as their saint, building a theology around my name, preparing for a return that would never come.

I chewed slowly, savoring the taste, and wondered how long I could keep the masks in place before they shattered.

---

The rest of breakfast passed in a blur of Alistair's stories and Seraphina's quiet observations. By the time I excused myself, the letter was burning a hole in my sleeve, a constant reminder of the danger I was in.

I retreated to my room, the familiar comfort of my four walls settling around me like a shroud. Baphomutt was still gone, no doubt skulking through the palace corridors in search of intercepted mail. The silence was almost peaceful.

I pulled the letter from my sleeve and read it again, my eyes tracing the florid script with growing disgust.

*"To the Saint of the New Dawn..."*

They had called me a saint. Me. Maledictus, the Demon Lord, the scourge of the Seven Heroes. The irony was so profound it made my teeth ache.

But beneath the irony, there was something else. Something colder.

 They no longer saw me as a vessel to be used. They saw me as a holy icon, a divine figure worthy of worship.

And that was dangerous in a way I hadn't anticipated.

They wanted to define me. And their definition was a lie.

The cold spot in my chest pulsed, a dull ache that spread through my ribs. I pressed a hand to it, feeling the void where my lifespan had been excised. The Word of Unmaking had cost me years I would never get back, and for what? To save myself from a cult that had turned around and worshipped me anyway?

"Mistress?"

Baphomutt's voice came from the window, small and uncertain. I turned to find him perched on the sill, his wings folded tight against his body, his eyes wide with something that might have been concern.

"Did you find anything?" I asked.

He shook his head. "No letters. No messages. Baphomutt checked everywhere. Very sneaky."

"Good." I tucked the letter back into my sleeve, my mind already turning. "Then we have a little time."

"Time for what?"

I looked at him, my expression hardening. "Time to figure out how to stop them. The cult thinks I'm their saint. They think I'm going to help them bring back their Lord. They're wrong, but they don't know that. And if I can't convince them, they'll keep sending letters, keep building their narrative, keep trying to define me."

"Baphomutt could eat them," he offered. "Very quick. Very efficient."

"Tempting, but no. Eating the cult would raise questions I don't want to answer."

"Baphomutt could make them disappear. Very sneaky."

"No." I paced across the room, my mind racing. "We need a different approach. We need to make them think I'm not worth worshipping. We need to make them lose interest."

"Mistress could be boring," Baphomutt suggested. "Very boring. Like watching grass grow. Like listening to courtier talk."

I paused, considering. "That's... actually not a bad idea."

Baphomutt's ears perked up. "Baphomutt smart?"

"Don't push it." I crossed to my desk, pulling out a sheet of parchment and a quill. "The cult's letter mentioned a 'New Dawn.' They're expecting something. A sign, a miracle, a confirmation of their beliefs. If I can give them nothing—if I can make my responses so bland, so unremarkable, that they lose interest—then maybe they'll move on."

"But mistress not boring," Baphomutt said, his voice earnest. "Mistress is terrifying and wonderful."

I felt a flicker of warmth at his words, quickly suppressed. "I'll take that as a compliment."

I dipped the quill in ink and began to write. The response was carefully crafted, a masterpiece of diplomatic tedium. I thanked them for their letter, expressed my gratitude for their support, and politely declined to engage with any of their theological claims. I signed it with my full title—Princess Liliana Celestia Lumengarde—and sealed it with the royal crest.

It was the most boring letter I had ever written. It was perfect.

"Take this to the palace scribe," I said, handing the parchment to Baphomutt. "Tell them it needs to be sent."

"Mistress, why scribe?"

"Because if I send it myself, the cult will know it came from me. If it comes from the palace, it looks official. Boring. Unremarkable."

Baphomutt nodded, his expression one of intense concentration. "Baphomutt understands. Mistress is playing long game."

"Exactly." I smiled, but the expression didn't reach my eyes. "The cult wants a saint. I'm going to give them a bureaucrat."

The imp took the letter and vanished through the window, leaving me alone with my thoughts and the cold spot in my chest.

I sat down on my bed, the silence pressing in around me. The letter from the cult was still in my sleeve, a weight I couldn't shake. 

And no matter how many boring letters I sent, I couldn't shake the feeling that their misunderstanding was only going to get worse.

The cult was a threat. Not because they wanted to hurt me, but because they wanted to define me. And in their zealous ignorance, they had stumbled onto a truth they couldn't possibly understand.

I was Maledictus. I was the Demon Lord. And no matter how hard I tried to bury that truth, it would always be there, waiting to surface.

At least when they had tried to kill me, I had known how to fight back.

Now, I wasn't so sure.

title: Summoning Failures
prose:
# Chapter 38: Summoning Failures

The ornamental garden was quiet at this hour, the kind of quiet that made the back of my neck prickle. Not the quiet of peace, but the quiet of a stage waiting for the actors to arrive. The morning mist still clung to the rose bushes, turning the thorns into tiny, glinting daggers. I knelt in the damp earth, my knees pressing into the cold dirt, and traced the summoning circle with the tip of my finger.

It was a small circle, barely larger than my palm. A trivial thing, really.  But I wasn’t a novice. I was Maledictus, the Demon Lord, architect of a thousand forbidden rituals, master of the Abyssal Halls. And yet, here I was, kneeling in the dirt like a child playing in the mud, attempting to summon something so insignificant it barely warranted the name *demon*.

A gnat.

Not just any gnat. A *Muscus audientis*. A demonic gnat. A creature of such minor power it was little more than a whisper with wings. But it would be *mine*. A servant, a spy, a first step toward reclaiming the power that had been stolen from me. And if I could summon something this small, this trivial, then perhaps I could begin to build something greater.

I took a deep breath, feeling the damp air fill my lungs, and began the incantation.

The words were guttural, ancient. The kind of words that tasted like smoke and iron on the tongue. I had spoken them a thousand times before, in a voice that could shake the foundations of the world. Now, I whispered them, my voice barely more than a breath, as if I were afraid to wake something sleeping.

The circle’s lines glowed faintly, a sickly, uncertain light that flickered like a dying candle. I could feel the mana trickling from my fingertips, a pathetic dribble compared to the roaring river I had once commanded. It was like trying to fill a bathtub with a teaspoon. The circle drank it in, hungry, but it wasn’t enough. The light flickered, sputtered, and died.

Silence.

The air remained empty. No gnat. No demon. No servant. Just the damp earth and the cold weight of failure pressing down on my chest.

I exhaled sharply, my breath fogging in the cool air. The frustration was a cold stone in my gut, sharp and heavy. I knew the theory. I knew the words, the gestures, the precise alignment of the circle’s lines. I had designed summoning matrices that could call forth armies from the depths of the Seven Hells. And yet, my body could not provide the spark. My mana was a trickle, a pathetic, insufficient thing. My mind held the cosmic architecture of a summoning, but my flesh was a prison, a frail, mortal cage that could not contain the power I once wielded.

I closed my eyes and let the frustration wash over me, let it settle into the cold spot in my chest where the Word of Unmaking had stolen a sliver of my lifespan. It was a reminder, this spot. A reminder of what I had lost, of what I could never reclaim. Not like this. Not while I was trapped in this body, this life, this gilded cage of a princess.

A rustle of fabric caught my attention. I opened my eyes and turned my head slightly, just enough to see the group of courtiers strolling along the garden path. They were a good distance away, their voices a low murmur carried on the breeze. But I could hear them. I always could.

“What is she doing?” one of them whispered, her voice tinged with curiosity.

Another, a lady-in-waiting with a perpetually smug expression, leaned in and offered a knowing smile. “Meditating, surely. Her tutors say she seeks inner calm. Such a delicate constitution requires balance.”

Delicate constitution. The words were a bitter joke. I was not delicate. I was a storm trapped in a teacup, a wildfire smothered beneath silk and lace. But the court saw what it wanted to see. A fragile princess, a prodigy, a miracle. Not a demon. Not a threat.

I seized the narrative before it could slip away from me. Closing my eyes, I adopted a serene expression, the kind of look one might wear while communing with the universe. I took a slow, deep breath, letting my shoulders rise and fall with exaggerated calm.

“Yes,” I murmured, just loud enough to be heard. “Meditating.”

The courtiers exchanged glances, their expressions softening with understanding. One of them, a young man with a perpetually flushed face, nodded sagely. “She is so wise for her years. A true philosopher.”

I bit the inside of my cheek to keep from laughing. A philosopher. If only they knew the kind of philosophy I practiced. The kind that involved summoning circles and forbidden grimoires, not quiet contemplation and inner peace.

But the game was working. The courtiers drifted away, their whispers fading into the morning air. I remained kneeling in the dirt, my hands resting lightly on my knees, my expression one of serene meditation. The failed summoning circle was still there, its lines faint but visible in the damp earth. A testament to my failure. A reminder of my limitations.

And then, of course, Baphomutt decided to “help.”

I heard the rustle of leaves before I saw him, the telltale sign of the imp’s presence. He emerged from behind a topiary shaped like a rearing horse, his mismatched eyes gleaming with mischief. His wings, tattered and bat-like, fluttered as he scurried toward me, his claws digging into the earth.

“Mistress!” he hissed, his voice a squeaky whisper. “Baphomutt sees! Mistress is making pretty circle!”

I sighed inwardly. Of course he had seen. Baphomutt saw everything, usually at the worst possible moment. He was like a particularly stupid guardian angel, one who had taken a vow of chaos instead of protection.

I opened my eyes and fixed him with a glare. “Baphomutt,” I said, my voice low and warning. “What did I tell you about interrupting?”

The imp’s ears drooped, his expression crestfallen. “Mistress said no interrupting. But Baphomutt wants to help! Mistress is making pretty circle, but it needs shiny!”

Before I could stop him, he reached into the pocket of his tattered vest and pulled out a glittering hairpin. It was silver, delicate, and unmistakably stolen. I recognized it immediately. It belonged to Lady Elara, one of the Queen’s closest attendants. The kind of woman who would notice its absence before the morning was out.

“Baphomutt found shiny!” the imp declared, his voice brimming with pride. “Shiny is good for circle! Makes it pretty!”

I lunged for the hairpin, but I was too late. Baphomutt scampered forward and placed it in the center of the summoning circle with a flourish. The moment it touched the earth, the circle’s lines flared to life, a sudden, violent burst of light that sent the imp tumbling backward with a yelp.

The hairpin glowed, its silver surface shimmering with an eerie, unnatural light. The summoning circle, now “complete” with Baphomutt’s offering, pulsed with energy, its lines burning bright against the damp earth.

I stared at it, my mouth slightly open. This was not how summoning circles were supposed to work. Offerings were meant to be symbolic, a gesture of intent, not a stolen hairpin dropped haphazardly into the dirt. And yet, the circle was reacting. It was alive, humming with a power that was not mine, a power that was not even demonic. It was the power of chaos, of Baphomutt’s idiotic enthusiasm.

And then, of course, Lady Elara screamed.

It was a high, piercing sound, the kind of scream that could shatter glass. The courtiers, who had only just drifted away, turned as one, their expressions a mix of shock and concern.

“My pin!” Lady Elara shrieked, her voice rising to a near-hysterical pitch. “That’s my pin! The one the King gave me for my birthday!”

She stormed toward me, her skirts swishing angrily against the gravel path. The other courtiers followed, their expressions ranging from amused to horrified. I remained kneeling in the dirt, my hands still resting lightly on my knees, my expression one of polite confusion.

“Your pin, Lady Elara?” I asked, my voice sweet and innocent. “I’m afraid I don’t understand.”

Lady Elara pointed a trembling finger at the summoning circle, at the hairpin glowing in its center. “That’s my pin! The one that was in my hair! The one that’s been missing for days!”

I blinked, my expression carefully blank. “I see. And you believe I took it?”

“Well, I—” Lady Elara faltered, her confidence wavering under my guileless gaze. “I mean, it was in your circle. And you were meditating. And—”

“And you think I stole your pin to use in my meditation?” I asked, my voice dripping with faux incredulity. “Lady Elara, I assure you, I would never. Meditation is a sacred practice. It requires focus, discipline, and above all, respect for the property of others.”

The courtiers murmured amongst themselves, their expressions shifting from accusation to doubt. Lady Elara’s face flushed a deep, embarrassed red. “I—I didn’t mean to accuse you, Your Highness. It’s just that the pin was in your circle, and—”

“And it is a very pretty pin,” I said, cutting her off with a gentle smile. “Perhaps it was drawn to the circle’s energy. The universe works in mysterious ways, Lady Elara.”

The courtiers nodded sagely, their expressions softening with understanding. One of them, an older woman with a perpetually sour expression, stepped forward. “The princess is right. The pin was likely drawn to the circle’s spiritual resonance. A sign of its power, perhaps.”

Lady Elara’s flush deepened, but she nodded, her expression sheepish. “Of course. I—I didn’t think of that. I’m so sorry, Your Highness. I didn’t mean to interrupt your meditation.”

I waved a hand dismissively, my expression one of serene forgiveness. “Think nothing of it, Lady Elara. The universe has a way of testing our patience, doesn’t it?”

The courtiers murmured their agreement, their expressions turning contemplative.  A stolen pin, a glowing circle, a princess in meditation. It was all so *mysterious*. So *profound*.

I stood slowly, brushing the dirt from my knees with deliberate care. I turned to the summoning circle, my expression one of polite disturbance. “Alas, the circle’s energy has been disrupted. Perhaps the universe was not ready for a gnat today.”

 “A gnat, Your Highness?” one of them asked, her voice hushed.

I nodded sagely. “A minor summoning. A test of my connection to the spiritual realm. But the pin’s presence has thrown off the balance. The universe has spoken.”

The courtiers exchanged glances, their expressions turning reverent. “The universe has spoken,” they murmured, as if repeating a sacred mantra.

I reached down and plucked the hairpin from the center of the circle, careful not to touch the glowing lines. The moment my fingers closed around it, the light faded, the circle’s energy dissipating like smoke in the wind. I turned to Lady Elara and held out the pin, my expression one of gentle apology.

“Here, Lady Elara. The universe has returned your pin. I hope it brings you luck.”

Lady Elara took the pin, her expression a mix of gratitude and embarrassment. “Thank you, Your Highness. I—I don’t know what to say.”

I smiled, my expression warm and understanding. “Say nothing. The universe has a way of working things out, doesn’t it?”

The courtiers murmured their agreement, their expressions turning wistful. They drifted away, their voices a low hum of conversation as they discussed the morning’s events. Lady Elara lingered for a moment, her expression uncertain, but I turned away, my attention once more on the summoning circle.

The moment she was gone, I exhaled sharply, my shoulders slumping. The hairpin was still warm in my hand, its surface smooth and cool against my skin. I turned it over, examining the delicate silverwork, the tiny sapphires that dotted its surface like stars.

Baphomutt, who had been cowering behind a rose bush, scurried forward, his expression sheepish. “Baphomutt sorry, Mistress. Baphomutt didn’t mean to cause trouble.”

I fixed him with a glare. “Baphomutt,” I said, my voice low and dangerous. “What have I told you about stealing?”

The imp’s ears drooped, his expression crestfallen. “Mistress said no stealing. But Baphomutt saw shiny, and Baphomutt thought—”

“You didn’t think,” I snapped, cutting him off. “That’s the problem. You never think.”

Baphomutt’s lower lip trembled, his eyes filling with tears. “Baphomutt sorry. Baphomutt will be good. Baphomutt will bring Mistress shiny that isn’t stolen!”

I sighed, my frustration draining away. It was hard to stay angry at Baphomutt. He was an idiot, but he was *my* idiot. And he meant well. Mostly.

“Just—” I began, but I was interrupted by the sound of footsteps on the gravel path.

I turned to see Queen Seraphina approaching, her expression unreadable. She was dressed in a gown of deep blue, the color of twilight, her hair pulled back in a simple braid. 

I dropped into a curtsy, my skirts pooling around my knees. “Mother,” I said, my voice soft and respectful.

Seraphina stopped before me, her gaze sweeping over the summoning circle, the disturbed earth, the hairpin still clutched in my hand. Her expression was carefully neutral, but I could see the questions in her eyes.

“Lily,” she said, her voice quiet. “What are you doing?”

I hesitated, my mind racing. Seraphina was the hardest to fool. She noticed things. The way my hands trembled when I cast a spell. The way my aura flickered with ancient malevolence when I was tired. The way my sketches sometimes bore more resemblance to pentagrams than to family portraits.

But she also loved me. And that love was a shield, a barrier that kept her from seeing the truth. She saw what she wanted to see. A prodigy. A genius. A miracle.

I held up the hairpin, my expression one of polite confusion. “Lady Elara’s pin, Mother. It was in my meditation circle. The courtiers think it was drawn to the circle’s energy.”

Seraphina’s gaze flicked to the summoning circle, to the faint lines still visible in the damp earth. Her expression remained neutral, but I could see the wheels turning in her mind. She was thinking, analyzing, piecing together the clues.

“And what were you meditating on, Lily?” she asked, her voice quiet.

I hesitated, my mind racing. “A gnat,” I said finally, my voice soft.

Seraphina’s eyebrows rose slightly. “A gnat?”

I nodded, my expression earnest. “A minor summoning. A test of my connection to the spiritual realm. But the pin’s presence disrupted the energy. The universe wasn’t ready.”

Seraphina’s gaze lingered on the summoning circle for a long moment. I could see the doubt in her eyes, the suspicion. But then she smiled, a small, gentle thing, and reached out to brush a strand of hair from my face.

“You are so wise for your years, Lily,” she said, her voice warm. “But perhaps it’s time to take a break from your studies. You’ve been pushing yourself too hard.”

I nodded, my expression one of grateful relief. “Of course, Mother. I’ll be more careful.”

Seraphina smiled, her expression softening. “Good. Now, come. Your father is looking for you. He wants to show you the new pony.”

I hesitated, my expression faltering.  The one that had arrived with a fading glamour on its eyes, a pony that was not quite what it seemed.

I had wanted a demonic steed, a creature of shadow and fire. What I had gotten was a pony with a bad temper and a habit of biting.

But I forced a smile, my expression bright and eager. “Of course, Mother. I’d love to see the new pony.”

Seraphina took my hand, her fingers warm and gentle against my skin. She led me away from the summoning circle, away from the damp earth and the cold weight of failure. The hairpin was still clutched in my other hand, its surface smooth and cool against my skin.
