As we walked, I glanced back at the summoning circle, at the faint lines still visible in the damp earth. The circle was dead now, its energy dissipated, its purpose unfulfilled. A testament to my failure. A reminder of my limitations.

But the game continued. And for now, at least, I was still playing.

I tucked the hairpin into the pocket of my dress, my fingers brushing against the cold spot in my chest. The spot where the Word of Unmaking had stolen a sliver of my lifespan. The spot that reminded me of what I had lost, of what I could never reclaim.

Not like this.

Not while I was trapped in this body, this life, this gilded cage of a princess.

But I would find a way. I always did.

And until then, I would keep playing the game.

title: Confessions of a Delusional Prince
prose:
# Chapter 39: Confessions of a Delusional Prince

The library’s western alcove was my usual sanctuary, but today the air itself felt tense, charged with a peculiar energy that had nothing to do with dormant ley-lines. I could feel it in the way the dust motes seemed to hang motionless in the slanted afternoon light, as if holding their breath. Master Theron knew to find me here when he needed my “opinion,” which meant when he needed a problem solved he’d been struggling with for weeks, then politely pretended the solution had been obvious all along.

Today, however, my sanctuary was under siege.

I heard him before I saw him. The heavy, deliberate footfalls that announced Prince Leo of the Beastfolk Plains like a herald announcing a particularly enthusiastic natural disaster. 

I kept my eyes on the page before me, a monograph on the migratory patterns of luminescent moths, and willed him to pass by. Perhaps he was looking for the armory. Perhaps he’d taken a wrong turn in his endless quest to find someone willing to arm-wrestle him. Perhaps the gods of misdirection and poor judgment would smile upon me and guide his feet elsewhere.

The footsteps stopped.

“Lily.”

His voice was uncharacteristically subdued. Normally, Leo greeted me with the enthusiasm of a hunting hound who’d cornered a particularly interesting fox, his words tumbling out in a rush of challenges and declarations. Today, he spoke my name like it was a sacred invocation, weighted with a solemnity that immediately put me on guard.

I turned a page. The moth monograph was actually quite interesting—apparently, certain species could navigate by starlight, which had implications for a scrying array I’d been considering—but I gave no indication that I had heard him.

“Lily.” He said it again, and this time I detected a tremor beneath the weight. “I must speak truth.”

I looked up.

He stood at the entrance to the alcove, his massive frame somehow folded into a posture of nervousness. His hands—those enormous paws that could crush rocks and had, on one memorable occasion, accidentally crushed a training dummy’s head—were fidgeting with the hem of his tunic. His amber eyes, usually bright with competitive fire, were darting around the alcove as if seeking an escape route.

He looked like a man preparing to charge a fortress with a butter knife.

“I have been thinking,” he said, “for many days. Many, many days. Leo has been thinking.”

This was unprecedented. 

“And what,” I asked, “has the great Prince Leo been thinking about?”

He swallowed. I watched his throat work, watched the way his ears—those expressive, wolfish ears that betrayed every emotion he tried to hide—flattened against his skull. He was terrified. Of me. This was either very good news or very bad news.

“You,” he said.

I waited.

“You are…” He paused, clearly searching for words. His hands clenched and unclenched at his sides. “You are like the winter sun. Bright and sharp. You are like the storm that breaks the drought. You are like—”

“Leo.” I cut him off before he could continue his meteorological metaphor. “What are you talking about?”

He took a step forward, then another, closing the distance between us until he stood at the edge of the table, looming over me. His shadow fell across the monograph, across my hands, across the careful fortress of indifference I had constructed around myself.

“My heart,” he said, “is a storm.”

I stared at him.

He stared at me.

The dust motes continued their lazy drift through the afternoon light.

“You have a condition,” I said carefully, “that requires medical attention.”

“No!” He slammed his fist on the table, and the monograph jumped. Several volumes on the shelf behind him wobbled dangerously. “My heart is a storm because of you, Lily! Because of your fierce spirit and your sharp tongue and your—your—” He gestured vaguely at me, encompassing, apparently, my entire existence. “Your everything!”

Ah.

Of course.

I had wondered when this would happen. Leo’s behavior over the past months had followed a predictable trajectory, from competitive challenge to grudging respect to an increasingly baffling series of “gifts” that included a dead rabbit (which, to be fair, had been skinned and cooked, and was actually quite good), a hand-carved wooden figure that was supposed to be me but looked more like a potato with hair, and a collection of polished stones he had gathered from a riverbed because they “reminded him of my eyes.”

I had assumed, in my vast experience with the courtship rituals of various species, that he would eventually either lose interest or escalate to a formal declaration. He had chosen the latter.

“The storm,” he continued, “has been raging for weeks. I cannot eat. I cannot sleep. I think only of you, of your clever words and your fierce spirit and the way you look at me like you want to kill me.”

My murderous intentions toward the prince had softened recently to something more akin to mild homicidal irritation, which was practically affection by my standards. But I did not say this.

“Your thorns,” he said, “are a challenge I welcome. Your beauty is a treasure I seek. I love you.”

The words hung in the dusty air, ludicrous and sincere.

I blinked. My jaw tightened. I could feel the heat of his gaze on my skin, and something else—a strange, unwelcome flutter behind my ribs, like a trapped bird beating its wings against bone. I ignored it. I was a master of ignoring such inconvenient signals.

“I have thought,” he said, his voice dropping to a raw, earnest whisper, “about the way you correct the tutors. The way you look at the stars. The way you hold a teacup with both hands, as if it is precious.” His amber eyes found mine and held them. “I see you, Lily. Not just the princess. I see the fierce rose within.”

The flutter behind my ribs went still.  And he was looking at me with such naked sincerity that it felt like a violation, like he’d bypassed all my defenses and seen something raw and unprotected underneath.

That was not acceptable.

“You are a delusional fool, Leo,” I said.

His face broke into a triumphant grin. His ears, which had been flat against his skull, shot upward with such force I half-expected to hear them snap.

“See!” He pointed at me, his voice filled with exultation. “Your spirit flames! You fight even my affection! It is perfect!”

I stared at him. The heat in my hand from where he’d been near it dissipated, leaving a strange, cool tingle in its wake.

He stared at me, beaming.

“Leo,” I said, with all the patience I could muster, “I am not fighting your affection. I am telling you that you are a delusional fool. These are different things.”

“No, no.” He shook his head, his expression one of profound understanding. “I see through your words to the truth beneath. You push me away because you are afraid. Because you have been hurt before. Because you do not trust that someone could love you for who you truly are.”

I had been hurt before, but not in the way he meant. I was not afraid. I was exasperated.

“I am not afraid,” I said. “I am exasperated. There is a difference.”

“Your exasperation is a shield,” he declared. “A shield forged in the fires of past pain. But I will break through it! I will prove to you that love can be trusted!”

The words formed on my tongue, ready to be deployed like arrows against his fortress of delusion.

And then I stopped.

Because explaining would break the fragile, absurd world he lived in. A world where the fierce glare of a princess was actually a sign of hidden affection. A world where every rejection was a challenge to be overcome. A world where the girl who had tried to poison him, trip him, and once accidentally set his tail on fire was actually just a shy maiden expressing her feelings in the only way she knew how.

It was a stupid world. It was a wrong-headed, nonsensical, utterly ridiculous world.

But it was also a world that protected me.

In that world, I was safe.

“Fine,” I said.

Leo’s grin faltered. “Fine?”

“Have your love.” The words felt foreign in my mouth, like speaking a language I had long since forgotten. “Call me what you will.”

The effect was immediate. His face transformed. His grin stretched so wide I thought his face might split, his ears stood at attention, and his tail, which I had not realized was wagging, began moving so fast it was almost a blur.

“Truly?” His voice cracked with joy. “You accept my courtship? You acknowledge my declaration?”

“Truly,” I said, because arguing was futile.

He seized my hand. His grip was enormous, but surprisingly gentle, as if he were handling a bird’s egg. He raised it to his lips and pressed a kiss to the air just above my knuckles, his breath warm against my skin.

“Then you are my fierce little rose!” he declared. “And I am your knight!”

“Fierce little rose,” I repeated.

“Yes!” He was practically vibrating with excitement. “Because you are beautiful and fierce and your thorns protect your heart! And I will be the knight who guards you, who fights by your side, who—”

“Leo.” I pulled my hand back, curling my fingers into my palm where his warmth lingered. “You should go. I have research to complete.”

He nodded eagerly, already backing toward the entrance. “Of course! Your brilliant mind must not be disturbed! I will tell my father! I will send word to the Beastfolk Plains! I will—”

“You will go,” I said firmly, “and allow me to read about moths.”

He went. His departure was a triumph of enthusiasm over dignity, a retreat that somehow managed to radiate victory. He nearly knocked over a book cart in his haste, caught it with a grace that surprised me, and disappeared down the main aisle with a final wave that was more like a military salute.

The silence he left behind was deafening.

I sat in my chair, my hand still tingling with a phantom warmth that had nothing to do with the afternoon sun, and stared at the monograph I had been reading. The words swam before my eyes, meaningless symbols that refused to cohere into sense. A fierce little rose. The label felt less like an insult now and more like a truth I’d been avoiding. Yes, I was fierce. And yes, I was a rose—a carefully cultivated flower in the garden of Lumengarde, beautiful and decorative and utterly trapped.

And my thorns? They were not a shield for my heart. They were a prison for my true nature, the only thing keeping the Demon Lord from consuming this fragile princess from the inside out.

I rose from my chair and crossed to the far end of the alcove, where a tall cabinet of dark wood stood against the wall. Its glass front was polished to a high shine, and in its surface, I could see my reflection—a small girl with dark hair and pale skin, dressed in a simple blue gown, looking every inch the delicate princess she was supposed to be.

Fierce little rose.

I met my own eyes in the glass. Behind them, the ancient soul burned with a cold, patient fire. The knowledge waited. The power, limited though it was, simmered in the depths of her fragile body. A slow, dry smirk touched my lips. He was right, in his own ridiculous way. I was fierce. I was a rose. And I was trapped in a garden of thorns, a beautiful cage of misunderstanding and affection I could not escape without destroying everything I had built.

But perhaps, I thought, as I turned back to my monograph and the fascinating migration patterns of luminescent moths, that was not such a bad thing. To be underestimated. To be loved by a fool. It was a kind of camouflage, sharper than any spell.

My fingers traced the title of the monograph, but my mind was elsewhere, turning over his words. *I see you, Lily. Not just the princess.* The words were wrong, profoundly wrong in their interpretation, yet they grazed the edge of a truth. He saw something. Not the Demon Lord, not the ancient evil, but the *fierceness*. The part of me that refused to be a mere ornament, even if he mistook it for romantic spirit rather than vengeful ambition.

It was irritating. It was dangerous. And, if I was being honest with myself in the privacy of my own skull, it was the first time in years anyone had looked past the *princess* to the *will* beneath, even if they’d mislabeled it.

The game continued. I was still playing. And now, it seemed, I had a new piece on the board—a smitten, delusional beastfolk prince who saw my thorns as a challenge and my glare as an invitation. A piece that could be useful, perhaps, if I could stop wanting to strangle him with his own earnest declarations.

The library door opened again, and I heard the distinctive, hurried footsteps of Eris of the Spire approaching. She was carrying a notebook, as always, and her eyes were bright with the fever of intellectual pursuit.

“Your Highness!” she called, her voice echoing through the stacks. “I have the most wonderful theoretical question to discuss with you!”

I sighed, pushing the lingering warmth in my hand and the irritating flutter in my chest down into the mental box where I kept inconvenient feelings. The box was getting crowded.

“Come in, Eris,” I said, my voice once again the soft, polite tone of the princess. “I’m all ears.”

The fierce little rose had work to do.

title: Brewing the Unbrewable
prose:
# Chapter 40: Brewing the Unbrewable

The garden was a crime against geometry.

 The crime was in the *waste*. Every inch of this manicured paradise was a squandered opportunity. The ley-lines hummed beneath the soil, thick as spilled ink, and here they were, coiling uselessly around rosebushes and marble benches while the court sipped tea and complimented the gardener on his "artistic vision."

I sat at a wrought-iron table that had been painted white to match the china, my fingers curled around a cup of Darjeeling that smelled of bergamot and surrender. Across from me, Eris of the Spire clutched her notebook like a holy text, her quill already dancing across the page before I’d even spoken. The title of her latest entry read, in her painfully neat script: *Theoretical Necromancy: Ethical Boundaries and the Preservation of Post-Mortem Consciousness.*

I took a sip. The tea was excellent. A pity it would do nothing to dull the headache I was about to give myself.

"Shall we begin, then?" I asked, setting my cup down with a delicate *clink*. "Let us assume, purely for discussion, that a soul’s signature persists post-mortem as a form of residual energy. Not as a sentient echo, mind you—more akin to the afterimage of a candle flame, lingering in the air long after the wick has gone dark."

 "The... the *afterimage* model. Yes. Yes, that aligns with the Spire’s observations on spectral decay rates. Though the Archmage would *never* permit such a discussion, not even in theory. She considers it—" She lowered her voice, though there was no one near enough to hear. "—*morally fraught*."

I allowed myself a small, private smile. Morally fraught. How quaint. As if morality had ever been more than a speed bump on the road to knowledge. "Morality is a luxury for those who can afford to ignore the implications," I said, keeping my tone light, almost playful. "If we *could* interact with these residual signatures, what might we learn? About memory, about identity, about the fundamental nature of consciousness itself?"

Eris’s eyes shone. She looked like a supplicant before an altar, which, in a way, she was. "Everything," she breathed. "We could *map* the soul. Trace its contours, its weight, its—its *texture*. The Codex Animarum suggests that consciousness isn’t a single thread, but a *tapestry*—" She caught herself, flushing. "Forgive me. I’m lecturing."

"Not at all," I said smoothly. "Your enthusiasm is... refreshing." And it was. Refreshing, and *useful*. Eris had spent years tiptoeing around the edges of forbidden knowledge, too afraid to take the leap. I was the bridge she’d been waiting for—the one who could turn her cautious steps into a sprint.

 "Consider the practical applications. If a soul’s signature can be *bound*, not to a corpse, but to a resonant object—say, a locket, or a mirror—what then? Could we create a vessel for the dead? Not reanimation, not possession, but... *conversation*."

Eris’s quill snapped.

She stared at the broken tip, her lower lip trembling. For a terrible moment, I thought she might cry. Then she reached into her satchel with shaking hands and produced a spare, her movements jerky with excitement. "A vessel," she repeated. "A *sustained echo*. Your Highness, do you realize what this means? The ethical implications alone—"

"Are vast," I agreed. "Which is why we must approach them with *rigor*." I plucked a scone from the tray between us and broke it in half, watching the crumbs scatter across the lace tablecloth. "The spell would require a focus of immense personal significance. Something tied to the deceased’s identity—an heirloom, perhaps, or a letter they’d written. And a caster of... exceptional clarity."

I let the words hang in the air, heavy as the scent of roses. Eris’s gaze flicked up to meet mine, her pupils dilated with something dangerously close to worship. "Clarity," she echoed. "Yes. The caster’s mind must be a *lens*, unclouded by doubt or emotion. A perfect conduit for the resonance."

I took a bite of the scone. It was dry. "Precisely. " I paused, letting the implication linger. "—it could *infect* the caster. Twist their own memories, their own sense of self."

Eris’s breath came faster. She was scribbling again, her handwriting devolving into a frantic scrawl. "Infection. Yes. The Codex mentions something similar—a case study from the Third Age, where a necromancer attempted to bind his dead lover’s soul to a harp. The harp *played itself* for three days, and when they found the necromancer, he was—" She swallowed. "—humming the melody. Backwards."

I set the scone down. "A cautionary tale," I murmured. "But not, I think, an insurmountable obstacle. With the right precautions, the right *theory*..."

Eris’s quill stilled. She looked up at me, her face pale beneath the freckles. "Your Highness," she said, and her voice was barely more than a whisper. "Do you... do you think *I* could ever achieve that kind of clarity?"

The question caught me off guard.  She wasn’t asking if she was *capable*. She was asking if she was *worthy*.

I should have lied.

 But the words stuck in my throat, tangled in the dry crumbs of the scone and the bitter aftertaste of my own hypocrisy.

 A state of being, as innate as the color of your eyes or the shape of your bones. And Eris’s mind was a cluttered attic of half-formed theories and desperate longing, every thought tripping over the next in its haste to please.

 The kind of clarity that came from knowing exactly what you wanted and exactly how to take it. 

The kind of clarity that was currently trapped in the body of a ten-year-old girl who couldn’t even cast a simple light spell without passing out.

I reached for my tea. The cup trembled in my grip. "Clarity is a practice," I said at last, forcing my voice into something gentle, something *kind*. "Not a birthright. You have the rigor, Eris. You have the *Codex*. Your contribution is in the verification, the grounding of theory in reality."

It was the right thing to say. The *kind* thing. The thing a mentor would say to a promising student.

Eris’s face lit up like a lantern. "You—you really think so?"

"I know so." I set my cup down and folded my hands in my lap, the picture of patient encouragement. "Theory is the skeleton. You are the flesh that gives it form. Without you, it’s just... words on a page."

Eris sniffed. A tear slid down her cheek, and she wiped it away with the back of her hand, leaving a smudge of ink on her temple. "I won’t let you down," she said fiercely. "I’ll study harder. I’ll—I’ll *earn* this."

I resisted the urge to sigh. Eris’s devotion was a double-edged sword.  One wrong word, one perceived slight, and she’d dissolve into tears or worse—into *doubt*.

And doubt, in a mind like hers, was a contagion.

I plucked another scone from the tray and held it out to her. "Eat something," I said. "You’ll need your strength for the research ahead."

Eris took the scone with reverent fingers, as if it were a sacred offering. "Thank you, Your Highness. For... for everything."

I waved a hand, dismissing her gratitude. "We’re scholars, Eris. Partners in discovery. Now—" I leaned back in my chair, letting my gaze drift toward the topiary rabbits. "—tell me more about this harp."

Eris launched into a detailed explanation of the Third Age necromancer’s folly, her voice rising and falling with the cadence of a sermon. I nodded along, making the appropriate noises of interest, but my mind was elsewhere.

The harp was a dead end. A curiosity, nothing more. What *mattered* was the principle—the idea of binding a soul to an object, of creating a vessel that could *hold* the dead without reanimating them. A sustained echo. A conversation.

A *weapon*.

Because if a soul could be bound to an object, it could be bound to *anything*. A sword. A crown. A *child*.

No. I cut the thought off before it could fully form. The backlash wasn’t the problem. The *mana* was the problem. My body was a sieve, a cracked cup trying to hold an ocean. Even the simplest spells left me gasping, my vision swimming with black spots. And the Word of Unmaking—the one spell that *didn’t* require mana—had already cost me a sliver of my lifespan. A cold spot in my chest, a void where a piece of my future had been carved away.

I flexed my fingers against the armrests of my chair. The wrought iron was cool beneath my palms, solid and unyielding. A reminder of the world I was trapped in—a world of tea parties and topiary rabbits, of scone crumbs and misplaced worship.

A world where I was *adorable*.

The thought was a spark in the dry tinder of my frustration.  They called me adorable when I drew pentagrams in the dirt. Adorable when I corrected the royal tutor on the proper incantation for a fireball. Adorable when I *failed* at magic, when my nose bled and my hands shook and the court clucked their tongues and said, "Oh, the poor dear, she’s *trying* so hard."

Adorable.

I was not adorable. I was a *conqueror*. A *scholar*. A force of nature that had bent kingdoms to its will. 

Eris’s voice cut through my thoughts. "...don’t you think, Your Highness?"

 A binding circle. A resonance matrix. A list of potential foci, ranked by emotional significance.

"I think," I said carefully, "that you’ve made an excellent start."

Eris beamed. "I’ll keep working on it. I’ll—" She hesitated, then added in a rush, "I’ll bring you the revised theory by the end of the week. If that’s all right."

"It’s more than all right," I said. "It’s *necessary*."

Eris packed up her notebook with the reverence of a priest handling relics. I watched her go, her robes fluttering behind her like the wings of a particularly earnest crow. When she was out of sight, I let my shoulders slump, just for a moment.

The garden was quiet. The bees droned lazily among the roses, the gravel paths crunched under the feet of distant courtiers, the ley-lines thrummed beneath the soil like a sleeping giant’s heartbeat. I closed my eyes and listened to the hum of it, the *potential* of it.

Then I opened them and looked down at my hands.

Small. Delicate. Capable of holding a teacup, of turning the pages of a book, of sketching a binding circle in the dirt.

Incapable of holding power.

I flexed my fingers again, watching the way the sunlight caught the fine bones beneath the skin. A child’s hands. A princess’s hands.

Not a conqueror’s.

Not yet.

---

The tea things had been cleared away by the time I made my way back to the palace, leaving only a faint ring of condensation on the tablecloth and the ghost of bergamot in the air. I walked slowly, my slippers scuffing against the gravel, my thoughts a tangled skein of frustration and calculation.

I needed a way to *store* power. Not in a crystal garden—that had been a disaster, a pretty lattice of mana-siphoning nodes that my father had proudly declared "Lily’s Rock Collection" and turned into a tourist attraction. Not in a grimoire, not in a locket, not in any of the usual vessels.

I needed something *living*.

The thought slithered into my mind like a serpent through tall grass. Something living. Something that could *hold* mana without breaking, without leaking, without—

A child.

The word echoed in the hollow of my skull, bouncing off the walls of my own hypocrisy. A child. A vessel. A *body*.

Not mine. Never mine. My body was a prison, a gilded cage of insufficient biology. But if I could find another—

No.

 No. The idea was monstrous. Unthinkable. Even for me.

And yet...

 If I could find a way to regulate the flow, to *control* the energy—

A rustle of fabric. A shadow falling across the path.

I looked up.

Queen Seraphina stood before me, her hands folded at her waist, her expression unreadable. The late afternoon sun haloed her hair, turning it to spun gold, and for a moment, she looked like something out of a saint’s hagiography—serene, untouchable, *holy*.

"Lily," she said. "You’ve been out here for hours."

I blinked. The garden had grown dim while I’d been lost in thought, the shadows stretching long and thin across the gravel. How long had I been standing here? Five minutes? Ten?

"I was thinking," I said.

Seraphina’s gaze flicked to the empty tea table, then back to me. "About necromancy?"

The question was so casual, so *ordinary*, that for a moment, I thought I’d misheard. Then the implications hit me like a bucket of ice water. She knew. She *knew*.

 There was no way—

"I beg your pardon?" I said, forcing my voice into something light, something *innocent*.

Seraphina stepped closer. She smelled of lavender and something sharper—rosemary, perhaps, or sage. The scent of a healer’s hands. "Eris of the Spire," she said. "She’s been seen leaving your chambers with a rather... *enthusiastic* expression. And a notebook filled with diagrams that look suspiciously like binding circles."

I felt the blood drain from my face. My fingers twitched at my sides, itching to curl into fists. "I—"

Seraphina held up a hand. "I’m not accusing you of anything, Lily. But I *am* asking you to be careful." She crouched down until we were eye level, her skirts pooling around her like liquid silver. "The Spire takes its restrictions seriously. And while I have no doubt your intentions are pure—" A ghost of a smile touched her lips. "—others might not be so understanding."

I stared at her. The cold spot in my chest pulsed, a reminder of the lifespan I’d spent to save myself from the cult. A reminder of the *cost*.

"I don’t know what you mean," I said.

 "Lily," she said softly. "I know you’re brilliant. I know you see the world in ways the rest of us can’t. But brilliance is a double-edged sword. It can cut you just as easily as it cuts others."

I swallowed. My throat was dry. "I’m just... curious."

"Curiosity is a wonderful thing," Seraphina said. "But some doors shouldn’t be opened. Not yet. Not by you."

I wanted to scream. I wanted to grab her by the shoulders and shake her until her teeth rattled. *I am not a child*, I wanted to say. *I am not your daughter. I am the Demon Lord, and I have walked through doors you can’t even imagine, and I have come back with knowledge that would make your hair turn white.*

"I understand," I said.

Seraphina studied me for a long moment. Then she nodded, as if she’d made a decision. "Good," she said. "Now come inside. It’s nearly dinnertime, and your father has promised to tell the story of the Siege of the Obsidian Plains again. I believe he’s added a new verse to his song."

I let her take my hand. Her fingers were warm, her grip gentle but firm. 

A door I couldn’t open. Not yet.

But doors, I knew, could be unlocked.

And I had a lifetime of keys.

title: Toys, Lies, and Alibis
prose:
# Chapter 41: Toys, Lies, and Alibis

I blinked. The garden had grown dim while I’d been lost in thought, the shadows stretching long and thin across the gravel. How long had I been standing here? Five minutes? Ten? "I was thinking," I said. Seraphina’s gaze flicked to the empty tea table, then back to me. "About necromancy?" The question was so casual, so *ordinary*, that for a moment, I thought I’d misheard. Then the implications hit me like a bucket of ice water. She knew. She *knew*. But no. That was impossible. Eris had been careful. I’d been careful. There was no way—

"I beg your pardon?" I said, forcing my voice into something light, something *innocent*.

Seraphina stepped closer. She smelled of lavender and something sharper—rosemary, perhaps, or sage. The scent of a healer’s hands. "Eris of the Spire," she said. "She’s been seen leaving your chambers with a rather... *enthusiastic* expression. And a notebook filled with diagrams that look suspiciously like binding circles."

 "I—"

Seraphina held up a hand. "I’m not accusing you of anything, Lily. But I *am* asking you to be careful." She crouched down until we were eye level, her skirts pooling around her like liquid silver. "The Spire takes its restrictions seriously. And while I have no doubt your intentions are pure—" A ghost of a smile touched her lips. "—others might not be so understanding."

I stared at her. The cold spot in my chest pulsed, a reminder of the lifespan I’d spent to save myself from the cult. A reminder of the *cost*. "I don’t know what you mean," I said.

Seraphina’s smile faded. She reached out and tucked a loose strand of hair behind my ear, her fingers warm against my skin. "Lily," she said softly. "I know you’re brilliant. I know you see the world in ways the rest of us can’t. But brilliance is a double-edged sword. It can cut you just as easily as it cuts others."

I swallowed. My throat was dry. "I’m just... curious."

"Curiosity is a wonderful thing," Seraphina said. "But some doors shouldn’t be opened. Not yet. Not by you."

"I understand," I said.

Seraphina studied me for a long moment. Then she nodded, as if she’d made a decision. "Good," she said. "Now come inside. It’s nearly dinnertime, and your father has promised to tell the story of the Siege of the Obsidian Plains again. I believe he’s added a new verse to his song."

I let her take my hand. Her fingers were warm, her grip gentle but firm. As we walked back toward the palace, I glanced over my shoulder at the garden, at the topiary rabbits frozen in their eternal leap, at the ley-lines humming beneath the soil. A door I couldn’t open. Not yet. But doors, I knew, could be unlocked. And I had a lifetime of keys.

***

The royal nursery was a riot of primary colors and plush toys, a stark contrast to the gnawing calculation in my head. Sunlight streamed through the tall windows, illuminating dust motes that danced like lazy sprites over a miniature kingdom of carved wooden blocks and velvet cushions. The air smelled of lemon polish, old fabric, and the faint, sweet scent of spilled juice that never quite left the rugs. It was, by all accounts, the safest, most innocent room in the entire palace.

Which made it the perfect theater for sedition.

I sat at a tiny, child-sized table, my knees bumping against the underside. Before me lay the tableau: three hand-carved puppets, each about six inches tall, crafted from polished wood and painted with meticulous detail. A king in crimson and gold, his tiny crown a fleck of tin. A queen in serene blue, her face a smooth oval of painted ivory. And a dragon, its scales a dark, mossy green, its eyes two pinpricks of obsidian.

My fingers, still feeling the ghost of Seraphina’s warning, moved with deliberate slowness. I positioned the queen a respectful distance from the king. Then I picked up the dragon. Its carved wood was cool against my palm. I moved it behind the king puppet, its felt claws—one of my own additions, painstakingly glued on with hide glue—hovering just above the king’s painted back.

"There," I murmured, my voice a whisper meant only for the puppets. "A shadow at the heart of power. A beast lurking behind the throne. So very... *theatrical*."

"What a lovely scene, Your Highness!"

The voice belonged to Nurse Elara, one of the nursery maids. She was a plump woman with kind eyes and hands perpetually dusted with flour from the kitchen. She leaned over my shoulder, her shadow falling across the table. "Are you telling a story?"

I looked up at her, tilting my head in the way that Alistair called "endearingly curious" and I called "calculated vulnerability." "The dragon is being naughty," I said, my tone serious, as if explaining a complex geopolitical situation. "He’s hiding. The king doesn’t know he’s there."

"Oh dear," Nurse Elara cooed, her hand coming to rest on her chest. "That *is* naughty. The poor king." She straightened up, smoothing her apron. "You have such a wonderful imagination, Princess. Just like your father with his stories!"

I offered a small, shy smile. Internally, I was mapping the palace staff hierarchy with the cold precision of a general planning a siege. Nurse Elara was kind, but not clever. Her loyalty was to the nursery routine, not to the crown’s security apparatus. She would mention the puppets in the kitchen, to the other maids. They would mention it to the steward. And the steward, a nervous man who sweated at the thought of displeasing *anyone* important, would eventually mention it to someone who mattered.

 Every time his agents returned empty-handed from investigating one of my little "conspiracies," his standing at court would dim a fraction more. The man was the Shadow Blade, a spymaster of legendary reputation. And I was turning him into the court jester, one crayon drawing at a time.

I nudged the dragon puppet a millimeter closer to the king’s back. The felt claws brushed the painted wood. A silent, imaginary threat. Perfect.

***

My next task required stealth, not of the physical sort—nursemaids and tutors were always hovering—but of the psychological variety. I needed to plant the seed of the puppet conspiracy in the mind of someone who would ensure its rapid, unfiltered dissemination to the upper echelons of palace administration. That person was Head Steward Grimsby.

Grimsby was a tall, thin man who moved with the brittle dignity of a dried twig. He visited the nursery once a day, ostensibly to inspect the linen and ensure the fruit bowl was stocked, but in reality, to absorb any intelligence that might filter down from the royal nursery and report it to the chamberlain, who reported to the queen. A perfect, if unwitting, conduit for misinformation.

I waited until the afternoon rest period. Most of the nursery staff were in the pantry, taking their tea. Nurse Elara was humming a lullaby to the infant prince in the adjoining crib. The main playroom was empty, bathed in warm, sleepy light. This was my window.

From the hidden pocket in my smock—a modification I’d sewn myself, my stitching clumsy but functional—I retrieved my weapon. It was a piece of parchment, folded twice. On it, rendered in the waxy, vibrant crayon I preferred for important communications, was a drawing. It depicted a puppet, much like the one on my table, but with one crucial difference. Its eyes were not simple black dots. They were two large, glowing red circles, radiating jagged lines that could be interpreted as either光芒 or menacing energy, depending on the viewer’s predisposition.

I moved to the nursery’s small bookshelf, a cheerful construction of painted wood holding a dozen or so storybooks with titles like *The Brave Little Squire* and *The Unicorn’s Picnic*. I selected the most popular one, *The Princess and the Pea*, and opened it to the middle. I tucked the folded drawing between the pages, leaving just a corner visible—not hidden, but not ostentatious either. It had to look like something a child might have tucked away and forgotten. A relic of playtime, not a manifesto.

Then I retreated to my small stool, picked up a wooden block, and began stacking it, my expression one of focused, childish concentration.

Grimsby arrived precisely at three o’clock, as he always did. His footsteps were a crisp, measured sound on the wooden floor. He nodded to Nurse Elara, inspected the fruit bowl (a single, disapproving look at a slightly bruised apple), and then his gaze fell upon me.

"Princess Liliana," he said, his voice a dry rustle. "Engaged in constructive play, I see."

"Yes, Steward Grimsby," I said, placing another block with exaggerated care. "Building a castle."

"Hmm. Very good." He began his perfunctory patrol of the room, his hands clasped behind his back. His eyes swept over the toy chests, the cushions, the sun-drenched floor. And then they landed on the bookshelf. Specifically, on the *Princess and the Pea*, with its telltale corner of parchment protruding.

I held my breath, my posture one of innocent absorption in my block tower. Internally, I was a connoisseur of human behavior, watching a specimen walk into a carefully laid snare.

Grimsby paused. His brow furrowed, a slight, almost imperceptible twitch. He was a man for order, for tidy spaces and predictable routines. A piece of paper sticking out of a book was a disruption. He walked over, his movements still precise but now tinged with a compulsive need to correct. He reached out, his long, thin fingers pinching the corner of the parchment, and drew it free.

He unfolded it.

The silence in the nursery stretched. I could hear the soft lullaby from the adjoining room, the distant caw of a crow in the palace gardens. Grimsby stared at the crayon drawing. His face, usually a mask of professional neutrality, underwent a subtle transformation. His lips pressed together. His nostrils flared slightly. It was the face of a man who has just discovered a spider in his sugar bowl.

I waited for the inevitable. The drawing was crude, the symbolism blatant. Glowing red eyes. A puppet. It was childish, yes, but it was *specific*. It took the "naughty dragon" game I’d been playing and gave it a sinister, almost occult overtone. To a mind already primed by Zephyr’s whispers of conspiracies—whispers I had so carefully cultivated—it would look like a clue. A sign.

Grimsby did not gasp. He did not cry out. He carefully, precisely, refolded the drawing along its original creases. He tucked it into the inner pocket of his tailored coat. Then he turned, his face once more an impassive mask, but his eyes had acquired a new, sharp quality. They darted to the puppet table, lingering on the dragon behind the king for a fraction of a second longer than necessary.

He cleared his throat. "A... tidy drawing," he said, his voice fractionally higher than before. "A princess should take care with her... artistic materials. Not leave them about."

"I'm sorry, Steward Grimsby," I said, lowering my eyes in a show of contrition. "I forgot it was there."

"Hmm. See that you are more mindful." He adjusted his coat, smoothing the fabric where the drawing now lay hidden. Then he gave a stiff nod to Nurse Elara and swept from the room, his footsteps sounding just a little less measured, a little more hurried, than before.

The door closed behind him. I picked up another block and placed it atop my tower. My hands were steady. Inside, a cold, familiar satisfaction settled in my chest, right next to the perpetual void left by the Word. 

He would receive a report: A crude drawing of a puppet with glowing eyes, found in the royal nursery. Associated with Princess Liliana’s "storytelling."

I smiled, a small, secret curve of my lips that I quickly suppressed. I was playing a game of grand strategy with pieces made of crayon wax and nursery toys. It was beneath the dignity of the Demon Lord. It was, however, devastatingly effective.

***

The walk back to my chambers was a study in contrasts. The palace corridors were busy with the evening rush—maids carrying linens, footmen lighting oil lamps, the distant, savory smells of roasting meat drifting up from the kitchens. I moved through it all like a ghost, a small, quiet figure in a world of adult bustle. My body performed its usual ballet of fragility: a slight stumble here, a hand braced against a wall there, a pause to catch my breath after climbing the grand staircase. The performance was automatic now, a second skin.

But my mind was elsewhere. It was mapping the flow of information. Grimsby’s report was the first domino. 

I reached the door to my chambers. It was tall, oak, and carved with the royal crest. To anyone else, it was a simple door. To me, it was the border of my sovereignty, the one place in this gilded cage where I could, for a moment, drop the mask of the fragile princess and simply be.

I pushed it open.

And was immediately assaulted by a small, foul-smelling missile.

"Mistress! Mistress is back! Baphomutt has brought treasures!"

The imp materialized from the shadows of a tapestry, his bat-like wings a blur, his green skin mottled and scaly. He was roughly the size of a large pigeon, with the temperament of a particularly enthusiastic terrier. In his spindly claws, he clutched a silver spoon.

He dropped it on my pillow with a clang. The spoon was large, ornate, and bore the faint, unmistakable sigil of the Shadow Realm’s embassy on its handle.

I stared at the spoon. Then I stared at Baphomutt, who was now hovering beside my writing desk, preening a patch of feathers from his underbelly with a look of supreme self-satisfaction.

"Baphomutt," I said, my voice utterly flat.

"Mistress is pleased?" he chirped. "Baphomutt saw the shiny. The tall, shadow man with the sad face keeps it in the shiny box. Baphomutt took it! For Mistress!"

I pinched the bridge of my nose. The "tall, shadow man with the sad face" was almost certainly Zephyr. The "shiny box" was his personal effects case. This imbecile had just stolen the personal property of the king’s spymaster and left it on my pillow. In the current climate, with Grimsby about to set the palace rumor mill churning over a crayon drawing, this was the diplomatic equivalent of throwing a lit match into a powder keg.

"Not now," I sighed, a genuine weariness settling over me. "I’m busy framing a spymaster for toy-based treason. Did I ask you to steal anything?"

Baphomutt’s lower lip, a wet, rubbery thing, extended in a dramatic pout. "Mistress said... Baphomutt remembers... Mistress was looking at the shiny man’s door. With the thinking face. So Baphomutt—"

"I was *mapping his patrol schedule*," I hissed, "not ordering a theft. There is a difference! A subtle one, I grant you, but one a half-witted imp ought to be able to grasp."

The imp’s eyes, yellow and luminous, welled with theatrical tears. "Baphomutt only wants to help! Baphomutt is a good imp!"

I closed my eyes. The spoon glinted on my pillow, a silver beacon of incompetence. My first, hot impulse was to hurl it out the window. My second, more pragmatic impulse, followed a second later. Zephyr would notice the spoon was missing. He would be furious. He would assume it was a targeted act of provocation, another piece in the puppet conspiracy puzzle he was now undoubtedly assembling. He would look for the thief. He would not find one, because the only witness was a feathered gremlin currently trying to eat a tassel from the bed curtain.

And then... an idea, sharp and cold and beautiful, began to form in the back of my mind. A spoon was a mundane object. But in the right context, with the right interpretation, any object could become a symbol. A threat. A message.

I walked over and plucked the spoon from my pillow. Its silver was cool, its engraving precise. "This was foolish, Baphomutt," I said, my tone making it clear that "foolish" was a vast understatement.

"But—"

"However," I continued, turning the spoon over in my hands, "you may have accidentally done something useful. Leave me now. And do *not* steal anything else today. I mean it."

The imp’s face lit up. He gave a jerky bow and vanished into the shadows with a triumphant squeak, leaving behind only the faint smell of sulfur and victory.

I sat on the edge of my bed, the stolen spoon weighing down my palm. I would keep it. I would use it. When the time was right—and that time was drawing near, with Zephyr now doubly distracted—I would plant it somewhere. Perhaps in the kitchens, near the site of the Crumble Conspiracy. Perhaps tucked into the pages of a book in the library. Or perhaps, with a final, insulting flourish, I would send it back to him in another fruit basket, with a note: *For your collection. Found it near the naughty dragon. — L*

The possibilities were delightful. I slipped the spoon into my hidden pocket, next to a smoothed river stone and a shard of obsidian. Tools for a trade I was only just beginning to practice in this life: the trade of misdirection, of turning the mundane into the menacing, of framing an entire security apparatus with nothing but stolen silver and crayon drawings.

 But tonight, as I heard Alistair’s booming laugh echo from down the hall, heralding his approach to tell his overwrought siege story, I felt something else alongside the cold. A flicker of something that might, in a lesser being, have been called satisfaction.

The puppet conspiracy was in motion. Zephyr’s investigation would soon be the laughingstock of the court, a farcical quest for subversive toys. His credibility would crumble. And I, the Demon Lord in a child’s body, would be sitting in the middle of it all, looking up at my father with wide, innocent eyes, and asking for another helping of roast potato.

The game was almost too easy. Which, of course, meant I should be prepared for it to become spectacularly, dangerously hard. But that was a problem for tomorrow. Tonight, I had a spoon to pocket and a siege story to endure.

I placed the spoon in my bedside drawer, beneath a stack of handkerchiefs embroidered with my initial. A secret weapon for a secret war. My lips curved again, this time holding the shape for a full three seconds before I forced them back to neutral.

Baphomutt would get his pat on the head eventually. For now, he had earned a silent place in my calculations. An idiotic, loyal, and utterly indispensable piece on the board.

The door opened before I could even stand. "Lily, my little lioness!" Alistair boomed, filling the doorway with his considerable presence. "Ready to hear about the time I single-handedly held the pass at Obsidian Ridge for three days on nothing but hardtack and sheer will?"

I looked up at him, the Hero of Dawn, the man who had slain Maledictus, now beaming with the uncomplicated joy of a father about to tell his favorite bedtime story. The warmth in his chest, which I could almost feel from across the room, tangled with the cold in mine.

"Ready, Father," I said.

And I settled in to listen, as the evening light faded and the first stars appeared, while the palace hummed with the quiet, building energy of a conspiracy that existed only in crayon and paranoia, meticulously crafted to waste the time of dangerous men. My time. My game. My slow, patient, utterly delightful revenge.

title: Firestarter Fiasco
prose:
# Chapter 42: Firestarter Fiasco

The morning air carried the smell of the gardens and the flat stone smell of the courtyard. I stood inside a circle of polished white stones, the sigil for *Ignis Minimus* already traced in the air before me, a thin line of orange light that flickered like a candle in a draft. The court had arranged itself in a loose ring, silks and medals and polite expectation, all of them gathered for a magical demonstration, another performance in the endless theater of being a princess.

Alistair stood at the front of the crowd, beaming like the sun had taken human form. "Show them your spark, little lioness!" he boomed, and a ripple of approving laughter ran through the courtiers.

My fingers trembled, not from fear but from the sheer indignity of having to prove myself to these people, these soft mortals who had once fled screaming from my citadel and now watched me the way they'd watch a performing dog. My father, the Hero of Dawn, had slain me—had slain *me*—and now he was cheering for a candle-spell like it was the climax of a tournament. I'd chosen *Ignis Minimus* precisely because it was the smallest flame in the lexicon, a candle-lighter, a party trick. Even a child with a spark of talent could manage it. The court expected a charming fumble, a few sparks, a delighted gasp.

They did not expect me to set myself on fire.

I began the incantation. The words came out clean, each syllable seated in its proper place, the cadence exact. I'd cast this spell a thousand times in my old life, a thousand thousand, and every syllable was carved into my bones. The sigil pulsed in response, its glow intensifying for a brief, hopeful moment. Then, with a sound like a wet cough, it sputtered. A single spark leapt from my fingertips, arcing through the air before landing directly on the sleeve of my dress.

The fabric smoldered. A thin thread of smoke curled upward, and the court gasped as one, a sound like wind through dry leaves.

By the Abyssal Halls, this is undignified. I once reduced an army to ash with a flick of my wrist, and now I can't even light a candle without setting myself on fire.

The cold spot in my chest pulsed, a dull ache that climbed into my jaw. The headache followed, a slow throb behind my eyes, the familiar price of forcing mana through a body with the conductivity of wet paper. My sleeve kept burning.

Alistair's laugh boomed across the courtyard. "That's my girl! Bold as a summer blaze!" He clapped, and applause rippled through the crowd like a wave. A lady near the front pressed a handkerchief to her lips. "So determined," she whispered to her neighbor, loud enough for me to hear. "She doesn't give up, does she?"

Seraphina reached me before the smoke finished its first curl. A damp cloth appeared in her hand (she always had one, I'd learned, a habit from a lifetime of healing) and she pressed it against the smolder with the efficiency of someone who had extinguished a thousand small disasters. The fabric hissed. The smoke died.

"Lily, dear," she said, her voice soft as a pillow and twice as dangerous. "That fabric is quite flammable."

I looked up at her, forcing my eyes wide, my mouth small. "I wanted to try something new. I didn't realize the fabric was so… delicate."

Her gaze held mine a beat longer than I liked, cataloging something in the space between my words. Then the physician arrived, small and balding, his satchel swinging, his expression already harried.

"Your Highness," he said, pressing his fingers to my wrist before I could offer it. His brow furrowed. "A bit rapid. Nothing alarming. I prescribe more naps and a lighter schedule. No magic for at least a week."

"A week," I repeated, letting my voice dip into something small and disappointed. Then I nodded, my chin tucked. "Of course, Doctor."

He patted my shoulder like I was a kitten that had fallen off a fence. "Good girl. A warm bath and a cup of chamomile tea should do the trick."

I let him lead me from the circle. As we passed the edge of the crowd, I saw Zephyr standing near the fountain, arms crossed, face unreadable. He wore that particular stillness, the one he adopted when he was filing something away. Another entry in the dossier he kept building. Another "suspicious behavior" to add to the pile. He met my eyes for half a second, and I saw the calculation behind his—the way he was already fitting this failure into a pattern that didn't exist.

Let him investigate. Let him chase his own shadow. The man couldn't tell a magical mishap from a child's clumsiness if both were wrapped in ribbon and handed to him with a bow.

The cold spot pulsed again, harder, and I stumbled. The physician's hand caught my elbow, steadying me.

"Steady now, Your Highness."

I nodded, swallowing the ache.

---

The physician's chambers smelled of dried herbs and old paper, a combination I'd cataloged as *mortal medicine* and filed under *useful, if slow*. He settled me on a cushioned stool beside a crackling hearth and pressed a steaming cup into my hands. The tea was pale gold, fragrant with honey over a bitter undertone.

"Drink," he said. "It will calm your nerves."

I took the cup, my fingers curling around the warm porcelain. The tea tasted like grass and regret, but I sipped it obediently, my expression never wavering.

He watched me, eyes softening. "You're a brave little thing. Not many children your age would attempt such advanced magic."

"I just wanted to make Father proud."

The physician chuckled. "Your father is already proud, Your Highness. You needn't push yourself so hard."

I nodded and took another sip, then another, until his attention drifted to his satchel. The moment his back was to me, I tipped the cup into the potted fern beside the stool. The leaves wilted almost immediately, drooping like they'd been struck by frost. He didn't notice.

He turned back with a small vial of clear liquid. "A few drops in your evening milk. No nightmares, I promise."

I tucked the vial into my pocket. "Thank you, Doctor."

He patted my head. "Off you go. And remember, no magic for a week."

I slid off the stool and made for the door, my steps even, my shoulders soft. The hallway swallowed me, and I let out a breath I'd been holding since the spark landed on my sleeve. A pair of courtiers passed me in the corridor, dipping into curtsies I barely registered. "Such spirit," one murmured to the other. "Turning a failed demonstration into a lesson in perseverance." I kept my smile small and my pace even, and filed the words away. They thought I was brave. They thought the fire was a teaching moment. The truth—that I was a demon lord trapped in a body that betrayed me at every turn—would have made them faint.

---

My chambers were quiet. The curtains stirred in the breeze, and the late afternoon light slanted across the desk, catching dust motes in gold. I closed the door behind me and stood there a moment, letting the silence settle.

The cold spot pulsed, slower now but still there, still hungry.

I crossed to the desk and pulled open the hidden drawer. The spoon lay where I'd left it, cool and smooth beneath my fingers. A silver weapon for a war of misdirection. I turned it over, watching the light catch the bowl, and let myself imagine the pastry chef's face when the accusations began. The Crumble Conspiracy would claim another victim. Zephyr would chase the shadow I'd painted for him, and the spoon would be waiting in the wings.

But the room was still. The courtyard below was still. And the crystal garden—my failed array, my beautiful, useless geometry—glowed faintly in the fading light, humming with power I couldn't touch. Alistair had declared it a work of art and installed a brass plaque. The mana crystals hummed their quiet song, and I couldn't reach a single note.

A knock at the door. I slid the spoon back into the drawer and tucked it shut.

"Come in."

Eris slipped through the door, her arms full of books, her cheeks flushed with the particular excitement she reserved for forbidden knowledge. "Your Highness," she said, breathless. "I brought the texts you requested."

I gestured to the desk. She set them down with trembling fingers, arranging them by size, a habit I'd noticed and chosen not to correct.

"Archmage Mira required three moonlit sermons," she said. "But they're the most advanced texts on theoretical necromancy in the Spire."

I picked up the top volume, running my fingers along the leather spine. The binding was worn, the title stamped in faded gold. Somewhere inside these pages was the key to a body that refused to channel what my mind already knew.

"You're smarter than you think, Eris," I said. "You just need the right teacher."

She blushed a deep, pleased red. "I'd be honored to learn from you."

I smiled and opened the book. "Then let's begin."

---

An hour passed in diagrams and margins, in the scratch of charcoal and the murmur of forbidden theory. Eris asked sharp questions, her brow furrowed, her mind quick. I answered her with patience, the kind I'd once extended to a hundred archmagi and found them all wanting.

But the cold spot kept pulsing. And the headache behind my eyes had settled into a dull, persistent throb, a counterweight to the ache in my jaw.

Eris gathered her things as the light began to fail. "I should go. Archmage Mira will be expecting me."

"Thank you, Eris."

She bowed, cheeks still flushed. "Anything for you, Your Highness."

The door clicked shut. I sat alone in the silence, the book open before me, the pages full of words I could read but not yet cast.

The cold spot pulsed.

I closed the book and stood, crossing to the window. The crystal garden hummed below, a pretty, useless failure. The spoon waited in its drawer. The vial of sleeping draught sat in my pocket, a tool I hadn't yet assigned a purpose.

I would find a way to break free. I would find a way to make this body obey. And when I did, they would all regret underestimating the girl who couldn't light a candle without setting herself on fire.

The headache throbbed, a dull counterpoint to the cold. I pressed my fingers to my temple and let the evening settle around me, patient as a blade waiting for its whetstone. Tomorrow I would ride out and take the measure of the garden's heart. Tonight I would rest, and plan, and let the court remember me as the brave little princess who set her sleeve on fire.

title: Shrines and Suspicion
prose:
# Chapter 43: Shrines and Suspicion

The morning sun had barely crested the eastern wall when I persuaded the stable boy to saddle Midnight for a ride through the royal gardens.  

"Your Highness rides early," he said, fumbling with the girth strap. Midnight stamped a hoof, impatient with his incompetence.

"The dew makes the roses smell sweeter," I said,  What I actually wanted was to examine the ley-line convergence at the garden's heart before the morning court convened and the space filled with gardeners, courtiers, and the inevitable parade of nobles who wanted to "admire the princess's pretty rocks."

  Midnight was not that. But she was black, which was the important part, and her eyes—once the glamour faded—would be red enough to satisfy anyone who knew what to look for.

The gardens sprawled across thirty acres of manicured excess, a monument to the Hero King's belief that peace meant turning every available surface into either a flower bed or a training ground. I guided Midnight along the gravel path that wound past the ornamental fountain, where a marble statue of Alistair held a sword aloft in a pose that suggested he'd just vanquished a particularly dramatic seagull. The fountain's water sparkled in the morning light, and I resisted the urge to channel a minor cantrip just to see the spray turn to ice.

The ley-line convergence was at the garden's eastern edge, near the hedge maze that Alistair had commissioned after a particularly boring diplomatic summit.  

But something was different today.

 It was small, no larger than a birdhouse, but it was unmistakably an altar. Black candles sat in bronze holders at its base, their wicks fresh and unburned. A crude statue stood at its center, a child's figure carved from dark stone, its features rough and unfinished. The eyes, though, were unmistakable.

Glowing red. A faint, pulsing luminescence that I recognized immediately.

 

Apparently, I'd overestimated their survival instincts.

The cold spot in my chest pulsed, a dull ache that had become as familiar as my own heartbeat.  I pressed a hand to my sternum, feeling the void beneath my ribs where a sliver of my future had been excised.

 

Midnight shifted beneath me, sensing my tension. I patted her neck, forcing my breathing to slow.

 

I was not, historically, a creature of sense.

But I was also not a fool.  

I rode past, my spine straight, my face arranged in the pleasant blankness I'd perfected over years of courtly endurance. The shrine watched me go with its crude stone eyes, and I felt its presence like a splinter beneath my skin.

---

I found Alistair in the solar, where he was attempting to read a diplomatic dispatch while simultaneously eating a scone and explaining to a visiting dignitary why the Lumengarde military's tactical doctrine was superior to the Beastfolk's "bite and claw" approach. The scone was winning.

"Ah, my little miracle!" Alistair's face lit up as I entered, the dispatch forgotten. The dignitary, a beak-nosed man from the southern duchies, turned to regard me with the wary expression of someone who'd heard stories. "Come, come! I was just telling Lord Vex here about your crystal garden. He thinks it's a fanciful waste of resources!"

"I think it's a fanciful waste of resources," Lord Vex said, his tone suggesting he was not accustomed to being contradicted by kings.

"It's a testament to the beauty of natural formations," I said, in the soft, slightly uncertain voice I used when I wanted adults to think I was being precocious. "The crystals align with the ley-lines in a way that promotes growth and harmony. It's almost as if the earth itself wanted them there."

Lord Vex blinked. Alistair beamed.

"Ha! She's got you there, Vex! My Lily is not just pretty, she's *smart*!" He swept me up in a hug that smelled of scones and old leather, and I endured it with the patience of a saint enduring a particularly tedious martyrdom. "Speaking of gardens, have you seen what the gardeners have done? A little shrine, right near your crystal garden! They said it was to honor our miracle."

The cold spot pulsed again, sharper this time.

"A shrine?" I kept my voice light, curious. "How lovely. What does it honor?"

"The miracle of your survival, of course!" Alistair set me down, his face alight with pride. "When those cultists tried to harm you, and you survived—well, the people wanted to show their gratitude. The gardeners, bless their hearts, they built it overnight. Black candles, a little statue of you—they even gave it glowing eyes, like you're watching over the garden."

My internal monologue was a scream of pure, undiluted horror. The gardeners. The gardeners had built a shrine to *me*, and they'd given the statue my face, and the cult had seen it, and now they were using it as an opportunity to test me, and Alistair thought it was adorable.

"It's… very pretty, Father," I managed.

"I knew you'd love it! Come, let me show you!" He grabbed my hand and towed me toward the door, Lord Vex trailing behind with the expression of a man who had realized he was going to be late for his next appointment.

The shrine was exactly where I'd left it, which was to say, exactly where I'd hoped it wasn't. Alistair gestured at it with the pride of a man unveiling a monument to his own magnificence.

"See? Black candles—they symbolize the darkness you overcame. And the statue—the gardener who carved it said she wanted to capture your 'quiet strength.' She gave it red eyes because, and I quote, 'Your Highness's gaze pierces the soul.'"

"Very artistic," I said aloud.

"I knew you'd approve!" Alistair beamed. "I've already ordered a permanent fixture to be built around it. A proper shrine, with a plaque and everything. We'll make it a tourist attraction! 'The Lily Shrine'—it has a nice ring to it, doesn't it?"

"Very nice," I said. "Father, could I spend some time here? I'd like to… admire it."

Alistair's face melted into an expression of such pure, paternal pride that I felt something twist in my chest. Not the cold spot—something warmer, more dangerous. "Of course, my little miracle! Take all the time you need. Vex, let's leave her to her devotions."

They departed, Alistair's voice booming about the shrine's "spiritual significance" and Lord Vex's replies growing fainter as they moved away. I stood alone before the altar, surrounded by the hum of ley-lines and the faint scent of black candle wax.

 

Or I could do something they didn't expect.

I reached into my pocket and withdrew a single black rose, plucked from the garden's shadowed corner where the sun never quite reached. It was a flower that shouldn't exist in this climate, a variety I'd cultivated in secret from seeds smuggled out of the Obsidian Plains.  The red eyes seemed to flicker, as if acknowledging my offering.

*I see you*, the rose said. *And you should be very careful what you wish for.*

---

The afternoon passed in a blur of courtly obligations. I sat through a tea with the Duchess of Marrow, endured a piano recital in which I was required to perform a piece I'd composed at age six (which was actually a simplified inversion of a siege-breaking cantrip, but no one had noticed), and smiled through a dozen conversations with nobles who wanted to talk about "how brave" I was for surviving the cult's "terrible attempt on your life."

 And then I'd used it to save myself from a fate I'd engineered in a past life, and the cold spot had settled into my chest like a stone dropped into still water.

Eris found me in the library after supper, her arms full of books and her face flushed with excitement.

"Your Highness! I've been researching the sustained echo theory, and I think I've found something!" She dropped the books onto my desk with a thud that made the candles flicker. "There's a passage in the Codex Animarum about anchoring a soul's residual energy to a resonant object, and it mentions a technique for—"

"Eris." I held up a hand, and she fell silent, her eyes wide with adoration. "We can discuss this later. Right now, I need you to tell me if you've noticed anything unusual in the palace."

"Unusual?" She frowned, her brow furrowing. "There's been a lot of talk about the new shrine in the garden. Everyone's saying it's a tribute to you, but—" She hesitated, biting her lip. "Your Highness, I don't mean to be presumptuous, but the statue's eyes look… wrong. Almost like they're watching you."

"They are watching me," I said. "The Cult of the Eternal Flame built that shrine as a test. They want to see if I'll respond."

Eris's mouth dropped open. "The cult? But they were arrested! The King declared them blasphemers and—"

"The public leaders were arrested. But cults are like hydras—cut off one head and two more grow in its place." I leaned back in my chair, steepling my fingers. "They've gone underground, but they haven't stopped. The shrine is their way of telling me they know who I am."

"Who you are?" Eris's voice was barely a whisper. "Your Highness, you're… you're the princess. The miracle. The—"

"I'm the only person who can read the Black Tome without going mad," I said, which was true and also a convenient way to redirect her attention. ""

Eris's face cycled through several expressions—confusion, horror, and finally a kind of fierce, protective determination. "Your Highness, I won't let them harm you. I'll—I'll tell the King, I'll—"

"You'll do nothing," I said, and her mouth snapped shut. "If you tell anyone, they'll think you're the one who's mad. And if the cult learns that you know about their activities, they'll target you next. Do you understand?"

She nodded, her eyes shining with unshed tears. "Yes, Your Highness."

"Good." I softened my voice, allowing a hint of warmth to creep in. "I trust you, Eris. That's why I'm telling you this. You're the only one who can help me."

"I—I'd die for you, Your Highness."

 But the cult was a problem that wouldn't be solved by sentiment.

That night, I dreamed of the Word of Unmaking.

 In the dream, I stood before the shrine, and the statue's red eyes were fixed on me with an intensity that felt almost hungry. 

The shrine dissolved. The candles snuffed out. The statue crumbled into dust, and the dust rose into the air like a cloud of glittering motes, and the motes swirled around me, and I felt the Word's power singing through my veins like a dark symphony.

I woke with a start, my heart pounding, my sheets tangled around my legs. The cold spot was throbbing, a dull, persistent ache that made me want to curl into a ball and never move again.

 

I smiled into the darkness, and it was not a pleasant smile.

*Let them watch*, I thought. *Let them wait. They have no idea what they're dealing with.*

title: The Steed from Hell
prose:
# Chapter 44: The Steed from Hell

The stable smelled of warm hay and old leather and the mineral tang of horse sweat,  I stood beside a dappled gray mare named Constance, whose long face regarded me with the bored tolerance of a creature that had survived three royal children's riding lessons and expected to survive mine. My fingers traced the coarse strands of her mane, following the ridge of her neck down to where the hair grew thickest. She snorted and shifted her weight, one enormous hoof scraping against the stone floor with a sound like a blade being drawn across a whetstone.

I had been coming to the stables for three weeks now, ever since I had decided that the time for subtle manipulation had passed and the time for direct action had arrived. Not, of course, that I could be seen requesting anything directly. The art of requesting was the art of appearing not to request, of planting the seed in someone else's mind so they could later claim the idea as their own. My tutors in the Abyssal Halls had called this "the doctrine of borrowed intention," and it had served me well for six centuries of infernal politics. It served me less well here, where the minds I was planting seeds in belonged to people whose primary hobbies were sword-fighting and pastry consumption.

"Father," I had said one morning at breakfast, three weeks ago, with the careful offhandedness of someone discussing the weather, "do you think a pony with red eyes would be too scary?"

Alistair had laughed—that enormous, room-filling laugh that rattled the silverware and made the wine in his goblet tremble like a frightened animal—and said, "Red eyes? Like a little demon horse? Oh, Lily, you do think of the most wonderful things!"

He had meant it as a joke. He always meant it as a joke. The Hero of Dawn, who had once cleaved my armies in twain with a blade forged in holy fire, now spent his mornings debating with the royal baker whether blueberry or raspberry was the superior filling for morning tarts. The man who had stood at the gates of my obsidian citadel and shouted challenges in the old tongue now could not locate his ceremonial belt without assistance from at least two attendants. 

I patted Constance's neck and moved to the next stall, where a bay gelding with a white blaze on his forehead was chewing hay with the methodical disinterest of a philosopher working through a treatise he had long since grown tired of. The stablemaster, a weathered man named Corwin whose face had been carved by decades of wind and animal odors into something resembling a particularly thoughtful piece of driftwood, was nearby, checking the fit of a saddle. He nodded to me with the deference that all palace staff had learned to afford the princess, even the small, quiet one who occasionally said things that made grown adults blink and tilt their heads like confused dogs.

"Your Highness," he said. "Constance is in good form today. Would you like to take her out for a walk in the courtyard?"

"She is a very handsome horse," I said, because acknowledging a creature's quality was a form of control, and because the court expected me to be polite. "I was actually hoping to speak with you about something, Master Corwin."

He straightened up, resting one hand on the saddle he had been adjusting, and gave me the full weight of his attention. I could see the calculation behind his eyes—not the sharp, dangerous calculation of a man like Zephyr, but the slower, steadier calculation of a man who had spent his life making sure that very expensive animals did not break very expensive equipment. He was wondering what the princess wanted and how much it would cost him in extra work.

"Of course, Your Highness. Anything you need."

 

"I would like to speak with Father first," I said, which was true and also a way of making sure that Corwin understood the hierarchy of command. Even in the stables, the chain of authority was sacrosanct.

"Of course, Your Highness. The King is in the east wing this morning, I believe. He was demonstrating his new sword technique to the Captain of the Guard."

Demonstrating his new sword technique. I had seen the demonstration the day before, in which Alistair had accidentally severed a decorative column and then blamed a draft. The court had applauded. The masons had sighed. The Captain of the Guard had picked splinters out of his hair with the quiet resignation of a man who had long since accepted that his job description included "standing near the King while the King does something impractical."

I thanked Corwin and made my way through the stable corridors, my boots clicking against the flagstones in a rhythm that I had learned to control. When I walked quickly, my heartbeat climbed toward the threshold where my body began to complain, a reminder that this vessel was built for thinking, not for moving.  I slowed my pace and felt the ache recede to its usual background hum, a constant companion, like the memory of my own death.

The east wing corridor was wide and sunlit, the windows tall arches of colored glass that cast jeweled patterns across the marble floor. I had walked this corridor a thousand times, counting each step the way a prisoner counts the stones in their cell, except that my cell was gilded and my warden brought me strawberry jam. The morning light caught a figure at the far end, leaning against the wall with one arm raised in a theatrical pose that I recognized immediately as Alistair practicing his "heroic stance," the one he struck for visiting dignitaries and portrait painters. He was alone, which meant I would not have to wait for an audience. Alone, my father was almost tolerable. Almost.

He saw me before I reached him, and his face split into the broad, unguarded grin that he reserved exclusively for me. It was, I had to admit, an impressive grin. The man had cheekbones that could cut glass and eyes the color of a summer sky, and he used these natural gifts exclusively for the purpose of making me feel simultaneously cherished and irritated. He straightened up from his pose as I approached, dropping his arms with a clatter of armored sleeves, and the grin widened until I worried it might reach his ears.

"Lily! My little miracle! What brings you to the training wing? Have you come to watch your old father demonstrate the art of the blade? I've just perfected a new technique I call the 'Sunset Arc'—it involves a forty-five-degree rotation of the wrist combined with a—"

"I would like a pony," I said.

The grin did not waver. If anything, it expanded, as though my words were a gift that had been wrapped in unexpected paper. He crouched down to my level—a habit that I found simultaneously touching and insulting, as though my height of four feet and two inches were an insurmountable barrier between us rather than a temporary condition of my current incarnation—and placed his hands on my shoulders. His palms were warm and large enough to cover both shoulders entirely, and I could feel the faint hum of his mana through the leather of his tunic, a rich, steady current like a river that had never known drought. It was infuriating. His mana pool could have supplied a small army's worth of spellcasting, and he used it primarily to make his sword glow at dramatic moments.

"A pony," he repeated, as though tasting the word. "Well, that sounds perfectly reasonable. You're growing up so fast, Lily. Before long you'll be riding into battle like your mother did at the Siege of the Scorching Fields—did I ever tell you about the time she—" He stopped, catching himself, and laughed. "But first, a pony. Tell me, what kind? What color? What size?"

I tilted my head and let my eyes go soft, the way I had learned to do when I needed something and could not yet afford to show that I needed it with anything more than a child's idle curiosity. "I have been reading," I said, which was true in the sense that I read constantly and also in the sense that it made everything I said sound precocious rather than calculating. "About ponies. In the royal library."

"Lily the reader! Of course you have. You know, when I was your age, I couldn't sit still long enough to read a letter, let alone a whole book. Your mother says it's because I have the attention span of a caffeinated squirrel, but I think—"

"Father." I paused, letting the silence do the work. Children were allowed to be interrupted. Children were allowed to be impatient. Children were allowed to redirect conversations with the casual ruthlessness of a field marshal adjusting troop formations. "I would like a black pony. With red eyes."

The words hung in the air between us, perfectly weighted, perfectly timed. I watched them land, watched the exact moment when Alistair's brain processed them, and I saw the gears turn behind his eyes—the initial surprise, the quick assessment, and then the full, delighted surrender of a man who had never been able to deny me anything and had never wanted to. He threw his head back and laughed, and the sound bounced off the corridor walls and rattled the stained glass, and somewhere in the distance a servant dropped a tray.

"Red eyes!" he howled, wiping tears from the corners of his eyes with the back of his hand. "Like a little demon horse! Lily, you magnificent creature, where do you come up with these ideas? You have the imagination of a poet and the courage of a warrior! Anything for my little miracle—anything at all!"

He pulled me into a hug that lifted my feet off the ground, and I let him, because resistance would have been suspicious and because—though I would sooner eat my own grimoire than admit it aloud—the warmth of his embrace was not entirely unpleasant. His arms were thick and solid, smelling of leather and the faintly metallic tang of sword oil, and I could feel his heartbeat against my cheek, strong and steady and oblivious. 

The universe has a cruel sense of humor. I have always known this. But the universe, I was beginning to suspect, was also a coward, because it had given me a father who loved me unconditionally and then made me the person who would eventually have to do something about it.

I did not think about that. Not yet. Not today. Today, I wanted a pony.

The Royal Stables occupied a square of the palace grounds roughly the size of a small battlefield, which was fitting because Corwin managed it with the same grim efficiency that a general brings to the defense of a critical pass.
