When Alistair and I arrived, still in the grip of his post-laughter euphoria, Corwin was waiting by the main doors with his arms folded across his chest and his face arranged in an expression that I recognized as professional caution. He had probably been listening. The stables were not large enough to contain Alistair's laugh without broadcasting it to every stall and tack room within a hundred yards.

"Corwin, my good man!" Alistair clapped the stablemaster on the shoulder with enough force to make him take a half-step forward. "My daughter has made a request, and I intend to fulfill it. She wants a pony. A black pony, with red eyes. Can you find one?"

Corwin looked at Alistair, then at me, then back at Alistair. His weathered face performed a complicated series of adjustments, like a man trying to rearrange furniture in a room while someone kept moving the walls. "A black pony, Your Majesty?"

"That's right."

"With red eyes?"

"Red as rubies! Red as sunset! Red as the heart of a hero!" Alistair spread his arms wide, as though personally commissioning the pony from the universe. "My daughter has excellent taste, Corwin. She knows what she wants."

"Your Majesty," Corwin said, and I could hear the careful, measured tone of a man choosing his words with the precision of someone defusing a explosive device. "A black pony with red eyes is... a very specific request. Such a creature would be unusual. Some might say it would be... unnatural."

I met his gaze and held it, letting my expression settle into the one I had perfected for occasions like this: wide-eyed innocence layered over a quiet, unshakable certainty, the look of a child who has read something in a book and will not be dissuaded by adult skepticism. I had used this expression with tutors, with physicians, with Queen Seraphina herself when she had asked me why my crayon drawings all featured the same recurring symbol (it was a pentagram, but she had called it "a creative use of circles"). The expression always worked. It worked because it was real, or at least close enough to real that no one could tell the difference. I was, after all, a child. My eyes were genuinely large. My face was genuinely small. The innocence was a mask, but it was a mask made of my own skin, and that made it nearly perfect.

"I have read about them in books," I said, and I let a note of shy determination creep into my voice, the verbal equivalent of a kitten showing its claws. "They are said to be very brave."

Corwin blinked. The professional caution in his expression flickered, and something else surfaced beneath it—a grudging, reluctant admiration, the kind that people felt when they realized that the small person standing in front of them had a will that exceeded their expectations. I had seen this before, in the faces of courtiers who expected me to be a fragile ornament and discovered instead that I was a fragile ornament with opinions. It was a useful expression to provoke. It meant that the person was less likely to argue and more likely to comply.

"Very brave," Corwin repeated, as though testing the words. He looked at Alistair, who was beaming with the incandescent pride of a father whose child has said something impressive. "Your Majesty, I will make inquiries. There are breeders in the eastern provinces who specialize in unusual stock. And I have contacts in the Beastfolk territories who might have access to horses of... distinctive temperament."

"The Beastfolk!" Alistair's eyes lit up. "Excellent! Ragnar owes me a favor anyway—saved his life at the Battle of the Hollow Chasm, you know. One time, he and I were fighting this enormous—"

"I will begin writing letters immediately," Corwin said, with the firm decisiveness of a man who had learned that the surest way to end one of Alistair's stories was to present him with a new topic. "It may take some time, Your Majesty. Finding a black pony with red eyes is not the sort of thing that happens overnight."

"Take all the time you need, old friend. Take whatever resources you require. The royal coffers can handle it—after all, what is money but a tool for making my little girl happy?"

I smiled at this, a small, grateful smile that made Alistair's eyes go soft and made Corwin's mouth twitch in what might have been the beginning of a smile of his own. Inside, behind the smile, I was doing mathematics. The "red eyes" would be the hardest part, because truly red eyes in a pony meant one of two things: a rare genetic mutation that produced unusually pigmented irises, or a creature that had been exposed to enough ambient demonic energy to change its physiology from the inside out. Corwin would search for the first. He would find the second, because the second was what I actually wanted, and because Baphomutt—bless his忠诚, idiotic heart—had already been laying the groundwork.

 Three weeks ago, I had mentioned to the empty air of my bedroom—because I knew the little demon was listening from inside the wardrobe, where he liked to sleep on a pile of my discarded stockings—that I thought ponies were "very pretty." I had then, as though struck by a sudden afterthought, mentioned that the ponies in the old texts had "such lovely eyes, glowing like embers in the dark." I had said this while I was brushing my teeth, spitting into the basin, and I had not looked toward the wardrobe because looking would have been unnecessary. Baphomutt would act. Baphomutt always acted.

Now I watched Corwin retreat to his office, already scribbling notes on a scrap of parchment, and I felt the particular satisfaction of a plan that was unfolding on schedule. The stablemaster would write to breeders. The breeders would draw a blank. And then, in a week or two, a traveling merchant or a nervous gift-giver or some other convenient vector would arrive at the palace gates with a small black pony that had eyes the color of fresh blood, and everyone would marvel at the coincidence, and Alistair would declare it destiny, and I would have my steed.

 The Word of Unmaking had cost me more than a few years of lifespan. It had cost me access. The demonic energies that I had once commanded as naturally as breathing were now muted, distant, like trying to hear a conversation through a wall. I could still reach them, but only just, and only in small ways—a whisper here, a nudge there, the subtle rearrangement of probabilities that would bring the right creature to the right place at the right time.

Alistair, oblivious to all of this, had returned to his "Sunset Arc" demonstration, performing the maneuver repeatedly for the benefit of a pair of bewildered palace guards who had not asked for a lesson and were now unable to leave without risking offense. I watched him for a moment from the stable doorway, his form silhouetted against the stained glass, the morning light turning his hair to gold and his sword to a band of white fire. He moved with the easy, unconscious grace of a man whose body was a weapon and whose mind was a garden, and the contrast between the two made something twist in my chest that was neither the cold spot nor the strange, guilty warmth that had taken up residence beside it.

I turned away and walked back toward the palace, counting my steps.

Three days later, I was summoned to the east courtyard.

The message had come from Alistair, delivered by a breathless page who had apparently run the entire distance from the stables. "Your Highness, the King requests your presence! Immediately! He says—" The page stopped, gulped air, and continued. "He says, and I quote, 'The miracle has arrived, bring Lily at once before Corwin changes his mind!'"

 I checked my reflection in the mirror and adjusted my expression to match: a mixture of excitement and demure surprise, the face of a child receiving an unexpected gift.  He had not been able to describe the creature in words—his vocabulary in Common was limited to approximately thirty words, half of which were variants of "Mistress" and "shiny"—but the images he had projected into my mind had been clear enough. A small pony, black as a moonless sky, with eyes that glowed like dying stars.

I reached the courtyard to find a scene of organized chaos. Alistair was standing in the center of the flagstones, his arms crossed, his chest puffed out, his expression one of pure, unfiltered triumph. Behind him, a wooden crate had been placed on the ground, and the crate was moving. Not dramatically—not shaking or rattling—but with the small, persistent shifting of a living creature adjusting its weight, testing the boundaries of its enclosure, preparing to step out into a world that it had not chosen but would, in time, come to dominate. The crate was plain, unmarked, and had been sealed with iron clasps that bore the faint scorch marks of a recent binding ritual. Someone had been careful. Someone had known that this particular cargo required extra precaution.

Corwin stood to one side, and his face told me everything I needed to know. He was pale—paler than I had ever seen him, his weathered skin gone gray at the edges, his lips pressed together in a thin line that suggested he was holding words in the way a dam holds back water. His eyes kept darting to the crate and then away, as though looking directly at it for too long might cause something to happen that he was not prepared to handle. He had found the pony. He had delivered the pony. And now he was experiencing the very reasonable suspicion that he had brought something into the palace that did not belong there.

"The breeders in the eastern provinces had nothing," Corwin said, his voice carefully controlled in the way that voices are when the speaker is afraid that the alternative is shouting. "I sent letters to every contact I had. Nothing. But two days ago, a merchant arrived at the palace gates—didn't give a name, didn't give a trade affiliation. He had a wagon, and in the wagon was this crate, and a note addressed to the Princess. The note said—" He pulled a scrap of paper from his vest pocket and read it, his voice thin and precise. "'For the one who remembers. A gift from the old roads.'"

The old roads. Baphomutt's idea of anonymity was to use phrases that I had taught him during one of my late-night sessions with the Black Tome, when I had been practicing the old Infernal dialect and the imp had been perched on my shoulder, absorbing words like a sponge absorbs water, only to use them later in the most inconvenient possible contexts. The note was a risk. I made a mental note to address this with Baphomutt at the earliest opportunity, which meant I would spend the next several days shouting at a creature that interpreted shouting as enthusiastic communication.

Alistair, of course, saw none of this. Alistair saw a mystery gift that had been delivered to his daughter, and mystery gifts were simply the universe confirming what he already knew: that Lily was special, that Lily was chosen, that Lily deserved wonderful things because she was wonderful. He strode to the crate, bent down, and pulled the iron clasps free with a grunt of effort, and the wood groaned and split, and the crate fell open like a blooming flower, and—

The creature that stepped out was black.

Not the soft, matte black of ink or charcoal, but the deep, absolute black of a sky without stars, the kind of black that seemed to absorb light rather than reflect it, that made shadows pool around its hooves like spilled oil. It was small, no taller than Constance at the withers, and its proportions were compact and powerful, every line of its body suggesting contained energy, coiled tension, the stillness of something that could move very quickly and very violently when it chose to. Its coat was not quite hair and not quite hide; it had a texture that caught the light in ways that made my eyes ache, as though the creature was slightly out of focus, slightly out of the world, a thing that existed in a space adjacent to the one I was standing in.

And its eyes.

The eyes were red. Not the dull, flat red of painted glass or dyed fabric, but a deep, luminous crimson that seemed to glow from within, like embers buried in ash, like the last light of a dying fire that refused to go out. 

*Hello*, I thought. *I remember you. Or rather, I remember what made you.*

The pony stood in the wreckage of its crate, its hooves scraping against the flagstones, and looked at me with those terrible, beautiful eyes, and I felt something that I had not felt since the moment I had spoken the Word of Unmaking and felt my future burn away: a sense of wholeness, of completion, of a missing piece sliding back into place. This creature was a thread connecting me to what I had been, a bridge across the gap between Maledictus and Lily, and for a moment—one brief, dangerous moment—I let myself feel the pull of it, the ancient, irresistible gravity of the Abyss calling me home.

Then Corwin stepped forward, his face ashen, and said the words that I had been waiting for.

"Your Highness," he said, and his voice was the voice of a man who has seen something that cannot be unseen. "This creature... it is not natural."

I looked up at him, my expression arranged in the careful configuration of innocent wonder that I had been practicing in the mirror for three days. "I have read about them in books," I said, and my voice was steady and clear and entirely appropriate for a child meeting a new pet. "They are said to be very brave."

The pony took a step toward me. Its hooves made no sound on the flagstones, a detail that Corwin noticed and that Alistair did not, because Alistair was too busy beaming with the radiant satisfaction of a father who has fulfilled his daughter's wish. The pony lowered its head and sniffed at my outstretched hand, its breath warm against my palm, and then it pressed its nose against my fingers in a gesture of recognition so deliberate and so precise that it could not have been anything other than what it was: an acknowledgment. The creature knew me. It knew what I was, even if the rest of the world did not.

I stroked its nose, feeling the strange, half-organic texture of its coat beneath my fingers, and I smiled. It was not a wide smile or a particularly warm one, but it was genuine, which was unusual for me, and I let it sit on my face for a moment before I caught myself and adjusted it to something more appropriately childlike.

"It's perfect," I said.

And behind me, Alistair's voice boomed across the courtyard like a war horn announcing a victory, which, in his mind, this was. "Just like you, my little miracle!" he cried, and the courtiers who had gathered to watch the spectacle burst into applause, and the stable hands exchanged glances that mingled admiration with unease, and Corwin stood very still with his hands at his sides and the look of a man who has delivered something to his doorstep that he cannot take back.

The pony nickered, a low, resonant sound that vibrated in my chest like a chord struck on an instrument tuned to the frequency of the Abyss, and I felt the cold spot pulse once, twice, in time with the sound, and I knew with the certainty of long experience that this was only the beginning.

Baphomutt, watching from the roof of the stables, chittered with delight.

Mistress had her night beast. The games could begin.

title: Riding into the Unknown
prose:
# Chapter 45: Riding into the Unknown

The morning light arrived like an accusation, thin and golden, slanting through my window in ribbons that made the dust motes dance.  The pony was waiting for me. I could feel it the way one feels a storm gathering beyond the horizon—a pressure in the air, a charge that made the hairs on my arms stand at attention.

Baphomutt materialized from the shadows near my wardrobe with a chitter that was meant to be discreet and succeeded only in being loud. "Mistress rises! Mistress rides the night beast today! Very important day!"

"Baphomutt," I said, not opening my eyes, "if you wake the entire palace with your enthusiasm, I will bind you to a teapot for the next century."

He had the decency to lower his voice to something approximating a whisper, though the effect was ruined by his excited hopping from foot to foot. "The night beast is ready. It stamped its hoof three times when the sun rose. It knows."

I opened my eyes and sat up slowly, swinging my legs over the edge of the bed. The floor was cold against my bare feet, a sensation I had grown accustomed to but never quite enjoyed.  This palace was full of cold surfaces, cold air, cold silences that I filled with calculated chatter and manufactured innocence.

"I know it knows," I said, reaching for the dress that Nurse Branna had laid out the night before. It was a riding habit in deep burgundy, practical and modest, with a matching jacket that had been embroidered with tiny silver flowers along the cuffs.  "The question is whether the court knows."

"Mistress will make them see nothing," Baphomutt said with the confidence of a creature who had never successfully kept a secret in his entire existence. "Mistress is very good at not being seen."

I pulled the dress over my head and began the complicated process of fastening the buttons that ran down the back.  I cursed under my breath in Infernal, a phrase that would have curdled milk if anyone had been close enough to hear it.

"Let Baphomutt help," the imp offered, already floating toward me with his clawed hands extended.

"Absolutely not. You'll tear the fabric or leave scorch marks, or both." I managed the button through sheer force of will and moved on to the next one. "What did you see when you checked the stables?"

"The night beast is calm. It does not like the stablemaster. It showed him its teeth when he tried to brush its mane." Baphomutt's chitter took on a note of pride. "It knows who its real master is."

Corwin had been unsettled by the pony since its arrival, and I could hardly blame him. The creature had arrived in a crate that had been sealed with wax bearing a sigil I recognized—a mark that had not been used in the mortal world for centuries, a signature from the old roads that connected the Abyss to the waking world. The merchant who had delivered it had been gone before anyone could question him, leaving only a note written in a hand I knew as well as my own.

*For the one who remembers.*

I had burned the note in my chamber pot and watched the ashes dissolve into nothing.

The pony itself was magnificent. Its coat was the color of midnight, so deep and dark that it seemed to drink in the light around it rather than reflect it. Its mane and tail flowed like smoke, and its eyes—those eyes—burned with a faint red glow that I had seen dimmed to a subtle ember whenever the courtiers were watching. The creature had been glamoured, its true nature veiled behind a thin layer of illusion that would fool anyone who did not know what to look for.

I knew what to look for.

 I had ridden creatures like this one through the Abyssal Halls, their hooves striking sparks from the ground as they carried me to battles that had reshaped the map of the world.

"Help me with the jacket," I said, and Baphomutt obeyed with more enthusiasm than skill, nearly knocking me over in his eagerness. I caught myself on the bedpost and gave him a look that would have made lesser demons flee. He simply chittered and floated backward, clearly proud of his contribution.

The walk to the stables took me through the eastern corridor, past the breakfast room where I could hear my father's voice booming with laughter at something one of the servants had said. I paused at the threshold, just for a moment, and watched him through the gap in the door.

 He was laughing at a joke that I could not hear, his broad shoulders shaking with mirth, and the sight of it made something twist in my chest that I did not want to examine too closely.

*This is the man who killed you,* I reminded myself. *This is the man who ended your reign and scattered your armies. This is the enemy.*

But the reminder felt hollow, like a bell struck in an empty room. 

I continued walking.

The stables were a bustle of activity when I arrived, with stable hands rushing to prepare the horses for the morning exercise and Corwin barking orders from the center of the commotion. 

"Your Highness," he said, bowing. "You're early."

"I wanted to see Midnight before the morning ride," I said, arranging my face into the careful configuration of childish eagerness. "Is she ready?"

"She's... ready." Corwin's hesitation was barely perceptible, but I caught it. "The grooms have been having some trouble with her temperament. She doesn't take well to strangers."

The stall where Midnight had been housed was at the far end of the stable, separated from the other horses by an empty stall on either side. The grooms had learned quickly that the black pony did not appreciate company, and they had given her a wide berth.

I approached the stall alone, ignoring Corwin's muttered protests. The pony was standing in the center of her stall, her head raised, her ears pricked forward. Her eyes glowed faintly in the dim light, and I felt the cold spot in my chest pulse in response.

"Hello," I said softly, reaching through the bars of the stall door. "Hello, beautiful."

The pony stepped forward, her hooves making no sound on the straw, and pressed her nose against my palm. Her breath was warm and smelled of smoke and old stone, and the recognition in her eyes was absolute.

*I remember you,* I thought. *I remember what you are.*

"Your Highness," Corwin said from behind me, his voice tight with barely concealed unease. "Perhaps you should let the grooms saddle her. She can be... unpredictable."

"I think she knows me," I said, and it was the truest thing I had said in days. "I think she's been waiting for me."

The pony nickered, a low, resonant sound that vibrated through my chest like a chord struck on an instrument tuned to the frequency of the Abyss. I felt the cold spot pulse again, stronger this time, and I did not pull away.

"Saddle her," I said. "I'm taking her out."

Corwin's face was a study in conflict, his loyalty to his king warring with his obvious discomfort. In the end, loyalty won, as it always did. He gestured to a groom, who approached the stall with the caution of a man approaching a sleeping dragon.

The saddling process took longer than it should have, because Midnight kept shifting her weight and rolling her eyes at the groom whenever he got too close. I stood at the stall door and watched, offering quiet words of reassurance in a language that no one else in the stable could understand. The groom thought I was cooing to the pony in baby talk. In truth, I was speaking the old tongue, the language of the Abyssal Halls, and I was telling her to be patient, to endure this indignity, to remember that we would be free soon enough.

When the saddle was finally in place, I stepped into the stall and took the reins. The pony's eyes met mine, and I felt the connection between us solidify into something tangible, a thread of shared purpose that bound us together across the gap of centuries.

"Let's go for a ride," I said.

The courtyard was crowded with courtiers when I emerged from the stables, their faces bright with anticipation. Word had spread that Princess Lily was taking her new pony for her first ride, and the court had turned out in force to witness the spectacle.

I mounted Midnight with the help of a mounting block, my legs too short to reach the stirrup otherwise. The saddle was warm beneath me, and the pony's muscles shifted with a liquid grace that spoke of power held in check. Baphomutt, who had been lurking in the shadows of the stable, chose this moment to make his presence known.

"Mistress rides the night beast! Very regal!" he chirped, landing on the saddle behind me with a thump that nearly unseated me.

"Baphomutt," I hissed, "you are not supposed to be here."

"Mistress needs company on her ride! Baphomutt will provide moral support!"

I could feel the eyes of the court on us, and I knew that any attempt to dislodge the imp would be interpreted as me playing with a beloved pet. I forced a smile and adjusted my grip on the reins.

"Very well," I said through gritted teeth. "But if you fall off, I am not catching you."

The pony stepped forward, her hooves silent on the cobblestones, and I guided her toward the path that led through the royal gardens. The courtiers waved from the balcony, their faces alight with pride, and I waved back with a smile that was practiced and perfect.

*They have no idea,* I thought. *They have no idea what they are watching.*

The gardens were in full bloom, the roses heavy with dew and the hedges trimmed into elaborate shapes that had been the pride of the royal gardeners for generations. I guided Midnight along the gravel path, feeling the strange silence of her hooves beneath me. The gravel should have crunched, should have scattered beneath her weight, but she moved as if she were walking on air.

The cult's shrine loomed in the distance, a structure that had been erected in the wake of my "miracle" at the ritual circle. The court had reclassified it as a tourist attraction, a monument to Princess Lily's divine protection, but I knew what it really was. The Cult of the Eternal Flame had placed it there as a test, a marker, a way of claiming the ground for their own purposes.

I had left a black rose at the shrine the night before, a silent acknowledgment of their presence and a warning that I was watching. The flower had been grown from seeds I had smuggled from the Obsidian Plains, and its petals were the color of dried blood.

Midnight's ears twitched as we approached the shrine. Her nostrils flared, and for a moment, her eyes burned brighter than they should have, the glamour slipping just enough to reveal the ember beneath.

*Not now,* I thought, tightening the reins. *Not here.*

The pony obeyed, her tension palpable but contained. She stepped past the shrine with a delicacy that belied her power, and I felt the cold spot in my chest pulse in time with her heartbeat.

"Lily!"

My father's voice boomed across the garden like a war horn, and I turned to see him striding toward me with a grin that split his face in half. He was wearing his ceremonial armor, the gleaming plate that he had worn during the final battle against Maledictus, and he was carrying his holy sword at his hip as if he expected to need it at any moment.

"Lily! Your pony is magnificent!" he cried, his voice carrying to every corner of the garden. "I've never seen such a fine beast! She looks like she could outrun the wind itself!"

I felt my expression soften despite myself, the practiced smile giving way to something more genuine. "Thank you, Father."

He reached us and reached up to pat Midnight's neck, and I watched his hand pass over the pony's coat with a strange sense of unreality. He could not feel what I felt. He could not sense the power that hummed beneath the surface of that midnight-dark coat, the ancient recognition that bound this creature to me across the centuries.

"She's a beauty, no doubt about it," Alistair said, his eyes shining with pride. "Just like you, my little miracle!"

The words hit me like a blow, and I felt something crack in my chest—not the cold spot, but something else, something that had been growing there despite my best efforts to keep it contained. I looked at my father, at the man who had killed Maledictus, and I felt the warmth spread through me like a tide.

"Thank you, Father," I said again, and this time the words came easily.

The moment was fleeting, but it lingered. The weight of his love pressed against me, a force as inexorable as the tide, and I felt myself drowning in it even as I fought to keep my head above the surface.

*You are the enemy,* I reminded myself. *You are the man who destroyed everything I built.*

But the reminder was growing weaker, the words losing their power to cut.

"Ride her well, my little rose," Alistair said, stepping back. "I'll be watching from the balcony."

I nodded and urged Midnight forward, feeling the pony's muscles bunch beneath me as she moved. The garden path stretched ahead, winding through the hedges and flower beds, and I let myself sink into the rhythm of the ride.

Baphomutt chittered from behind me, his claws digging into the saddle with a grip that was more enthusiastic than comfortable. "Mistress rides well! The night beast is pleased!"

"Quiet," I murmured, aware of the courtiers watching from the palace. "You are a pet, remember? Pets do not speak."

"Baphomutt is a very quiet pet," the imp said, at a volume that could only be described as a shout.

I sighed and focused on the ride, guiding Midnight through the gardens with a precision that came naturally to me. The pony responded to my every cue, her movements fluid and graceful, and I felt a sense of wholeness that I had not experienced since before the Word of Unmaking had carved its cold price from my future.

The shrine was behind us now, and I allowed myself to relax just slightly. The ride had been uneventful, the court had been suitably impressed, and Baphomutt had—for once—not caused a catastrophe.

The stables appeared ahead, and I guided Midnight toward them with a sense of reluctant finality. The ride was ending, and with it, the brief moment of peace that I had allowed myself.

I dismounted with the help of the mounting block, my fingers brushing against Midnight's neck as I descended. The pony nuzzled my hand, her breath warm and strangely familiar, and I felt the cold spot pulse one final time before settling into stillness.

"Thank you," I whispered, so softly that even Baphomutt could not hear. "Thank you for remembering."

Baphomutt leaped from the saddle to the stable roof with a chitter of excitement, his eyes already scanning for something to steal. I watched him go, my mind a whirl of calculations and contradictions.

The imp was a liability, a constant threat to my carefully constructed cover. And yet, I could not bring myself to be rid of him. He was a thread connecting me to what I had been, a reminder of the power that had once been mine.

I walked back toward the palace, my steps slow and deliberate. The morning sun was warm on my face, and the gardens were beautiful in the way that all well-tended things are beautiful—a beauty that was maintained, curated, controlled.

I caught Seraphina's gaze as I approached the palace steps. The Queen was standing on the balcony, her hands folded in front of her, her expression unreadable. But her eyes were sharp, watching me with an intensity that made my skin prickle.

I met her gaze, my own face a mask of innocence, and I smiled.

"Good morning, Mother."

Her lips curved in response, a smile that was equal parts warmth and calculation. "Good morning, my dear. Did you enjoy your ride?"

"Very much," I said. "Midnight is wonderful."

"She does seem to have taken a liking to you," Seraphina observed. "The grooms were concerned about her temperament, but she seems quite docile with you."

*Docile,* I thought. *If only you knew.*

"I think she just needed someone to understand her," I said, and the words were truer than she would ever know.

Seraphina's eyes lingered on me for a moment longer, and 

The game continued.
